Goodbye.

Good morning, everyone, and welcome to Skerry Point Nature Reserve. My name is Fiona, and I'm the warden here. Thank you all for giving up your Saturday. Before we go out, I'd like to explain how a volunteer day works, and then tell you where we need help.

First, timing. Shifts used to start at half past seven, but the early start put quite a few people off, so from this season we begin at 8 o'clock. We finish at about three, with a lunch break in the middle. Lunch is provided by the Friends of Skerry Point, so you don't need to bring sandwiches, but do bring a bottle of water.

Next, parking. Please don't use the car park beside the visitor centre. It's reserved for visitors and for people with limited mobility. The track down to the old lighthouse is closed at the moment, so the best place is the village car park, which is only a five minute walk. There's no charge for volunteers if you show the badge I'll give you today.

Now, what to wear. We'll lend you a bright jacket, and gloves if you need them. What we can't lend you is footwear. The ground is very wet at this time of year, so please wear waterproof boots. Ordinary trainers won't last ten minutes on the marsh, I promise you.

A word about the paths. The east path along the cliff is closed until the end of August. Arctic terns have nested on the grass beside it, and they're very protective of their eggs. Some of you may have been told the path is closed because of erosion. That was true last year, but this year it's the birds. Please keep to the signed routes and don't go looking for them.

So what will you actually be doing today? Our original plan was to count seals on the beach. But the seals haven't come ashore yet, so that will wait until next month. We'd also thought about repairing the fencing, but a team finished that last week. What we really need is help with sea buckthorn. It's a thorny shrub that spreads across the dunes and crowds out the smaller native plants, so we'll be clearing it by hand.

Let me now take you round the reserve in your minds. We'll start at the bird hide, which looks over the estuary. A small group will be based there. Their job is to record the numbers of each species they see, and they'll fill in the sheet every half hour. You don't need to be an expert. There are pictures of all the common birds on the wall.

From the hide, a boardwalk runs across the soft ground to the beach. It was built twenty years ago, and several of the planks have gone soft and slippery. Two volunteers will replace the worst ones. Carpenters are very welcome, but I'll show anyone how to do it.

Halfway along the boardwalk you'll see the pond. In winter we cut back the reeds there, but that's finished, so today the job is something different. We take water samples to check how clean the water is, and a student from the university will show you how to use the testing kit. It's easier than it sounds.

Then there are the dunes. That's where the sea buckthorn is, as I said. Gloves are essential, please, because the thorns are sharp. Whoever works there will probably end up the muddiest, but also the proudest.

Finally, the visitor centre. We have a lot of families on Saturdays, so we always need one or two people at the door to hand out leaflets and answer questions. If you're happier talking to people than pulling up bushes, that's the place for you. We don't ask anyone to paint signs today, because the new ones haven't arrived yet.

Safety next. Always work in pairs. Radios are in the box by the door, and the emergency number is written on the back of your badge. If the tide comes in over the causeway, don't try to cross. Wait, and call me. The tide tables are pinned up in the hut, and I'll walk through them with you now.

There will be tea and biscuits at the hut at eleven, and at the end of the day we'll look at what you've found. Last month, a volunteer found a rare moth on the dunes, and that made the local paper. So keep your eyes open. Right, does anyone have any questions before we set off?
Good. Then let's choose pairs, collect your jackets from the hut, and head out. Mind the steps. They are slippery.
Come in, both of you. Sit down. So, you wanted to talk about the river project. How did the fieldwork go?
Mostly well, Dr Patel, though we had a few problems. We studied bank erosion on the River Wharfe, just outside Otley.
Hannah wanted to change the site halfway through, which caused some trouble.

That's not quite fair, Liam. The first site was upstream by the weir, and when we got there the bank had been covered in concrete. There was nothing natural to measure, so we moved to a bend two kilometres further down.
Yes, that's true. I was cross at the time, but looking back it was the right decision. The new site had a proper outer bend, with a steep eroding bank.
Good. Outer bends are exactly where you'd expect the fastest erosion. How did you measure it?
We used erosion pins. We pushed thirty of them into the bank in three rows, and then measured how much of each pin was showing.
Thirty seemed like plenty to me. But I've been thinking, and maybe it wasn't enough. We only had one visit, so we can't show change over time.

Well, a single visit is a limitation, certainly. But thirty pins is a reasonable sample for a student project. I wouldn't worry about the number. I'd worry more about repeating the measurements. Could you go back in two weeks?
We could, if the river doesn't flood. It's been raining a lot.
That would be ideal, actually. A flood would give you fascinating data. But before you go back, remember the safety form. Did you complete a risk assessment the first time?
Yes, we did, and we wore life jackets near the water, though the bank was only knee deep at the edge.
I felt a bit silly in mine, but Hannah insisted.
Quite right. Rivers rise very quickly, and the department will not let you work alone. Take a third person with you if you can, and tell someone where you are going.
We'll ask Priya from our group. She wanted to come anyway.
Good. Now, what about the equipment? Did anything go wrong?
Quite a lot, really. The GPS unit ran out of battery after an hour, so we only have grid references for the first ten pins.

And I thought the tape measure was too short for the wide section, but in the end we managed with two people. The bigger problem was the pins. Some of them had worked loose by the time we measured them. The soil was so soft that they moved.
Yes, and I'd say that's more serious than the battery. We can't trust those readings.
So the pins that moved are a problem for accuracy, while the GPS is only an inconvenience. You can mark the missing positions from your photographs. Did you take any?
Plenty. Although my phone fell into the water on the second day, so I lost half of them.
Luckily mine are fine. We have the whole bank covered.
Excellent. Let's talk about the missing readings. Would you leave them out, or try to estimate them?
I'd estimate them from the neighbouring pins.
I disagree. I think it's better to leave them out and say so honestly. If we make numbers up, the results lose their value.

Liam is right. Never invent data. Leave the gaps, and explain them in your discussion. Now, let's look at your draft. I read it last night. Your introduction first. It's clear, but at the moment it's much too long. Cut it by about a third.
We included lots of background reading.

I can see that. In fact your use of the literature is very strong, which is a real credit to you, but you must be selective. The methods section is what I'd like to praise most. It's detailed enough that someone could repeat your work.
That's good to hear. I wrote most of it.
The results are where you need to improve. The tables are fine, but your diagrams are hard to read. The labels are tiny. A clear map showing your pins would help too.
We do have a map, but it's in the appendix.
Then move it into the results. And finally the discussion. You must say what the weaknesses are. Be honest about the single visit and the loose pins. Markers always reward that kind of honesty.
So the missing readings go there as well.
Exactly. Your conclusion should also answer your original question directly. What was it again?
Whether erosion is faster on the outer bank.
And on our evidence it looks as if it is, though only two rows show clear change.
Then say exactly that, and no more. Don't claim more than the evidence shows. One more thing about timing. Many students leave the writing too late. How are you planning to share out the work?
Liam will write up the results, and I'll do the discussion and the introduction.
Actually, I'd prefer to try the discussion myself, if Hannah doesn't mind. I did the methods, and I'd like to practise something more analytical.
That's fine with me. I'll take the introduction and check all the references.

A sensible plan, as long as one of you reads the whole thing at the end so that it sounds like a single voice. The deadline is Friday week, so you have time. Come back on Wednesday if you'd like me to read it again.
Thank you very much.
Yes, thanks. That was really helpful.

Good afternoon, everyone. Today I'd like to talk about one of the quiet revolutions of the nineteenth century, the reform of the British postal system. We tend to take the post for granted. But for most of history, sending a letter was expensive, slow and surprisingly unfair. Let me begin by explaining how things worked before 1840.

In those days, the person who paid for the letter was not the person who wrote it. The charge was paid by the recipient. You can imagine what that meant. If a letter arrived, you had to pay before you were even allowed to read it. And if you didn't want the news, or couldn't afford it, you could simply refuse the letter. Some clever people used this to their advantage. They would write a secret message on the outside of the envelope, and then the receiver would read it and send the letter back without paying a penny.

The price itself was complicated. It depended mainly on how far the letter travelled, but also on the number of sheets of paper inside. A letter of one sheet cost less than a letter of two sheets, so people wrote on both sides, crossed their lines, and used the thinnest paper they could find. An envelope counted as an extra sheet, so most people didn't use one. They folded the letter and sealed it with wax.

The reformer who changed all this was Rowland Hill. Hill was a teacher by profession. He had run a school near Birmingham, and he understood both mathematics and the daily life of ordinary families. Later he moved to the Post Office, and what he found there astonished him. The real cost of carrying a letter, he argued, was tiny. Most of the expense lay in the handling and in collecting the money at the door.

In 1837 he published a pamphlet called Post Office Reform. It made a simple proposal: charge a single low price, one penny, for any letter up to half an ounce, anywhere in the country, and make the sender pay in advance. Many officials thought the idea was ridiculous. They believed the Post Office would lose a fortune. But the public was strongly in favour, and after a long campaign Parliament agreed.

Pre-payment needed something to prove that the postage had been paid. That is why the first adhesive postage stamp was invented. The Penny Black went on sale in 1840. Stamps were printed on large sheets, and each sheet held 240 stamps. That number was chosen deliberately, because there were 240 pennies in one pound, so a whole sheet cost exactly one pound. There were no perforations at that time. Post office clerks and customers had to separate the stamps with scissors, and if you look at old stamps today, you will often see uneven edges.

The design was simple and elegant. It showed a small portrait of the young Queen Victoria, who was only eighteen when she came to the throne. The same portrait was used on British stamps for the next sixty years, even though the queen herself grew old. Hill wanted a picture that was hard to copy, and a royal portrait was one of the best ways to make that possible.

Did it succeed? Spectacularly. In 1839, the last year of the old system, about 76 million letters were sent in Britain. A year later, in 1840, the figure had more than doubled to 169 million. In the following decade it doubled again. Letters became part of everyday life. People who had never written to a distant relative now sent birthday wishes, news of illness, and invitations. Love letters and business letters flowed together through the same sacks.

Of course, there were a few problems. The Penny Black was cancelled with red ink, but red ink can be hard to see on a black stamp, and people soon found they could wash it off and use the stamp again. So in 1841 the colour was changed. The new stamp was the Penny Red, with the cancellation printed in black. It stayed in use for nearly forty years.

Another improvement came with perforations. In 1854 the first perforated stamps appeared, with tiny holes between each stamp so that they could be torn apart easily. It sounds a small thing, but it saved countless hours for clerks and shopkeepers, and the idea quickly spread to other countries.

One last development I want to mention is the way people posted their letters. In the early days, you had to take your letter to a receiving office, and these were few and far between. The solution was the roadside pillar box. The first ones in Britain appeared in the 1850s, and a Post Office official who helped introduce them was the novelist Anthony Trollope. He saw them as a practical way of bringing the service to people's doors.

So, to sum up, the Penny Post began as a simple idea from a teacher, but it changed how a whole society communicated. Next week we'll look at the telegraph, and ask whether the same kind of change happened again.
Harbourside Arts Centre, Owen speaking. How can I help you?
Hello. I saw a poster for your evening pottery classes, and I'd like to sign up for one, if there are any places left.
There might be. Let me open the enrolment form. Can I take your name?
Yes, it's Nadia Szymanski.
I'm sorry, could you spell the surname for me?
Everyone asks! It's S-Z-Y-M-A-N-S-K-I. Szymanski.
S-Z-Y-M-A-N-S-K-I. Got it, thank you. Now, which course were you thinking of? We run a wheel throwing course and a hand building course, and both are for beginners.
I'd really like the wheel, because I've always wanted to make bowls on one of those spinning wheels.

I'm afraid the wheel course is full until the spring. There's a waiting list, if you'd like me to add you to it. Hand building still has a few places. You make things from coils and slabs of clay, and a lot of people find it easier to begin with.
Well, in that case I'll take hand building, and I can try the wheel later on.
Wonderful. The class is on Tuesday evenings, from seven until nine.
Oh dear. I work late on Tuesdays. Is there any other evening?
Let me look. Yes, there's a second group on Wednesday evenings, at the same times. I can put you in that one.
Wednesday is perfect.
Lovely. The Wednesday course starts on 14 January and runs for ten weeks. There are twelve people in each group, so you'll get plenty of attention from the tutor.
And how much is it?
The standard fee is £180. But if you join the centre as a member, which is free for the first year, you get £15 off. So for you it would be £165.
Then I'll join as a member. Is the clay included?

Yes, all the clay, the glazes and the firing are included. The only thing you need to buy is a basic tool kit, with a sponge, a wooden knife and a few other bits. It costs £12, and you pay the tutor in the first week.
That's fine. Where do the classes take place? I haven't been to the centre before.

The pottery studio is on the second floor, at the back of the building. The main entrance is on the harbour side, next to the café. There's a lift if you'd rather not use the stairs. The number 5 bus stops right outside, and there's a small car park, although it fills up quickly in the evenings.
I'll probably take the bus. Do you need my address?
Yes, please. We send the confirmation by post as well as by email.
It's 17 Harbour Street, Bristol. Oh, wait. Sorry, that's my old flat. I moved in September. It's 17 Harbour Street, no, I mean 71 Marsh Lane. Sorry, I keep forgetting.
No problem. So that's 71 Marsh Lane. And the postcode?
BS1 5RW. That's B-S-1, then 5-R-W.
B-S-1, 5-R-W. Thank you. And have you done any pottery before?
Only once. When I was at school we made a bowl, but it cracked in the kiln. I wasn't very good at it!

Don't worry, everyone starts somewhere. The tutor, Mrs Patterson, is very patient. One important thing: please bring an apron, because clay gets everywhere, and wear clothes you don't mind getting dirty. You can leave your work on the drying shelves between classes.
What happens if I miss a class?

Then you can come to a catch-up session on the first Saturday of each month, free of charge. You just need to tell the tutor beforehand. We also have an open studio on Sunday afternoons, if you want extra practice.
That sounds great. Will we be able to take our pots home?
Yes, in the last week, after they have been fired. Most people leave with four or five pieces.
Brilliant. Do I need to pay today?
We'll send you a payment link by email within the hour. If you pay in the next two days, your place is guaranteed.
I'll do that tonight.
Then welcome to the Harbourside Arts Centre, Nadia. We'll see you in January.
Thank you, Owen. Goodbye.

Good afternoon, everyone, and welcome to the Liffey Science Centre. My name is Aoife, and I'll be introducing our new exhibition, which is called Under the Surface. It's a journey from the sunlit shallows of the ocean to the darkest places on Earth, and I hope you'll enjoy every minute of it.

Before we go in, let me explain a few practical things. First, opening times. The exhibition is open from ten until five every day. On Thursdays, however, we stay open late. Some of you may have heard that we close at nine on those evenings, but that was only during the opening month. From now on we close at eight o'clock, so please plan your visit accordingly.

Now, about tickets. You can buy a ticket at the desk on the day, but we often sell out of the busiest time slots, so I'd strongly recommend booking online in advance. It's cheaper that way as well, and you can choose your time. If you do arrive without a ticket, we will do our best, but we can't promise.

A word about photography. You're very welcome to take photographs, and many visitors like to share them on social media. The one thing we ask is that you switch off your flash. Some of our displays include light-sensitive specimens, such as old preserved sea creatures, and a bright flash can damage them over time. Some people believe it disturbs other visitors, and of course that's true, but the real reason is the displays.

Many of you have asked about the audio guide. The good news is that you don't have to pay for it. It's a free app, and you can download it onto your own phone. If you don't have a phone with you, or if you'd like headphones, you can borrow a set from the desk for a small deposit. I'd suggest you download the app before you go in, because the signal inside the building is quite weak.

One more piece of news. Next month, our planetarium will begin showing a new film about deep sea volcanoes. It's been made by a team of Irish scientists, and it is spectacular. The cinema will stay open at weekends only until the end of the year. So if you'd like to see it, you may want to book a seat now.
Right, let me tell you about the exhibition itself. It's divided into five zones, and you walk through them in order, rather like descending in a submarine.

The first zone is called the Shallows. This is where most of our younger visitors spend their time, because it's the one place where you can pick things up. There are trays of real shells and sponges and pieces of coral, and you're welcome to touch them. Please wash your hands afterwards, because the basins are just outside.

The second zone is the Reef. Here we've built a long glass tunnel, and as you walk through it you're surrounded by tanks full of tropical fish. The tank in the middle is home to a small shark, whose name is Murphy. It was named by a school group, and it has been very popular ever since.

Next comes the Twilight Zone, where the light fades away. It's a dark room, and the only sound is the music of the ocean. Here you can sit down and listen to recordings of whales and dolphins that researchers have collected from the Atlantic. Many people tell me this is their favourite part, because it's so peaceful after the busy reef.

Then you arrive in the Deep. The walls are black, and the only light comes from a model of a research submarine. Visitors take turns steering it with a joystick, and the aim is to find a hidden creature on the sea floor. It's much harder than it looks, so don't be disappointed if the submarine gets stuck. You might also be disappointed to hear that the diving suit display is under repair, so you won't be able to try the equipment on this month.

Finally, there's the Lab. It's the last room of the exhibition, and it's where visitors do some of their own science. On the big touch screen, you choose different animals and connect them to build a food chain, from tiny plankton up to the largest whales. If you make a mistake, the screen shows you what would happen to the whole ocean. A lot of adults enjoy this one more than the children do.

Now, please remember that the exhibition is on one level, and all of the areas are accessible for wheelchairs and buggies. The toilets are near the exit, and the café is on the ground floor. If you'd like to leave a coat or a large bag, the cloakroom is free, and the staff can look after your things until closing time.
That's everything from me. If you have any questions at all, one of my colleagues in a blue shirt will be happy to help. Thank you for listening, and enjoy Under the Surface.
Come in, Imogen. Hello, Dev. Sit down, and let's talk about your sleep study. I've read your outline, and I have a few questions. First of all, who are your participants?
We're planning to use first-year students. We want to find out whether going to bed earlier helps people remember new words.
And first-years are the easiest group to reach, because we can contact them through the course forum, and the department already has a list of volunteers.
That's true, but there's another reason. Most of them are about the same age and have similar timetables. That means fewer things that could change the results.

Fair enough. I'd say the second reason is the more convincing one. Convenience is not a scientific argument by itself. Now, I assume you won't be asking them to go to bed at a certain time without checking?
No, we'll ask them to keep a sleep diary for two weeks. They write down when they go to bed and when they wake up.

Last term I did a similar exercise for another module, and the problem was that people forgot to fill the diaries in. They tried to remember everything at the end of the week, and the information wasn't reliable.
That's why I think an app would be better. It can send a reminder every morning.
I agree. Paper diaries are always a problem. And the length of the study? Two weeks?
Actually, I wondered about four weeks. We'd see more patterns.
I think that's too long. We hardly have enough time to analyse the data. One week would be easier.
One week isn't enough to show a stable pattern, but four is more than your timetable allows. Two weeks is a good compromise. So keep your plan as it is.
Okay. Two weeks it is.
Now, the memory test. What exactly will participants do?
We'll show them a list of twenty words for two minutes, and then they have to write down as many as they can remember the next morning.
Twenty words is sensible. Some students suggest a story or a set of pictures, but those are much harder to mark objectively. A word list gives you a simple score.
We thought so too.
One more thing about the words. Make sure they're all about the same length and equally common, otherwise some will be easier than others.
We found a published list that has already been checked, so we'll use that.
I think that's safer than choosing our own.
Exactly. And think about how participants will behave at night. Tell them not to review the words before bed.
We'll put that in the instructions, in capital letters!

My main worry, though, isn't the type of test. It's the time of day. If some participants are tested at nine in the morning and others at four in the afternoon, you'll see a difference that has nothing to do with sleep.
I hadn't thought of that. We did think about caffeine, because people who drink a lot of coffee might sleep badly.
Caffeine matters too, and you can ask about it in the diary. But it's something you can record. The testing time you must control. Test everyone in the same two-hour window.
We can do that. Imogen has already booked the room for Tuesday and Thursday mornings.
Good. And is twenty participants enough? That's small.
It is small, but we can only manage so many in the time. It's a limitation, and we'll say so.
We could ask for thirty if the panel has enough volunteers.
Then ask for thirty and see how many reply.
Fine, as long as you say so. Now, what happens next? You have a lot to do before you start. Let's go through it. The ethics form is the first job. Nobody can recruit before the committee approves it.
I've nearly finished it. I'll submit it by Friday.
Excellent. Then the recruitment email. Dev, you offered to write it?
Yes, I'll draft it tonight. Do I send it to everybody?
No, please don't. The department has a participant panel, and all recruitment messages go through it. They will send it for you, and they know who has already volunteered for other studies.
Right, I'll contact the panel, then.
And the diary app. I'm afraid I don't know how to set one up. Ask Mr Brennan, the technician. He built one for a project last year, and he may be able to adapt it.
I'll email him this afternoon. Dev, do you want me to print the consent forms as well?
There's no need. The forms will be online, and participants tick a box. It saves paper and the data is already in a file. Finally, the analysis. Have either of you used the statistics software?
Not properly. I've only watched a video.
Then I'd go to the workshop on Monday afternoons. It's free, and it will save you hours later.
We'll both go. Thanks very much, Dr Whitaker.
You're welcome. Dev: When do we need to start collecting data?
Not before the middle of next month, because of the approval process. Come back and see me after the ethics decision, and we'll talk again.

Good morning, everyone. In today's lecture I'd like to look at a question that surprises many people: why are some British cities better places for bees than the countryside? We usually imagine bees in meadows and orchards, not on busy streets. But research over the last fifteen years suggests the picture is more complicated.

Let me start with some background. When people say bee, they usually mean the honeybee, the insect that lives in a hive and makes honey. But in Britain there are about 270 species of bee altogether. Only one of them is the honeybee. About twenty-five are bumblebees. All the rest, more than two hundred species, are quite different, and I'll come back to them in a moment.

Most of these remaining species are solitary bees. A solitary bee has no queen, no workers and no hive. Each female builds her own nest, usually a small tunnel in the soil or in a hollow stem, and lays her eggs there. They are often tiny, some of them smaller than a grain of rice, and they rarely sting. Many people have never noticed one, but they are some of our most important pollinators.

Now, what happens in cities? A few years ago, my own team carried out a survey of green spaces in Bristol. We counted bees in parks, gardens, cemeteries and allotments. The result that surprised us most was that the allotments had the greatest number of species. Allotments are small plots where people grow vegetables and flowers, and they are usually managed without heavy chemicals, so the soil is rich and undisturbed.

Why are cities so good? The key reason is variety. A farm field may contain a single crop, which flowers for only three weeks. A city garden, on the other hand, has hundreds of plants, chosen by hundreds of different owners. Something is in flower from early spring until the first frosts of the autumn. Bees need food over a long season, and a city can provide it.

There is one more advantage that has been less discussed. Cities are warmer than the surrounding land, because buildings and roads store heat. In a large city, the temperature can be several degrees higher than in the nearby countryside. For a cold-blooded insect, that means an earlier start in the year and a longer flying season. There's also the question of chemicals. In gardens, people use far less spray per square metre than farmers do, and many city councils have stopped using weedkiller in their parks. This too makes a real difference.

That brings me to honeybees. In the last decade, keeping honeybees has become fashionable, and thousands of hives have appeared on the roofs of offices, hotels and even department stores. I think it's a wonderful hobby. It gets people interested in nature, and it produces honey of excellent quality. But there is a problem. If too many hives are placed in a small area, the honeybees compete with the wild bees for nectar, the sugary liquid that flowers produce. Honeybees are very efficient foragers, so they win the contest. In some parts of London, researchers have found that there are simply not enough flowers for all of them.
So my advice to anyone thinking of getting a hive is to check how many are already nearby. And the best thing you can do for bees in general is not to keep them at all, but to help the wild ones.

How might you do this? The first step is easy: leave a patch of your lawn uncut. Long grass and clover provide food, and it also gives shelter. Some of you may find this untidy, and your neighbours might complain, but the bees will thank you.

Second, provide places to nest. You can buy or make what is called a bee hotel. The best ones are made from pieces of bamboo, cut to the length of your hand and bundled together, with one end closed. Solitary bees move in and lay their eggs inside. Avoid hotels made from plastic, which can trap water and encourage mould.

Third, think about the plants you choose. Lavender is among the best, along with borage, and wild flowers like foxglove. Choose single flowers rather than the double ones in garden centres, because the double ones often contain little nectar.

Finally, and most importantly, avoid pesticides. Even a small amount of chemical spray can kill a bee, or damage the nest that she has built. If you must deal with pests, use natural methods, such as encouraging ladybirds, or picking the insects off by hand.

I'd also like you to remember that the evidence isn't perfect. Our survey covered a single year, and a different summer might give a different picture, so always be careful before drawing a general conclusion.

To summarise, cities are not the bee deserts that many people imagine. With the right care, they might become some of the most important refuges for these insects. In next week's lecture, we will move on to the question of butterflies, and ask whether a similar story can be told.
Good morning, Seaview Cottages, Bethan speaking. How can I help?
Good morning. I'm hoping to book a cottage for the summer holidays. I saw one on your website, but I'm not sure whether it's still available.
Of course. Let me take a few details first, and then we can look at it together. Could I have your name, please?
Yes, it's Quentin Thackeray.
Could you spell your surname for me?
Certainly. T-H-A-C-K-E-R-A-Y. Thackeray, like the novelist.
T-H-A-C-K-E-R-A-Y. Thank you, Mr Thackeray. Which cottage were you interested in?
I think it was called Honeysuckle Cottage, the one with the blue door and the garden going down to the water.

Ah, I'm sorry, Honeysuckle is already taken for the whole of July. But I have a very similar cottage in the same village. It's called Primrose Cottage, and it also has a garden that leads to the harbour wall.
That sounds just as good. Is there a bedroom for each of the children? We have three.
There are three bedrooms, one double and two twins, so that works well. When would you like to arrive?
I was thinking of Saturday 5 July.
Hmm, let me check. I'm afraid Primrose isn't free that weekend. A family is staying until the eleventh. The first Saturday available is 12 July.
That's fine, actually. The schools break up a week later than I thought, so 12 July is better.
Lovely. And how long would you like to stay? Most people take a full week, from Saturday to Saturday.
We'd like a bit longer, if possible. Perhaps fourteen nights.

Hold on, let me look at the calendar. Ah, someone else has booked it from the twenty-sixth, so you could stay up to the twenty-second at most. That would be 10 nights, from the twelfth to the twenty-second.
Then 10 nights it is. That's fine.
Perfect. How many people will be staying?
Five of us. Myself, my wife and the three children. Oh, and my mother has just said she would like to join us, so it will be 6.
Six is no problem. The cottage sleeps up to eight.
And what's the price?

For a week in July it's normally £680. But I should explain how it works. The cheaper rate applies only until the end of June. From the first of July the cottages move into the high season, so the weekly price goes up to £720. For ten nights, we calculate it by the day, so I'll work out the total for you in a moment.
All right. So £720 is the figure for July.
That's right, per week. I'll send you the full total by email. Now, are you bringing any pets?
We'd like to bring our dog. She's a small spaniel, and very well behaved.
That's fine. We allow one dog in this cottage, and there's an extra charge of £25 for the stay. It covers cleaning.
That seems reasonable.
Did you want to know about the beaches?
Yes, please. The children are keen on swimming.

The nearest beach is Polgwidden Cove. That's spelled P-O-L-G-W-I-D-D-E-N. It's about ten minutes on foot, down the lane behind the cottage. It's sandy, and there are rock pools at low tide. There are bigger beaches a few miles away, but they get very crowded in the summer.
Polgwidden Cove sounds perfect.
One thing to mention is that dogs aren't allowed on the cove between May and September. But there's a path along the cliffs where she can run.
Oh, that's a shame, but we'll manage. How do we collect the key?
There's no need to come to the office. The key is in a safe beside the back door. The code is 4719. I'll confirm it in writing nearer the date.
4719. Good. And when can we arrive?
The cottage is normally ready from 3:00, but the cleaners are very busy on a Saturday, so I would plan for 4:30 to be safe. If you arrive earlier, you can leave your bags in the garden shed.
4:30 is fine. Thank you very much.
I'll send the booking form by email, and a deposit is due within seven days. Thank you for calling, Mr Thackeray.
Thank you. Goodbye.

Good morning, everyone, and welcome to the briefing for the Leith Harbour Food Festival. I'm Morag, the festival manager, and I want to run through the main points so that you can answer visitors' questions. The festival takes place over three days, from Friday to Sunday, and we expect about twelve thousand visitors.

First, the opening hours. The programme says we open at ten o'clock on Friday, but that has changed. Several of the stallholders are travelling from the Highlands, and the delivery trucks can't reach the site until the morning, so we won't open until noon. On Saturday and Sunday we open at ten as usual. Please tell visitors that if they ask.

Now, how do visitors pay? Entry to the festival is free. Inside, you can buy full meals from the stalls, and most of them accept cards. But the small tastings, the samples that cost a pound or two, work differently. Visitors buy tokens at the main gate. A strip of ten tokens costs eight pounds, and each tasting takes one or two tokens. That keeps the queues moving, and it also means the stalls don't have to handle a lot of coins.

Another change concerns the cookery theatre. Last year it was in the big white tent near the water, but that was damaged in the winter storms and the cost of repair was too high. So we've moved the theatre to the old warehouse behind the market. Please make sure that you give visitors directions, because the signs at the gate haven't been updated yet. Some visitors may think it's moved because of noise from the stage, but that's not the reason.

Waste is a big issue for us. All the hot drinks are served in cups that can be composted, but we'd prefer to use none at all. So if visitors bring their own reusable cup, we give them fifty pence off the price of a drink. It's not much, but people seem to like it, and we gave away hundreds last year.

Finally, our main theme. Many festivals raise money for charity, and a few focus on training young chefs. Those are good aims, but this year our priority is education. On Friday morning, before we open to the public, six primary schools will visit, and each class will meet a farmer, handle fresh ingredients and make a simple lunch. The purpose is to show children where their food comes from. So if you see groups of children on Friday, please be extra patient.

Now let me take you round the site, so you know what's where. We're standing at the main gate. If you walk straight ahead, you'll reach the Harbour Market. For years this was famous for fish, and you might expect to find a seafood tasting there. That was cancelled this year because the main supplier withdrew. Instead, the market will be full of farmers selling their vegetables directly to the public, with no shop in between. Prices are lower, and the produce is usually picked the same morning.

Turn left at the market and you'll find the Orchard Tent. This is a new addition. About a dozen fruit growers from Fife and the Borders have come, and visitors can taste apple, pear and plum juices, and talk to the people who grew them. The most popular drink last year was a cloudy apple juice with a hint of ginger. I'd recommend it to anyone who asks.

Next to the Orchard Tent is the Cookery Theatre, as I explained, in the old warehouse. It has seats for two hundred people, and chefs from restaurants across Scotland will cook in front of the audience. Visitors can watch and ask questions, but they don't take part. If a visitor wants to join in a baking session, I'm afraid we haven't organised one this year. We hope to have it next time.

On the far side of the market you'll see Street Food Row, a long line of vans and small kitchens. They serve dishes from all over the world: Indian curry, Mexican tacos, Polish dumplings and many more. It gets very busy at lunchtime, so I'd advise visitors to go early, or to try it on Sunday when it's quieter.

And right at the end, beside the old lighthouse, is the Dairy Corner. Here you can taste cheeses made on small farms across Scotland, from soft cream cheeses to a very strong blue one that is quite an acquired taste. Each stall will give you a small piece, and if you like it, you can buy a whole one to take home.

A few practical points. First aid is in the blue cabin by the gate. Lost children should be brought there, too. Toilets are on both sides of the market. All volunteers wear a green T-shirt, and you should have your badge on at all times. If anything goes wrong, my phone number is on the back of the badge.

Lunch for volunteers is served at one o'clock in the staff tent, and there's free tea and coffee all day. I'd ask you to be friendly, patient and above all enthusiastic. Visitors remember a smile far longer than they remember the exact answer. Right, are there any questions before we begin?
Hello, Callie. Hello, Rohan. Come in. I've been looking forward to hearing how the brewery project is going. Remind me, which company did you choose in the end?
Harrow Lane Brewery. We chose it because it has just launched an alcohol-free beer, and we wanted to see how a small company introduces a completely new product.
Originally I was in favour of a bigger firm, because we'd have more data. But a new launch gives us a clear question, so I think Callie was right.
A sensible choice. New products are the best place to study marketing. And what have you done so far?
We designed a questionnaire and sent it to about two hundred people in the city. We got ninety-four replies.
That's a respectable response rate. Were there any problems with the questions?

Yes. Some of the people who replied weren't in the target group at all. The brewery wants to reach adults between twenty-five and forty, but about a third of our replies came from students who were under twenty-one. We should have checked that at the start.
I'd say that was a bigger problem than the wording. A few questions were confusing, but we fixed those after the first twenty replies.
You can simply exclude the younger replies, as long as you explain why. Now, let me ask about the results. Did anything surprise you?
Two things, really. The first was that most people had never heard of the brewery. We assumed that, being local, it would be well known, but over sixty per cent said they didn't recognise the name.

And the other surprise was about price. We expected that cost would be the main factor, but it was only the third most important reason for choosing a drink. Taste and the look of the bottle came first.
Interesting. What about the differences between men and women? Many studies suggest women are less likely to try alcohol-free beer.
We found the opposite, but the difference was too small to mean anything. And the age groups were about the same.
There was one more thing, but it wasn't a surprise. Most people preferred bottles to cans.
That's well known, so I wouldn't spend time on it. Did you also speak to anyone at the brewery?
Yes, we interviewed the owner, Mrs Dalgleish, for half an hour. She was very open about the sales figures, but she asked us not to publish them.
So we'll show them only as percentages, and I think that's acceptable.
It is, provided you tell your reader that you've done it. Keep a copy of her written permission as well.
She emailed us last week, so we have that.
Good. Now, the recommendations. The company has a small budget. What do you suggest?

We thought about five options. The first was advertising on social media. At first I was keen, but when I looked at the cost, it was far more than they can afford. Even a small campaign costs thousands.
Local radio is cheaper, but the listeners are mostly older. So it's not a good match with the target group.
And tasting events?

That was the most popular idea in our survey. Respondents said they'd be more willing to try the beer if they could taste it first. The only difficulty is that someone from the brewery has to stand there all afternoon, and they only have three employees.
Discount vouchers have already been tried by almost every other drinks company in the area, so customers are used to them. They don't create much excitement any more.
And the last one?

Changing the label on the bottle. Here we have to be careful, because there are rules about what you can claim on alcohol-free products. For example, they can't say the drink is healthy. The brewery would have to check with a lawyer.
That's a good point, and many students miss it. I suppose you also considered the tourist season?
Yes, the summer is the busiest time, and the tasting events would work very well then, since visitors are looking for local products.

Excellent. Now, about the report. I'd like your recommendations to come near the beginning, not at the end. Many readers only read the first page. And please keep the literature review short. Two pages is plenty.
Should we include the raw questionnaire in the appendix?
Yes, but not the individual answers, only the questions. And remember to mention the limits of your sample. Ninety-four replies isn't large, and you removed some of them.
We'll make sure we do that. Should we also compare the brewery with a competitor?
Only if you have time. One company studied properly is better than two done badly.
Is it all right if we include a short section on what we would do with a larger budget?
Briefly, yes. But keep it to one paragraph. The marker wants to see that you can work within the limits you were given.
That makes sense. We'll keep it short.
Good. Send me a draft by the end of next week, and I'll give you feedback within three days. Well done so far.
Thank you, Professor.
Thanks very much.

Good afternoon. Today's lecture is about an energy source that is more predictable than almost any other: the tides. Britain is surrounded by water, and it has some of the biggest tides in the world, so it's no surprise that engineers have been dreaming of harnessing them for more than a century. Let me start with the basic science.

Tides are caused mainly by the gravitational pull of the Moon, although the Sun plays a smaller part. As the Earth turns, the Moon's pull drags the oceans into a bulge on the side nearest to it. There's a second bulge on the opposite side. The result is that in most places there are two high tides and two low tides. Because the Moon is moving round the Earth at the same time, a full cycle takes about 25 hours, not twenty-four. That is why tide times move later each day.

The difference in height between high and low tide is called the tidal range. In the open ocean it's small, but in certain shaped coastlines the water is funnelled and the range becomes enormous. The Bristol Channel and the Severn Estuary have one of the largest tidal ranges anywhere in the world, up to fourteen metres. That makes them very attractive for energy.

The first type of technology is the tidal barrage. A barrage is a long wall built across an estuary, rather like a dam. At high tide, water flows in through gates, and when the tide goes out the water is released through turbines, which generate electricity. The best known example is La Rance, in northern France. It opened in 1966 and has operated for more than half a century. In fact, for many years it was the largest tidal power station on Earth.

So why don't we have barrages everywhere? The main answer is the environment. A barrage changes the flow of water in the whole estuary. The mudflats, which are the feeding grounds for thousands of wading birds, may be covered for longer, or may no longer be exposed at all. Fish migration is another concern, because salmon and eels must pass through the turbines. For the Severn, a barrage has been proposed several times, but each time it has been rejected, because the cost was enormous and the damage to wildlife was considered too great.

That leads me to the second technology, which is much more popular today: tidal stream turbines. These look very similar to wind turbines. They have large blades fixed to a tower, but the tower stands on the sea floor and the blades are turned by moving water, rather than by air. Water is about 800 times denser than air, so even a slow current has a lot of power. A turbine with blades only half the size of a wind turbine can produce the same amount of electricity.

The best sites are places where the tide runs fast through a narrow channel. A good example is the Pentland Firth, between the north of Scotland and the Orkney Islands. There, the current can reach 5 metres per second, but most turbines need only around 3 metres per second to work efficiently. The first array of turbines was installed there in 2016, and it now supplies electricity to thousands of homes.

What are the advantages? The first is certainty. Unlike wind or sunshine, the tides can be predicted, and engineers can forecast the output of a tidal plant for decades in advance. We know when the next high tide will be in the year 2100. Compare that to the weather, which can change within hours. The second advantage is that the machines are mostly hidden below the surface, so they don't spoil the view, and there is less opposition from local residents.

And the disadvantages? The most important is cost. Building and installing a turbine in strong currents is difficult and expensive, and the equipment has to survive corrosion, storms and marine growth. Even more important in the long term is maintenance. A turbine on the sea floor can only be reached by ship, and in rough weather that may be impossible for weeks. So the total cost of the electricity is still higher than from a wind farm.

There's also the question of marine life. Early studies suggested that seals and fish could be injured by moving blades. More recent monitoring has found that most animals avoid the turbines, but we need more evidence, especially in the case of larger arrays.

Where does the technology go from here? Some engineers are developing floating turbines, which are attached to the surface by cables and are much cheaper to install. Others are looking at tidal lagoons, which are walls enclosing a smaller area of water, away from the main estuary, so the effect on wildlife is smaller. Whether they will work at scale is still an open question.

To sum up, tidal power is not going to solve our energy problems alone. But because of its reliability, it may be a very useful partner to wind and solar. In next week's lecture, we will look at wave power, and ask whether the same arguments apply. Thank you.
Good morning, Wythenshawe Leisure Centre. This is Daniel. How can I help you?
Hello. I'd like to join the gym, please. I've just started a new job nearby, and I want to get fit.
Great. I can help you with that. Let me open the membership form. Could I have your name, please?
Yes. Priya Kowalczyk.
Sorry, how do you spell your surname?
It's a little unusual. K-O-W-A-L-C-Z-Y-K. My husband is Polish.
K-O-W-A-L-C-Z-Y-K. Thank you, Mrs Kowalczyk. Now, there are several types of membership. Would you like full membership? That gives you the gym, the pool and all the classes, at any time.
Yes, I think so. Actually, wait. I'll probably only be able to come in the daytime, because I work evenings on three days a week. Do you have something cheaper for that?
We do. It's called off-peak membership. You can use everything between nine in the morning and four in the afternoon, and after eight at night. It's a good choice if your hours are flexible.
That sounds better. I'll take the off-peak one.
Lovely. The full price for that is £35 a month. But are you a student, or over sixty?
I'm actually doing a part-time degree, so I have a student card.
Then you get a discount. With a student card, it's £28 a month.
That's good. Is there a joining fee?
Normally there is. It's £25. But we have an offer this month, so you pay only £15. I'd join now if I were you.
Then I'll join today, in that case. What happens next?
Every new member has a free induction. A member of staff will show you the equipment and write a personal programme for you. It takes about forty minutes. Do you want to book that now?
Yes, please. Could I come on Monday?
Hmm, Mondays are fully booked, I'm afraid, because it's the busiest day. We have places on Tuesday, though.
Tuesday is fine, actually. Even better, because I finish early that day.
And what time would suit you?
Any time after about six, I think.
I have a gap at 6:45. Would that work?
That's perfect.
Brilliant. I'll put you down for 6:45 on Tuesday. Now, are there any classes you're interested in? We have spinning, aerobics, boxing and yoga.
I'd love to try yoga. I've done a little at home, but I'd like a proper teacher.
The evening yoga class is very popular, so book early. But you can take it with your off-peak card, as it starts at 8:15.
Wonderful. And what about the pool? I'd like to swim in the mornings.
Lane swimming starts at 6:30 in the morning, but your membership only covers the pool after nine. If you'd like early swimming, you would have to upgrade.
No, that's fine. I'll swim later in the day. Is there somewhere to leave my things while I'm training?
Yes, there are lockers in the changing rooms. You need a pound coin, which you get back when you open the locker. We also have a café on the first floor, and the hot showers are free.
Lovely. And do you have parking?
There's a large car park at the front. The first two hours are free for members, but you must enter your registration at the desk.
Good. Now, I need your address for the membership card.
It's 12 Ashby Road, Manchester.
Could you spell Ashby?
A-S-H-B-Y.
Thank you. And the postcode?
M14 6TQ. That's M, then 1-4, and then 6-T-Q.
M14 6TQ. Got it. We also need an emergency contact, in case you have an accident.
I'll put my brother. His name is Marek, that's M-A-R-E-K.
Marek. And his phone number?
I'll have to look for it. I don't remember it. Can I give it to you on Tuesday?
Of course. Just bring it with you, together with your student card. Oh, and a pair of clean trainers. We ask everyone to use different shoes in the gym than they wear in the street.
Right. I'll remember that.
Thank you very much for calling, Mrs Kowalczyk. We'll see you on Tuesday.
Thank you, Daniel. Goodbye.

Good evening, everyone, and thank you for coming. My name is Hugh Marlowe, and I'm the transport officer at the county council. Tonight I'd like to explain our plans for the Riverside Greenway, a new cycle path along the River Cam. I'll talk for about fifteen minutes, and then I'll be happy to answer your questions.

Let me start with the timetable. The plan was to open the path at the end of March, and you may have seen that date in the local newspaper. Unfortunately, the heavy rain this winter flooded the site, and the building work has been delayed by several weeks. We're now aiming to open the whole path in June. That's a firm date, and we have the contractors' agreement.

The path will be nine kilometres long, from the railway station in the south to the village of Waterbeach in the north. Some people have asked why it isn't longer. We did consider extending it to eleven kilometres, but that would have meant crossing private land, and negotiations with the owners would have taken years. Nine kilometres is a good start, and we hope we can add more later.

As for the cost, the total is about four million pounds. The largest part, around sixty per cent, comes from a government grant for sustainable transport. The council contributes about a third, and the rest has been donated by local businesses, including the college and the science park. I'd like to thank all of them for their support.

Let me now describe the route, starting at the station. As you leave the station, you'll find covered cycle parking for four hundred bikes. At the moment, as many of you know, the racks are always full, and bikes are left leaning against the railings. The new shelter will solve that problem. It also has cameras, so your bicycle will be safe.

From there the path runs north, along the old railway line, until it reaches the river at the Mill Bridge. This is the most expensive part of the project. The old bridge is too narrow and in poor condition, so we are replacing it with a new wide bridge with two lanes, one in each direction. It will be built of steel and wood, and local designers have been involved.

Past the bridge, the path crosses Riverside Meadow. This is a beautiful area, and the wildlife groups were worried about the effect of the path. We listened to their concerns, and as a result we've made a small pond beside the track. It will attract frogs, dragonflies and water birds, and we'll put up information boards for walkers and families.

Some residents asked for a separate lane for walkers, but there isn't room on the Meadow. The existing footpath stays where it is, and the cycle path runs beside it, and the two are divided by a low hedge. We also thought about putting benches along the route, but we have decided to wait and see where people actually stop. We can add them later.

Next comes Orchard Lane. This is a quiet road, but it's dark in the evening, because the trees are tall and there are no street lights. The council is installing new lights along the full length of the lane. They are low energy, and they will only turn on when someone is nearby. So the lane will be safe in winter, without disturbing the neighbours with a bright glare all night.

The last part of the path leads into the market area. This is where cyclists and pedestrians will mix, so we have introduced a few rules. When you reach the market, please get off your bike and walk. It is only a couple of hundred metres. A small bell is welcome, but it's not enough on its own. At the entrance to the market we'll install a repair stand with a pump and basic tools, which anyone can use free of charge.

Now, a word about how you can have your say. We held a public meeting last week, and about one hundred and fifty people attended. But we know not everyone can come in the evening, so we've also set up an online survey, which will stay open until the thirtieth of this month. The address is on the leaflets by the door. Please fill it in, because the results will help us decide on the details, such as where to put the signs.

Finally, safety. The advisory speed on the path will be ten miles an hour. This is not a race track, and it's meant for families as well as commuters. We'll review the arrangements after the first year, and we'll make changes if there are problems.

I know many of you have questions, and I'm sure some of you are worried about noise and traffic during the construction. I'll cover those in a moment. First, does anybody have a question about the route itself?
Come in, Zainab. Hello, Tom. Sit down. You wanted to talk about your presentation on Great Expectations. Let's hear what you have so far.
Thank you, Dr Brennan. We chose the novel because it's the one we both enjoyed most on the course. I'd read it as a teenager, and I wanted to see whether I'd understand it differently now.
For me it was partly the film. I saw a film version first, and it made me curious about the original.
Many students come to Dickens that way. Be careful, though, with the film. Some details are quite different from the book, and the examiners notice that.
That's what I said to Tom. I think we should refer only to the text.
I agree. I was thinking of showing a short clip, but I think it would take too much time.
Good. And which edition are you using?
The one from the course reading list.
Quote page numbers from that same edition, so that nobody gets confused. You have twenty minutes, including questions. What are you going to focus on?
We discussed several themes. At first we thought of guilt, because Pip feels guilty throughout the novel. But then we realised that was too big for twenty minutes.
So we decided on social class and ambition. They're connected, because Pip wants to become a gentleman, and that's what drives most of the plot.
A wise decision. Those two themes together give you a clear argument. Guilt would have been a mistake in so short a time.
I also considered crime, because of Magwitch. But I think that belongs to a different essay.
Quite right. Have you read any critical writing on the novel, or only the text itself?
Two articles. One argues that Pip is a snob, and the other says he's simply a young man who is easily influenced by those around him. I find the second one more convincing.
I'm not so sure. I think he has a choice, and he makes bad choices. But I'd rather present both views and let the audience decide.

That's the right approach, as long as you say which one you favour at the end. A presentation without a position is rather dull. Also, give the full details of each article on a final slide. Now, let's talk about the characters. How will you use them?
Pip, obviously, is the centre. His ambition makes him leave his family and become, in a way, ashamed of them.
And Miss Havisham shows how the past can control a person. She stops all the clocks on the day she was left at the altar, and she never moves on.

I'd also like to discuss Magwitch. He seems frightening at the beginning, but later we learn that he has been secretly paying for Pip's education. His generosity is hidden, and Pip finds it humiliating.
That's a strong analysis. I'd say Magwitch is the most interesting of the three, and don't be afraid to spend more time on him. So, what about your slides?
We've prepared twelve. I tried to put quotations on most of them.

Hmm. That may be too many. Twelve slides is fine for twenty minutes, but you have a lot of words on each. When people read the screen they stop listening to you. Cut the text by half, and use quotations only when you really need them.
I had thought the text was too small, too, but Zainab says it's all right on the projector. She also wants to include a picture of the author, which I think is a waste of space.
I'd agree. A picture adds little. Keep the space for ideas.
It's not the size so much as the amount. Another thing is the colour. The dark red background is hard to read. Choose something lighter.
I'll change that tonight.
And finally, practise out loud. Time yourselves. Most students go over time, and then the end of the talk is rushed. The conclusion is what the audience remembers.
We're going to rehearse on Thursday, in the seminar room.
Good idea. Also, think about who will speak when. Don't just alternate every slide. Divide it by sections, so each of you owns a part.
I'll do the introduction and the part on class, and Tom will take ambition and the conclusion.
That works for me.
One more practical point. Will you take questions during the talk or after it?
After, I think. If people interrupt in the middle, we'll lose time.
But a few questions in the middle could help us check that people are following. Maybe we could stop once, halfway.
I like that. Plan one pause, after the section on class. It also gives you a breath. And what is your final sentence?
We haven't decided.
I'd like to finish with a quotation from the last chapter.
Good, but choose a short one, something the audience can remember.
Excellent. I'm looking forward to it. Don't forget, the presentation is on the twelfth, at two o'clock, and I'll be sitting at the back. Good luck.
Thank you, Dr Brennan.
Thanks. See you on the twelfth.

Good morning, everyone. In today's lecture I want to take you to the north coast of Northern Ireland, to a place that looks as though it was built by giants: the Giant's Causeway. It's one of the most visited natural sites in the British Isles, and it's also a wonderful example of how geology and legend can explain the same landscape in two very different ways. I'll start with the science.

The story begins about 60 million years ago, at a time when this part of the world was very different. The Atlantic Ocean was just beginning to open, as the continents of Europe and North America slowly moved apart. As they did so, the Earth's crust was stretched and cracked, and molten rock from deep underground forced its way to the surface. For several million years there were huge volcanic eruptions across the area that is now Antrim.

The rock that flowed out was a kind of lava called basalt. Basalt is dark, very fluid, and it runs a long way before it stops. It poured out in sheets, filling valleys and covering the older rocks. Over time, layer upon layer built up, and today those layers form high plateaus along the coast.

Now to the columns. The Causeway is made of about 40,000 of them, packed tightly together like the cells of a honeycomb. Most of the columns have six sides, though some have four, five, seven or even eight. The tallest are about 12 metres high, and the rock is so regular that visitors often find it hard to believe nature made it.

How did that happen? When the thick lava flow began to cool, it also began to shrink. Think of what happens when you leave a bowl of wet clay in the sun. It dries, and as it dries it contracts. If it can't shrink evenly, it cracks. The same process occurred in the lava. As it cooled from the top and the bottom, it contracted, and cracks formed in the shape of hexagons. Then the cracks slowly grew downward through the rock, forming the columns.

That analogy with drying mud is not simply a nice comparison. Scientists have actually done experiments with wet starch, and they produce miniature columns that look remarkably like the real thing. In both cases, the cracks tend to meet at angles of about one hundred and twenty degrees, which is exactly what you find at the Causeway.

So much for the science. What about the legend? According to the old story, the Irish giant Finn McCool built the causeway as a path across the sea to Scotland, because he wanted to fight a rival giant who lived there. When Finn reached the other side, he found that the Scottish giant was much bigger than he was. Finn ran home, and his wife disguised him as a baby. When the Scottish giant saw how large the baby was, he thought the father must be enormous, and he fled, tearing up the causeway behind him. The story is told a little differently in different villages, and in some versions it is Finn's rival who builds the bridge.

Of course, it's a legend, but there is a surprising link with real geology. Across the sea in Scotland, on the small island of Staffa, you can find exactly the same kind of columns, from the very same lava flow. Fingal's Cave, on Staffa, is a sea cave lined with basalt columns. So the story of a bridge between the two countries isn't completely wild. The two places were once part of the same landscape.

Let me turn to protection. The Causeway was named a World Heritage Site in 1986. Recognition like that brings visitors, and today about 1 million people come every year. That creates problems of its own. The columns can be damaged by walking, and rare plants grow in the cracks. The managers have built paths, and visitors are asked to keep to them, but pressure remains.

The site is managed by a charity, which depends on money from its visitor centre. The centre has exhibitions that explain the geology, a café and a shop. Many visitors buy a ticket for the centre and never realise that the path along the shore is open to everyone.

There's another threat which can't be controlled by paths, and that is the sea. Waves have been eroding the coast for thousands of years, and storms are growing stronger. A number of columns have already fallen. Monitoring teams use laser scanners every year to measure how fast the cliffs retreat.

I'd like to leave you with a question. Why do you think so many cultures produce legends about places like this? My own view is that when the shapes of nature seem too perfect, people look for a human explanation. We'll talk about this further in the seminar, and I'd like you to read the article on the reading list before then.

Next week, we'll move on from Ireland to Iceland, where the same process of crust-stretching can still be seen. Please come to the lecture with the notes from today, because we'll compare the two places in detail.
