Hello, everyone, and welcome to the Alhambra Street Theatre. My name's Iain, and I'll be your guide for the next little while. I've worked here for twenty-two years, first as a stagehand and now as the head of tours, so I know every corner of this building, including some corners the audience never see.

Let's begin with the practical details. The tour normally lasts ninety minutes, but today there's a rehearsal on the main stage, and we can't go on until two o'clock. So we'll be a bit shorter this afternoon, about an hour and a quarter. If you have to leave early, just tell me and one of my colleagues will show you out.

Please don't carry your bags round the building. The corridors are narrow, and there are cables and equipment in many places. You can leave them in the lockers beside the stage door. They take a pound coin, which you get back when you open the locker. The cloakroom in the foyer is only for people attending shows, so it won't be open.

I'm afraid I'll have to ask you not to take photographs inside the auditorium today. Sometimes we allow it, but when a rehearsal is in progress the performers have asked for privacy. You can take as many pictures as you like in the rest of the building, though. Some people think it's about copyright, because the set was designed by a famous artist, but really it's about the rehearsal.

A little about the building. The theatre opened in 1884, which makes it about one hundred and forty years old. It was built for music hall, with a crowd of two thousand packed into a space that now holds fewer than nine hundred. It survived two fires and a bomb in the war, and it has been restored several times. Some of the old ironwork you'll see backstage is original.

There's good news about the future, too. Next year, we'll replace all of the seats in the auditorium. Many of them date from the nineteen seventies and are rather uncomfortable. We did consider building a small studio theatre beside the main one, but there isn't enough money at present. Perhaps in a few years.

Right, let me tell you where we're going. We start at the stage door, the entrance used by actors, musicians and crew. Look at the walls here. They're covered with signed posters from the last fifty years: comedians, dancers, rock bands, and even a famous magician. Everyone who has performed here has been asked to sign, and it's become a tradition. Please feel free to look for your favourites.

From the stage door we walk down the corridor to the wardrobe department. This is a big room with racks and racks of costumes. Some are from productions that are seventy years old. The costume makers still repair them, and they lend them to schools and amateur groups. You'll be able to try on some of the smaller pieces, such as hats and gloves, but I'm afraid not the big ones.

Next we visit the scenery workshop, where the sets are built. It's huge, because it needs to take a whole street or a castle wall. At the moment, the painters are working on a backdrop for the next pantomime, and you're welcome to watch them. The painting is done flat on the floor, then lifted up, so you can see how large it is.

After that, we go up a flight of stairs to the green room. It's called that for reasons nobody really knows, and it isn't green at all. It's a comfortable room with sofas, a kettle and a screen that shows what's happening on stage. This is where performers relax and wait for their turn. You may well meet a few of them, though I can't promise.

Our last stop is the lighting box, at the back of the circle. From here the technicians control all of the lights, and you can see the console. There are four hundred and twenty buttons on it, and each one has a purpose. If you ask nicely, the technician may let you test one or two lights from the desk. It's a popular part of the tour.

I should also mention the old trapdoor in the middle of the stage. It was used for ghosts and villains in Victorian plays. Unfortunately, it's been closed for safety reasons, so I can only show it to you from above.

A few last reminders. Stay with the group, and don't touch any equipment unless I say you can. There are steps in several places, so please watch your feet. If anyone needs a lift, tell me now, and I'll arrange it. And if you have any questions, ask at any time. Right, if everyone has put their bags away, let's go through the stage door.
Morning, Aisha, morning, Fraser. I heard that your bridge didn't survive the test. Tell me what happened.
It broke at a lower load than we expected, Dr Gibson. We were hoping for about twenty kilograms, but it failed at twelve.
Which was a bit of a shock, because the calculations looked fine. We chose a truss design, mainly because it's the simplest to analyse. We could work out the force in every member by hand.
That's a sensible reason. A truss is a good choice for a first project. An arch might look better, but the mathematics is much more demanding. Where exactly did the bridge fail?
At one of the joints in the middle, where two diagonal pieces meet the bottom beam. The glue gave way, and then the whole span collapsed.
I think that's the whole story. The glue was weak. We used a quick-setting type, and it just wasn't strong enough.

I'm not convinced, Fraser. I think the real problem was that we cut some of the pieces slightly too short. The gap at the joint was too wide, and the glue had to fill it. A thick layer of glue is always weaker.
Aisha's explanation is more convincing. If a joint is cut accurately, even a mediocre glue is surprisingly strong. A badly fitted joint will fail with any glue. Did you measure the gap?
About two millimetres.
There you are. That's enough to cause the problem. Did you apply the load evenly?
Yes, we used a sandbag hung from the centre, and we added sand slowly. We were very careful about that. We weren't in a hurry.
Good. So that's one source of error you can exclude.
We also checked the weight of the sandbag on the scales, so the readings should be reliable.
Excellent. Did you record the temperature or humidity on the day? Balsa wood absorbs moisture, and damp wood is weaker.
No, I'm afraid we didn't. The workshop was quite cold, though.
It was dry, I think. The heating was on.
Then it's probably not an issue, but write it down next time.
By the way, the materials cost us about eleven pounds.
That's well within the budget, so don't worry about that. Now, let's think about the second model. Do you have time to build another?
Yes, we've got about two weeks. We can strengthen it.
What are you going to change?
First, the diagonals. They were only five millimetres thick, and one of them began to bend before the joint failed. We could make them thicker, maybe eight millimetres.
And I'd like to add cross-bracing between the two sides. At the moment, the bridge moves sideways when the load is high, and that may have added stress to the joints.
What about using a different glue? I still think a stronger one would help.

You can, but I'd advise against changing two things at once. If you change the glue, the diagonals and the bracing, you won't know which one made the difference. Keep the same glue, improve the cutting, and make the other two changes.
That makes sense. We'll do that.
Should we reduce the span? We could make it shorter, and then it would be easier to build.
No. The span is set by the assignment. Shortening it would be cheating.
Right. I just wondered.
Now, the report. Let me give some advice on each section. Start with the introduction. Keep it short, and say what you were trying to find out. Don't give a history of bridges. Nobody wants that.
We'll just state the aim and the design brief.
Should we explain the calculation method in the introduction as well?
No. Put the calculations in an appendix, and refer to them in the text. The reader should reach your results quickly.

Good. For the results section, include a photograph of the failed joint. A picture of the failure tells the reader more than a paragraph of explanation. And include the graph of load against the sagging of the beam.
We took photos, so that's easy.
Fraser also took a short video of the collapse on his phone. Can we include a link to it?
A link is fine, but don't rely on it. Choose a few still images from the video and put them in the report.

The conclusion is where most students go wrong. Don't just repeat the results. Compare what actually happened with what you predicted from the calculations, and explain any difference. That's the point of the whole exercise.
So we say we predicted twenty kilograms and got twelve, and that the difference was due to the poorly cut joints.
Exactly. And if you aren't sure of the cause, say so honestly. Engineers learn more from failures than successes.
My father says the same thing. He works on bridges.
Then he'll be pleased that you've chosen this field.
Thank you. That's helpful.
Come and see me when you've tested the second one. I'd like to see how it goes.
When is the second test?
The lab is booked on the twentieth. Make sure you arrive early, because the equipment takes time to set up.
We'll be there at nine.

Good morning, everyone. Every spring and every autumn, billions of birds set off on journeys that cross whole continents and oceans. Today's lecture is about bird migration: why birds do it, how they find their way, and what dangers they face. I'll try to keep the story simple, because the science is still full of surprises.

Let me start with the question of why. People often assume that birds fly south in winter because it is cold. But most birds can cope with cold. What they cannot cope with is hunger. In northern countries, the insects disappear in winter, and for birds that feed on flies, beetles and caterpillars, there is simply nothing to eat. They have to leave, or die. The same birds return in the spring, because the long days of summer in the north bring an enormous supply of food, and that is a good place to raise chicks.

The next question is how they find their way. This is a puzzle that scientists have been working on for decades. We now know that birds use several different methods at once. They navigate by the position of the Sun during the day, and by the pattern of the stars at night. But they also seem to sense the Earth's magnetic field, rather like a built-in compass. Experiments show that if you place a small magnet near a bird in a cage, it will confuse its sense of direction.

Some migrations are astonishing. The champion is the Arctic tern, a small sea bird that weighs less than a hundred grams. It breeds in the far north, and spends the northern winter near Antarctica, which is about 70,000 kilometres of flying every year, if you include all the detours it makes. Over its lifetime, which can be thirty years, it travels the equivalent of three round trips to the Moon.

Another record belongs to the bar-tailed godwit, a wading bird. In one famous journey, a godwit flew from Alaska to New Zealand without stopping once. It took 8 days, and it covered more than eleven thousand kilometres. During all that time, it couldn't eat, drink or rest, and it lost almost half of its body weight.

Closer to home, let me say something about the swallow. This is the bird most British people associate with the beginning of summer. Swallows usually arrive in April, and you'll often see them gathering on telephone wires in the autumn, before they leave. They spend the winter in South Africa, thousands of kilometres from their nests, and many of them return to the very same barn every year.

How do they prepare? Before departure, birds eat much more than usual and store fat. Some species almost double their weight in just a few weeks. Fat is the most efficient fuel, because it contains more energy for its weight than anything else. A bird that doesn't gain weight in time simply won't survive the journey.

How do we know all this? In the past, scientists relied on rings fixed to the legs of birds, and they could learn only where a bird started and where somebody found it. Today the technology is far better. We can attach tiny devices called geolocators, which weigh less than a gram. They record the light levels during the day, and from this we can work out the bird's position. When the bird returns to its nest, we recover the device and download the entire journey.

This technology has also shown us where birds are in danger. One serious problem is light. In big cities, bright lights at night confuse birds that navigate by the stars, and they circle the buildings until they are exhausted. Some cities have started to turn off the lights of tall buildings during the main migration weeks, and the results have been encouraging. Another approach is to design windows that birds can see, with a pattern on the glass.

Probably the greatest long-term threat is the loss of places to rest. Migrating birds need regular stopovers where they can feed, and many of these are wetlands. Over the last century, more than half of the wetlands in many parts of the world have been drained for farming or building. Without those stopovers, a bird that has flown for a thousand kilometres may have nowhere to land.

The picture isn't entirely gloomy. International agreements now protect some of the key sites, and volunteers help to count birds every year. Your own gardens and local parks can also help, so long as you provide water and leave some wild patches.

To sum up, migration is a mixture of instinct, navigation and endurance, and we are only beginning to understand it. For next week, please read the article on the reading list, and think about how climate change might affect the timing of the journeys.

0412 555 038. Got it. Now, the wheel throwing course runs on Tuesday evenings, from six until eight.

Great. And where exactly is the studio? I only know it's somewhere near the harbour.
We're at 62 Whaler Street, in the old fishing district.
Sorry, was that 26 Whaler Street?
No, it's 62. Six, two. It's the green building with the big sliding door, just opposite the bakery.
Got it. And what's the postcode, so I can put it in my phone?
It's 6160, the same as the rest of central Fremantle.
Perfect. Is there anything I need to bring on the first night?
Just an apron, because you'll get covered in clay, and it helps if you keep your fingernails short. We provide all the tools and the wheels, so there's no need to buy anything yourself.
Okay, I'll dig out an old apron. What about parking?

There are a few bays outside the studio, but they're limited to two hours, and your class is longer than that. Most of our students use the Dock Street car park. It's free after five o'clock, and it's only a two-minute walk.
That sounds easy enough. Do you ever hold an exhibition of the students' work?
We do. At the end of every term we put on a small show in the front room, and family and friends are welcome. Some of our students even sell a few pieces.
Ha, I don't think mine will be ready for that. But I'm looking forward to it.
You'll be surprised how quickly you improve. Is there anything else you'd like to ask?
No, I think that's everything. Thank you very much for your help, Marcia.
You're welcome, Tom. I'll send that email now, and we'll see you in July.

Good morning, everyone, and welcome to the Fernbrook Farm open day here in the Huon Valley. My name's Gwen, and I look after our visitors, so if you have any questions today, just look for the people wearing the green caps. Before you head off to explore, I'd like to go through a few practical things.

First, parking. Some of you have already left your cars in the river paddock, which is where we used to send people. However, we've had a lot of rain this week and the ground down there is very soft, so for the rest of the morning please use the top paddock, next to the main gate. It's a little further to walk, but there's a free trailer ride every ten minutes, pulled by one of our tractors, which the children usually enjoy more than the farm itself.

Now, entry. Adult tickets are 12 dollars, and children between five and fifteen pay 6 dollars. Children under five are free. A few people have asked about discounts for library members or for people on our mailing list, but I'm afraid those only apply to our winter events, not today. Your ticket is a wristband, so keep it on, because you can leave and come back as often as you like.

A word about dogs. I know many of you would love to bring yours along, but because we have lambs and calves around, we can't allow dogs on the farm at all, even on a lead. We've built a small fenced pen next to the car park, with water and shade, so you can leave your dog there, but please check on it every so often.

Next, the cheese. Many of you have come specifically for our cheese-making demonstration, and I'm happy to say that you don't need to book in advance, which is what people often ask. But please note that it only runs once, at eleven o'clock, and the cheese room holds just thirty people, so I'd suggest arriving early. Children are very welcome, by the way, although they have to stay with an adult.

Another thing people ask about is the shearing demonstration, which you'll see on the programme is at two o'clock. Some of you have wondered why it isn't in the morning, when it's cooler. People often assume it's because the shearer is busy elsewhere, but no, he's here all day. The real reason is that the sheep need to be completely dry. The paddock was soaked by rain overnight, and shearing wet wool is difficult for the shearer and bad for the sheep. So we wait until the afternoon.

Now let me tell you what's on offer at each stop, so you can plan your day. Just inside the gate, on your left, is the dairy shed. Milking takes place at half past one, and you can watch our cows being milked by machine. Children can also see how the milk travels into the cooling tank. I should warn you that you can't taste the milk there, because it's raw, but there's fresh milk for sale in the shop.

Further along the lane you'll find the orchard. The apples are in season right now, and we have three varieties ready. Pick up a basket at the entrance, choose your own fruit straight from the trees, and we'll weigh it on the way out. Please try not to climb the trees, because the branches are fragile. Bear in mind that the plant stall, where you can buy seedlings and herbs, is up by the car park, not in the orchard.

The third stop is the cheese room itself. It's open all day, not only during the demonstration, and you can taste the cheeses, yoghurt and honey that are produced right here on the farm. People tend to buy a lot, so do leave room in the car.

After that, follow the track up the hill to the sheep paddock. Our ewes had their lambs about three weeks ago, so if you walk in quietly, you'll be able to see the newborn lambs close up. I'm afraid we can't let you feed them, because they're still too young. We're not running guided walks this year, by the way, so you're free to wander at your own pace, but please keep to the marked tracks.

And finally, there's the old barn, which was built in the eighteen nineties. The local historical society has put together a display of photographs showing the farm over more than a century, along with the tools that the early settlers used. You may recognise some of the faces, because several families in the valley still have relatives in the pictures.

The café is next to the barn, and it's serving lunch from half past twelve. If you would like to have lunch at the long tables outside, please remember to put your rubbish in the bins, because the wind can carry it into the paddocks. That's everything from me. Enjoy your day, and thank you for supporting a family farm.
Come in, you two. Right, let's go through your project proposal. Remind me, it's about Māori words in New Zealand English?
That's right. We want to find out how often people our age use words like kai, whānau and mahi in everyday conversation, and whether the habits differ between regions.
It's a good topic. How did you come up with it, Aroha? Was it the sociolinguistics lecture last term?

Well, that gave me the vocabulary to describe it, but no, the real start was my job. I work in a café on weekends, and customers drop those words into their orders all the time without thinking about it. I started noticing it and I couldn't stop.
And I just thought it would be easier than my other idea, which was accents in sport commentary.
Honesty is always welcome, Ben. Now, the questionnaire. I've read the draft. It has thirty questions, which is far too many for people to answer in a few minutes.
We thought that more data would be better.
More data is only better if people actually finish. I'd cut it down to about twenty. Also, you haven't asked where participants grew up, and for a regional comparison that's essential.
You're right, we forgot that completely. We can add it at the top.
What if we asked people to answer out loud instead of writing? I think they'd be more natural.
It's an interesting idea, but you'd have to transcribe every answer, and that would take weeks. Stick with written responses.
What about offering a small prize? Like a gift voucher for one lucky participant?
Possibly, but you'd need extra approval for that, and you don't have a budget. I'd leave it out.
Okay, so shorter, plus the question about where people grew up.
Exactly. Now, the second part of your plan is recording real conversations.
Yes, and I'm a bit worried about that part. People tend to go stiff and formal as soon as they know a recorder is switched on, so we won't hear how they really talk.
But we could do it in a café, where everybody's relaxed.

That's the observer's paradox, and every researcher faces it. Recording in a relaxed place helps, and so does starting with a few minutes of small talk that you don't use. I wouldn't worry too much about the transcription either, since you'll only be transcribing short extracts.
And the permission forms?
They're a bit tedious, but they're quick once you have the template.
Speaking of the café, my manager has said we can record there on Sunday mornings, as long as we put a notice on the door.
That's very helpful, and it's worth mentioning in your methods section. Make sure that the notice also explains what the recording is for, and who will hear it.
Should we also give people a chance to say no afterwards, once they've heard themselves?
Yes, you should. Participants need to be able to withdraw their conversations for a couple of weeks afterwards. Put that on the permission form, in plain language.
We'll add a line about it, and a contact email, in case anyone changes their mind.
Good. Also think about how many recordings you need. Ten short conversations is a sensible target, rather than aiming for something huge.
Ten is much more realistic than the twenty we first wrote down.
Now, about the literature review. Should we focus on research from the last twenty years? Most of the interesting studies are recent.
I'd be careful about that, because you'd miss the foundation. Begin with a short history of the contact between Māori and English, no more than a page, and then move to the recent work.
Could we compare with Canada? There's research on how Canadian English borrowed words from Indigenous languages.
It's tempting, but it would take you away from your question. Keep to New Zealand.
Fine. Could we go through the timeline now? I've drawn up a plan.

Please. Let's start with the ethics application. You'll fill in the form, of course, but it can't be submitted until the head of department has signed it, and she's often away, so don't leave it until the last minute.
Understood. Then we planned a pilot survey about three weeks after that.
Good. I'd suggest you test it on the other group working on the phonetics project, so you get honest feedback quickly. Don't just try it on your friends.
Okay. We've allowed two weeks for collecting data.
I think that's optimistic. Recruiting people always takes longer than students expect, so I'd allow at least a month.
That will make things tight, but we'll manage. For the analysis, we were going to use the statistics software in the computer lab.
You don't need to. You can reach it through the university website from home, so you can work whenever you like.
That's a relief. Finally, there's the presentation, and we thought we might just improvise.
Please don't. Practise it at least twice in front of your classmates, because you'll find the awkward moments that way. A handout is optional, but a good one always helps.
Right. Thanks, Doctor Hughes. This was really useful.
You're welcome. Send me the revised questionnaire by Friday, and I'll take another look.

Good afternoon, everyone. Today I want to talk about kelp forests, which are among the most productive ecosystems on the planet, even though most people never see them. I'll start with the basic biology, then look at what lives in them, and finally at why they are disappearing and what we might do about it.

First, a common misunderstanding. Kelp is not a plant. It's a type of brown algae, and it belongs to a group that is only distantly related to the plants on land. Kelp has no true roots, stems or flowers, and it takes in nutrients directly from the surrounding water through its surface. That is why it is found mostly in cool, nutrient-rich water. In general, kelp grows best where the water temperature stays below 20 degrees Celsius. Above that, it becomes stressed and its growth slows.

Within those limits, kelp can grow astonishingly fast. Giant kelp, which is the species we see around southern Australia and the Pacific coast of Canada, can grow up to 60 centimetres in a single day. A strand can reach thirty or even forty metres in length within one growing season, which makes it one of the fastest growing organisms on Earth.

Let me describe the structure, because it explains a lot. At the bottom, kelp is anchored to rocks by a root-like structure called a holdfast. Many people assume this absorbs nutrients like a root does, but it only holds the kelp in place, and a great many small animals actually live inside it. Above the holdfast is a long stalk, and along the stalk are the blades. Each blade has a small gas-filled bladder at its base, and these bladders keep the fronds floating upwards, so that the blades stay near the surface where the sunlight is strongest. That arrangement allows the kelp to photosynthesise efficiently even when the water below is dark.

Now, what lives there? A kelp forest is a three-dimensional habitat, a bit like a rainforest under the sea. The canopy shelters fish from predators and from strong waves, and the water beneath it is calmer than the open ocean. Young fish use the forest as a nursery, and so do juvenile rock lobster, which are an important commercial species in both Tasmania and New Zealand. Larger animals, such as seals and many seabirds, hunt in and around the forest, and the whole system supports a huge fishing industry.

But kelp forests are fragile, and one of the key reasons is a small animal, the sea urchin. Urchins feed on kelp, and normally the amounts they eat are not a problem. However, when urchin numbers explode, they can strip the seabed of almost all its kelp. What is left is called an urchin barren, a rocky area covered in urchins and almost nothing else. Once a barren forms, it can stay that way for decades, because the urchins can survive on very little food and they stop young kelp from re-establishing.

What controls urchin numbers? In many places, it's predators. On the Pacific coast of North America, for example, sea otters eat urchins, and where otters were hunted almost to extinction, the kelp forests collapsed. When otters were reintroduced to parts of British Columbia, the kelp slowly returned. In Australia, rock lobster and large fish play a similar role, which is why overfishing can indirectly damage kelp.

The other big threat is warming water. Along the east coast of Tasmania, the East Australian Current has been pushing warm water further south for several decades. The giant kelp forests there were once huge, and the loss has been dramatic. Surveys show that about 95 percent of the giant kelp has disappeared since the nineteen sixties. Warm water has two effects. It stresses the kelp directly, and it also allows urchins from further north to spread south, so the problems feed each other.

So, what can be done? There are several approaches, and I'll mention three. First, divers have been removing urchins by hand from small areas, which allows kelp to recover quickly. That works, but it's slow, and it costs a great deal. Second, scientists are collecting kelp that has survived in warmer water, and breeding it in the laboratory, hoping to produce strains that tolerate heat. And third, researchers are testing ways of restoring forests by growing young kelp in tanks and then attaching it to ropes, which are laid out on the seabed. The ropes protect the young plants from grazing until they are large enough to survive, and early trials in Tasmania look promising.

Let me finish with a point about the value of these forests. Apart from their role in the food chain, kelp absorbs carbon dioxide, and it also softens waves, which protects shorelines during storms. Some companies are even harvesting kelp for food and fertiliser, though there is a debate about whether harvesting wild kelp is sustainable. For next week, please read the two articles on the course page, and think about whether restoring a kelp forest is realistic or whether we should instead put our effort into reducing the causes of warming. We'll discuss it then.

Good evening, everyone, and welcome to Canal Frost Weekend. My name's Nadia, and I'm one of the organisers. We're delighted that so many of you have braved the cold, and I'd like to take a few minutes to tell you what's on, and to give you some practical information, so you can make the most of the next two days.

The festival is spread along about two kilometres of the canal, and it's divided into five areas. Let me start at the western end, where you'll find the skating loop. The ice is smooth and well maintained, and every hour, on the hour, our instructors run a lesson for beginners. It's free, and you don't need to book. If you've never been on skates before, this is the place to start, and you'll be amazed how quickly you pick it up. Skates can be hired from the hut by the entrance, although I should say that the queue is usually long on Saturday afternoons.

Next to the skating loop is the market tent. Here you can buy food from local producers, such as maple syrup, smoked fish and pastries, as well as crafts made by artists from the region. Many of the stalls accept cards, but a few only take cash, so it's worth carrying some.

Moving east, we come to the sculpture park, which is for many people the highlight of the festival. Teams of carvers from across Canada have spent the past week turning huge blocks of ice into sculptures, and over the weekend you can watch some of them finishing their work. They'll be giving carving demonstrations every afternoon, and you can ask them questions. Please don't touch the sculptures, though. Fingers and gloves damage the surface.

At the centre of the festival is the main stage, where there's live music from local bands all weekend. The line-up on the printed programme has changed slightly, so do check the screen beside the stage, because a couple of the Sunday acts have swapped times.

And finally, along the eastern bank you'll find the warming huts. These are small wooden shelters, each designed by a different architecture student, and inside you can warm up beside a heater and have a free hot drink, thanks to our sponsors. They're very popular with families, so be prepared to wait a few minutes at busy times.

Now, some practical points. How do you get here? I'd strongly advise leaving your car at home. The streets beside the canal are closed to traffic for the whole weekend, and the nearest car parks fill up by ten o'clock. The best way to arrive is on one of our free shuttle buses, which leave from the central station every fifteen minutes. Some people prefer to walk from the city centre, but it's about forty minutes, and it can be very cold, so most visitors choose the bus.

As for tickets, I'm happy to say that entry to the festival is completely free. However, some of the activities have a small charge, such as skate hire and the guided night tour, and the food and drink in the market tent are of course not free either.

Next, what should you wear? Everyone knows that you need warm clothes, and I hope you're all wearing several layers. But my most important advice is about footwear. The paths between the areas are covered in packed snow and ice, and they get very slippery by the end of the day. Please wear proper boots with a good grip, rather than trainers or smart shoes. We've seen a few sprained ankles in previous years, and we'd like to avoid that this time.

Tomorrow evening, there's the fireworks display, which has always been the most popular event of the weekend. It was originally planned for eight o'clock, but we've moved it to nine o'clock, so that it doesn't clash with the children's lantern parade, which will finish at about half past eight. The best place to watch is on the bridge, but it gets crowded, so the banks on either side are also excellent.

Finally, something new this year. We've developed a festival app, which you can download for free before you arrive. It has a map of the site, but the main feature is that it shows the waiting times for the most popular activities, so you can see at a glance whether it's worth joining the queue for the skating lessons or whether you'd be better off visiting the market first. If you have any trouble with it, there's a help desk next to the main stage.
That's all from me. If you have any questions, ask any of our volunteers in the orange jackets. Please enjoy the festival, stay warm, and thank you for coming.

Hello, Leila, hello, Ravi. Come in and sit down. I've read your outline for the history project, so let's talk through it. You're focusing on Chinese miners on the Victorian goldfields, is that right?
That's right. We wanted to look at their daily lives in the eighteen fifties and sixties, rather than just the big events.
It's a good topic. What made you choose it?

Well, honestly, we first thought about the Eureka uprising, because it's the famous one. But Leila found that the local museum has a collection of objects from the Chinese camps, and almost nobody has written about it.
Yes, I went to look at it last month. The curator told me that hardly any students ever ask about it. So we thought we could actually add something new.
That's the best reason to choose a topic. Now, what about your sources? Where will the information come from?
Mostly from the state archive, which holds the court records and the newspapers. The problem is that the archive has quite limited opening hours, and it's an hour's drive from here.
And the other difficulty is that a lot of the documents are in Chinese. We can't read them, and we don't have a translator.

You're right to worry about that. I'd suggest you contact the Asian languages department. Some of their postgraduates are looking for projects like this one, and they might be happy to help with a few key documents. As for the opening hours, I wouldn't worry, because you can book a reading room and the staff will bring the files to you.
Oh, that's useful. I thought we had to turn up and wait.
Not at all. Now, for the section on daily life, which sources will you use?
We were planning to use the newspaper advertisements, because they show what miners were buying and selling. And possibly letters, because some of the families kept them.
But the letters are in private collections, aren't they? We'd have to contact the families, and that could take months.

Exactly. I'd skip the letters. The court records are a much better source, because they list the names, the jobs and the addresses of the people involved. And the photographs held at the museum are excellent, so I'd definitely include those. The newspaper advertisements are interesting, but you'll find they mostly describe the European customers, so they won't help much with the Chinese miners.
All right. Court records and photographs, then.
One more worry. Some of the court records mention people only by English nicknames, and the spelling changes from one document to the next.
That's a classic problem. Keep a spreadsheet with every spelling you find, and note the date and the page. Over time patterns emerge, and you can often match one person across several documents.
We could divide the work. I'll take the court records from the eighteen fifties, and Leila can take the following decade.
A sensible plan, although I'd suggest you both read a few records from each decade first, so that your methods are consistent. Otherwise, your two halves may read like two different essays.
Good point. We'll meet every Thursday to compare notes.
Excellent. That kind of routine saves a lot of trouble near the deadline.
Good. Now, how are you going to present the work in class?
I'd like to do a short film, with photographs and a voiceover. It would look much more interesting than slides.
I'm not so sure. A film takes ages to make, and we have to submit the essay as well. I'd prefer a poster, and then we could each talk for five minutes.
I think the poster is the more realistic choice, but Ravi, you can still use a few of your best images on it. Make sure it isn't crowded with text.
Fair enough. A poster it is.

One more thing, about the essay itself. The limit is three thousand words, and students nearly always try to cover too much. Choose three or four strong examples and treat them in depth, rather than trying to mention everything.
That makes sense. Could you suggest some books to start with? We found a lot, but we aren't sure which are reliable.

Certainly. Let's go through your list. The first one, the general history of the goldfields, is well written, but it's very broad, and it only has a few pages about the Chinese miners. It's fine for background, but you won't find much detail.
And the second one, the book by the local historian?

That one is the opposite. It's rather old, from the nineteen sixties, and some of its conclusions have been challenged, so I'd use it carefully. But the third one is very good, because it includes tables of statistics from the census, showing how many miners came from each region. You'll definitely want that.
Great, we'll start with the third one, then.
Excellent. Send me a draft of the first section in two weeks, and I'll give you feedback. And please let me know if the archive staff cause you any trouble.
Thank you, Professor Wallace.

Good morning, everyone. Today's lecture is about urban heat islands, a phenomenon that affects almost every large city, and which will matter more and more as the climate warms. A heat island is simply an urban area that is noticeably warmer than the rural land around it. The difference is largest at night. On a calm, clear night, the centre of a big city can be up to 7 degrees Celsius warmer than the countryside nearby. During the day the gap is smaller, usually two or three degrees, but it still has a real effect on how people feel and how much energy they use.

So why does this happen? There are several causes, and it's important to understand each of them, because the solutions depend on them. The first is the materials we build with. Roads, car parks and roofs are mostly made of dark materials such as asphalt and concrete. These absorb a lot of the sun's energy during the day, and then release it slowly after sunset, which is why the nights stay warm. A grass field, by contrast, reflects more light and stores much less heat.

The second cause is the loss of vegetation. Plants cool the air in two ways. They provide shade, and they release water vapour through their leaves, which is rather like sweating. When a city replaces a park with a paved car park, it loses both. Studies in Sydney and Vancouver have found that suburbs with plenty of trees can be several degrees cooler than similar suburbs without them.

The third cause is waste heat. Every air conditioner moves heat from inside a building to the outside, and the engines of vehicles produce a lot of heat as well. In a busy city centre in summer, this adds up to a significant amount, and it creates a vicious circle: the hotter it gets, the more people use air conditioning, which makes the streets hotter still.

The fourth cause is the shape of the city itself. Tall buildings built close together form what we call street canyons. In a canyon, heat that is released from the walls and the road gets trapped between the buildings, and there's very little wind to carry it away. At night, the buildings also block the view of the sky, so the heat can't radiate away into space as easily.

Now, why does it matter? It isn't only about comfort. Heat waves are one of the leading causes of weather-related deaths in Australia, and elderly people and young children are most at risk. Hot nights are especially dangerous, because the body doesn't get a chance to recover. There are also economic effects, because electricity demand rises sharply in hot weather, and power networks can fail.

Let's turn to solutions. The simplest is to change the colour of surfaces. A cool roof is one that reflects most of the sunlight instead of absorbing it, and the cheapest way to make one is to paint a normal roof white. In trials, white roofs have lowered indoor temperatures by several degrees, and the cost is very small compared with air conditioning.

A second solution is the green roof, which is a roof covered with soil and plants. On a hot day, the surface of a green roof can be up to 30 degrees cooler than a conventional dark roof. Green roofs also absorb rainwater, which reduces flooding, and they provide a habitat for insects and birds. They're heavier and more expensive to build, however, so many cities use rules and incentives to encourage them. In Toronto, for example, a by-law requires a green roof on every new building with a floor area of more than 2000 square metres. It was the first rule of its kind in North America.

A third solution is simply to plant more trees. Melbourne has an urban forest strategy, which aims to increase the tree canopy to 40 percent of the city by 2040. That's an ambitious target, because many of the city's older trees are dying in the drought, and planting trees in the middle of a busy street is surprisingly difficult. The roots need space, water and protection from traffic.

Finally, a word about how researchers measure all this. In the past, scientists relied on thermometers at a small number of weather stations, which gave a very limited picture. Today, they use thermal images taken by satellites and aircraft, which show the temperature of every street and every roof. Planners can use these maps to identify the hottest neighbourhoods, which are very often the poorest, and to decide where new trees and cool roofs will have the greatest effect.

For next week, please read the two case studies on the course page, and consider this question. If a city has a limited budget, should it invest in trees, in cool roofs, or in helping people buy air conditioners? There's no single right answer, and I'd like you to be ready to defend your choice.

So that's Saturday 19 September. Now, what time would you like the party to start?
We'd like people to arrive at seven, I think. Actually, my wife prefers a bit later, so let's say half past seven. 7:30.
That's fine. You can have access to the hall from six o'clock, so you'll have an hour and a half to decorate and set out the food. On Saturdays the hall must be empty by midnight.
That should be plenty. We'll start clearing up at about eleven.
How many guests are you expecting?
Around sixty, I'd say. Although, hold on. My wife has a very big family. Once I count all the cousins and the neighbours, it's probably closer to 85.
That's no problem. The hall seats up to 90 at tables, or 120 if everyone is standing, so you have plenty of room.
Great. And what will it cost?
For a Saturday evening, the hire fee is 380 dollars. However, we offer a twenty percent discount to members of local clubs and associations. Do you belong to anything in the area?
I'm a member of the Fairview Bowling Club.
Then you qualify. If you bring your membership card when you collect the keys, the fee comes down to 304 dollars.
That's a nice surprise. Is there a deposit?
There's a refundable bond. It's normally 200 dollars, but if you plan to serve alcohol, it goes up to 300.
We'll have wine and beer, so 300, then.
Yes, that's right. It's returned within a week, as long as the hall is left clean and nothing is damaged. Do you need the kitchen?
Just the fridge and the oven, because the food is being delivered by a caterer.
That's included. Now, is there going to be any entertainment? I ask because of the noise rules.
I was thinking of a DJ, but my wife's brother plays in a band, and he's offered to perform. So I think it'll be a live band.
That's lovely, but the music has to finish by eleven o'clock, and you'll need to keep the doors closed once the band starts, because there are houses nearby. Will that be all right?
I'll make sure he knows. Where exactly is the hall? I haven't been since the community fair years ago.
We're at 23 Wattle Avenue.
Was that 32?
No, it's 23. Two, three. It's the brick building next to the library.
Okay. And the postcode, for the invitations?
Perfect. And when do I pick up the key?

Keys are not collected from here, because our office is only open on weekdays. You collect them from the library, between four and five on the Friday afternoon, and you return them there on Monday morning.
The council office, did you say?
No, the library, which is right next door. The staff will ask to see your membership card, so please don't forget it.
Understood. What about parking? I'm worried about eighty-five people trying to park.
There's room for about twenty cars behind the hall, and the school across the road lets people use their car park on weekends, so most guests manage fine.
Wonderful. Thank you, Gillian, you've been very helpful.
My pleasure. I'll send you an email with a booking form to sign, and we'll see you on the nineteenth.

Good morning, everyone, and welcome to Mount Larch Provincial Park. My name's Ranger Singh, and I'll be taking you through the main points you need to know before you head into the backcountry. It will take about ten minutes, and I'd ask you to listen carefully, because some of the information has changed since last summer.

Let's begin with permits. Many of you reserved your campsites online, and you've brought a printed copy of your confirmation. That's useful, but it isn't enough. Before you set off, every group must come to this visitor centre to collect a backcountry permit, which has to be attached to your pack. Rangers do check on the trails, and we do turn people back. You don't need to register again at the campgrounds themselves.

Next, wildlife. This park has both black bears and grizzly bears, and in the past few weeks we've seen more activity than usual around the campgrounds, because the berries are late this year. Please keep all your food, toothpaste, and anything with a smell, in the metal lockers provided at each campground. A few years ago, we advised people to hang their food from a tree, but bears learned how to get it down, so we no longer recommend that. And please, never keep food in your tent, even a chocolate bar.

A related matter is fire. As the summer has been unusually dry, there is a fire restriction in force across the park. You may not light a fire anywhere except in the metal fire pits at the Larch Lake campground. We've provided firewood there, so you don't need to gather any from the forest. Gas stoves are permitted everywhere, but please take care with them, and keep a bucket of water nearby.

Now, water. Most of the creeks look beautifully clean, but they can contain parasites, so all water has to be treated. Some people use tablets, and others carry filters. Both work, but the filters can fail if they have frozen overnight, and tablets take a long time to work in cold water. So the most reliable method is to boil your water for at least a minute. It takes a little more fuel, but you can be sure it's safe.

Let me finish with the trails themselves, because several of them have special conditions this season. The Larch Lake loop is the easiest, and it's the only trail with a smooth, wide surface, so it's suitable for wheelchairs and pushchairs. It takes about an hour, and there are benches along the lake.

Eagle Ridge is a very different story. It is a spectacular hike with views over three valleys, but there is one steep section, about halfway up, where you'll need to pull yourself up using fixed ropes. They're in good condition, but if you have a fear of heights, or you're carrying a heavy pack, you might prefer another route.

Cedar Falls was a favourite with many of you, I know, but I'm afraid the trail is closed for repairs. A bridge was damaged in the spring floods, and the crews are working on it now. We hope to reopen it by the end of the month, but please check the notice board before you plan anything. I should add that the longest route in the park is the Highland Traverse, which takes four days, and I'm not covering it today, because it needs a separate permit.

The Marten Creek trail is lovely, but you must be aware that there is no bridge over the river about two kilometres from the start. You'll have to wade across, and in the spring melt the water can be knee-deep and very cold. Take a pair of sandals, and always undo the waist strap on your pack before you cross, in case you fall.

Then there's the Old Quarry track, which is short, but it's the best place in the park for watching wildlife. If you're there at dawn, you have a good chance of seeing deer, and sometimes even a moose, drinking at the pond. Please keep your distance and stay quiet, because the animals are easily frightened.

One last thing about Silver Creek campground. It's a beautiful spot, right beside the water, but I must stress that the pump there is out of order, and so there is no drinking water at all. Bring everything you need from Larch Lake, or be prepared to treat creek water, as I mentioned.
If you have any questions, I'll be here for a few minutes. Otherwise, please collect your permits from the desk, and enjoy your trip.
Right, Hannah, Jamal. Let's talk about your experiment on sleep and memory. Hannah, could you remind me of the main idea?
Of course. We want to test whether a short nap after learning a list of words helps people remember more of them later, compared with people who stay awake.
It's based on a study from Canada, which found that even a twenty-minute nap improved recall. But we're not sure it was a fair test.
Which study was that? I know a few from Toronto.
A paper from Toronto, yes, published about ten years ago. They tested forty volunteers, and the nap group scored about a fifth higher.
Our lecturer in first year called it a classic, but said it had never been properly repeated.
That is exactly why a small replication like yours is worth doing. Even a modest result tells us something, as long as the design is sound.
A healthy attitude. Let's go through the design, then. Who are your participants?
First-year psychology students. They get course credit for taking part, so recruitment is easy.

That's convenient, but it's a weakness. Students are young, they sleep irregular hours, and they're not typical of the wider population, so your results may not apply to older adults, for example. You'll need to say so in your discussion.
I did wonder about that, but we don't have time to recruit anyone else.
Fine. Just be honest about it. What's the memory test?
A list of fifteen common words, which participants study for two minutes and then try to recall.

I'm worried that it's too easy. In my experience, people remember most of fifteen common words whether or not they've slept, and then you'll have no difference to measure. I'd use at least thirty words, or choose less familiar ones.
I thought a short list would be less stressful, but I see your point.
Alternatively, we could make the words more abstract.
Possibly, but start with a longer list. Now, how will you measure the sleep itself?
We've borrowed some wristbands from the sports science department. They record movement, and the software estimates whether someone is asleep.
That's the right idea, but remember what they actually measure. They detect movement, not brain activity, so they can't distinguish light sleep from simply lying still. That might blur your results.
Could we borrow the electrode equipment from the lab instead? It reads the brain directly.

I wouldn't. It's booked for months, and the setup takes an hour for each participant. I'd keep the wristbands, but I'd also ask your participants to write down how long they think they slept. That doesn't replace the data, but it gives you a second source.
A sleep diary, you mean? That's easy enough. We'll do that.
Next, the timing. Some people will be tested at nine in the morning, and some at two in the afternoon, I see.
That's just because of the timetable.
But the morning group will probably have had coffee, and caffeine can affect both sleep and memory. Either test everyone at the same time, or ask people to avoid caffeine on the day.
We'll ask them to avoid it. Everyone is free at two, so we could also move the morning group.
I'd rather keep both times and just ask them. It's more flexible.
Well, whichever you choose, put it in your method section. And the last point is the control group. You've planned for eight people in each group.
Yes, because it's a small project.
That's very small, and a single unusual person could change the result. Aim for at least fifteen per group, even if you have to spread the testing over several days.
That's a big increase. Well, we'll try.
If we run sessions on two afternoons a week for three weeks, we could just manage it.
And we should book the testing room now, before other groups take every slot.
Sensible. The booking system opens on Monday, so be quick, and remember that the room has to be left exactly as you found it.
Good. So where does that leave the design? What are you going to change?
I think we should double the length of the word list. We'll do that first.
Agreed. And as for the wristbands, we'll keep them, but add the diary, so we're not relying on a single source.
What about the controls? Shall I contact more students about the extra participants?
Let's wait until the ethics committee approves the plan. We shouldn't contact anyone until then.

Quite right. Now the ethics application. It's short, but there are two things the committee will look at carefully. The first is how you'll store the data, which should be on the university server and not on your own laptops. The second is how you will recruit participants. They'll want to see the exact wording of your invitation. You don't need to list the names of participants, since the data will be anonymous, and the test materials can be sent later.
That's clear. We'll write it this week.
Excellent. Send me a draft by Friday, and I'll look it over before you submit it.

Good afternoon, everyone. In the last lecture, we looked at how much electricity solar panels and wind turbines can produce. Today I want to look at the other half of the problem, which is what to do when the sun isn't shining and the wind isn't blowing. In other words, storage.

Let me start with why storage matters. An electricity grid has to match supply and demand at every moment. With coal or gas, we simply burn more or less fuel. But solar power peaks in the middle of the day, whereas demand peaks in the evening, when people come home, cook dinner and switch on lights, and the sun has already gone. That mismatch is the central challenge, and that's why the evening peak is the focus of most storage projects.

There are many ways to store energy, but two technologies dominate: pumped hydro and batteries. Let's take pumped hydro first. It's an old idea, and the principle is simple. You have two reservoirs, one high up and one low down. When electricity is cheap, you use it to pump water uphill. When electricity is expensive, you release the water, and it flows downhill through turbines and generates power. Round-trip efficiency is typically around 80 percent, which means that you get four-fifths of the energy back. That's excellent for something so simple.

Pumped hydro plants are also extremely durable. A well-built scheme can operate for 50 years or more, much longer than any battery. The largest projects can store enough energy to supply hundreds of thousands of homes for many hours. A major scheme in the Snowy Mountains of Australia is an example, though its cost has increased several times since it was first announced, and that's a warning about the risks involved.

The main drawback of pumped hydro is geography. You need the right landscape, with a large height difference between two reservoirs, and you need water. Many cities are nowhere near mountains. Building a scheme takes many years, and it can raise environmental concerns, as it involves flooding valleys or damaging habitats. So although it's the cheapest storage per unit of energy, it can't be built everywhere.

Now, batteries. Most grid batteries today use lithium-ion technology, the same as in your phone, but on a far larger scale. Their great advantage is speed. A battery can respond to a change on the grid in milliseconds, which is thousands of times faster than a gas power station. That makes them ideal for stabilising the grid, and not only for storing energy.

A famous example is a battery in South Australia, which was installed in just 100 days after a series of blackouts. Within a year it had saved consumers many millions of dollars in grid stabilisation costs. It's a striking demonstration of how quickly batteries can be built, compared with the many years for a hydro plant.

But batteries have limitations too. They don't last as long. A typical grid battery lasts about 15 years before its capacity falls significantly, and it has to be replaced. Their cost has fallen dramatically, by almost 90 percent over the past decade, but the materials, such as lithium and cobalt, are mined in places where the environmental and social conditions are often poor. And when batteries do reach the end of their life, we need to dispose of them safely. At present, the main challenge is recycling, because only a small percentage of lithium-ion batteries are recycled properly, and the technology to do it cheaply is still being developed.

Batteries also store energy for relatively short periods, usually between two and four hours. They're excellent for smoothing out the evening peak, but not for the long gaps, such as a week of cloudy, windless weather in winter. For that, we need something else.

This is where hydrogen comes in. The idea is to use surplus solar and wind power to split water into hydrogen and oxygen, store the hydrogen in tanks or underground caverns, and burn it or use it in fuel cells when it's needed. Hydrogen can be stored for months, and that makes it attractive for seasonal storage. However, the round-trip efficiency is poor, often below 40 percent, and the infrastructure doesn't yet exist. So for the long-term future it may be vital, but for the next decade, it's mainly a research topic.

To sum up, there's no single solution. Pumped hydro offers cheap, long-lasting storage but depends on geography. Batteries are fast and flexible but expensive and short-lived. Hydrogen could fill the gap over weeks and months but is not yet ready. Most experts now believe that a grid with a high share of renewable energy will need all three. For next week, I'd like you to read the two reports on the course page, and prepare a short comparison.
Good morning, Westside Aquatic Centre, Bridget speaking.
Hi there. I'd like to enrol my daughter in swimming lessons for next term, please. Are there still places?
Yes, there should be. Let me open the enrolment form. Could I start with your surname?
It's Donnelly.
Is that D-O-N-E-L-L-Y?
Almost. There are two Ns. It's D-O-N-N-E-L-L-Y.
Is this her first time at our centre?
Yes. We've only just moved to Brisbane from Wellington, and she learned a little at a school pool there, but she's been away from the water for about a year.
That's quite common, and children usually pick it up again very quickly.
Thank you. And how old is your daughter?
She's seven. Well, she'll be eight in February, but she's seven at the moment.
That's fine. We group the children by their age at the start of term, so I'll put 7. Can she swim at all?
A little. She's happy putting her face in the water, and she can swim a few metres with a kickboard, but she can't do freestyle without it.
Then she'd go in Level 2. Level 1 is for children who are just learning to float, and Level 3 is for children who can swim a full length by themselves. So Level 2 sounds just right.
Great. Which days are the classes?
Level 2 runs on Tuesdays and Thursdays. Tuesday afternoon is very popular and it's already full, I'm afraid. I have a few places on Thursday.
Thursday's fine. She finishes school at three, so we could easily get here by four.
There are two Thursday classes. One starts at four o'clock, but that's for Level 3. The Level 2 class is at 4:15, and it lasts forty minutes.
So 4:15. That's ideal.
Wonderful. Now, the fee. A term is ten weeks, and the cost is 216 dollars.
Right. Is there any discount?
There is. If you pay for the whole term before it starts, instead of paying week by week, we take 24 dollars off. So you'd pay 192 dollars.
That's a good saving. I'll pay it all upfront.
Lovely. The new term begins on Monday 26 January, but that's a public holiday for some of our classes. Yours is a Thursday, so the first lesson will be on 29 January.
Sorry, the twenty-ninth?
That's right, 29 January. Please arrive about ten minutes early so she can get changed.
Okay. Is there anything I need to tell you about her health?
Yes, we ask every family. Does she have any medical conditions we should know about?
She has mild asthma. She carries an inhaler, and I'll make sure she brings it every week.
Thank you, that's really helpful. I'll make a note so the instructor knows, and she can keep the inhaler beside the pool. Is she allergic to anything?
No, just the asthma.
Good. Now, I need your home address, for our records.
It's 47 Lomandra Street, in Toowong.
Sorry, was that 74?
No, 47. Four, seven.
Thanks. And the postcode?
Perfect. I'll email you the confirmation and a receipt as soon as the payment goes through. Do you have a few more minutes? I'd like to tell you about the changing rooms and parents' area.
Sure, I'd like to know.

Well, there's a family change room just inside the entrance, which has lockers that take a two-dollar coin. Parents can watch the lessons from the viewing area upstairs, which has a window onto the pool. There's also a small café there, and it serves coffee and snacks.
That sounds lovely. And what should she bring?
A swimsuit, a towel, goggles if she likes them, and a swimming cap if she has long hair. It's also a good idea to bring a drink bottle, because the pool is warm and the children get thirsty.
Also, if she misses a lesson because of illness, she can attend a make-up class in the same term, as long as you call us before four o'clock on the day.
That's very good to know.
Thank you. I think that's everything.
You're welcome, Mr Donnelly. We'll see you on the twenty-ninth.

Good morning, everyone, and welcome to the final briefing for the Harbour to Park Fun Run. My name's Keira, and I'm the race director. First of all, thank you for choosing to run for such a good cause. Every dollar you've raised goes to the children's hospital, and last year we raised over a hundred thousand dollars between us.

Let me go through the course, section by section, so you know what to expect on Sunday. The race is eight kilometres. We start at Waterfront Park, and you'll see the big inflatable arch from a long way off. On the ground there's a timing mat, and I'd ask you to run across it, because that's how your time is recorded. If you're walking with a pram, please start at the back.

From the park, the route follows Pohutukawa Drive, along the water's edge. This is the flattest section, and the best part for settling into a rhythm. There's a local band playing at the roadside, and last year, many runners said they sped up when they heard the drums.

At about the three kilometre mark, you turn up Bluff Road, and I should be honest with you. This is a steep hill, nearly half a kilometre long. Don't try to run up it as quickly as the flat. Slow down, take smaller steps, and keep your head up. Remember, it's the hardest part of the course, and once you're at the top, it's mostly downhill.

After the hill, you reach Sandy Bay, where the road runs along the beach. The water station is here, in the middle of the beach car park. Please take a cup, drink it, and put it in the bin. We don't want to leave rubbish on the beach. There'll be a second station near the finish.

At six kilometres you cross the old Mill Bridge. The bridge is only two metres wide, so it's very narrow, and it's difficult to overtake. If you're running faster than the people around you, please wait until you're over the bridge before you try to pass. Everyone's finish time is recorded by the timing mat, so a few seconds won't matter.

The last stretch takes you into Memorial Lawn, where the finish line is. The photographer will be standing near the line, and the photos will be on our website by Monday, free of charge, so remember to smile. Unfortunately, the ice-cream van that was there last year can't come this time, but there will be fruit and sports drinks for everyone.

Now, some practical information. First, where do you leave your things? If you've brought a bag, you can leave it at the bag drop beside the start. It's free, but please put your name on a label, and don't leave anything valuable in it, because we can't be responsible for phones or wallets. We'd suggest you keep your keys in a pocket.

Next, the fundraising. Many of you have been collecting money online, and thank you. If you're still collecting sponsors, you can continue until Friday after the race. Anyone who raises more than 200 dollars receives a free T-shirt, which you can collect at the finish.

And please don't forget to warm up. The race begins at nine o'clock sharp, and we'll lead a short warm-up at the start line at a quarter to nine, with music. It's a lot of fun, even for people who don't think of themselves as athletes.

A word about the medals. This year, for the first time, they're made from recycled materials. They were designed by students at the local art school, and every finisher receives one, whether you run, jog or walk. We'd like to thank the school for that.

The final point is about volunteers. We're still short of about twenty marshals for the course, especially at the bridge, and at Sandy Bay. If you have a friend or family member who isn't running and who'd like to help, please ask them to sign up at the table by the door. Volunteers get a free breakfast and a cap, and they're a very important part of the day.

Finally, the weather. At the moment the forecast looks good, but it can change quickly at this time of year, so please check the website on Saturday evening. If there's a thunderstorm, we may delay the start, but we'll let you know by text message. Thank you for listening, and good luck on Sunday.
Hello, Mei, hello, Oscar. Come in. I've read your draft report on the rainwater system for the community garden. Overall, it's a good start. Let's go through it.
Thanks, Doctor Barrett. We'd like to check that the design is realistic before we finish the report.
Remind me why you chose the garden at the primary school.

Mainly because Perth gets so little rain in summer, and the garden uses a huge amount of drinking water. We thought that if the roof of the hall could supply the garden, we'd save the school quite a lot.
And the teachers were really keen. They've even offered to let us test the system once it's built.
That's valuable. Now, let's start with the gutters. You've drawn the standard plastic ones.
Yes. We've chosen them because they're cheap and easy to fit.

That's fine, but make sure you mention maintenance. In Perth, the gum trees drop leaves and bark all year, and the gutters clog quickly. They'll need cleaning at least twice a year, so you should put that in your maintenance schedule.
Okay, we hadn't thought about the maintenance at all.
Should we also include a cleaning plan for the tank itself?
Yes, briefly. Every few years someone has to empty it and check the inside for sludge, and the school should know exactly who is responsible for that.
Next, the first-flush diverter. Why is it in your design?
It sends the first few litres of rain away, because that water washes the dust and bird droppings off the roof.

Exactly. And note that in Western Australia it's required by the building regulations for a system that supplies garden taps, so you can't take it out, even if you're short of money. Make that very clear in the report.
Right. Now, the tank. I was hoping to bury it, to save space.

I understand, but an underground tank is much more expensive, because of the excavation, and it's harder to inspect. For a school budget, an above-ground tank is the better choice, and it's easier to clean.
Fine. I'll change that.
And the pump?
We've specified a small electric pump. At first, we thought of running it from solar panels, to make the whole system independent.

It's a nice idea, but at this scale the panels would cost more than the pump, and the saving is tiny. Stay with the mains. And, by the way, the pump you've chosen is a good deal. I've looked at the prices, and it's cheaper than you estimated in your table.
Oh, good. Then we might have some money left for other things.
Lastly, the overflow pipe. When the tank is full, the extra water goes through the pipe, and you've shown it open at the end.
Yes, so it drains into the garden bed.
That's fine, but mosquitoes love tanks, so the end of that pipe must be covered with fine mesh. Otherwise they'll breed in the water, and the school will have a problem.
Understood. I'll add that to the diagram.
Now, let's talk about the report itself. I like the structure, but it's missing a few things. Tell me what you plan to change.
Well, the introduction is too long, isn't it? It's nearly two pages.
I wouldn't cut it. The background on Perth's climate is important. I think the problem is in the later sections. We need a diagram of the layout, because it's hard to follow without one.

I agree with Oscar. A clear diagram showing the roof, the gutters, the diverter and the tank would help a lot. And you also need a table of costs, so the reader can see the price of each part and the total at a glance.
All right. We'll add both. I think the introduction can stay as it is, and the conclusion is fine too.
It is, but do add a sentence about future work. Now, what will you do next?
We have to decide how to test it. I was going to suggest we measure the amount of water collected after each storm.
But there might be no storms before the deadline. I'd rather build a small model and test it with a hose.
That's a good compromise. If it rains, record the real results as well, but don't depend on it. And please book the workshop now, because it fills up quickly.
We'll book it today.
One more question. How many references do you expect in the final report?
At least ten, and preferably more from recent Australian sources. The council guidelines on rainwater use were updated last year, so check you have the latest version rather than the old one.
I found a government website with a calculator for roof catchment. Could we use that for our estimates?
Yes, but explain your assumptions, such as the roof area and the average rainfall per month. A number with no explanation is worth very little.
We'll set that out in an appendix.
Good. And think about the school's needs, too. A system that works on paper but that the teachers can't maintain is not much use, so keep the instructions short, with plenty of photographs.
Maybe a one-page guide for the caretaker.
A very good idea.
Excellent. Send me the revised report in two weeks.

Good morning, everyone. Today I'd like to talk about glaciers in the Southern Alps of New Zealand, and what is happening to them. New Zealand is a good place to study this, because its glaciers are unusual. They flow down from high mountains to quite low altitudes, so they respond quickly to changes in the climate.

Let me begin with the biggest one. The longest glacier in the country is the Tasman, which is about twenty-three kilometres long and runs down the eastern side of Aoraki Mount Cook. Visitors often take boat trips on the lake at its end. But that lake is itself a sign of change. Since the early nineteen nineties, the end of the Tasman Glacier has retreated by more than 5 kilometres, and the meltwater has collected in front of it, forming a lake that is growing every year.

Why does this matter for glaciers? Well, a lake at the front accelerates the process. The water is warmer than the air, and it melts the ice from below. In addition, pieces of ice break off, which scientists call calving, and float away. So once a lake forms, the glacier can lose ice much faster than before.

How do we know all this? Researchers use several methods. The most famous is the annual snowline survey. Each year, at the end of summer, a team flies along the Alps in a small plane and photographs the snowline on about fifty glaciers. The snowline is the boundary between the snow that lasts through summer and the bare ice below. If the snowline moves higher up the mountain, the glacier is losing mass. These photographs go back to nineteen seventy-seven, so they're a very valuable record.

To work out how thick the ice is, scientists use radar equipment. A radar unit is pulled over the surface, or carried by a helicopter, and it sends signals into the ice, which bounce off the rock beneath. The time they take to return tells us the depth. Some of the glaciers are more than five hundred metres thick, but the ice at the end is thinning rapidly.

Another tool is satellite imagery, which can show the whole length of a glacier at once, though it is less precise than a person with a measuring tape standing at the edge. Local guides also contribute, because many of them have photographed the same ice for twenty years, and their pictures show changes that no instrument recorded.

And what is causing the loss? The main factor is temperature. Since 1900, the average temperature in New Zealand has risen by about 1 degree Celsius. That sounds small, but for a glacier it's very significant. A warmer climate affects glaciers in two ways. More ice melts in summer, and in winter, more of the precipitation falls as rain rather than snow, especially at lower altitudes. That means there is less snowfall to replace the ice that has melted. If the snow doesn't build up, the glacier cannot feed itself.

A useful way to think about a glacier is as a bank account. Snowfall is the income, and melting is the spending. For several decades now, the account has been overdrawn, and the balance gets smaller every year.

Now, let's look at the consequences. The first is on rivers. At the moment, melting glaciers send extra water downstream, and this has increased the risk of flooding in some valleys, because more water enters the rivers in a short time. Local councils have already built stronger banks in several places. In the long term, however, the opposite will happen. When the glaciers have shrunk, summer flows will fall, and some rivers will become much smaller.

That matters because many of these rivers are used by people. Farmers on the Canterbury Plains rely on glacier-fed rivers for irrigation, and several hydropower stations also depend on them. If the flow drops in summer, when demand for water is at its highest, there could be serious problems for both farming and electricity.

There are also effects on tourism. Glacier walks and helicopter flights bring in many millions of dollars each year. At Franz Josef, the track to the end of the glacier has been moved several times, and the glacier is so much shorter that guides now take visitors by helicopter to higher parts of the ice. Some businesses are already adapting, but others fear for the future.

So what does the future hold? The models vary, depending on how much greenhouse gas we emit. In the most pessimistic scenario, New Zealand's glaciers could lose up to 90 percent of their volume by the end of this century. Even if emissions fall quickly, we are likely to lose about half. In other words, some change is already certain, and the question is how much more we allow.
For next week, I'd like you to read the two papers on the course page, and consider how the data from the snowline survey could be used to explain this to the public. Thank you.
Pier Street Café, Maureen speaking.
Oh, hello. I saw on your website that you do catering for events. I'd like to order lunch for a staff meeting at our office.
Certainly. Let me bring up the catering order form. Is this for a company?
Yes, it's an accounting firm. We hold a big meeting for all the staff twice a year, and this time I've been put in charge of the food.
Lovely. Could I have your surname, please?
It's Gallagher.
And how do you spell that?
G-A-L-L-A-G-H-E-R.
Thank you, Mr Gallagher. And what date is the meeting?
It's on Thursday, 13 November. Or, hold on. Let me check my diary. No, I'm sorry, they've moved it. It's Friday now, so it's 14 November.
Friday 14 November. Good, we're not too busy that day. How many people should I plan for?
At first I was told thirty. But a few more people from the Dartmouth office are coming, so it's now 36.

Thirty-six. It's always better to order a little extra. Now, what would you like to eat? Our most popular lunch for groups is the soup and sandwich option, and the soup of the day is a seafood chowder, which is made with fresh haddock and scallops from Nova Scotia.
That sounds perfect, and I'm sure a lot of people will want it. Is there anything for people who don't eat fish?
Yes, there's a vegetable soup as well, and that's included. But I need to know about any special dietary needs in advance. Do any of your guests have allergies or other requirements?
Two of them are vegetarian, which the vegetable soup covers. And one person can't eat wheat, so we need gluten-free meals for her.
Fine. We make gluten-free bread, so we'll prepare one of those for her. I'll note that on the form. Do you want drinks as well?
Just coffee and tea, if you can.

Certainly. Now, the price. The soup, the sandwich platter and the coffee and tea come to 16 dollars per person. If you'd like dessert as well, we do lemon squares and fruit, and that brings it up to 18 dollars per person.
I think we'd better have dessert. People always remember dessert. So, 18 dollars.
Great, so 18 dollars a head, plus tax. The total comes to 648 dollars, before tax.
