Okay. And what time would you be able to deliver? The meeting starts at noon.
We could come at 11:30, but the problem is that our van is out on another delivery until a quarter to twelve. So the earliest possible time is 11:45. Is that all right?
That's a bit tight, but I think we can manage. I'll ask the others to set up the tables before then.
Good. Where do we deliver to?
We're at 250 Lorne Street.
Was that 205?
No, 250. Two, five, zero. It's on the third floor, and there's a lift.
And the postal code?
It's B3K 2R8. That's B as in Bravo, 3, K as in Kilo, 2, R as in Romeo, and 8.

Thank you. I've got B3K 2R8. Now, for orders of this size we ask for a deposit when you confirm. For orders over five hundred dollars, it's 50 percent, but for smaller ones, it's a quarter. Yours is above that limit, so we need half.
Oh, I thought it was less. So 50 percent?
Actually, I've just looked at the notice on my screen. We changed the policy this month. The deposit is now 25 percent for every order, large or small, which is 162 dollars for yours.
That's even better. Can I pay by card over the phone?
Yes, I can take it now if you like, or you can pay online using the link in your confirmation email. Whichever you prefer.
I'll pay online this afternoon, if that's all right.
No problem. And one more thing. If you need to change the numbers, please let us know at least two days before the event, because we buy the fish fresh.
Understood. Thank you so much for your help, Maureen.
You're welcome. We'll see you on the fourteenth, Mr Gallagher.

Good morning, everyone, and welcome to the Central Library. My name's Fiona, and I'm the community librarian. I'm delighted to see so many new faces. Before we start the tour, I'd like to tell you a few practical things about becoming a member, and then we'll walk through the building floor by floor.

First of all, joining. A library card is free for everyone who lives in the city, and all you need is a document showing your address, like a utility bill. If you live outside the city, you can still join, but there's an annual fee. Children can get their own card at any age, as long as a parent signs the form.

Now, let me tell you about borrowing. Until recently, members could borrow twenty books at a time, but that was a bit limiting for the keen readers among you, so we've raised it to 30 books. The limit for DVDs hasn't changed. It's still five. There's a higher limit of fifty items for teachers, but that doesn't apply to most people.

If you want to keep a book for longer, you can renew it. You used to be able to do this by phone, but we've closed the phone service, because hardly anyone was using it. Instead, you can renew online, using our website, or on the library app, which you can download for free. Of course, you can also renew your books at the desk, if you're here in person.

Right, let's go on to the building. We start here, on the ground floor. This is the main entrance, and you can see the reading lounge on your left. It's where we keep the newspapers and magazines, and there are comfortable armchairs. Many regulars spend the whole morning here, and the café is next door, so you can bring a coffee in, as long as it has a lid.

If you take the stairs or the lift, you'll find the first floor, which is the busiest part of the library. It's where you'll find our public computers, and a printing station. Using the computers is free for an hour a day, and you just need to sign in with your library card. Printing costs ten cents a page, and if you need help, a member of staff is always on duty.

On the second floor we have the quiet study area, which is very popular with students. There are twelve small study pods, each with a desk and a power socket, and you can book one for up to three hours through the website. They're often fully booked during exams, so I suggest you plan ahead.

The third floor is the most unusual, and it's my favourite. Here we have the local history archive, where you can look at old maps, photographs and newspapers from Winnipeg going back to the eighteen seventies. Some families come to trace their ancestors, and our archivist can help. It's open Tuesday to Saturday, and you need to make an appointment.

You may have heard that there are plans for a makerspace with 3D printers and sewing machines. It's a lovely idea, but the funding has been delayed, so I'm afraid that it's been postponed. We'll announce it on the website when it's ready. And if you're looking for conversation groups for people who are learning English, those take place at the community centre next door on Wednesday evenings, not here.

Finally, down in the lower level, we have the children's library. This is a bright space, with low shelves and beanbags, and there are storytelling sessions for the youngest children on Tuesday and Saturday mornings. Parents are welcome to stay, and there's a quiet corner for breastfeeding.

Now, a few announcements. Some of you may remember paying fines for returning books late. I'm very pleased to say that we no longer charge late fees on any item. If you are late, we'll send you a reminder, and you simply can't borrow more until you've returned the overdue books. It's made a huge difference, and many people who had stopped visiting have come back.

Another thing. Next month, the library will be closed on Monday mornings, as we're replacing the carpet on the first and second floors. We'll be open as usual in the afternoons. The notice is on the website, and we'll put signs on the doors. Sorry for any inconvenience.
That's all from me for now. Please feel free to explore, and ask any of the staff if you can't find something. Enjoy the library.
Good afternoon, Ines. Good afternoon, Marcus. I've read your outline for the marketing project. It's about reducing single-use packaging at the food trucks on campus, is that right?
That's right. We want to find out what would persuade students to use less packaging, and then recommend a plan to the truck owners.
Ines, what drew you to the topic?

I worked for a summer on a food truck in Halifax. At the end of every shift we threw away bags and bags of containers and cups, and I thought there must be a better way. The owner was interested, but he said he didn't know what customers wanted.
And for me it was more about the business side. I think sustainability will be a big selling point in the next few years.
Good. Now, tell me about the survey you're planning.
We'll ask about two hundred students whether they'd prefer reusable containers, and what they'd be willing to pay.

I'm a bit worried about that, though. People often say they care about the environment, but when it comes to paying fifty cents extra, they behave differently. So the survey might give us an over-optimistic picture.
But we can't really observe what they'd do without actually running a trial.

That's a fair point, Marcus, and it's a well-known problem in market research. I'd suggest you do both. Use the survey to find out what people say, then spend two lunchtimes watching what they actually do at the trucks. Count how many people bring their own cups, for example. That would give you a much stronger result than interviewing the owners, which I know you were considering.
I'd thought of the interviews because the owners know their customers well.
They do, and you might still talk to one or two. But it's the customers' behaviour that matters most.
Okay. Should we look at the different types of packaging in the report?
Yes, that would be useful. Let's go through the ones you've listed. Start with the paper cups.
We found that most of them have a thin plastic lining, so they look recyclable, but they aren't.
Exactly. In most Canadian cities, they can't be recycled, because the plastic can't be separated from the paper. That surprises many people, so it's worth explaining carefully.
Then there are the compostable containers. They're the obvious solution, but they cost nearly three times as much as plastic.
Which is a serious problem for a small business, with very thin margins. You'll need to show how the owners could afford it. What about the reusable bowls?
We thought we'd charge a deposit. The customer pays two dollars, and gets it back when they return the bowl.

It's a good model, but be careful about who returns them. In similar trials, it was mostly the regular customers who brought them back. Visitors and occasional customers tended to keep them, or throw them away.
So the scheme only works if you have a loyal group.
Right. Next, the cardboard trays.
They're cheap and they're recyclable, but there's one problem.
They go soggy. If you put hot food in them, like curry or noodles, they start to collapse within ten minutes.
Precisely. Mention that, because it affects how customers see the product. And the wooden cutlery?
That's the surprise. In our pilot survey, it was the most popular change, because people thought it felt nicer than plastic, and it was only a tiny extra cost.
That's a useful finding, and an easy win for the owners. Now, what recommendations will you make at the end?
I think we should recommend a discount for people who bring their own cup. Even a small amount, like twenty cents, might change behaviour.
And we could suggest a partnership with a composting company, so that the trucks don't have to dispose of the containers themselves.
Those are both realistic. What about banning single-use packaging altogether?
I'd like to, but the owners would never agree.
And a social media campaign could help, but it's not really the key.
Should we also include a section on the costs of our own recommendations?

Definitely. An owner will only act if he can see the numbers. Work out how many cups a truck sells in a week, what the discount would cost, and how much it would save on packaging. Even a rough calculation is better than none.
I could ask the owner I worked for. He'd probably let us see his sales figures if we promised not to publish his name.

That's a good idea, but get his agreement in writing. And think about the length of your report. The limit is four thousand words, and the best reports I see are usually closer to three thousand five hundred, with clear headings and short paragraphs.
We'll aim for that.
What about the presentation? Should we use slides?
Yes, but keep them simple, with one main idea per slide, and perhaps a photograph from your observation days. A picture of a full rubbish bin makes the point better than a paragraph of text.
Agreed. Concentrate on the discount and the partnership. Send me a draft of the survey by next Wednesday, and I'll give you some feedback before you launch it.

Good morning, everyone. Today I want to talk about wool, which is one of the oldest textile fibres in the world, and also one of the most interesting from a scientific point of view. Both Australia and New Zealand built their economies on wool, and it still matters a great deal to farmers in both countries, so I'd like us to understand why it behaves as it does.

Let me start with a little history. The sheep that produce the finest wool are called merinos, and they came originally from Spain. The first merinos arrived in Australia in 1797, brought by a small group of settlers, and within a few decades, the colony had become the world's largest producer of fine wool. The animals adapted very well to the dry climate, and the industry grew rapidly.

What does fine mean? The quality of wool is measured by the diameter of the individual fibres, in a unit called the micron, which is one thousandth of a millimetre. A human hair is about seventy microns across. The finest merino wool is less than 19 microns, which makes it soft enough to wear next to the skin. Coarser wool, which is used for carpets, can be more than thirty microns.

Now, what makes wool so special? Let's look at the structure. If you looked at a wool fibre under a microscope, you would see that its outer layer is made of overlapping scales, which together are called the cuticle. They are rather like the tiles on a roof. This is important for two reasons. It makes the fibre slightly water-repellent, so rain runs off, and it is also the reason wool can felt, which is what happens when a woollen jumper shrinks in a hot wash. The scales catch on each other and lock together.

Inside the fibre, there is another feature, which is the natural crimp, or waviness. Because the fibres are curly, they don't pack together tightly, and they form tiny pockets that trap air. That is why wool is such a good insulator. Air is a poor conductor of heat, so the trapped air keeps the warmth in on a cold day.

At the same time, the fibre is able to take in moisture. Wool can absorb up to 30 percent of its own weight in water vapour before it even feels damp. That's a lot more than cotton, and far more than synthetic fibres, which hardly absorb anything. This is why a wool garment keeps you comfortable when you sweat, instead of making you feel clammy.

Wool has some other useful properties. For one, it is naturally resistant to fire. It's hard to ignite, and when it does burn, it tends to go out by itself, so it's often used for uniforms and for furnishings in public buildings. It also resists odours, because the fibre doesn't hold bacteria in the way that synthetic fibres do.

Let's turn to sustainability, which is where wool has attracted a lot of interest recently. One concern with synthetic clothes is that every time they're washed, they release tiny pieces of plastic into the water. These are called microplastics, and they end up in rivers and oceans. Wool doesn't release microplastics, because it's a natural protein fibre, and in the right conditions, it breaks down in the soil, and returns nutrients.

However, we shouldn't be uncritical. Sheep farming has its own environmental costs, including methane emissions and land use. A typical merino sheep is shorn once a year, and it produces a fleece weighing about 4 kilograms, which is enough for several jumpers, but not a great deal in global terms. So the industry is working on reducing its emissions.

There has also been a lot of discussion about animal welfare. One issue concerns a practice called mulesing, in which a strip of skin is removed from around the sheep's tail area. The purpose is to prevent a serious condition called flystrike, which happens when flies lay their eggs on damp, dirty wool, and the maggots attack the animal. Mulesing is painful, and many consumers and retailers now refuse to buy wool from farms that practise it. Farmers are looking at alternatives, such as breeding sheep with smoother skin, or using better treatments.

Finally, a word about new uses. For decades, the main use of wool was clothing and carpets, but demand for those has fallen. In New Zealand and Australia, there is growing interest in using wool as building insulation. It's natural, it regulates humidity, and it doesn't release harmful dust. Several companies already sell wool insulation batts, and early results are promising, though they cost more than the standard fibreglass.
For next week, please read the two articles on the course page, and think about whether wool can compete with synthetic fibres on price, or whether it should be marketed purely as a premium product.
Kia ora, Kauri Learning Hub, Isla here. Are you calling about a class?

Oh, hello. I hope you can. I'm ringing about the study skills workshops you advertise. I'm a mature student, I've just started a part-time degree, and I haven't written an essay in about twenty years.

Then you've phoned the right people. We run three series at the moment. There's Exam Technique, there's Writing Clearly, and there's Note-Taking Essentials. Do you know which one you're interested in?

I think I'd have said Exam Technique, because that's what frightens me most. But my first test isn't until June, so I suppose the first problem is simply getting everything down in lectures. Could I take the notes one instead?
Of course. Honestly, most people say that note-taking is the better place to start. It makes all the others easier. I'll pull up the enrolment screen. And your name is?
It's Gareth Lomax.
Sorry, was that Lo-max, or Lowe-max?
Lomax, L-O-M-A-X. It rhymes with "no Max", if that helps.
Lovely, thank you. Right, so that's the Note-Taking Essentials series. It starts on Tuesday the second of April.
Oh dear. I'm away that week, visiting my brother in Wellington. Is there any other start date?
Let me look. The second of April group is actually full anyway, but we have a second group starting a week later, on the ninth of April. There are still four places left in that one.
The ninth would be perfect. And what time of day is it? I work until five, and the traffic into town is terrible.
It was advertised as six o'clock, but the tutor has asked for a slightly later start so people can get across town after work. So it's now half past six, finishing at eight.
Half past six is much better, thank you.

And the classes are in the Totara Room, which is on the first floor, just beside the lift. You'll see a sign. Some people go to the Rimu Room by mistake, because that's where our computer courses are held.
Totara Room, I've got it. How many sessions are there altogether?

It's a five-week series, one session each week. The first four are teaching sessions, and the fifth is a practice session where you bring your own lecture notes and compare methods with the others. People tell us the last one is the most useful, which surprised us at first.
That sounds sensible. What does it cost?
The standard price is ninety-five dollars. But you're a student, so you qualify for the learner rate, which is eighty-five dollars. I'll just need to see your student card on the first evening.
That's fine. I can pay by card, I suppose?
Yes, you can pay on the night, or you can pay online beforehand if you'd rather. Either is fine.
I'll do it on the night. Is there anything I should bring?

Please bring a pen, a highlighter if you have one, and an A4 pad. Not a laptop, I'm afraid. The tutor wants everybody writing by hand, at least for the first two weeks. She says it forces you to listen properly and decide what matters, instead of typing every word.
That's interesting. I'd always assumed a laptop was quicker.
It's quicker, certainly, but not always better. Now, may I ask how you heard about the workshops? We like to record that.

Let me think. I saw something on Facebook, I think. No, wait, that was the library's page. It was actually a flyer. I picked it up at the student centre on campus, pinned to the noticeboard by the coffee cart.
A flyer, wonderful. Thank you. And one last thing. We send a reminder the day before each session. Would you like that as an email, or would you prefer a text message?
Text message, please. I never seem to check my email on weekdays. Should I give you my mobile number now?

There's no need, we already have it from your call. So that's you booked in for the ninth of April, half past six, Totara Room. We'll see you then, Gareth. And don't worry about the twenty years. Most people in that room have the same fear, and they're surprised how quickly it passes.
Thank you so much, Isla. You've been really helpful.
My pleasure. Goodbye for now.

Right, can everyone hear me at the back? Wonderful. Welcome to Karamea University, and welcome to Peer Mentor Week. My name is Jess, and I coordinate the mentoring programme. I'm also in my third year of a psychology degree, so I was sitting exactly where you are two years ago, feeling exactly as nervous.

First, a word about timing. This week is orientation, so you'll be collecting timetables, finding your lecture halls and getting lost. Mentor groups don't begin this week. Lectures start on Monday, and your group will meet for the first time in the week after that, so in your second week at the university. That gives you a few days to settle in first.

Next, the groups themselves. Last year we had twelve students in each group, and it was too many. The quieter people never got a word in. So this year every group has eight students and two mentors, and I think you'll find it far friendlier.

You might wonder who decides which group you're in. You don't get to choose, but nor is it decided by your faculty, which is what some people expect. When you enrolled online, you were sent a short questionnaire about your interests, your course and the kind of support you thought you'd need. We use that to match you. If you skipped it, please see me after this talk and I'll put you through it today.

Now, what do mentors actually do? We explain how the university works, such as how to use the learning platform, where to find the counsellors, and how to get an extension if you're ill. We tell you what we wish we'd known. We also help you set up study habits that suit you. What we do not do is proofread your assignments. People ask us every year, and the answer's always no, because then you'd never learn to catch your own mistakes. We'll happily talk through a draft with you, but we won't correct it.

Let's talk about your first session. You'll receive an email with the room and the time. Please don't bring a laptop, because we want you talking, not typing. Some people think they need their student card, but you don't, we'll know who you are. What you do need is your timetable, so that your mentors can help you plan your week. And please come with a list of questions. They can be about anything at all, from where to buy cheap textbooks to how many hours you should study. Those lists are the best way to get conversation going.

I'd like to take you through what happens over the first half of the term, because every group follows the same plan. In the second week, the session is about the learning commons. We take you on a short walk to find the quiet floors, the group study rooms and the borrowing desk, so you'll never have to ask for directions again.

In the fourth week, we turn to time. Together you'll build a reading schedule for one of your own courses, and you'll see how many hours there really are in a week. Most first-years are astonished, and mostly in a good way.

By week six, the first assignments will be arriving, so we practise something that is quite scary, which is speaking up. Each of you gives a short talk of two minutes on a subject of your choice, and the group gives friendly feedback. It sounds worse than it is. Last year, someone talked about her pet tortoise and got a standing ovation.

And in week eight, the mid-term exams are close, so the session is about sharing revision methods. You'll hear how other students cope, and you'll steal the ideas that work. Please note that we don't invite lecturers to the sessions. Some groups ask, and we feel the point is that students speak freely among themselves.

A few practical points before we finish. Your mentors are volunteers, and they give up their evenings, so please be on time, and let us know if you can't come. You can message your mentors in between sessions through the programme app, but they won't answer after ten at night, because they need to sleep too.

If anything goes wrong, or you simply feel the match isn't right, please speak to me. I can arrange a change in the first month, and nobody will be offended. Now, are there any questions? Yes, the gentleman by the door.
Sorry, Priya, Sam, I've kept you waiting. Come in, sit down. Right, your project on peer assessment. I've read the proposal twice, and I think there's a good idea in it. Tell me where you've got to.
Well, we've decided what we're comparing. We want to find out whether first-year students give feedback on each other's essays that is as useful as the feedback they get from a tutor.

We had a long argument about the word "useful", actually. Priya wanted to ask the students whether the comments felt helpful. I thought that was too subjective, so we've agreed to look at whether the next draft improved.

Good compromise. Though be careful, a draft can improve for lots of reasons, such as simply having more time. You'll need to say that in your limitations. So how many students are you hoping to recruit?
Sixty, originally. But Sam spoke to the first-year coordinator, and she said that's probably too ambitious in the time we've got.
She suggested forty, which would still give us twenty pairs. It's not huge, but I think it's enough for a student project.
I agree. Forty well-run pairs are worth far more than sixty messy ones. And where will the essays come from?
From the Introduction to Sociology course. The lecturer has agreed to let us use the first assignment, as long as everything is anonymous.
That's helpful. Now, the rubric. Are you using the one the lecturer wrote?

That was our plan, but it's quite long, and the students would need an hour just to read it. We'd rather write a shorter one from scratch, with four criteria, so the peer reviewers don't get overwhelmed.
I'd be cautious. If you design your own rubric, your results may only tell us about your rubric. Why not trim the lecturer's one, and say clearly what you removed?
Oh, that's easier, and probably more honest. Yes, let's do that.
Next, training. Will the peer reviewers get any?
A short session, twenty minutes, where we show them two sample essays and talk through the feedback. Nothing more, otherwise it stops being peer review and becomes tutoring.
Sensible. And I like that you'll keep the tutor's feedback hidden from the reviewers. Otherwise they'll simply copy it. Now, what about analysis? How will you decide whether a comment is useful?
We're going to code each comment into categories. Is it specific? Does it suggest a change? Does it mention the argument or only the grammar?
Fine, but make sure you both code a sample independently, and then compare. If you each classify things differently, you need to find out early. Is there anything about the project that worries you?
Have you thought about a pilot? Even two pairs, before you commit the whole group.
We hadn't, to be honest. Would it really make a difference?

A great deal. In my experience, something always goes wrong the first time. A form that nobody understands, an instruction that can be read two ways, a file that won't open. It's far better to discover that with two pairs than with twenty.
That's fair. I'd forgotten that last year's group lost a week because their online form wouldn't load on phones.

Exactly. So run the pilot in the first week, change what needs changing, and then begin the real exercise. It will cost you three or four days, but it will save you much more than that. Anyway, you mentioned a worry.
Yes, honestly, our schedule. The recruitment message goes out next week, but the essays aren't due until the end of the month, and the report is due six weeks after that.

That's tight but possible. Something I'd suggest is to stagger the work, so you're not analysing everything in the last fortnight. Here's how I'd plan the stages. Recruiting is the easy part, so prepare the message now, and speak to the coordinator again about sending a reminder a few days later.

When you collect the essays, scan every one the same day and give each a code number immediately, so nothing gets muddled. For the rubric, as we said, adapt the lecturer's version and check your changes with her before you use it.

For the analysis, book a second coder. Perhaps a friend on the course who isn't part of the project. And when you present your results, don't hide the disappointing ones. Students and examiners respect honesty more than a neat story.
That makes sense. What about the ethics form?
Ah, yes. That has to be approved before you recruit anyone, so please don't send the message until I've signed it. Bring it to me tomorrow, and I'll look at it straight away.
We'll do that. We were also wondering whether the students should pick their own partners for the swap, because friends might be kinder than strangers.
Good question, and you'll need to decide. My instinct is to pair them randomly, so that friendship doesn't colour the comments, but whichever you choose, write down why.
Random it is. Thanks, Dr Hollis.
You're welcome. Email me if anything changes, and I'll see you both next Thursday.

Let me start with a question. When did you last learn something really well? Not well enough to pass a test, but well enough that it stayed with you for years? I suspect that, for most of you, the answer involves explaining it to somebody else. Today's lecture is about why that is, and how universities can make better use of it.

I'll begin with a phenomenon that psychologists call the protégé effect. That's p-r-o-t-e-g-e with two accents, if you want to look it up. The idea is simple. People who study material because they expect to teach it to someone tend to organise it better and remember it for longer than people who study the same material for a test. The learner's own effort is the same. What changes is the purpose.

Of course, nobody invented this idea recently. Back in 1984, the educational psychologist Benjamin Bloom reported that students who were taught one to one by a tutor performed dramatically better than students in a conventional class. The average tutored student did better than about ninety-eight percent of the others. Bloom called it a problem, because no school could afford a tutor for every child. And that raised a question. Could ordinary classmates offer part of the benefit?

To understand why they might, we need a theoretical idea from the Russian psychologist Lev Vygotsky. He argued that learning happens best at a level just beyond what a person can do alone, but within reach if somebody helps. He called this region the zone of proximal development. Spell it with me, p-r-o-x-i-m-a-l. A classmate who understood the topic five minutes ago is often better placed to help than an expert, because the expert has forgotten how hard it was.

Now let me describe one practical method, which is called peer instruction. It was developed in the early nineteen nineties by Eric Mazur, a physics professor at Harvard. Mazur noticed that students could recite formulas but could not apply them, and that his clear explanations were not helping. So he changed the format of his lectures.

This is how it works. He asks a short conceptual question, and each student votes for an answer privately. In his early years he used flashcards, but now it's usually clickers, which are small handsets, though phone apps do the same job. If most people are right, he moves on. If the votes are split, he asks the students to turn to a neighbour and persuade each other. They talk for about two minutes, and then vote again.

What happens next is the interesting part. The correct answers usually rise, often substantially, and they rise even when nobody in the pair knew the answer at the start. In explaining their reasoning to someone else, students find holes in it, and fix them.

A fair objection at this point is that peers can be wrong. If a classmate explains something incorrectly, the listener may learn the mistake. That is a genuine risk, and it is why the questions are designed with one clearly correct answer, and why the lecturer always reveals and explains that answer at the end, so that errors do not survive the discussion.

Peer learning is not magic, however, and I'd like to spend a few minutes on when it goes wrong. Research on group work suggests that size matters. Pairs are very effective, but for a longer task, groups of five often split into a pair and a trio, and groups of three tend to leave one quiet person out. Groups of four are the usual recommendation.

Next, roles. If everybody is simply told to work together, a few people will do all the work. So effective teachers give each member a specific role, such as the person who records, the person who questions, or the person who checks the sources, and they rotate the roles from week to week.

Even so, you may hear students complain that one member did nothing. Psychologists call this social loafing, l-o-a-f-i-n-g, and it is a real effect, not just a complaint. It becomes more common in larger groups, and when individual contributions cannot be seen.

What can a teacher do about it? Several things, but the most successful, in my view, is asking each group to write a short reflection on how the work was shared. It needs only a paragraph, but it makes people think about their own contribution, and it gives the teacher something to read besides the final product.

To summarise, learning by teaching works because it asks for organisation, explanation and retrieval all at once. Peers can be unexpectedly good at helping because they remember the struggle, and structure turns casual chatting into real learning. In next week's session, we'll look at what happens when the peers are online, and why that changes more than you might think. Thank you.
Hollowbrook Repair Café, Martin speaking.
Oh, hello. I saw a notice in the post office window asking for volunteers, and I wondered whether you still need anyone.
We always need people. Do you have a few minutes? I can take your details while we talk, and tell you how it all works.
Yes, of course. I've just retired, and I'm looking for something useful to do with my Saturdays.
Well, you've picked the right group. Let me start with the form. Can I have your surname?
It's Pettigrew. P-E-T-T-I-G-R-E-W.

Thank you, Mrs Pettigrew. Now, what could you repair? We've got volunteers who fix bicycles, toasters, lamps and radios. Some people think you must be a trained electrician, but you don't. It's mostly patience.

Well, I used to repair electrical things when my husband was alive, but I'm very out of practice, and I'd rather not touch anything with a plug. What I do really well is sewing. I was a dressmaker for thirty years.

A dressmaker! That's wonderful. Sewing is the table with the longest queue. People bring in coats with broken zips and trousers they've grown out of, and we only have two people on that table at the moment. So, sewing, I'll put down.
Lovely. When do you meet?
Once a month. It used to be the last Sunday of the month, but too many volunteers had family commitments, so we moved it. It's now the first Saturday of every month. Would that suit you?
Saturday is perfect. And what time does it start?
Doors open to the public at ten, and we stop at one. But volunteers arrive earlier, at half past nine, so we can set up the tables and have a quick briefing over a cup of tea.
Half past nine, fine. And where is it held?
In the Linden Hall, on Millbrook Road. Not the Church Hall, which is what everyone assumes, because we used to meet there. We moved last year after the roof was replaced.
Linden Hall, I know it. Is there anywhere to park? I'd be bringing a sewing machine.

You can use the machines we have, so there's no need. But, yes, there's free parking behind the pharmacy, just a one-minute walk from the hall. The car park by the supermarket is a pay car park, so avoid that one.
Good to know. Is there any training? I'd feel better if I knew what to do if someone cut a finger or something.

Yes, we run a short safety session for every new volunteer, covering first aid, how to handle materials, and what to do with electrical items. The next one is on the twenty-first of May. It lasts about two hours. Is that a date you can do?
The twenty-first, let me check. Yes, that's fine. I'll put it in my diary.

Good. Another question. Should you bring anything yourself? We supply needles, thread and pins, and we've got a lot of buttons that people have donated over the years. But please bring your own scissors. Ours tend to go missing, and a dressmaker will want her own.
Naturally. I've had my favourite pair for about thirty years, and nobody is going to get hold of them.

Ha, quite right. Now, expenses. We're a small charity, so we can't pay for petrol, but if you come by public transport we'll pay for your bus fares. Just keep your tickets and give them to our treasurer at the end of the day.
I'll probably walk, it's only fifteen minutes, but thanks.
Lovely. The last thing I need is an emergency contact. It's a requirement for our insurance, and it's only used if something goes wrong.
Well, my husband passed away some years ago, so it should be my daughter. No, she lives in Canada. Better put down my sister, who is ten minutes from me. She's called Gwen.
Thank you. I'll put down your sister, Gwen. We'll send the rota and the training details by email to the address you've already given me.
Perfect. Thank you for being so welcoming.

Not at all, we're delighted. Our youngest customers are always astonished that a pair of trousers can be mended instead of thrown away, and you'll find it very rewarding. We'll see you on the twenty-first, Mrs Pettigrew.
Looking forward to it. Goodbye.

Thank you all for coming out on such a wet evening. I'm Marguerite Ashby, the library services manager for the council, and tonight I want to explain, as clearly as I can, what is happening to the Harbour Library, and what we hope will replace it.

First, the timetable. A lot of rumours have been going round, so let me be exact. The old library will close its doors on the thirty-first of July. Some people have said June, and I understand why, because that was the original plan, but the builders have asked for an extra month to move the shelving. There'll be a temporary service in the community centre until the new building opens in the spring.

Why are we doing this at all? Many of you love the old building, and so do I. But it was built in 1964, and its biggest problem has nothing to do with the roof or the heating. It's access. It has no lift, there are stairs at the front and the back, and every week, parents with prams and people in wheelchairs have been turned away from half the collection. That's something we can't accept in a public service.

Now, the money. I know some of you will want to know whether this is paid for by your council tax. Part of it is, but not most. The biggest share, around sixty percent, comes from a government regeneration grant, and what's left is split between the council and local donations. We've been touched by the donations, some of them very small, and each is recorded on the wall of the new foyer.

The new building will be longer and lighter, with big windows facing the harbour. And, importantly, it will be open for longer. Today we close at six, which is no use for anyone who works. From next spring, the library will be open until nine every weekday evening. Some other councils have gone to a card system, where members can enter without staff at night, but we've decided against it for now, because we want a person on the desk at all hours.

Now, the question I'm asked most. What will happen to the books? I can promise you that we aren't throwing them out to make room for computers. The number of different titles will stay about the same. What we will do is hold fewer duplicate copies of the most popular novels, so that shelf space can be used for other things. And we'll keep every local history book, including those in the basement archive.

Let me take you through the plan of the building. The main entrance faces the street, on the north side. Immediately inside it, on the left, is the café. We put it there on purpose, so that people who come in for a coffee see the books on the way. At the back of the ground floor, away from the entrance, is the children's area, with low shelves and a small stage for story time. We've put it there so that noisy toddlers don't disturb the readers.

Upstairs, at the top of the stairs, you'll find the quiet study room, which will have forty desks and no phones allowed. Next to the lifts on the same floor are four small meeting rooms, which community groups can book for free. There's a big window in each one, so people can see that they're in the middle of the library.

And downstairs, in the basement, the part we're most excited about. We call it the makerspace, and it's where people can use sewing machines, 3D printers and tools that most people couldn't afford to buy. It's in the basement because of the noise, and because the floor can carry the weight of the machines. A group of teenagers asked for the roof terrace to be used for it, but we felt that the neighbours might not appreciate the sound of drills at midnight.

There is a roof terrace, by the way. It will be a reading garden, and it will be open from May to September. And the space on the harbour side of the ground floor, which I know some of you will ask about, will be a newspaper and magazine room, with comfortable chairs, free to everyone.

So that's the plan. I'd like to take your questions, and then there's tea and biscuits at the back. Please don't be shy. If you think we've got something wrong, I'd rather hear it tonight than after the building is finished.
Chloe, Ravi, good to see you. Take a seat. You wanted to talk about your questionnaire for the library project.
Yes. We've finished a draft, and we're a bit stuck on who to ask. Our topic is why people stop using the public library after they leave school.
Which, to be fair, was my idea, because I did exactly that. I used the library every week as a child, and then I just stopped when I went to university.
Many people do. I think it's a good topic, because it's about a real gap. Before the survey, though, tell me about your background reading. What have you found?

Mostly reports from library associations, which tend to be very positive, and a few academic papers on young adults. There's one study that says teenagers drift away at about fifteen, usually when homework moves online.
That fits my experience, actually. By that age I could get everything I needed from my phone, so the library felt like a detour.
Interesting. But be careful with reports written by library associations. They have a reason to present good news. Look for independent studies as well, and say in your report which is which.
We'll do that. We also found out that many councils don't record why members leave. They only record that they've left.
Then your project fills a gap, and you should say so in your introduction. Now, who will you survey?
We thought we'd stand outside the main library on Saturday mornings and ask people as they come out.
Hmm. That's a problem, isn't it? You'd be asking only the people who are still using it. If you want to know why people stopped, you need to speak to people who aren't there.
That's a good point. We hadn't thought of it like that.
So perhaps the shopping centre instead? There are lots of people there, and they're all ages.

Better, certainly. Or, even better, both. Use the library entrance to ask current users, and the shopping centre for everyone else, and then compare the two groups. That would actually make your project more interesting.
And we could add an online version as well, I suppose, through the student union newsletter.

You could, but I'd be careful. Students are a very particular group, and they are not typical of the public. I'd drop that idea unless you have time to do a proper analysis. Now, let's look at the questions. I've read through them. Question six, "Do you think libraries are boring?" Please don't use that.
Why not? It seemed a direct way of finding out.
Because it's a leading question. It tells people what answer you expect. Try something neutral, like "How would you describe the library to a friend?" and let them answer in their own words.
That's much better. What about the long list of reasons for not visiting? We have about twenty.

That's too many. Nobody will read twenty options. I'd cut it to eight, group the similar ones, and always add an "other" box. And keep the whole thing short. If it takes more than five minutes, people will walk away.
We'd wondered about a prize draw to encourage people.
I'd avoid that. It can attract people who just want the prize, and give you careless answers. You can offer a small thank-you, perhaps a bookmark, but no more.
A bookmark, that's quite fitting.
One more thing. How many people do we need? A friend on the maths course said a hundred in each group.

A hundred in each group is ambitious for two students working over a few weekends. Aim for sixty in each, and be honest about the limits in your discussion section. A smaller sample, carefully taken, is better than a larger one that's rushed.
Sixty each, so a hundred and twenty altogether. That's manageable if we both work on Saturdays.
And one practical point. Ask permission from the shopping centre manager first. They can be strict about people with clipboards, and I'd hate you to be moved on halfway through a Saturday.
Good thinking. We'll email the manager this week.
Do it today. These things take longer than you expect.

Now, the process. I'd like you to do three things before you start. First, test the questionnaire on five friends, and ask them what confused them. Second, get the ethics form signed, even for a short survey, because you'll be talking to members of the public. Third, practise your introduction, because most people will decide in the first ten seconds whether to speak to you.
And what about the analysis?
Keep it simple. Count the main reasons people give, compare the two groups, and use two or three charts. And if the interviews turn up something unexpected, please follow it up.
Thank you. That's given us a lot to do.

Also, keep a short diary of what happens each Saturday: the weather, how many people refused, which questions caused confusion. Those notes are surprisingly valuable when you write up your method, and they cost nothing.
We'll start a shared document tonight.
Good. Come back in a fortnight and show me the revised version. I'd like to see the pilot results too.
We'll bring them. Thanks again.

Good morning. Today I'd like to ask a question that sounds old-fashioned. Will we still have public libraries in thirty years, and if we do, what will they be for? Newspapers regularly tell us that libraries are dying, killed by the internet, and councils with limited budgets sometimes behave as if that were true. I'd like to argue that the real picture is more interesting, and more hopeful.

Let's start with some history, because the library we know today is quite a recent idea. In Britain, the Public Libraries Act of 1850 allowed local councils to raise money to open free libraries, and the movement spread quickly. Across the Atlantic and beyond, the steel businessman Andrew Carnegie paid for about 2,500 libraries between 1883 and 1919. His rule was that the town had to provide the land and the running costs, so it had to want the library.

The purpose of these early libraries was to educate working people, and for a hundred years that remained the central idea. The library was a place to borrow a book. But in the 1980s, sociologist Ray Oldenburg offered a different way of thinking about public buildings. He argued that, besides home and work, people need what he called third places, where they can gather informally and meet others on equal terms. Cafés and pubs were his examples, but libraries fit the description very well. Think about that phrase, third places, because I'll come back to it.

Let's look now at what is happening in some of the most admired modern libraries. In Helsinki, the central library, Oodi, opened in 2018 and was not primarily designed as a place for books at all. Yes, there are books, on the top floor, but the ground floor has a cinema, a café and a large hall for events. On the middle floor there are workshops where people can borrow not just books but sewing machines, laser cutters and 3D printers. Notice that these are things people want to use occasionally, but would never buy. That is the old library principle of sharing, applied to equipment.

Not every town can afford a building like that, of course. Oodi cost nearly a hundred million euros. But the idea travels. A small library can share a tool collection with a hardware shop, or lend telescopes and musical instruments from a single cupboard. What matters is the principle, not the budget.

What of digital services? It is true that fewer people borrow printed books than twenty years ago in many places. But I want to give you an example from a region of New Zealand that I'll call the Tasman network. There, e-book loans rose by about forty percent in five years, so reading has not disappeared, it has just changed form. And librarians tell me that the thing which hasn't changed is the need for guidance. People want a trusted person to help them find what is reliable.

That leads me to a serious difficulty, which is the digital divide. In the same Tasman region, about twenty percent of households have no reliable internet at home. For those families, the library computer is the only way to apply for a job, fill in a tax return or do homework. So the argument that the internet makes libraries unnecessary is exactly backwards. The more services go online, the more people need somewhere free to get online.

Now, I should be fair and describe the risks. The first risk is staffing. In some places, councils have tried to extend opening hours by allowing members to enter without staff, using their membership cards to unlock the doors. It looks good on paper, because the building is open for more hours, but without staff, the library cannot do what makes it special, which is helping people. A second risk is mission creep. Critics say libraries are being asked to replace social services that have been cut. Librarians now find themselves dealing with people in real distress, with little training and no extra money. It is a compliment to libraries that people trust them so much, but it should not be an excuse for councils to do less elsewhere.

So what will make libraries survive? I'd suggest three things. Libraries must keep their promise of being free and open to everybody. They must continue to offer what the market doesn't, such as shared equipment, quiet space and expert help. And above all they must be trusted. In a world of misinformation, and of services that watch what we do, a place that lends without asking questions is quite precious. If libraries lose that trust, no building, however beautiful, will save them.

Next week, we'll look at a case study of one rural library, to see how these ideas work when the budget is small and the nearest town is two hours away. Please read the paper on the reading list before then.
Cwm Derwen Field Centre, Gwyneth speaking.
Oh, good afternoon. I'm hoping to book a residential trip for some of my geography students, and a colleague told me you're the people to talk to about urban ecology courses.
We are, although I'd say we're better known for rivers and woodland. We started the urban course three years ago, and it's very popular. Could I start with your name?
It's Whitcombe. W-H-I-T-C-O-M-B-E. David Whitcombe.
Thank you, Mr Whitcombe. And which school are you from?
Ravenscroft High School, in Bristol. It's a state school, about a thousand students.
Lovely. And when were you thinking of coming?
We wanted the second week of October, so we'd arrive on the fourteenth. But I suppose the Monday after the half-term holiday is when most people want it.

I'll check the diary. The fourteenth is taken, I'm afraid, because we've got a university group in. But we have the whole centre free from the fifteenth, so you could arrive on the Tuesday, the fifteenth of October, and stay until the Friday.
The fifteenth would be fine. That means four days, which is what we'd hoped for.
And how many students are you bringing?

At the moment we have forty names, but I'm quite sure that will fall. Last year we lost several at the last minute because of the cost, and a couple always get ill. I'd say it's likely to be thirty-six by the end.
Let's book it for thirty-six, and you can tell us if it changes. We won't charge you for a few absences if you let us know a week before. And the staff, how many adults?
Four, including me.
Perfect, that's well within our ratios. In terms of rooms, our bunk rooms hold six, with three bunks in each. If you want smaller rooms, there are a few that sleep four, but they cost a little more.
Six is fine for the students. The staff will want something smaller, if possible.
We have single rooms, they're in the old farmhouse. Now, meals are all included, and our cook is very good. Do any of your party have special dietary needs?
We've got three vegetarians, I know, and one boy who is vegan. And a girl who needs halal meat. I hadn't thought about that until now. Is that going to be a problem?
Not at all. We cater for halal several times a month, and we'll get the meat from a supplier in Cardiff. Just send us the details with the booking form.
Excellent. Now, equipment. Do the students need to bring their own?

Mostly waterproof jackets and warm clothing, and please tell them not to bring trainers, because the sites are muddy. We can lend wellingtons in most sizes, and we charge four pounds a pair for the week. We supply the nets, quadrats and identification guides.
Wellingtons for everyone, then. I'm sure some will forget.

We'll make a note. And for the evening activity, there are three choices. People often ask for the moth trap, because it's quick and the students enjoy seeing what they've caught. There's also a pond survey, but that's difficult in the dark in October. The most popular one, though, is a bat walk, where we use detectors that pick up their calls. In October it's the last chance, because they go into hibernation in November.
A bat walk, then. I'm not sure the students will have done anything like it before.

They never have, and it's usually the highlight of the week. Now, the cost. The full price for four days is two hundred and eighty pounds a student. We ask for a deposit of 350 pounds when you confirm, and the balance a month before arrival.
Three hundred and fifty. Right. Can I pay by school purchase order?

Yes, if your finance office sends it to us by email. Lastly, how will you travel? We can arrange a minibus from the nearest station, which is Penmaen, P-E-N-M-A-E-N. It's about twenty minutes by road from here. If you come by coach, you can come right to the door.
We'll come by train, I think, because the coach is too expensive. So the minibus from Penmaen would help.
Wonderful. I'll send the booking form this afternoon. Is the email address on your school website the best one?
Yes, that's fine. Thank you very much for your help.
You're welcome. We look forward to seeing you in October.

Right, can everybody see me? Good. Can I have a bit of hush at the back, please? Thank you. Welcome to Hazelwood Park, and welcome to our first ever BioBlitz. For those who've just arrived, I'm Dougal, and I'm the park's ecology officer. A BioBlitz is a simple idea. We try to find and record every living thing in the park, within twenty-four hours, with the help of as many people as possible. By tomorrow lunchtime, we'd like to have a list that nobody has ever had before.

Let me say how the park is organised, because we've divided it into four zones, and each is looked after by a team. I'll tell you what each is for, and then you can choose. First, the old meadow, which is behind me, with the long grass. Here we're looking for insects, in particular bees and butterflies. Most of you will have a net, but please look first and net only if you must, because butterflies are delicate. The meadow team will record them on a numbered sheet.

The second zone is the lake. It's actually a pond, though everyone here calls it the lake. The lake team will take samples of the water, and examine them under a microscope for tiny animals. It sounds dull, but I promise you it isn't. There's a whole world in a bucketful of pond water. We think there may be some rare species of dragonfly nymph.

The third zone is the woodland, at the bottom of the hill. For the woodland, we're focusing on fungi and lichens. Autumn is the best time of year for mushrooms, and last year the university identified more than forty species from a single afternoon's work. Please don't pick anything. Take a photograph and record the location, and one of the experts will identify it. Some of these species are poisonous, and I don't want any of you to be tempted.

The last zone is the car park and the paths, which is the least glamorous but possibly the most interesting. The team there will survey what lives in the cracks and edges, plants and tiny creatures that people never notice. You might be surprised how many species live in a patch of pavement.

A few words on equipment, since people always ask. Each team leader has a box with hand lenses, field guides, plastic tubs and a clipboard. If you've brought your own binoculars or a camera, you're welcome to use them, but please don't leave them lying about, because the park can't be responsible for anything that goes missing. Gloves are in the blue crate by the gate. Children are very welcome in the meadow and the car park teams, and our youngest recorder last year was five. She found a beetle that none of the experts had ever seen in the park, so never assume that experience is what counts.

Now, practical matters. The event starts at three o'clock this afternoon. Most of you will work until six, and then we'll have a break for supper, which is provided and is being served in the tea room. At eight o'clock there'll be a torchlit walk for bats and moths. Please note that the walk isn't suitable for small children, because the paths are uneven. Those who want to take part overnight will find tents in the picnic area, but you must bring your own sleeping bags.

Please download the BioBlitz app before you start. Take a photograph of everything you find, and the app will suggest what it is. But treat the suggestion as a first guess only. It's wrong about one time in five, particularly with moths and mosses. We have a team of experts, and they'll check the doubtful ones. What matters most is that you record the place and the time, because a species without a location is hardly any use to science.

Some of you have asked why we're doing this. There are two reasons. First, the park will be redeveloped in two years, and the council has promised that nothing rare will be bulldozed. But to protect a species, we need to know it's there. Second, a BioBlitz teaches people to look. When you've held a bumblebee that's covered in pollen, you don't walk past a flower in the same way again.

A word about safety. Please keep to the paths in the woodland, and don't enter the water. If you're stung, tell a team leader. And please don't touch the wild animals, even if they seem tame. Any questions? No? In that case, collect your badge from the table, choose your team, and let's get started.
Come in, Freya, Tariq. Sit down. I've seen your fieldwork plan, and I'd like to understand how you got to it. You're comparing invertebrates on green roofs with those at ground level, is that right?
Yes. Our research question is whether the number of species on a green roof is lower than on an equivalent patch of grass nearby.
We started with six roofs around the city, but only two of the building managers answered our emails.
That's the first lesson of fieldwork. Access is always the real problem. What happened with the others?
One said it was a health and safety issue. Another wanted us to pay for insurance, and two just never replied.
And the two you have?

One is on top of the library, which is a sedum roof, mostly low succulents. The other is above the new sports centre, and that one has meadow planting. The library roof is about six years old, and the sports centre roof is only two.
Right, so your two roofs differ in age and in planting. If you find fewer species on one than the other, you won't be able to say why.
We did worry about that, actually. Tariq thought we should just add a third roof, but there isn't time.
I'd still rather have three than two. But I do see that it won't fix the problem of age.

What it does is give you some idea of how variable roofs are. But I think you're better off stating plainly that you can only compare two roofs and treat the work as a case study. Don't try to claim a pattern for all green roofs.
That makes sense. Now, the ground-level sites. We were going to use the park next to the library.
Why that one?
It's close, so we can move equipment quickly between sites. But the park is mown every fortnight, whereas the roof is never mown.
Exactly, and mowing affects insects far more than most people expect. Is there an unmown area nearby?
There's a strip beside the railway, behind a fence, that nobody cuts. It's about twenty metres from the sports centre.
That sounds far more comparable. Can you get access?
I'll have to ask the rail company. I think that could take a month.
Then ask today. Now, your method. You mentioned pitfall traps.
Yes. We bury plastic cups in the ground, level with the surface, and leave them for a week. Insects and spiders that walk about on the surface fall in.
Fine, but on a roof you can't dig. What will you do about the substrate?
We've only got a few centimetres of soil on the library roof, so we can't bury a cup. We were thinking of using sticky traps, but that may harm more insects than we need.

What about pan traps? Coloured bowls filled with soapy water. They sit on the surface, they catch flying insects as well, and they're easy to set up. You can use the same traps at ground level, so the method is identical in each place.
That's cleverer. We'll need yellow, white and blue ones, I think.
Before we go on, have you thought about what happens to the insects? Pan traps kill what they catch, and the department's ethics committee will want to see that you've minimised that.
We'll empty the traps every twenty-four hours, so nothing sits in the soapy water for days.
Daily emptying is better, certainly, but it doubles your workload. Think about whether you can really commit to it, especially on a roof, where you'll need two people for safety.
We'd have to share it between the two of us and a friend. We'll ask a first-year, perhaps.
Fine, as long as they've been through the safety briefing too.
And how many traps per site?
Six. Two of each colour.
That's reasonable, but space them at least three metres apart, otherwise one trap will take insects that would have gone to the next.
And how long should the sampling go on?
A single week won't tell you much. Insects vary with the weather. Ideally you'd do three rounds, a fortnight apart. If you can only manage two, be honest about it.
Two will be all we can manage, because the term finishes in November.

Then plan two rounds, one in the first week of October, and one in the last. And weather matters, so record the temperature and rainfall for every day the traps are out. That information will explain some of the differences you find.
Is it a problem that we won't be able to identify everything to species?

Not at all. Group your insects at the level you can be confident with. Beetles, flies, bees, and so on. It's a legitimate approach as long as you explain what you did. What isn't acceptable is naming species you can't be sure of.
We'll ask the university's entomologist to check a sample of specimens.

Good. Then I think the main steps are clear. Send me the revised plan by Friday. Include the names of the sites, the dates, and a risk assessment for working on a roof. Please don't go onto either roof until I have seen that.
One more thing. Keep a field notebook with dates, weather and a sketch of each site. Your examiners will ask to see it.
Understood. Thank you very much.

In earlier lectures, we've talked about how cities change the places animals live. Today I'd like to look at something that is easy to forget, because we notice it so little ourselves, and that is noise. A city is a very loud place, and for birds, which communicate mainly by sound, noise isn't just an annoyance. It can affect whether they find a mate or defend a territory.

To see why this matters, think about what a song does. For most small birds, singing has two jobs. Males use it to announce that a territory is taken, so that rivals stay away without a fight, and they use it to advertise their quality to females. If neighbours can't hear the warning, there are more fights, and if females can't hear the advert, there are fewer matches. Both are costly, so any bird that can solve the noise problem has an advantage. The interesting question is how they do it.

I'll start with one of the best-known studies. In the early 2000s, two researchers working in the Dutch city of Leiden recorded great tits. That's Leiden, L-E-I-D-E-N. They compared birds in noisy streets with birds in quiet woodland outside the city. What they found was that the city birds sang at a higher pitch than the woodland birds. The explanation is simple. Traffic noise is mostly low-frequency, so a bird that sings at a higher pitch has a better chance of being heard above it.

A second strategy is volume. In Berlin, researchers studied nightingales, and found that the males sang louder on days when traffic was heavier. On quiet days, they sang more softly. That is exactly what you do yourself when you speak in a noisy café, and it's called the Lombard effect, after the French doctor who described it a century ago.

A third strategy is timing. In Sheffield, scientists noticed that robins living in the noisiest, brightest areas were singing at night, which is unusual, since traditionally they sing at dawn. The researchers suggested that the birds were singing when it was quieter, because the day was too noisy for the song to carry. Later work suggested that artificial light plays a part too, so it's likely that both factors contributed.

Now, you could say these birds are simply adapting, and that's good news. But there's a cost. Higher-pitched songs may be less attractive to females, because in some species, low notes signal a larger, healthier male. Singing louder uses more energy, and singing at night may cost the bird sleep. So adaptation isn't free.

One of the most striking pieces of evidence came, strangely enough, from the global pandemic. In spring 2020, traffic in San Francisco fell dramatically, and noise levels dropped to the levels last seen in the 1950s. Researchers who'd been studying white-crowned sparrows for decades were able to compare recordings made before and after. They found that during the quiet period, the birds sang more quietly, and the songs were of higher quality, with a wider range of frequencies. It seems that when the noise went away, the birds were free to sing the way they would naturally.

How do researchers actually measure these effects? The basic tool is a decibel meter, which records the sound level at the place where the bird is singing. Many teams also use automatic recorders left in the field for weeks, and then use software to pick out individual species. It's far more reliable than relying on human listeners, who tend to hear what they expect to hear.

So what can planners do? People often suggest planting trees and hedges beside roads. Unfortunately, vegetation absorbs only a small amount of noise, particularly low-frequency noise. It does help to hide the road from view, which makes people feel calmer, but for birds that doesn't matter. A more effective strategy is to deal with the source. One of the most useful measures is lower speed limits, because the noise from tyres and engines rises quickly as speed increases. Another is to resurface roads. Quieter road surfaces, which are made with a particular mix of stone and bitumen, can reduce the noise by several decibels.

I should add that researchers disagree about how much of the change is learned and how much is inherited. In some species, young birds simply copy the higher songs they hear from their neighbours, which means a change can spread within a few years. In others, the evidence points to birds with naturally higher voices doing better in cities. Probably both processes are at work, and sorting them out is an active area of research.

Of course, none of this means that cities are hopeless for birds. Many species do well in them, and some even do better than they do in the countryside. What I'd like you to take away is that noise is a form of pollution, and it affects more than just human health. Next week we'll look at light, which turns out to be just as important.
Hi there, you've reached the Tandem Table. This is Bronwyn.
Oh, hello, Bronwyn. I found your website last night, and I wondered whether I could still join the language exchange. I'm new in Melbourne, and I don't know many people yet.
Of course you can. We take new members at any time. Would you like me to fill in the registration form while we talk? It only takes a few minutes.
That would be great.
Lovely. First, your surname, please.
It's Kowalczyk. It's a Polish name, so it's tricky. K-O-W-A-L-C-Z-Y-K.
Thanks, I'll read that back later. And which language can you offer to a partner? You told me on the website form that you were interested in more than one.

Well, Polish was my first language, because my parents came from Gdańsk. But honestly, it's not a language many people here want to learn. I grew up in Germany, so my German is much better, and I think that's what people would find more useful. So put down German.
German it is. Now, which language would you like to learn?

I'd originally thought about Korean, because I watch a lot of television in Korean. But I'm going to have a work trip next year, so I think I'd better do something practical. I'd like to learn Japanese.
Japanese, great. We have lots of Japanese speakers who want to improve their German, and it's one of our most popular pairs. Where's the trip to?
Osaka, in the spring. I'd assumed it would be Tokyo, which is where our head office is, but the project is actually in Osaka. So I've got about seven months.
That's plenty of time to learn the basics. And which evening would suit you? We run sessions on Tuesday, Wednesday and Thursday.
I play football on Tuesdays, so that's out. I'd prefer Thursday, because I finish work early, but I'm told the Thursday sessions are mostly advanced speakers, and I'd feel out of my depth.
That's right, you're better off with a group at your own level. The Wednesday sessions are mixed, and they're much more relaxed. I'd put you down for Wednesday.
Wednesday it is, then. Where do you meet?

In the Carlton Library, in the meeting room at the back. We used to meet in a café on Lygon Street, but it got too noisy, and the library lets us have the room free of charge. There's tea and coffee, and a few biscuits, but we ask everyone to bring a small contribution.
That's a nice idea. And how much does it cost to belong?
The standard membership is forty-five dollars a term. But we have a concession rate for students and pensioners, which is thirty dollars. Are you a student?
I'm doing a postgraduate degree part-time, so yes, I think I qualify.
Then it's thirty dollars. Please bring your student card on your first night so we can check.
Of course. How do you decide who's paired with whom?

Everyone fills in a short profile when they join. We don't match people by age or by job. We match by interests, because people talk more freely when they care about the same things. If we match a twenty-year-old with a retired engineer who loves football, they'll do very well, as long as they both like football.
That's reassuring. I do love football, as you've probably gathered.

I'll make a note of it. Between sessions, our members keep in touch through a chat group. We used to use WhatsApp, but a lot of members complained about privacy, so now we use Telegram. Do you have it?
I don't, but I can download it tonight.
Perfect. I'll send you the link by email. Now, the next group begins on the sixth of March. That's a Wednesday, so it will suit you well. We start at half past six and finish at eight.
The sixth of March. I'll put it in my calendar.

One last piece of advice. People often arrive a little nervous, because they think their language isn't good enough. Please don't worry. Everyone here is learning, so no one will judge you, and the first session is mostly games and introductions.
That does make me feel better. Thank you very much, Bronwyn.
Not at all. We'll see you on the sixth, Stefan.

Kia ora, everyone, and welcome. Please grab a cup of tea if you haven't already, and find a seat. I'm Moana Heke, and I coordinate the exchange programme here in Dunedin. Tonight is for the host families, which means you, and I'd like to explain what to expect over the next three months, and what we'd ask of you. Don't worry, nobody has failed at this yet.

Let's begin with the arrivals. The students will land at Dunedin airport on the second of February. A few of you may have heard that the flight comes in at noon. It's actually delayed this year, so they won't reach the airport until a little after four. I'll send you a message to confirm. The programme will arrange the bus from the airport, and the students will arrive at the school hall, where you'll collect them.

Now, how many students are there? We have eighteen this year, from three schools in Japan, and each will stay with one family. Some of you asked whether you could take two students, so that they could keep each other company. We've decided against that, because we find that two students from the same country tend to talk to each other, rather than to you, and it defeats the purpose of the exchange.

The students are aged fifteen to seventeen. Most have studied English for several years, but they've mostly done it in classrooms, and the first week can be exhausting. Don't be alarmed if your student seems quiet at first. They're listening very hard. Speak at normal speed, but try to use simple sentences, and don't be afraid of repeating yourself. If you use slang, explain it, because a student who says "Sweet as" may not know what it means.

A few practical matters. First, meals. Please do ask what your student likes. Many Japanese teenagers aren't used to a cooked breakfast, and they might prefer rice or toast. Don't make a fuss, and don't assume that because they're polite, they enjoy everything. It's better to find out in the first week. You'll receive a small allowance to cover the cost.

Next, transport. Most of you live a short distance from school, but a few are on the other side of the harbour. We can arrange a bus pass for those students, which you can collect from the school office. Please don't drive them unless it's raining heavily. Part of the point is learning to travel independently.

Third, going out in the evening. We ask that the students are home by nine o'clock on school nights, and by ten on weekends. These rules apply to your own children as well, I suppose, but exchange students are in a foreign country, and we have a duty of care. If they're going to be late, they must phone you, and you must have their number.

Next, the internet. Many families ask about this. Students will want to keep in touch with their parents, and I think that's perfectly reasonable. But I'd suggest agreeing on a set time each day, so that the student isn't on their phone all evening, speaking Japanese. Some families set a rule that phones are put away at meals, and that works well.

Money is another question. The students bring their own spending money, so you're not expected to pay for outings or souvenirs, though a family trip to the beach will always be appreciated. Please don't give them money. If a student runs out, they should contact me.

Finally, illness. If your student is sick, don't wait. Phone the school first, and then the programme office, and we'll arrange a doctor. All the students have insurance, and the school nurse will help with the paperwork.

I'd like to end by saying what you will get out of this. Of course the students learn English. But host families often tell me they learn just as much, about patience, about their own culture, and about how strange the ordinary can look through someone else's eyes. One family told me last year that their student had made them realise how little they knew about their own city. They went to the museum together for the first time in twenty years.
Now, do we have questions? Yes, the woman in the green cardigan.
Amara, Ben, come in. I've got your draft proposal here, and I wanted to go through it with you. It's about language exchange, isn't it?
Yes. We're interested in whether students who do a tandem exchange, where two people teach each other their own languages, make faster progress than those who only attend classes.
We both took Spanish at university, and I think I only really learned it after I started meeting a friend from Mexico every week.

That's a good starting point, but it's also exactly the kind of personal experience that can mislead you. Plenty of people feel they learned more through conversation, but they might simply have been more motivated. How will you handle that?
We wondered about that. We thought we could compare two groups of first-year Spanish students, one with a weekly exchange partner, and one without.
And how will you decide who goes in which group?
We were going to let them choose, but that would mean the keener students end up in the exchange group.

Precisely. If you let people choose, you'll have no way of knowing whether any difference is because of the exchange, or because of the kind of person who chooses it. I'd draw names from a hat, or use a random number generator. It's not always easy to do, but it's the only way to be sure.
The department might not like us deciding who gets a partner, though. Some students might feel it's unfair.
Then offer the exchange to the second group at the end of the term. That's perfectly standard, and it's fair.
That's a great idea. Now, what about the test? We wanted to give a speaking test at the start and again at the end.
Sensible. But who will mark it?
Both of us, I suppose.

That's a problem. If you know which students had a partner, you may be biased in their favour without realising. Ideally, the marker shouldn't know which group a student is in. Could you ask someone from the language department to do it?
I could ask Dr Reyes. She taught our Spanish course, and she's very helpful.
Good. Make sure she uses a standard scale, such as the university's own speaking descriptors. Now, how long will the project run?
Ten weeks. The students will meet their partners once a week, for an hour.
You should also expect some students to drop out. If twenty start and fifteen finish, can you still compare the groups?
We hadn't really thought about that. We'll recruit a few extra at the beginning, to be safe.
Good idea. Record who leaves and why, because if the less motivated students leave the exchange group, your results could look better than they really are.
That's a subtle point. We'll keep a note.
And how will you record how often they actually meet? In my experience, partners start with great enthusiasm and stop turning up after a month.
We'd planned to ask the students to keep a diary.

Diaries are unreliable. People forget, or they fill in a week's entries on the final day. Could the partners sign a short log sheet each time they meet? It's a small thing, but it gives you real data.
Yes, that's far better. We'll make a simple form.
Have you thought about consent? Students must know that they might end up in the group without a partner, and that taking part is voluntary.
We've written an information sheet, and everyone signs a consent form before the first test.
