Good. And make clear that their results won't count towards their course marks, otherwise some will be anxious and others won't take it seriously.
Dr Reyes mentioned that as well. We'll put it in bold on the first page.
Then there's the question of the partners themselves. Where will you find native speakers of Spanish?
The university has an international society, and a lot of Spanish-speaking students are members. We've contacted the president, and she's promised thirty volunteers.
Make sure they're also learning English, so the exchange is genuinely two-way. If one side is only helping, they'll lose interest.
We'd already thought of that, and the volunteers have all said they want to improve their English.
Excellent. Now, let me ask about what you expect to find. What's your hypothesis?
That the exchange group will improve more. But we haven't decided how much more.

Then I'd leave that open. Don't guess a number. And be ready for the opposite result. If the exchange group doesn't do better, that's still an interesting finding, and you should report it in the same way.
Right. One more thing. Our schedule is very tight. Could we start with just the first group, then add the second later if we have time?

I'd rather you did a smaller study properly than a bigger one badly. Cut the numbers if you must, but keep the random allocation and the blind marking. They're the two features that make your work convincing.
Agreed. We'll send you a revised version by Monday.
Good. And remember to describe the limitations honestly. That's what separates a strong report from a mediocre one.

Good afternoon. In the last lecture, we considered whether children and adults learn languages in the same way. Today I want to take a more practical approach, and ask what actually helps a person to learn a second language, and why immersion, living in the language, seems to be so effective. It's a question with considerable consequences, because how we answer it determines how we organise classes, exchanges and even whole school systems.

Let me start with a famous experiment. In 1965, in a suburb called St Lambert, near Montreal, a group of English-speaking parents persuaded their local school to teach their children entirely in French from the first day. This was the beginning of the immersion movement in Canada. The children were taught maths, science and history in French, and they were not taught about French as a subject. By the end of primary school, they spoke French far better than children in conventional classes, and their English had not suffered. That is a remarkable result.

One early explanation came from the linguist Stephen Krashen. He argued that we acquire language mainly through understanding messages, and that what learners need most is what he called comprehensible input. That is language that is slightly above their current level. He expressed it as a formula: i plus one, where i is the learner's present level, and the plus one is the next step up. If the input is too easy, nothing is learned. If it is too hard, nothing is understood.

Krashen's idea was very influential, but it soon ran into a difficulty, and the difficulty came from the Canadian classrooms themselves. A researcher called Merrill Swain studied children in French immersion, and found something puzzling. They understood French beautifully. But when they spoke and wrote, they made basic mistakes that never went away. So input alone, she concluded, was not enough.

Swain's explanation, which she published in 1985, was that learners also need to produce language, and in particular to be pushed to say things that they can't yet say easily. She called this pushed output. When you try to say something and realise you don't have the words, you notice the gap, and that makes you pay attention the next time you hear the missing word.

Around the same time, Michael Long proposed that the most important thing is neither input nor output on its own, but the interaction between people. When two people talk and one of them doesn't understand, they ask for clarification, repeat, rephrase, or slow down. Long called this the negotiation of meaning. The conversation breaks down, and it is repaired, and in the repair the learner receives exactly the input they need.

A fourth idea, from Richard Schmidt, is that none of this works unless the learner actually notices the feature in question. Schmidt argued that learners must notice a form in the input before they can learn it. You can hear a past tense a hundred times, but unless you notice it, it may pass you by.

Does all this mean that going abroad is automatically the best way to learn? Not necessarily. Studies of students who spend a year overseas show large gains on average, but also wide variation. Those who made friends among local people improved far more than those who lived and socialised with fellow countrymen. In other words, the quantity of contact matters less than its quality.

How does all this apply to language exchanges? Quite directly. Imagine you're speaking Japanese with a native speaker. If you say a sentence incorrectly, a good partner won't stop and lecture you. They'll say the correct sentence back to you, in a natural way, and carry on. That technique is called a recast, and research suggests it is one of the most effective forms of feedback, provided the learner notices it.

But exchanges have weaknesses. The first is that the stronger language tends to take over. In most cities, one partner has a better command of English than the other has of their target language, and the conversation drifts into English. It's easy and comfortable, and the learner thinks they've had a wonderful evening, but they've actually spoken very little of the language they came to practise.

There's a fairly simple solution. Many successful exchanges adopt a firm rule: thirty minutes in one language, then thirty minutes in the other, with a timer. It feels artificial at first, but it keeps the balance fair, and it forces each person to be both the learner and the expert.

Finally, I'd like you to think about what this tells us about motivation. Immersion and exchange work partly because the learner wants to understand a real person, not just pass a test. That desire to communicate may be the most powerful tool of all. Next week we'll turn to the role of age, and ask whether it really is too late for adults.
Kauri Street Careers Centre, Gemma speaking. How can I help you?
Oh, hi there. I'm hoping to book a place on one of your interview workshops. I've got my first proper interview in a couple of weeks and, to be honest, I'm feeling a bit nervous about it.
Well, you've come to the right place. That's exactly what our Interview Essentials sessions are for. Are you a current student?
Yes, I'm in my final year at the university.
Lovely. Let me take a few details, then. Can I have your name, please?
It's Ravi Whitcombe, and that's spelled W-H-I-T-C-O-M-B-E.
Thanks, Ravi. And a mobile number, in case we need to change anything at short notice?
Okay, so that's 021 555 0178. Now, which degree are you doing?
A Bachelor of Science, at first, but I switched across to Commerce in my second year, so that's what it will say on my certificate.
Right, Commerce. And what sort of company is the interview with? It helps us choose practice questions that are relevant.

Um, a freight business, I think. The email called it a shipping company, but hang on, I'll check. Yes, here it is. Harcourt Logistics. So it's a logistics company, really, and the job is in their finance team.

Perfect. We've got a good set of questions for that kind of role. Now, the workshop runs on Tuesday evenings and Thursday evenings, but I'm afraid Tuesday is already full this month. I've only got spaces left on Thursday.
Thursday is fine. That's actually better for me, because I have a lab on Tuesdays.
Great. It used to start at quarter past six, but we've moved it earlier, so it's now 5.45. That way people can catch the later bus home.
That's good to know. And is there a fee? I'm on a pretty tight budget at the moment.
It's normally 25 dollars, but for current students it's 15, and you can pay on the night. Cash or card, either is fine.

That's very reasonable, thank you. I was half expecting it to cost a lot more, since it's evening work. What actually happens in the session? Is it mostly listening, or do we have to do things ourselves?

There are two parts. For the first hour, our adviser, Tracey, talks through the kinds of questions you're likely to be asked and how to structure your answers. After a short break, you'll do a short practice interview in front of a small group, and everyone gives you feedback. Most people find that second half a bit scary, but also the most useful.
Oh dear. Well, I suppose that's the point. Where do we meet? Is it the main hall?
No, the hall is being repainted. You'll be in the Rimu Room, on the second floor, at the end of the corridor. There's a lift if you need it.
Rimu Room, got it. Should I bring my CV?

Not this time, we already have it from the careers portal. What you do need is a copy of the job advertisement, so that Tracey can see exactly what the employer is asking for. You can print it, or just show it on your phone.
No problem. I'll print it out. I should probably highlight the main points too.
That's an excellent idea. Right, last thing. We'll send you a confirmation letter, so could I have your postcode?
It's 3216. No, sorry, I always mix them up. It's 3261.
3261, thank you. That's the postcode for Fairfield, isn't it?
That's right. I'm in a flat just behind the shopping centre.

Wonderful. You'll get the letter within two working days, and an email reminder the afternoon before. If you need to cancel, please let us know at least 24 hours ahead, because there's a waiting list.
Understood. Thanks so much, Gemma. You've made me feel a lot calmer already.
That's what we're here for. Good luck with the interview, Ravi, and we'll see you on Thursday.

Good morning, everyone, and welcome to Dunmore Regional Council. My name is Helen Castellan, and I coordinate our graduate recruitment. Thank you all for coming, and congratulations on getting this far. Before the day properly begins, I'd like to run through how it will work, so that nothing comes as a surprise.

First, a quick word about where you are. Most of you will have come in through the main doors on the ground floor and been pointed upstairs. If you haven't signed in yet, please do that now. Some candidates in the past have tried to sign in with the security staff, but they only deal with deliveries and contractors. The sign-in desk is in the lobby on the third floor, just beside the lifts, and you'll find your name badge there as well. Please wear it all day, because it's how our staff know who you are.

Now, timing. The day was originally planned to run until half past four, but we've shortened it, and you'll all be free to leave at four o'clock. That means those of you with a long journey home should miss the worst of the traffic. We will be on schedule, so please don't wander off during the breaks.

Next, lunch. In earlier years we gave everyone a sandwich box, but a lot of it was wasted, so this year we're trying something different. Each of you has been given a voucher, which you'll find in your welcome pack, and you can use it at the Harbour Cafe on the ground floor. It covers a main meal and a drink. Of course, if you've brought your own food, that's absolutely fine, and the staff kitchen has a fridge you're welcome to use.

A few practical points about phones. I know many of you will want to check messages, and I understand that. But during the exercises, phones must be switched off and left in your bags. You may use them during the coffee and lunch breaks, and I'd ask you to keep the volume low in the corridors, because there are staff working on this floor.

Now, what happens afterwards? I'm sorry to say that we can't give results on the day. The panel will meet tomorrow morning, and every candidate, successful or not, will receive an email from me within a week. If you'd like detailed feedback on how you performed, you can ask for it in your reply, and one of the assessors will send you some written comments. I'd encourage you to do that, whatever the outcome, because it's the quickest way to improve.
Right, let me tell you about the shape of the day and where each part takes place. You've all got a map of the third floor in your pack, but I'll go through it.

We start with welcome drinks, and these are served in the Atrium, which is the big open space you walked through when you arrived. Do help yourselves, and do talk to each other. Several of our current staff will be there too, and they were all in your position not long ago, so they're happy to answer questions.

At about ten o'clock you'll move to the written exercise. This takes place in the Library, which is the quiet room at the far end of the corridor. You'll be given a short briefing paper and forty minutes to write a recommendation. There are no trick questions, we just want to see how clearly you can set out your thinking.

After a short coffee break comes the group task. For this, you'll be divided into teams of five, and each team will work in the Innovation Lab, which is the glass room with the round tables. I should mention that it's often noisy in there, so please speak up, but don't talk over your teammates. The assessors will be watching how you work together, not who talks the most.

After lunch, the interviews themselves. These are held in Room 4, which is the small meeting room just next to the lifts. Each interview lasts about twenty-five minutes, and you'll be seen by two members of the panel. You'll be told your time slot on the morning, and while you wait you can sit in the Cedar Room, which has comfortable chairs and plenty of magazines. Please don't use that time to revise frantically; honestly, you'll do better if you relax.

Finally, at about quarter to three, there's a tour of the building, led by one of our graduate trainees. That starts in the Boardroom, which, as you'd expect, is the room with the very long table on the corner. It's not part of the assessment, so you can ask whatever you like, and many candidates tell us it's their favourite part of the day.

One last thing. If you have any special requirements, such as dietary needs or help with access, please tell me or one of the staff in blue lanyards. We would much rather know now than discover a problem later. And if you feel nervous, that's completely normal. Everyone here has been through an assessment day, including me. Remember that we want you to do well, and we've designed the day so that you can show us your best.
Right, if there are no questions, let's head down to the Atrium for coffee. Please follow me, and don't forget your badges.
Come in, both of you. Joel, Mei, sit down. So, I understand you want to talk about your presentation on how graduates prepare for first interviews.
That's right, Mrs Adeyemi. We've done the survey, and we've got the results, but we're not completely sure how to present them.
And we hit a couple of problems on the way, so we wanted your advice before we go further.
Of course. Remind me how you collected the data. I thought you were going to ask employers.
That was our first plan. We emailed about forty companies, and only three replied, and two of those said they were too busy.
So we switched to recent graduates instead. We contacted people from last year's cohort through the alumni network, and a hundred and twenty answered.
That's a good response rate. Was it a problem that you changed direction?
I was worried about it at first, but in the end I think it works better. Graduates remember what it felt like, whereas employers tend to say what they think candidates ought to do.
That's a fair point, and you should say so in your introduction, because the examiners will want to know why you made the change.
Okay, I'll add that. Now, something that really surprised me was how many people said they'd only practised answers in their heads. Barely a quarter had said anything out loud before the interview.
Yes, I'd assumed most would have rehearsed with a friend or a tutor. It turns out people feel silly doing it.
That doesn't surprise me at all. But it's a striking result, so I'd put it near the start of your findings. Was there much difference between courses?
Not really. Engineers and arts students were almost the same. The only group that stood out was nursing, because they have practice interviews built into the course.

Mm, that makes sense. Now, one thing I wanted to ask. In your draft, you recommend the STAR method, where candidates describe the situation, the task, the action and the result. Have you thought about its weaknesses?
I think it's very useful. It gives people a structure when they're panicking.
It is useful, but I've seen candidates stick to it so rigidly that they sound like they're reading from a script. Interviewers notice that. So I'd say use it as a loose frame, not a rulebook.
That's a good point. We could say candidates should practise it until it's natural, rather than just memorise it.
I'd also like to talk about the length of the questionnaire. Some respondents said it was too long, and quite a few stopped halfway through.
How many questions did you include?
Twenty-eight. We were thinking of cutting it to about fifteen if we do a follow-up.
I'd go lower than that, if you can. Anything over ten tends to lose people. But you've already done the survey, so for now just describe the limitation honestly in your report.
Right, we'll do that.
Now, the most interesting part. What did people say went wrong in their interviews?
The most common complaint was that they didn't know enough about the company. Nearly half said they'd only looked at the home page.
And the second biggest was not asking any questions at the end. People said they froze and said, "No, I think you've covered everything."
Both very typical. What about lateness? I'd have expected that to come up.
It did, but only a few people mentioned it. Most had allowed plenty of time. And hardly anyone said they'd spoken too fast, which I thought would be more common.
We also asked about clothes, but nobody really thought that had mattered.
Good. Then let's talk about how you structure the presentation. I've read the outline you sent, and I have a comment on each section.
Great. Let's start with the introduction.
Your introduction is fine in content, but it's far too long. You spend four slides on the background, and the audience will want to reach the results. I'd squeeze it to one.
Okay. What about the method section?

That one needs the opposite approach. It's too thin at the moment. You don't say how you chose the participants or how you tested the questions, and examiners will definitely ask. A little more detail there would help.
That's fair. We did a pilot with ten people, but we forgot to mention it.
Exactly the sort of thing to include. Now, your findings. The charts are good, but you've got a table on slide seven that nobody will be able to read from the back of the room. Turn it into a chart.
That's easy enough to fix.
And the recommendations. These are sensible, but at the moment they're just a list. I'd like you to link each one to a specific finding, so that it's clear where the advice comes from.
Oh, that would make it much stronger.
It would. Finally, think about rehearsing. Do the presentation aloud, in front of someone, at least twice. Given what your survey found, it would be a little ironic if you didn't.
We'll practise on each other tonight. Thank you, Mrs Adeyemi.
Yes, this has helped a lot.
You're welcome. Send me the revised slides by Friday, and I'll take another look.

Good afternoon, everyone. Today I want to look at something that every one of us has experienced, and that most of us underestimate: the first impression. Specifically, I want to ask what happens in the opening minutes of a job interview, and what the research tells us about how candidates should prepare for them.

Let me begin with a well-known type of study, often described as thin-slice research. The idea is simple. Researchers record a full interview, then cut it down to a tiny fragment, and ask observers to judge the candidate from that alone. In one early version of this study, the clips lasted thirty seconds. Later researchers asked whether even that was necessary, and they found that observers could form a confident judgement from clips lasting just 20 seconds.

Now, here is the striking part. When these quick judgements were compared with the scores given by interviewers who had sat through the complete interview, the two were remarkably close. In other words, the first few seconds appear to predict the final result, at least much of the time. That is uncomfortable for anyone who believes interviews are won by the clever answers that come later.

You might wonder what observers were actually responding to, especially as the clips were silent. Several cues were tested. Eye contact, which you would naturally expect to matter, turned out to be less important than people assumed. Facial expression mattered, but it wasn't the strongest signal either. The cue that most consistently influenced the ratings was the candidate's posture. Candidates who sat upright but relaxed were rated as more competent, even though observers couldn't hear a word they said.

So why do first impressions stick so firmly? Part of the explanation lies in how interviewers behave after the first few minutes. Once they've formed a view, they tend to look for evidence that supports their initial judgement, and to ignore anything that contradicts it. Psychologists call this confirmation bias. It's not a sign of laziness or dishonesty; it's simply how human attention works. An interviewer who has decided that a candidate seems nervous will interpret a pause as a lack of knowledge, whereas the same pause from a candidate who looked calm will be seen as thoughtfulness.

Organisations are aware of this problem, and many have tried to reduce its effects. The most widely adopted solution is the structured interview. Every candidate is asked the same questions in the same order, and answers are scored against agreed criteria. The evidence suggests that structured interviews predict job performance much better than informal conversations do. They don't remove first impressions entirely, but they limit how far a good or bad impression can distort the final decision.

Another strategy is to use more than one interviewer. A panel of three is less likely to share the same bias than a single person, because each member notices different things. But I should add that panels bring their own difficulties. Candidates often find them more intimidating, and one forceful member can still sway the others.

Let me turn now to what all this means for candidates. The practical advice that follows from the research is, I think, quite reassuring, because most of it is about preparation rather than personality.

First, timing. Many people believe they should arrive as early as possible, and some turn up half an hour before their slot. But arriving that early can make you more anxious, and it can be awkward for the receptionist. Most career advisers recommend arriving about ten minutes early. That gives you time to settle, but not enough time to start worrying.

Second, preparation about the organisation. Many candidates in surveys say they only read the home page. A far better source is the annual report, because it explains what the organisation is proud of, where it is struggling and what its plans are. If you can refer to something specific from it, you immediately stand out, because very few people do.

Third, evidence. Interviewers are far more convinced by examples than by claims. If you say you work well in a team, they will take it with a pinch of salt. If you describe a particular project, they will believe you. So I suggest preparing three short stories from your past experience, each of which can be adapted to a range of questions. Practise telling them aloud, because the research shows that rehearsed speech sounds noticeably more fluent than speech produced on the spot.

Finally, think about how you end. Interviewers often remember the last few minutes almost as well as the first. When you're asked whether you have any questions, don't say no. Ask something that shows you've been listening. And when you leave, thank the panel and, if you can, use each person's name. It's a small gesture, but it signals confidence and courtesy, which are exactly the qualities the first impression was trying to measure.

To sum up, the first impression matters, but it is not destiny. Candidates who prepare thoroughly, who practise aloud and who give the panel something concrete to remember can change how an interview unfolds. In the next lecture, we'll look at how these ideas apply to online interviews, where the first impression is made through a screen. Thank you.
Tamar Quay Workspace, this is Kirsty. How can I help?
Hi, Kirsty. I'm after some information about your memberships. I've been working from my kitchen table for about two years now, and I'm starting to go a bit stir-crazy.
Ha, you're not the first person to tell me that. Most of our members started out at home. Would you like to sign up over the phone? It saves you filling in the form online.
That would be great, thanks.
Lovely. Can I start with your name?
Marcus Lindqvist. That's L-I-N-D-Q-V-I-S-T.
Thanks, Marcus. And what do you do for a living? We like to know, because we try to seat people so that they won't disturb each other with phone calls.

I'm a freelance illustrator, mostly children's books and some magazine work. I used to be a graphic designer in an agency, but I went solo a couple of years ago. So it's very quiet work. No calls, just a lot of drawing.

Perfect, you'll fit in beautifully. Now, there are two kinds of membership. A dedicated desk is yours alone, and you can leave your things on it overnight. A hot desk means you sit wherever there's a free space each day, and you clear it when you leave.
I was thinking dedicated, because I've got quite a lot of equipment, but what does that cost?

Hmm. That's more than I'd like to pay. I do have a decent bag, and there are lockers, aren't there?

Then I'll go for the hot desk, I think. It makes more sense while I'm still working out how often I'll come in.
Good choice. And how many days a week do you expect to use it? You can come in as often as you like, but the price depends on whether you choose a part-time or full-time plan.

Three days, then. That's our part-time plan, and it comes to 180 dollars a month, with the first month's fee taken on your start date.
Okay, so 180. That seems fair. When could I start?
We're quite quiet at the moment, so you could start as soon as next week. Is Monday the 4th of March any good?
It's the 4th, is it? Then yes, 4 March is perfect. I'll have finished a job by then.
Great, I've put that down. You also get some free time in our meeting rooms every month. Last year it was five hours, but we've increased it, so it's now ten hours, which you book through the app.
That's useful. I sometimes need to meet publishers, and my kitchen isn't exactly impressive.
Well, ours has a nice view of the river, so that should help. One more thing. We ask for a deposit for the key card, which you get back when you leave. It's 20 dollars.
That's fine. Can I pay that on my first day?
Yes, no problem. Now, just a couple of questions for our records. How did you hear about us? We like to know which of our efforts are working.
I thought I'd seen you in the newspaper, but actually it was a podcast about freelancing. The host mentioned that she'd used your space while she was setting up. I've been meaning to ring ever since.
Brilliant, I'll note that. And finally, we need an emergency contact, in case there's an accident in the building. It can be anyone who lives locally.
Um, my brother lives in Hobart, which is a bit far away. My sister is in Launceston, though, so she'd be better. Her name's Annika.
That's fine. I'll put your sister down, and take her number when you come in.
Perfect. Is there anything I need to bring on the first day?

Just some photo ID and the deposit. We'll give you a tour, show you where the kitchen and the lockers are, and introduce you to a few people. Most of our members are friendly, and there's a lunch every Wednesday if you feel like joining in.
That sounds wonderful. Thanks very much, Kirsty. I'm really looking forward to it.
Our pleasure. See you on the 4th, Marcus.

Good morning, everyone, and welcome to Pinecrest Digital. For those of you I haven't met, I'm Ailsa Drummond, and I look after staff onboarding. I know it feels slightly odd to be welcomed by a face on a screen, and some of you are probably sitting in your living rooms right now, but we've done this for a long time, and I hope that by the end of this session you'll feel a little more settled.

I'd like to cover four things: how the company keeps in touch, what to do in your first week, the equipment we help you with, and the tools we use. Please type questions in the chat as we go, and I'll try to answer them at the end.

First, how we keep in touch. Everybody joins a whole-company meeting. For years that happened every week, but people said it took up too much time, so it's now every fortnight, on a Thursday. It lasts about forty minutes, and it's recorded, so if you can't attend, you'll catch up afterwards. Besides that, each team has its own meeting, which is run by your team leader, and the schedule is up to them.

Now, your first week. On the first morning you'll be sent a welcome email with a list of tasks. The most important, and the one I always ask people to do first, is to set up two-factor authentication on your account. It takes about five minutes, and it protects company data, so it can't wait. After that, you can personalise your profile, add a photo, and so on, but those things are less urgent. Your team leader will then introduce you to your buddy, who's an experienced colleague, and you'll have a short chat with them every day for the first month.

A word about cameras. I know that's a sensitive topic for some people. In small team meetings, we ask that you switch your camera on, because it makes conversation so much easier. But in the big all-company meetings, or in training sessions, it's completely up to you. Nobody will think any less of you if you leave it off.

Now, equipment. Pinecrest provides you with a laptop, and we'll courier it to you before your start date. Beyond that, we offer an allowance so you can make your working space comfortable. You can claim for a proportion of your broadband costs every month. You can also claim up to 200 dollars towards a monitor, which most people find makes a big difference. Chairs, however, we don't pay for, because it's difficult to say which ones are suitable, but we can arrange for you to borrow one from our office if you'd like. And I'm afraid snacks and coffee aren't covered, however tempting. There's also a small day-pass budget for coworking spaces, but your team leader has to approve it in advance.

Finally, the tools. We use quite a few, and it can feel overwhelming, so let me explain what each one is for. You'll hear people say 'ping me on Beacon'. Beacon is our messaging system, and it's the best place for quick questions. If you have something that needs a thoughtful answer, send an email instead, but for anything fast, use Beacon.

For project work, we use Taskboard. That's where every project's deadlines live, and it shows who is doing what, so you can always check where things stand without bothering anybody. If you want to see when something is due, look there first.

For writing, we've got Notebook. It's a shared document space. Meeting notes go there, and so do plans and policies. The rule is simple: if a decision's been made, it should be written down in Notebook, so everyone can find it later.

You'll also meet Huddle, which is our video system, and Loop, which is for sharing files with clients. Most of you won't need Loop for a while, and Huddle you'll pick up in minutes, so I won't dwell on either.
Passwords are kept in Vault. Please don't store them in a spreadsheet, or worse, on a sticky note, however convenient it seems. Vault generates strong ones and fills them in for you.

And last, a tool called Pulse. It's a very short anonymous survey, sent every month. It asks how you're feeling about workload and about the team, and nobody can see who said what. The results go straight to senior managers, and they've changed things because of it, so please do answer it honestly.

That's everything from me. A couple of small points before questions. Please don't feel you have to be online all day, because we don't measure presence, we measure what gets done. And if you feel isolated, tell your buddy or your team leader, because it's very common in the first few months, and there are simple things we can do. Now, who would like to go first with a question?
Hello, Sophie. Hello, Kwame. Come in and sit down. Your project on remote teams, how's it going?
Quite well, thank you, Dr Farrow. We've now interviewed five teams, and we've got a lot of material.
But we're still deciding how to organise it, so we hoped you could give us some advice.
Of course. Before we get to that, remind me why you chose interviews. I thought you were going to run a survey.
That was the original plan, but with only five teams it wouldn't have given us anything meaningful.
Right, and also we really wanted to know why things happen, not just whether they do. A survey can't tell you that.
Yes, I think that's a sound justification. Mention it in the method section. So, tell me about the teams.

Well, the first was a design studio with about twelve people in three countries. Their most unusual habit is that they record almost every meeting, even small ones, and people watch them later at double speed.
Interesting. And does it work?
They say so. It means nobody misses anything, and people in different time zones don't feel left out.
The second team was a call centre. That was very different. The manager phones every single member, individually, every morning, just for five minutes.
Every morning? That sounds exhausting.
She said it was, but the staff turnover is the lowest in the company, so she keeps doing it.
The third was a software firm, and there the biggest issue was time zones. Their developers are in Europe and Australia, so the team only has two hours a day when everybody's awake.
Do they cope?
They do, mainly because they've got very clear written processes, so most of the work doesn't depend on live conversation.

The fourth was a charity, and that one surprised me. Most of the people on the team had never actually met each other. They'd worked together for three years, entirely online, and had never been in the same room.
That's quite remarkable. How did they feel about that?
Pretty relaxed, actually. One of them said that she knew her colleagues' voices better than she knew most of her neighbours'.

And finally a research lab, where roles change every month. Whoever chairs the meeting this month won't do so next month, and the same applies to taking notes. It keeps everyone engaged, because everyone has to take their turn.
It sounds as though you've collected a very rich set of cases. I'd be interested to know whether you noticed any pattern in how the teams described their own problems.
Mostly they talked about loneliness and about interruptions at home, not about the technology. Nobody mentioned software at all, which I found rather striking.
Yes, even the team with the worst connection said it was a minor inconvenience compared with not knowing what their colleagues were doing.
That fits what the literature says, so draw the link explicitly in your discussion. Now, you said there were problems with the interviews.
Yes. We intended to record all of them, and we asked each participant for permission. Two people refused, one because of company policy, so we ended up taking notes by hand.
That's not unusual. As long as you explain it in your method, it won't weaken your work. But there's something else I want to ask. How did you find these five teams?
Through a business network. We emailed the group, and managers volunteered their teams.

I thought so. And that's the real weakness in your sample. Teams volunteered by their managers are almost certainly the ones that are doing well. You need to acknowledge that your sample is likely to favour success, and be careful about what you conclude.
That's fair. We can't claim to show what causes failure, only what successful teams happen to do.
Exactly. Now, on the matter of time zones, Sophie, you mentioned you thought that was the biggest difficulty?

I did, at first, but after the interviews, I've changed my mind. The teams with overlapping hours coped just fine. What seemed to make a difference was whether people trusted each other to deliver work without being watched.
I like that. Make it a major theme of your discussion. Is there anything you're unsure about in the data?
Yes, one thing. The call centre manager said the daily calls were popular, but two of her staff told us privately that they found them a bit intrusive. We're not sure how to handle that.
That's an interesting discrepancy. I wouldn't ignore it. Could you contact the call centre again and ask a few follow-up questions? If you do that, you'll have a much more balanced picture.
We could do that this week. We'll ask whether the staff would prefer a different arrangement.
Good. And when you write it up, include a short table of the five teams and their main features, so the reader can compare them at a glance.
Will do. Thanks very much, Dr Farrow.
You're welcome. Send me a draft by the end of next week, and we'll go through it together.

Good morning, everyone. Last week we looked at how remote working spread across different industries. Today I want to ask a more difficult question: what actually makes a distributed team perform well? And to answer it, I'd like to start by looking at what researchers got wrong.

In the 1990s, when the first large studies of virtual teams were carried out, there was a strong belief that the problem was technology. The argument went like this: if people are separated by distance, we simply need better tools to bring them together. Faster connections, sharper video, more reliable software. It's an attractive idea, and a lot of money was spent on it.

But when researchers started to test it, the results were disappointing. One often-cited study examined 80 teams in several industries, and found that the quality of the technology was a surprisingly weak predictor of performance. Some teams with very basic equipment did extremely well, while some with the latest systems struggled badly. Clearly, something else was going on.

So what mattered more? Well, the first factor, and I think the most consistent one across studies, was a clear shared goal. Teams that knew precisely what they were trying to achieve, and why, coped far better with distance. When people can't see each other working, they need an unambiguous idea of what counts as progress. Without it, they drift apart.

The second factor was what researchers now call working agreements. These are written statements about how the team operates: when people are expected to reply, how decisions are made, which tool is used for which purpose. It sounds terribly dull, and in some ways it is. But teams with clear agreements waste far less time on misunderstanding. In an office, you can lean across a desk and check what a colleague meant. When working remotely, those small repairs are much harder, so it pays to prevent misunderstandings in advance.

The third factor is trust. Now, trust normally grows slowly, over years of shared experience. But distributed teams are often put together quickly, with people who have never met. Researchers noticed that, surprisingly, many of them developed what was called swift trust. In these cases, people didn't trust each other because of personal history, but because of roles. Each person assumed that a colleague with a particular job title would behave in a professional way. The danger is that swift trust is fragile. One missed deadline, one unanswered message, can damage it badly, because there's no personal history to fall back on.

Let me turn to communication itself. A key distinction here is between synchronous communication, such as a meeting or phone call, and asynchronous communication, such as email or messages. Asynchronous methods are essential for teams working in different time zones, but they bring their own problems. One is uncertainty about how quickly a reply is expected. If one person assumes an hour, and another assumes a week, resentment builds. Many successful teams therefore set a simple standard. A message should be answered within one working day, and if something is truly urgent, it should be flagged as such.

A second problem with remote communication is visibility. In an office, a quiet person is still present; you can see them working. In a distributed team, a quiet person can disappear entirely. Researchers who interviewed such team members found that they often reported feeling invisible, and that this was a stronger predictor of leaving the team than their workload or their pay. Managers need to find ways of noticing people who say very little.

Video meetings deserve a mention too. Following the rapid growth of video calls, researchers began to study what has been called video fatigue. The suggestion is that keeping the camera on all day, looking at a grid of faces and also at your own, is mentally draining. Several studies found that participants who had the option to turn their cameras off reported significantly less fatigue, without any loss in their performance.

So what practical conclusions can we draw? I'll offer three. First, the beginning of a meeting matters. Instead of launching straight into the agenda, leaders can begin with a short check-in, where each person says one sentence about how they are. It takes only a couple of minutes, but it gives everyone a voice at the start, and it helps the quieter members to join in later.

Second, think carefully about when meetings are really needed. Many teams find that they can replace a good half of their meetings with written updates, and use the time saved for work that benefits from conversation, such as solving problems or planning something new.

Third, don't underestimate the value of meeting face to face, at least occasionally. Even teams that are entirely remote often arrange for everyone to get together in person twice a year. Evidence suggests that these occasions have a lasting effect on trust, and that the benefit continues for months afterwards.

To sum up, the evidence suggests that distributed teams succeed not because of the sophistication of their technology, but because of the clarity of their goals, the quality of their agreements and the care they take of the relationships between people. In next week's seminar, we'll look at a case study of a team that got all of this wrong, and I'd like you to think about what you would have done differently. Thank you.
Glenmorven Wind Farm Visitor Centre, Beth speaking. How can I help you?
Good afternoon. My name's Neil Haldane, and I teach at a secondary school near Perth. I'd like to bring a class to see the wind farm, if that's possible.
Oh, we'd love to have you. School visits are one of my favourite parts of the job. Let me get the booking sheet up. Could I have your surname again, and how it's spelled?
Haldane, that's H-A-L-D-A-N-E.
Thanks, Mr Haldane. And the name of your school?
Ravensdale High School. We're about forty minutes' drive from you, so it's fairly easy to reach.
Ravensdale, lovely. Which year group are you bringing? We have a different worksheet for each stage.
I was going to say Year 9, because they're doing a unit on energy, but our head of science has now asked me to take the older ones, so it's Year 10. They're studying renewable power for their exams.
Perfect, Year 10 it is. And how many students will there be?
Forty-five was the plan. But two have dropped out because they have a clash with a music exam, and one is away, so it'll be 42 altogether, plus three staff.
So 42 students and three adults. That fits nicely into two groups. Now, dates. We usually have room in spring. Are you thinking of May?
Yes, ideally. I've been told the first week is out because of exams.
Let me see. I can offer you the 13th, but I'm afraid we have a group of engineers booked in for the morning of that day. The 14th, though, is completely free.
Then let's go for the 14th. The 14th of May would suit us well.
14 May, excellent. What time would you like to arrive? Our tours start at ten o'clock.
If we could, we'd like to arrive a bit later than that. Our coach doesn't leave until nine thirty, so I think we'd be at the centre at about a quarter past ten.
That's fine. We'll start the first group at 10.15, then, and the second group will go up to the turbines while the first group does the workshop. What about the cost? Schools pay per student.
What's the price at the moment?
It was eight pounds last year, but we've received a grant, so we've been able to reduce it. This year, it's six pounds per student, and teachers come free.
That's very good news. I'll let the head know, because the budget was a worry.

Now, lunch. Where will the students eat? You can bring packed lunches, but you'll need somewhere to sit. We have a small cafe, but it only holds about thirty, so it's not really big enough for a school group.
What other options are there?
There's the old barn next to the car park. It's been converted into a picnic space, with long tables, and it's warm and dry. Most schools use that.
The barn sounds ideal. We'll eat there, then.
I'll put you down for the barn. Now, do any of your students have special requirements I should know about? Some of the path up to the turbines is quite steep.
Yes, actually. We have one girl who uses a wheelchair, so we need to know whether she can get around. We don't have anyone with a hearing problem, and I think the others are all fine.

Thank you for telling me. The path to the lower turbines is surfaced, so she'll be able to join the group, and we'll have a wheelchair accessible minibus for the upper viewpoint. I'll make a note to arrange that.
That's wonderful, thank you so much. It makes a big difference to her.

Finally, parking. Your coach can use either car park, but Car Park A is closed at the moment because of roadworks. So please ask the driver to park in B, next to the barn. That's the one with the green gate.
Car Park B, got it. I'll pass that on.
Good. I'll send you a confirmation email, together with a risk assessment and a worksheet pack. Please have a look through those, and ring me if there's anything you'd like to change.
Thank you very much, Beth. You've been extremely helpful.
My pleasure. We look forward to seeing you on the 14th, and I hope the students enjoy it.

Good evening, everyone, and welcome to the open evening at Eastfield Renewable Skills Academy. My name's Greg Tanaka, and I'm head of apprenticeships here. In a moment I'll take you on a short tour, but I'd like to begin with a quick overview of the building, so that you can find your way around, and then talk about the apprenticeships themselves.

Everyone should have a plan of the site in their hands. As you can see, the main building is shaped like a letter L. You came in through the main doors, and the reception is immediately on your left, on the ground floor, just beside the entrance. That's where you sign in each morning, and where visitors collect their badges.

If you look along the east corridor, you'll see a pair of big doors at the very end. That's the welding workshop. It's quite noisy, and the sparks can be dramatic, so we keep it away from the classrooms. You'll visit it later on the tour, and you'll be given safety glasses before you go in.

Next, the solar training area. Some people expect that to be in a field, but it's actually on the roof, which we reach by the stairs beside the library. We have eight real panels up there, connected to the grid, so that apprentices can practise installing and testing them. You'll get a good view of the valley, as long as it isn't raining.

The battery laboratory is in the basement. It's a controlled environment, with limited access, because of the safety requirements, but the apprentices are trained to work there from their first term. The corridor to it starts opposite the lifts.

Finally, the common room, where apprentices relax, is on the first floor, directly above the reception. It has sofas, a games table, and a kitchen, and the apprentices have decorated it themselves. If you ever want to know what they really think of us, that's where you'd hear it.

Now, let me talk about the apprenticeships themselves. The question I'm asked most often is how long they last. In the past, many of our programmes took four years, but we've redesigned them, and the standard apprenticeship is now three years. A few specialised courses are longer, but most people finish in three.

People also ask how the time is divided. Some imagine an apprentice spends most of the week in a classroom, but that isn't the case. Apprentices spend four days a week with their employer, and just one day here at the academy. In the first year, there's also a six-week introductory block, but after that it's the usual pattern.

Then, the question of pay. Apprentices are employees, so they're paid from the first day. In your first year, you'll receive at least the legal minimum wage for your age, but many of our employers pay more than that, particularly the larger companies. Your wage rises each year, and in the final year it's usually close to that of a qualified worker.

What about entry requirements? We don't ask for a degree, of course, and you don't need a science qualification, though it helps. What we do require are passes in maths and English at the standard level, or, if you haven't got them, you can sit a short test in our centre. If you're nervous about it, we run a revision session in February.

And what should you do next? If you'd like to apply, the first step is to complete an online profile on our website, which takes about twenty minutes. Some people think they have to send a CV at this stage, but you don't need to. Instead, we'll invite you to a selection day, where you'll try some practical tasks and meet a few employers. The deadline for the profile is the end of this month, so there isn't long.

Before we start the tour, a word about who we're looking for. Employers frequently tell me they'd choose a reliable, curious person over someone with a perfect exam record. If you like working with your hands, enjoy solving problems, and care about the environment, then clean energy might be right for you. Many of our current apprentices had no idea what they wanted to do until they visited a place like this.

Right. If you'd like to follow me, we'll start with the welding workshop, and then go up to the roof if the weather holds. Please stay together, and do ask questions along the way. The apprentices who'll show you around are very happy to answer them.
Hello, Isla. Hello, Tariq. Do take a seat. I've had a look at your dissertation proposal on apprenticeships in offshore wind. It's a promising idea, so let's talk it through.
Thank you, Professor Whelan. We're really keen on it, but we've got a few things to sort out.
Mainly the data, and how we're going to handle it.
Fine. First, remind me why you've chosen this topic. There are plenty of subjects in energy policy.
Well, Tariq's cousin did an apprenticeship with a turbine maintenance company, and he told us the training was excellent but that hardly anyone in his school had even heard of it.
Yes, that's the gap we're interested in. We want to find out why people don't know about these careers, even though demand is growing.
That's a good question. Have you decided how to collect your data?
We'd like to interview apprentices, and we've found a company that's agreed to let us contact twelve of them. But we wondered whether twelve is enough.
For interviews, I'd say twelve is perfectly reasonable, provided they're varied. What worries me more is that the company chose them. They'll probably pick the happiest people.
That's what we thought. So we'd like to ask a second company as well, and perhaps ask some who left the programme.

Yes, former apprentices would be very valuable, though they'll be harder to find. Try contacting the training provider, and see if they'll pass on a message. Now, tell me what you expect to find. What do the apprentices say they like?
From the pilot interviews, we heard two things most often. Firstly, they liked being paid while they learned. Several said they'd have found it impossible to study without an income.
And secondly, they liked doing real work from the start. They didn't feel like they were just sitting in lessons, and they said that made the theory easier to remember.
Those are both common findings. Did anyone mention the opportunity to travel? Offshore work is often portrayed as adventurous.
One did, but that was really a minor point. Several said they were nervous about being at sea, and one said she found the long periods away from home hard.
Hm, that's worth recording, though I'd be careful not to generalise from one comment. What about the employers' side? Are you planning to talk to them?

Yes, two managers have agreed. One of them told us that finding supervisors is the biggest difficulty, because experienced technicians don't always have time to teach. And he also said the cost of safety training is much higher than people realise.
The other manager mentioned a different problem, which is that apprentices sometimes leave as soon as they're qualified, so the company loses its investment.
So the main problems from the employers' perspective are the demand on supervisors and the cost of the safety training. Is that right?
That's right. The leaving issue is more occasional.

One more point before the timetable. You'll be promising the participants that their names won't appear anywhere. That has to be real. A manager reading your report mustn't be able to work out who said what, so be careful with job titles and place names.
That's a good point. We were going to say 'a senior technician at a Scottish wind farm', and there can't be many of those.
We could say 'a technician at an offshore operator' instead, and give each person a number rather than a name.
Much better. It's a small detail, but supervisors do check it, and it matters a great deal to the people who've trusted you with their stories.
Fine. Let's talk about the timetable, because it matters. Your project is due in April, and you need to build in time for analysis. When do you plan to complete each stage?
We'd like to have the ethics form submitted by the end of this month. That's the first thing, and I think it's the easiest.
Yes, and please get it done early, because it can take weeks to be approved.
The interviews with apprentices are the next stage. We can't begin until the form's approved, but we hope to finish them before the mid-term break.
That seems realistic. And the employer interviews?
Those will be a bit later. The managers are busy until after Christmas, so we plan to finish them before then, in the first half of December.
Hmm, that's tight, but possible. And the transcription and analysis?
We'd leave that for the new semester, so that we can concentrate on writing in the spring.
Good. I'd also like you to think about whether you want to include a short questionnaire for school pupils. It might strengthen your argument about awareness.
We hadn't thought of that. It might be too much work, though.

Perhaps. Think about it over the next fortnight, and send me an email with your decision. In the meantime, start on the literature review, because that's something you can do without anyone's permission.
We'll do that. Thanks very much, Professor.
Not at all. I'm looking forward to seeing how it develops.

Good afternoon, everyone. In this lecture I'd like to look at a problem that sits at the centre of the clean energy transition: not the technology, which is advancing rapidly, but the people needed to install, maintain and repair it. In particular, I want to ask whether apprenticeships can close what's commonly called the skills gap.

Let me begin with the scale of the challenge. A recent industry forecast estimated that the sector will need around 40,000 additional workers over the next decade. That includes electricians, engineers, technicians and people to manage large projects. Now, that figure is uncertain, as all forecasts are, but even the most cautious estimates suggest a shortage.

Part of the difficulty is demographic. The workforce in the skilled trades is ageing. In one national survey, the average age of experienced electricians was found to be 52. Many of these people will retire within fifteen years, and they take decades of practical knowledge with them. At the same time, the sector is growing, so we are losing skills just as we need more of them.

Which areas are affected most? Wind and solar attract the headlines, but one of the fastest-growing areas is heat pump installation. Millions of homes will need to replace gas boilers, and each installation requires a trained person. At present, there are simply not enough of them, and the shortage is expected to get worse before it improves.

So how do apprenticeships fit in? Let me explain briefly how they work, for those who are unfamiliar. An apprenticeship combines paid employment with formal study. The apprentice is an employee, and the great majority of their learning happens on the job, working alongside experienced colleagues, with a smaller proportion spent in a college or training centre. At the end, the apprentice receives a recognised qualification, which can be used anywhere in the industry. That portability is important, because it gives apprentices security and employers confidence.

I should stress that this is not a new idea, and nor is it limited to one country or one industry. What is new is the urgency, because the target dates for cutting carbon emissions are fixed, while the supply of trained people is not.

The model has a long history, and the most celebrated example is in Germany, where what's called the dual system has operated for generations. There, around half of young people enter some form of apprenticeship, and it has a high social status. Many countries have tried to copy it, with mixed results, partly because the model depends on a culture of cooperation between employers, unions and schools that can't be created overnight.

Now, what are the obstacles? I'd like to highlight three. The first concerns employers. Taking on an apprentice is an investment. You must pay a wage, release your most experienced staff to supervise, and accept that, for the first year or so, the apprentice may cost you more than they produce. Smaller companies, in particular, worry about the cost, because they cannot afford to lose their investment if the apprentice later leaves.

The second obstacle concerns image. In surveys of school pupils, many describe skilled trades as a second-best choice, something you do if you've failed to get into university. Parents and teachers often share that view. That's unfortunate, because many clean energy roles are highly technical, and they involve digital skills as well as practical ones. Yet this perception persists, and it limits the number of applicants.

The third obstacle is diversity. The sector remains heavily male. Among apprentices in clean energy, only 9 percent are women, and for some trades the figure is lower. This isn't only a question of fairness. The industry cannot fill its vacancies if it ignores half the population. Several studies suggest that women are put off not by the work itself, but by a lack of visible role models, and by a sense that the culture will not welcome them.

So what can be done? Researchers and policy makers have proposed a number of measures. One that has shown promise is the taster week, in which school pupils spend several days working alongside apprentices in a real workplace. Evaluations suggest that these weeks change attitudes more effectively than leaflets, careers talks or websites, because pupils can see for themselves what the work involves.

A second measure is to make the progression routes clearer. If an apprentice knows that they can continue to higher qualifications, perhaps even to a degree, the trade seems less of a dead end, and the second-best image begins to fade. Some universities are already working with employers to design such pathways.

In conclusion, apprenticeships are not a complete answer to the skills gap, but they're an essential part of it. Their success will depend less on the design of the training than on whether employers invest in them, and whether young people, and their parents, regard them as an attractive first choice. In next week's lecture, we'll look at how the picture differs in rural areas. Thank you.
Ferndale Markets, Pauline speaking. What can I do for you?
Oh, hi. I'm thinking about taking a stall at one of your markets, and I wanted to find out how it works. I've never done it before, so I'm a bit in the dark.
No problem at all, we get new stallholders every month. What do you sell?

Well, I do quite a few things, to be honest. I teach yoga three mornings a week, I do some bookkeeping for small businesses, and in my spare time I make cards. That's what I'd like to sell at the market.
Sounds like a busy life. Right, shall I take your details first? What's your surname?
Mulcahy. M-U-L-C-A-H-Y.
Thanks, Declan. And a mobile number?
Got it. And what kind of cards are they?
They're printed by hand. I used to do screen-printed designs, but they take ages, so now I carve the pictures into lino and print them one at a time. Linocut cards, they're called.
Lovely, those always sell well, especially around birthdays.

Now, we hold two markets. There's one on Sunday, in the park, and one on Saturday, in the old station car park. The Sunday market is bigger, but the stalls cost more, and it's mostly food. Cards would do better on Saturday, I think, because that's where the craft stalls are.
Then Saturday it is. I'd also rather keep my Sundays free.
That's fine. How big a stall do you want? The standard width is three metres, but you can have more.
I thought three would be enough, but then I remembered that I've got two big display racks, so I think I'd better have four metres.

Four metres, no problem. That's a corner pitch, actually, so it should be easy for people to see you. Now, the price. Normally a four-metre pitch is 45 dollars a day, but new stallholders get a discount for their first month, and it's 35 dollars.
That's very good. Does that include the table?

Yes, we supply one trestle table per stall. What we don't supply is cover. So, you'd need to bring your own gazebo, in case of rain, and it has to be weighted down, not just pegged, because of the car park surface.
I've got a gazebo, but I'd have to check that it's the right size. It's a three-metre one.
That's fine for a four-metre pitch. Most people have a three-metre one.
Good. And when could I start? Is there a waiting list?
There's a short one, but there's a cancellation this month, so you could begin on 21 June. That's a Saturday.
That's perfect. I'll have a stock of cards ready by then. I'd planned on starting a week earlier, but it takes me a while to print them.

It's better not to rush. You'll have a few more things to sort out before then. For example, the council requires every stallholder to show evidence of public liability insurance. It's quite cheap, and you can get it through your bank or online. Without it, I'm afraid we can't allow you to trade.
I wasn't aware of that. Do I have to send it to you in advance?
Yes, a scanned copy by email will do. You'll also need to have your trading details, but we can talk about that when you've got the insurance.
All right. I'll sort that out this week.

Wonderful. One other thing. Stallholders can't park in the market car park, because it's used by the stalls. So you should unload there, and then take your vehicle to Alder Street. It's about two minutes' walk.
Alder Street, okay. I thought I might use Elm Street, because it's closer to my flat.
Elm Street is blocked on Saturdays, because of the road works, so Alder Street is the best place. It's free, but arrive early, because spaces go quickly.
Thanks, that's really useful. What time should I arrive to set up?
The market opens at eight, and stallholders can arrive from six thirty. Most people like to be set up by half past seven.
That sounds fine. I'm used to early starts, with the yoga.
Excellent. I'll email you the form and a map of the pitches. Thanks for calling, Declan, and I hope the first market goes well.
Thank you, Pauline. You've been a great help.

Good evening, everyone, and thank you for coming along to this information evening at Brookvale Community Learning Centre. My name's Hamid Rasool, and I manage the centre. I'd like to tell you about our winter programme of short courses, many of which are designed for people who make their living in more than one way, such as part-time employees, freelancers and people running small businesses on the side.

First, a few words about the timetable. The winter programme begins in July, not in June as it did last year. We moved the start so that it doesn't clash with the end of the school term, because a lot of our students are parents. It then runs for ten weeks. All courses are in the evening, and every class is held in the main building on Mill Road.

What's new this year? Over the past two years, many of you asked us to introduce online classes, and we've done that, but they're only for a few subjects. The real change is that we've added a creche. If you've got children under five, you can leave them with our trained staff while you attend a class, and it doesn't cost anything extra. We also considered weekend classes, but there wasn't enough demand, so we've left those for now.

Now, fees. Each ten-week course costs 120 dollars, which is the same as last year. People who are unemployed, and pensioners, pay half. Full-time students pay 90 dollars, if they show their card. If you want to take more than one course, we offer a ten per cent discount on the second, so it's worth thinking about combining them.

And how do you enrol? Some people ring us, and some come to the front desk, but this year we're asking everyone to enrol online, through our website. It's much quicker for our staff, and you receive a confirmation immediately. If you don't have a computer, though, don't worry. Our front desk has a terminal, and one of the team will help you.
Now, let me describe the courses, and the evenings on which they take place. As you'll see on the sheet you were given, we have six this term, and I'll mention the day for each of them.

The first is Bookkeeping Basics. This is for anyone who needs to keep records of their own income and expenses. It's taught by a qualified accountant, and it's always popular, so it meets on Monday evenings, when we have the biggest room available.

Next, Building a Website. You don't need any technical knowledge. By the end, you'll have a simple site of your own, which many people use to display a portfolio of their work. It meets on Tuesday evenings. We offered it on Wednesdays last year, but several people said that clashed with their other commitments.

For people who feel nervous about presenting themselves, there's Public Speaking, which runs on Wednesday evenings. It's practical, and not at all frightening, I promise. Everyone speaks at every session, but in small groups.

Then, Writing Contracts and Quotes. That's a very useful one for freelancers, who often find it difficult to put a price on their work, or to put it in writing. It's run by a solicitor and meets on Thursday evenings.

For those of you who promote your work online, there's Social Media for Small Business. It's taught by a woman who has built a successful following for her own craft business, so she knows what she's talking about. That meets on Friday evenings, though I admit that isn't everyone's favourite evening.

And finally, Photo Editing. It's useful if you sell products online and want them to look professional. That's the only course which doesn't meet on a weekday. It's held on Saturday mornings, in the art studio, and it's the one I'd encourage you to try if you've never edited a picture in your life.

One last practical point. We have a limited number of places on each course, usually twenty, and the most popular ones fill quickly. I'd advise you not to leave it too late. If a course is full, you can join a waiting list, and we'll contact you if somebody drops out. And if you're not sure which course is right for you, our advisers are in the foyer after this talk, and they'll be glad to help. Thank you very much for listening.
Come in, Akira. Ben, sit down. Right, your presentation on portfolio careers is next week. How are you getting on?
We've nearly finished the research, Dr Reyes. We interviewed a woman called Maya, who combines four different kinds of work.
She's really interesting, and I think she'll make a good case study. But we've got a few questions about how to present her.
Fine. Tell me about her first. What does she do?
She works part-time as a nurse, she teaches music privately, she plays in a band at weekends, and she writes freelance articles about health.
That's a lot. Why did she choose to work that way? Was it a deliberate plan?

Not really. She said it started after a restructuring at the hospital, when her hours were cut. But she says she'd never go back to a single job now. Two things came up most often when she explained her decision. One was the flexibility. She can arrange her week around her family and her health.
And the other was that she got bored easily. She said that doing the same job for twenty years would have driven her mad, and that moving between her different roles keeps her fresh.
Good, so flexibility and avoiding boredom. Did she mention money as a motive? Did she hope to earn more?
No, in fact she earns slightly less than she did before. But she says that's a fair price.
That's useful, because it suggests the motive wasn't financial at all, which is rather unusual in the literature. Now, you mentioned a problem with the data.
Yes. We recorded the interview, but the file's quality was poor. There was a lot of noise from the cafe where we met, and about ten minutes of the discussion about her finances can't be heard at all.
That's irritating. Can you go back to her?
We've emailed to ask whether she'll answer a few follow-up questions in writing. She's said yes, but she's busy this week.
Good, that's the sensible approach. Now, let me raise a more theoretical question. You use the phrase 'portfolio career' throughout. Are you sure everyone will understand it in the same way?
I thought it was quite clear.

It's not, I'm afraid. Some writers use it only for people who've chosen to combine jobs, and others include anyone with more than one source of income, even if they didn't want it. Your case study falls in the first group. I'd like you to define the term in your introduction, and say which meaning you're using.
That makes sense. Otherwise, someone's bound to ask in the discussion.
Exactly. What about the financial side? Do you have anything on income security?

That's actually the most interesting part. Maya said she'd expected to feel insecure, but she feels safer in this way of working than she ever did in her hospital job. If one source of income dries up, the others carry on.
I'm not sure I'd agree, though. Her income is steady because of nursing, and the other jobs are unpredictable. Without that stable base, I think it would be much riskier.
That's a good point, Ben, and I'd like you both to put that disagreement into the presentation. It makes it more honest and more interesting.
Okay. We could present it as a debate.
Excellent. Now, let me ask about the structure of the case study. I'd like you to tell the audience about each of her jobs, and what role it plays in her working life. What did she say about them?
Well, the nursing is clearly the foundation. She said it provides her with a regular income, so she can take risks with the other work.
The private teaching is the one she's thinking of giving up. She said the travelling between students' houses wears her out, and she's considering moving to online lessons instead.
Performing in the band is the least reliable financially. Some months she makes very little, and she says she does it for the love of it, though it does bring in a few bookings.

And the writing was actually the one that led to the others. She started writing a blog about her work, and a magazine saw it. Without that, she might never have started the freelance articles at all.

That's a nice detail. It shows how the pieces of a portfolio feed into each other. I'd suggest a simple diagram on one slide, with the four jobs as circles and arrows showing which led to which. Audiences remember pictures far better than lists, and it will save you a minute of explanation. Finally, what do you plan to say in your conclusion?
We thought about saying portfolio careers suit everyone, but that seems too strong.
So we're going to say they suit people who value independence and can cope with some uncertainty, and that it's much harder for people who need a predictable income.
That's a more careful conclusion, and much easier to defend. Good. Go and rehearse it, and let me know if you need anything else before next week.
Thanks, Dr Reyes.
Thank you. That's been really helpful.

Good morning, everyone. Today I'd like to look at a way of working that is becoming increasingly common, and which challenges some of our assumptions about what a career is. I'm referring to the portfolio career, in which a person combines several different jobs or income streams, rather than depending on a single employer.

Let me begin with the origins of the idea. The phrase was popularised in 1989 by a British management writer, who argued that the traditional job for life was disappearing. He suggested that, in future, many people would spend their working lives assembling a portfolio of different activities, a bit like an investor with a range of shares. At the time, many people regarded that as a rather eccentric prediction. Today it seems almost conventional.

What exactly does it involve? A portfolio worker typically does several kinds of work at once, often for different employers, and sometimes for themselves. A person might, for example, work two days a week for a company, run a small consultancy and teach an evening class. The key point is that no single source of income defines them.

Why has this pattern become more common? There are several reasons, and I'd like to mention four. The first is the rapid growth of gig work, meaning short-term, task-based jobs that are often arranged through online platforms. These make it much easier to find small amounts of work, and combine them, than it was thirty years ago.

The second reason is that people are living and working for longer. Many young people today expect to be working until the age of 70, and few believe they will spend all those years in one organisation. A long working life almost demands a succession of different roles, and some people prefer to hold them simultaneously.

The third is a change in what workers want. Surveys repeatedly show that younger employees value autonomy, the ability to decide for themselves how, when and where they work, more than they value a high salary. Portfolio work offers a degree of control that is very hard to find within a single organisation.

What are the benefits? One, I think, is resilience. Someone who depends on a single client is in a vulnerable position, because if that relationship ends, their income disappears. A portfolio worker, by contrast, can lose one client and still have others. In this sense, a portfolio can be more secure than a single job.

A related benefit is that it is easier to survive redundancy. People who've already built several sources of income find that losing one job is a setback, rather than a disaster. Studies of workers who were laid off found that those with a portfolio recovered much faster than those who had relied on one employer.

But there are risks, and I'd be misleading you if I presented only the attractive side. The most obvious is financial unpredictability. Income varies from month to month, and that makes planning difficult. Banks, in particular, are often reluctant to lend to people with irregular earnings, so it can be very hard to get a mortgage.

There is also a human cost. Because portfolio workers are always aware that they're not earning when they're not working, they tend to say yes to everything. Many report working very long hours, with no clear boundary between jobs, and some suffer burnout. This is probably the most serious risk, and it receives far less attention than it deserves.

So what skills does a portfolio worker need? Researchers have identified several. They need to be able to market themselves, to negotiate, and to manage their own finances. But the one that people mention most often is organisation. When you're juggling several commitments, you cannot rely on a manager to tell you what to do next. Successful portfolio workers tend to plan their lives with a weekly schedule, set aside time for rest, and are firm about what they will and won't accept.

Let me end with a point about identity. When someone asks 'What do you do?', the person with a portfolio career has no simple answer. Some find that liberating. Others find it confusing, and say that they miss belonging to a single professional community. Research suggests that those who thrive are the ones who build a sense of identity around their skills rather than their job titles. So I'd suggest that, in a portfolio career, what you can do matters more than where you work.

None of this means that a portfolio career is simply a good or a bad thing. It is a trade-off, and whether it is the right one depends on the person, on their circumstances, and on the support available to them.

In our next session, we'll look at how educational institutions might need to change in order to prepare students for this kind of working life. Please read the two articles on the reading list before then. Thank you.
Penrhos Library, Sian speaking. How may I help?
Good morning. I saw a poster in your window about a scheme where young people help older ones with computers. I wondered if I could put my name down.
Oh, the Digital Buddies. Yes, of course. We've had a lot of interest this year. Shall I take a few details now?
Please. I'm not terribly good on the phone, so bear with me.
Not at all, you're doing fine. First of all, your surname?
It's Pryce, P-R-Y-C-E.
Lovely. And may I ask your age? It's only so we can match you with the right group.
I'm 71, though I'll be 72 in March. Does it make a difference?
