Not at all. We have people from sixty to ninety. Now, are you retired?
Oh yes, for about six years now. I was a surveyor for most of my life, measuring land and buildings. I started out as a joiner, actually, but I moved into surveying in my thirties.
Interesting, so you'll appreciate precision. What would you like the students to help you with? Most people want to learn a particular thing.

Well, I can just about manage my email, thank you. What I'd really like is to learn how to make a video call. My daughter lives in Canada, and she keeps asking me to speak to her on the screen, but I can't work out how it goes.
That's a very common request, and it's a lovely one. We'll make sure you're paired with someone who's good at that. Now, when would suit you? We run sessions on Tuesday and Wednesday afternoons.
Tuesday is difficult, I'm afraid. I play bowls on Tuesdays, and I don't like to miss it. Wednesday would be much better.
Wednesday afternoons, then. Sessions begin at half past two. They used to last an hour, but that was too long for some people, so now they're 45 minutes.
Forty-five minutes sounds right. I'd probably start to get tired after an hour, to be honest.
Most people say that. Where would you like to meet? There are two places. We can use the cafe downstairs, which is quite lively, or the reading room on the first floor, which is much quieter.
I think the cafe would be too noisy for me, because I'm slightly deaf. The reading room, please.

The reading room, then. It has a big table and good light, so it works well. Now, I should say that we provide the tablets, so you don't need to bring one. But we ask people to bring their own headphones, because it's difficult to hear on a video call otherwise.
I've got a pair of those. My granddaughter gave them to me last Christmas, and I've never used them.

Then it's an ideal time to try them. Right, let me see who I can pair you with. I have a student called Leila, who's seventeen and studying for her exams. She's brilliant at explaining things, and she's very patient. Would you like to be paired with her?
That sounds splendid. Will she mind if I ask the same question several times?
Not in the slightest. She says she's learned a lot herself from the older people she's met. It really is a two-way exchange.
That's good to hear. I'd feel awful if I thought I was wasting her time.

You won't be. Now, shall we choose a start date? The next session is on the 2nd, but it would be better for you to begin after the induction evening, which is on the 9th. So the first session would be on 16 October.
16 October. I'll write that on the calendar. What will happen at the induction evening?
It's very informal. You'll meet the students, have a cup of tea, and we'll explain how the scheme works. It's on the evening of the 9th, at seven o'clock, in the main hall.
I'll definitely go to that. Thank you for being so kind, Sian.
You're very welcome. I'll send you a leaflet in the post, with a map, in case you haven't been to the library recently.
I've been coming here for forty years, so I think I'll find it.
Of course you have. We'll see you on the 9th, Mr Pryce.

Good morning, everyone, and thank you so much for volunteering for the Millbrook Skills Swap Day. My name's Margaret Oyelaran, and I'm one of the organisers. This is the briefing for all volunteers, so it's important that everyone hears it, even if you've done something like this before. I'll try to keep it short, because I know people are keen to get started.

First, timing. We'll open the doors to the public at ten o'clock, but I'd like all volunteers to arrive by nine. That gives us an hour to set up the tables, put out the signs and have a cup of tea. Last year we opened early, because people were queuing, but it caused confusion, so we're going to stick to ten this time.

Now, where to leave your belongings. The cloakroom by the front entrance will be locked, because the caretaker has to keep the main doors open, so please don't use it. Instead, there's a store room behind the stage. I'll give the key to one of the team, and everything can be left there. Please don't bring anything valuable, in any case.

You'll all have been given a bright yellow T-shirt. If you're wearing one of those, you're a guide. Your job is to welcome people, explain what each table is about, and direct them. If somebody asks you something you can't answer, don't make it up. Just bring them to me, or to one of the people in green, who are the team leaders.

Let me explain the shape of the day. The whole idea is that older and younger people swap skills. Some of the older participants will teach things like knitting, cooking and woodwork, and some of the younger ones will teach things like coding and photography. We've also got a chess table, which is popular with both generations. Most of these activities take place in the main hall, but not all. The cooking and knitting will be in the small hall, because they need space for stoves and a lot of wool, and the photography will be outside, if the weather's fair.

So, two of those activities, the coding and the chess, will be in the main hall, along with the information table. I'd ask you to keep the noise down, because chess players need concentration, and I know it can be tricky when the coding workshop is next door.

At two o'clock, there'll be a short presentation by the youth council, in the main hall. They'll talk about a project to record the memories of older residents. It lasts about twenty minutes, and then the activities continue until four. You don't need to attend, but it would be nice if some of you could help the audience find their seats.

Now, a more delicate point. Occasionally, a participant gets upset, usually because they've found something difficult, or because they feel embarrassed in front of others. If that happens, please don't try to deal with it by yourself, and don't just walk away. Stay with them calmly, and then fetch one of the team leaders. We'll make sure they're looked after. It's much better to be honest about it than to pretend nothing has happened.

Lunch. In the past, volunteers had to bring sandwiches, and we've been criticised for that. This year, a local bakery is providing a lunch for everyone, which will be served in the small hall at one o'clock, in two sittings. If you're helping at the time, you can go to the second sitting. There's a vegetarian option, and if you've got any other dietary needs, please tell me before the end of today.

A word about photographs. We'd love to have pictures of the day, because we want to show the council what the event achieves. But we must have written permission from anyone whose picture is taken, and that's particularly important for children. So, if you're taking pictures, please carry the consent forms, and only photograph people who've signed. The forms are on the information table, and I'll give each of you some.

Finally, feedback. At the end of the afternoon, we'd like every participant to fill in a short form saying how they found it. In previous years, these were handed out at the door, and many people forgot them. This year, we'll put them on every table, with a pen, and ask the guides to remind people before they leave. Please don't push anyone to answer, but do encourage them to say what they think, because that's how we improve.
That's everything for now. If you have questions, I'll be at the information table. Otherwise, let's get the tables out. Thank you again, everyone.
Come in, all three of you. Hollie, Femi, Zoe, sit wherever you like. I wanted to talk about your group project on reverse mentoring.
Thanks, Dr Salazar. We've collected our data, and we're trying to decide how to analyse it.
And there are a couple of things in the design we'd like to check with you.
Of course. Remind me how you found your participants. I seem to remember it was tricky.

It was. We began by writing to about thirty companies, and nobody replied. In the end, it was through Hollie's mother, who works in human resources at a hospital. She introduced us to people at four organisations.
Which was lucky, because those four had all run reverse mentoring schemes, so we knew they had relevant experience.
Good, that's a reasonable way to start. Now, I recall you were going to use a questionnaire as well as interviews.
We did, but the response rate was low. We sent it to sixty people, and only nineteen replied.
Partly because it was too long, and partly because we sent it just before the holidays, which was a mistake.
You're not the first to make that mistake. Mention it in your limitations, and rely mainly on the interviews. Now, what did you notice that surprised you?
For me, it was how strongly the older people, the senior staff, felt about it. I expected them to be sceptical, but several said it was the best training they'd had in years.

I was surprised by something different. The young mentors were more nervous than I expected. One said she'd lain awake the night before her first session, worrying about telling a director what to do.
That's a theme I'd expect. Which brings me to terminology. You call the scheme 'reverse mentoring', but at least two of your organisations didn't use that term. One called it 'two-way learning'.
Yes, we noticed. We thought it was just branding.

Perhaps, but I'd be careful. The word 'reverse' suggests that the usual direction is the natural one, and that this is an unusual arrangement. Some participants may dislike that. I think you should acknowledge the different terms rather than treat them as identical.
That's a fair point. We'll add a short paragraph.
And tell me about the people who were less enthusiastic. Were there any?

A few of the senior participants said they'd found it hard at the start, because they weren't used to being taught by someone so much younger. But most had changed their minds after a couple of months.
One man in his sixties told us that, at first, he nodded at everything his mentor said, because he didn't want to look foolish. It took him weeks to admit that he hadn't understood a word.
And his mentor said almost the same thing in her interview, that she was never sure whether he was following. Neither of them had said anything to the other.

That's a lovely example of mutual politeness getting in the way. Use it, anonymised, in your discussion, because it illustrates the point better than any statistic. Did you notice any difference between men and women?
Not a clear one. We had too few people to say. The women were slightly more likely to describe the relationship as a friendship, but that could just be chance.
Then don't claim anything about it, though you could mention it as an area for future research. Now, what did the organisations do to support them?
The best approach seemed to be a short briefing for both sides before the scheme started. The two organisations that skipped it had more problems.
That fits with the literature. Now, let's talk about the four organisations individually. How did each one use the scheme, and what happened?
The bank was the one with the most formal arrangement, and also the happiest participants. They scored very high on satisfaction, mostly because the scheme was voluntary on both sides.
The hospital was different. Their scheme ended after a year, mainly because the funding was cut, even though the staff liked it.

The publisher used it for a more specific purpose. The directors wanted to understand how younger readers use social media, and the young mentors showed them. It was less about training and more about market research.
And the engineering firm struggled with timetables. The mentors and mentees worked shifts, so they could rarely find a time to meet, and many sessions were cancelled.
Good. That's a useful comparison, and it gives you a clear structure. Now, how are you going to finish?
We thought of recommending that all organisations introduce the scheme.

I wouldn't go quite that far. Your sample is small and not at all random. I'd say that reverse mentoring appears to benefit participants when it is voluntary and supported, and that more research is needed. That's an honest conclusion.
That makes sense. We'll rewrite it.
Excellent. Send me a draft in two weeks. And do check that you've anonymised everything. People will recognise their own stories.
We will. Thanks very much, Dr Salazar. We'll also rehearse the presentation together this weekend, so that all three of us are comfortable with every slide.
Sensible. Splitting the sections evenly will help, too, so that nobody ends up speaking for the whole time.

Good afternoon, everyone. In today's lecture I'd like to examine mentoring, and in particular the idea that learning between the generations can run in both directions. Most of us picture mentoring as an older, experienced person guiding a younger one. But in recent decades, a quite different model has emerged, and I'd like to compare the two.

Let me begin with the traditional model. The word itself comes from an ancient poem, in which a character called Mentor is asked to advise the young son of a king while the king is away at war. So from the very start, the concept involved an older person passing on knowledge to a younger one. And for most of history, that is how mentoring has worked, whether in a craft guild, a profession or a family business.

The traditional model has real strengths. The mentor shares hard-won experience, helps the younger person avoid mistakes, and opens doors to a network of contacts. Studies show that people who have had a mentor tend to be promoted faster and to report higher job satisfaction. But it has one weakness, and that is that the flow of information is one-directional. The mentor teaches, and the mentee learns.

It is worth pausing on that weakness, because it tells us something about how we usually think of expertise. We tend to assume that wisdom accumulates with age, and in many areas it does. But in fast-changing fields, a young person may know more than someone with decades of experience.

In the late 1990s, a different idea appeared. A large American company, which was worried that its senior managers were out of touch with new technology, asked some of its youngest employees to teach them. This was the first major example of what's now called reverse mentoring. The younger person is the mentor, the older person the mentee, and the subject is usually something the older generation hasn't had the chance to learn.

What do the younger mentors teach? In the first schemes, the answer was technology. Executives wanted to learn about the internet, email and later about social media. But many schemes have since broadened, and mentors now discuss things such as attitudes to work, new ways of communicating, and how younger people see the world.

That brings me to a second advantage. Seniors who take part often say that they gain a clearer understanding of younger customers. A retailer, for instance, can't expect to sell to young people if nobody in its leadership team understands how they shop. A reverse mentoring scheme provides a direct line to that world, without the cost of formal market research.

What does the evidence say? A well-known study followed 120 mentoring pairs in several organisations over eighteen months. The researchers found that both sides reported gains, which is the most important point. But the gains were different. Younger mentors reported a considerable increase in confidence. Many had never spoken to a senior executive before, and found, to their surprise, that they were taken seriously.

Older mentees, in contrast, valued the experience of being listened to as a learner. At their level of seniority, they are rarely in a situation where they can admit that they don't know something. The scheme gave them a safe place to ask basic questions, and many described it as a relief.

Now, it would be misleading to suggest that these schemes are without problems. The most obvious is the imbalance of power. A junior employee in a mentoring relationship with a director may feel nervous about saying anything critical, or even about correcting a mistake. If the mentor is afraid, the relationship becomes a performance, and the benefits disappear. Organisations that handle this well usually take care to separate the mentoring from any form of performance review, so that nothing said in the sessions can affect anyone's career.

Another challenge is making time. Both people are usually busy, and a mentoring session is easy to postpone. The research suggests that schemes work best when pairs meet monthly, with a fixed date in the diary, rather than leaving it to chance. Pairs who meet less often than that tend to drift apart, and the scheme quietly fades.

Finally, I'd like to say something about the language we use. Even the phrase 'reverse mentoring' can be problematic, because it implies that the natural direction is from old to young. Several organisations have therefore adopted the term 'mutual mentoring', which expresses more accurately what actually happens. The label may seem a small matter, but it shapes how people see their role, and what they expect to get from the relationship.

To conclude, mentoring across generations is most successful when it is a genuine exchange, not a ceremony. Both generations have something to teach, and both have something to learn. In next week's seminar, we'll look at how the same principle has been applied in schools, and I'd like you to bring one example from your own experience of learning from someone much older or much younger than yourself. Thank you.
Schoolwise Furniture, Kieran speaking. What can I sort out for you?
Hello, Kieran. I'm a teacher at a primary school in Brisbane, and I'm hoping to get a quote for some new furniture for my classroom. A colleague said you do adjustable tables.
We certainly do. It's one of our best-selling lines, particularly with schools that have children with different needs. Could I take a few details? I'll fill in the quote request as we go.
Of course. My name is Alison Mackintosh. M-A-C-K-I-N-T-O-S-H.
Thanks, Alison. And which school is it?
Banksia Park Primary School. People often think it's Banksia Park State School, but it was renamed a few years ago.
Banksia Park Primary, got it. And which classroom are we furnishing?

Room 14, which is the one at the end of the Year Three corridor. We've been given a small grant to make it more accessible, because next year we'll have a boy who uses a wheelchair, and a girl with a hearing impairment.

That's a great project. So what are you looking for? Most schools start with desks, but I'd steer you towards the height-adjustable tables. They can be set for a child in a wheelchair, and then lowered for a smaller child in the next lesson. A fixed-height desk won't do that.
That's exactly what I was hoping to hear. I'd thought about desks originally, but I agree that tables are more flexible. How many would you recommend?
What's your class size?

Twenty-four children, but we plan to seat them in pairs, so twelve tables would be enough. I'd first said fifteen, so that we could have a few spare for group work, but the room just isn't big enough.
Twelve is plenty, and it'll leave you space to move around, which matters if you have a wheelchair in the room. Now, colour. We have blue, grey, and a pale green.
The children would love blue, but I read that strong colours can be distracting for some pupils, especially those with sensory sensitivities. So I think I'd go for the pale green, it's calming.

Good thinking. Pale green it is. What about chairs? Ours come with a back support, or with armrests for children who need to push up when they stand. Most schools go for the plain back support, and that's all you need unless a child has particular needs.
I'll take the plain ones. But my main worry is noise. The girl with a hearing aid says scraping chairs are painful, because the aid amplifies everything. Is there anything we can do?

Yes, we fit felt pads on the feet of every chair for that reason. They're much better than the rubber tips we used to supply, which wore out in a year and made a squeaking sound on vinyl floors. With felt, you'll hardly hear a chair move.
Perfect. Are there any other products that would help? I've seen rugs and wall panels advertised.

We sell acoustic rugs, which are thick and absorb sound. In a hard-floored room, they make a big difference. We also sell wall panels, but those are quite expensive, and I'd start with the rugs and see how it goes.

Then I'll add two rugs, to absorb noise. I'll leave the panels for now. When could everything be delivered? Term starts on the twenty-ninth of July, and I'd like the room ready at least a week before.
Our usual delivery date is the fifteenth, but with the number of orders at this time of year, we're running about a week behind. I can promise you the twenty-second of July, if you confirm this week.
The twenty-second is fine. That gives me a few days to arrange the room before the children arrive.
Now, the price. With twelve tables, twenty-four chairs, the felt pads and two rugs, the total comes to five thousand two hundred dollars. But schools get a discount, which brings it down to $4,860.
That's within the grant, thank goodness. Do you need a deposit?
No, we invoice after delivery. If you send me your email address, I'll send you the quote this afternoon, and you can show it to your principal.
Wonderful. Thank you so much for your help.
You're very welcome, Alison. I hope the new room goes well.

Good evening, all, and thanks very much for turning out. For those I haven't met, I'm Helen Marsh, the deputy head of Parkview Primary School. Tonight I'd like to take you through the new east wing, which opened this term, and explain why it looks the way it does. You'll see it in person in a few minutes, but I find that a few words first make the tour more useful.

How did this begin? Some people assume it was a response to building regulations. In fact, it started five years ago, when a group of parents surveyed the school and listed the barriers they found. They counted heavy doors, steps, noisy corridors and signs that were too small to read. When the governors saw the list, they realised that no regulation was needed, because the evidence was in front of them. The work began in January last year and finished two weeks late, because the lifts were delayed in transit.

Let me explain some of the choices. First, light. Each classroom has dimmable lighting, which teachers can adjust with a simple dial by the door. Some children are sensitive to bright light, and others, such as those with limited vision, need it brighter. The old fluorescent tubes have all gone, because they flicker in a way that some people notice, even if they can't say why. Instead, we've used LED panels, and every room has a large window.

Second, the corridors. We widened them by half a metre, and we painted the floors in colours, with a different colour for each year group. A child who finds it hard to read signs can simply follow the green line to the Year Two classrooms. We were told that the colour-coding might look childish, but the children love it, and visitors say it helps them too.

Third, noise. This was the part that took the longest to resolve. Our first idea was to lay carpets throughout, because they absorb sound. But the school nurse reminded us that carpets collect dust, and several children have asthma and allergies. So the floors are hard, and we've fitted acoustic panels to the ceilings instead. They've halved the echo in the classrooms, and teachers say they no longer have to raise their voices.

Now, the features you'll see in every classroom. Each room has a quiet corner, with a beanbag, a lamp and a few books, where a child who feels overwhelmed can sit for ten minutes. There are height-adjustable tables, as well. Some people have asked about hearing loops, and they're installed in the school hall and the library, but not in every classroom. Interactive whiteboards have been fitted in the upper years only, to start with, and sinks at two heights are in the art room, not in the general classrooms.

A few practical points for tonight and the future. When you arrive, you will sign in at reception, and please wear your visitor badge at all times. The building has three entrances. If you use a wheelchair, or push a pram, please use the east entrance, which has a ramp and a button for the automatic door. The west entrance has a gentle slope, but it's quite steep in wet weather, so we don't recommend it. The front entrance has two steps, though a portable ramp is available on request.

Assistance dogs are very welcome, and we've set up a water station outside the east entrance, with a bowl that's always full. And for parents who find loud events difficult, such as the end-of-year concert, we have a supply of ear defenders, which you can borrow at the door. You don't need to explain why. Many of our teachers use them too.

Several of you have asked about cost. The whole wing cost slightly more than a standard refurbishment, but the extra was less than five percent of the budget, and the governors agreed that it was money well spent.

To end, I'd like to say that none of this was done for a single child. Every one of these features helps a great many of them. The colour-coding helps young children find their way, the quiet corner helps those who are tired, and the dimmable lights help all of us who have a headache. That's the idea we'll look at tonight. Now, if you'd like to follow me, the first stop is the Year Two classroom, just along the green corridor.
Jasmine, Owen, come in. Sorry about the mess. I've been marking all morning. So, your design project. Where have you got to?

We've chosen the classroom, a Year Five room in a primary school. We're going to design it for a class of twenty-eight, where three children have significant needs. One has a hearing impairment, one has dyslexia, and one uses a wheelchair.
And we've started drawing the floor plan. But we've run into a disagreement, which is why we wanted to talk to you.
Good. Disagreement is useful. What is it?
Owen wants to arrange the desks in a horseshoe, so that everybody can see everybody. I want groups of four, because that's how modern classrooms work.
But a child with a hearing impairment has to see the speaker's face to lip-read. In groups, someone will always have their back to the teacher.

That's a real concern, and it's one that gets overlooked. But you've made a false choice. Why not combine them? A horseshoe for whole-class teaching, and a way for the groups to form from it when needed. If the tables are on wheels and light enough to move, you can switch in a minute.
Oh, that's clever. We'd assumed we had to choose one.

And also think about where the teacher stands. If they speak with their back to a window, their face will be in shadow, and lip-reading becomes almost impossible. So put the board on a wall with no windows, and keep the teacher's face lit.
Right. I'd not thought of the light at all.
There's another point that students often forget, which is storage. Where do the children keep their bags and coats?
We've put hooks along the back wall, with a row of lockers underneath.

Think about reach. Hooks at the height of a standing adult are useless to a child in a wheelchair, and even to a small seven-year-old. Put them at two heights, or use low shelves. And keep the floor clear. A pile of bags in the middle of a route is an obstacle for a wheelchair, and a hazard for anyone with low vision.
We'll move the lockers into an alcove, then.
Let's discuss the floor. You've drawn a gap of seventy centimetres between the tables. What width does a wheelchair need?
I looked it up. About ninety centimetres to pass through, and a hundred and fifty to turn around.

Then seventy won't do. Please aim for a metre at least. And I'd like to see a clear route from the door to every seat, not just the first row. A student who has to ask classmates to move their chairs every time soon becomes self-conscious.
We could place the wheelchair user's table near the door, so there's less need to move around.
That solves one problem but creates another. If the child is always by the door, they're excluded from the centre of the room. I'd rather widen the routes and let the child sit where they choose.
Fair enough. Now, the dyslexia. We were thinking of coloured overlays for the textbooks.

Hmm. The evidence for overlays is much weaker than people assume. A more reliable approach is to change the text itself. Use a clear sans serif font, plenty of space between the lines, and cream paper rather than bright white. And for dyslexic students, listening to a recording of a text can be as valuable as reading it. Do you have audio options in your design?
We hadn't included those. We could add a listening station.
Better still, make sure all class materials exist in two forms, and anyone can use either. That way no one is singled out.
And for the hearing impairment, we've specified a hearing loop and carpet.

The loop is a good idea, but be careful about the carpet. Many hearing aid users prefer hard floors with acoustic ceiling tiles, because the echo is the real enemy. Also, think about the position of the loop. If you put the microphone at the front, but the teacher moves around, it won't work. A teacher should wear a small microphone.
So hearing loop, plus microphone, plus ceiling panels.

Exactly. Now, I'd like you to remember one thing. All of these features should be available to everyone. You're not designing a special corner for the three students. You're designing a room in which they don't have to ask for anything.
One more suggestion. Before you finalise anything, try to speak to people who actually use these features. Is there a disability support officer at the university?
Yes, there's an office on the second floor of the library.

Ask if somebody would look at your plan. A fifteen-minute conversation with someone who has lived with a hearing impairment is worth more than a week with a textbook. And listen carefully, because the answer won't always be the one you expect.
We'll book an appointment tomorrow.
That's a lovely way of putting it. We'll revise the plan and send it to you.
Please do. I'd like to see a second version before the end of the month, with measurements this time, not just sketches.
We'll get it done. Thanks, Dr Faulkner.

Good morning. Let me begin with a small piece of street furniture that you've all used without noticing: the dropped kerb. That's the place where the pavement slopes down to the road. Now, who do you think those were designed for? Wheelchair users, yes. But think about who actually uses them. People pushing prams, travellers with suitcases, children on scooters, delivery workers with trolleys. Designers call this the curb-cut effect, and it's the foundation of today's lecture, which is about designing classrooms, and teaching, so that fewer people need special treatment.

The term universal design was coined in the 1970s by the American architect Ronald Mace. Mace was a wheelchair user himself, and he was frustrated that buildings were designed for an imaginary average person, then adapted afterwards, at greater cost and with worse results. His principle was that things should be usable by everyone from the start, without needing adaptation. It's a simple idea that's hard to put into practice.

I should say a word about cost, because that is the usual objection. Retrofitting is expensive, but designing something in from the start adds only a small fraction to the budget. A ramp built into a new entrance costs far less than a ramp added later, and a classroom with good acoustics costs little more to build than one without. The expensive option is nearly always to do nothing, and then to deal with the complaints afterwards.

In education, the idea was developed by a research organisation called CAST, based in the state of Massachusetts. In the 1990s, researchers there started asking what it would mean to apply universal design to learning itself, not just to buildings. They suggested Universal Design for Learning, or UDL, and it rests on three principles, which I'd like you to remember.

The first is engagement, which is about the why of learning. People are motivated by different things, so teachers should offer choices. For example, students might be allowed to choose the topic of an assignment, or the order in which they do the tasks. Even small choices make a significant difference to motivation, particularly for children who find school difficult.

The second principle is representation, the what of learning. Information should be presented in more than one format. If you give a lecture, provide a transcript. If you provide a text, also provide an audio recording or a diagram. This helps students with visual or hearing difficulties, but it also helps the student who didn't understand the first time, or whose first language isn't English.

The third principle is action and expression, the how. Students should be able to show what they know in different ways. One student might write an essay, another might record a podcast, a third might make a poster. As long as the learning outcome is the same, the format can vary. Obviously, if the outcome is a skill like handwriting, you can't offer an alternative, and this is a point critics are quick to make.

Now let me turn from teaching to the physical room. Take noise first. Research on classroom acoustics indicates that background noise should stay below 35 decibels. That's quieter than a library. To put it in perspective, a typical classroom with an air conditioner and some chatter in the corridor is often twice that. The other factor is reverberation, or echo. For a typical classroom, a reverberation time of about 0.6 seconds is recommended. Many are over a second, which means that a child who is listening in a second language, or with a hearing impairment, simply cannot catch the ends of words.

Light is the third factor. Natural light is best, but it needs to be controlled, with blinds, so that it doesn't produce glare. Older fluorescent lights are best avoided, because they flicker in a way that can cause headaches and distraction for some children, especially those on the autism spectrum. Modern LED fittings are far better, particularly if they're dimmable.

What ties all this together? A well-designed room means that fewer students have to request special treatment. The best adjustment is the one nobody has to request. If the student with a hearing impairment can hear, and the student with dyslexia can read, and the student in the wheelchair can move around, then none of them has to explain, and none of them has to wait for permission. In that sense, accessibility is not a favour, but simply good design.

Before you go, a short reading list. Please look at two things this week: the CAST guidelines, which are free online, and the acoustic standard for classrooms that your own education department publishes. Neither is long, and both are more readable than you might expect.

In the seminar this week, you'll each be given a classroom plan and asked to find ten barriers. I'd like you to begin by looking at the room as a first-year child would, and then as a parent with a pram, and then as a teacher who is losing her voice. Thank you.
Hello? Sorry, I think I've been put through from the main line. Is this the pass office?
It is. Gareth speaking, Calderbrook Buses pass desk. The main line sends us every pass query, so you're in the right place. Are you after a new pass or a renewal?
A new one. I've just started a job on the other side of town, and I'd much rather leave the car at home. Parking round there is a nightmare anyway.

Forty-six Alder Lane. Sorry, no, Alder Close. Everybody gets that wrong, because there's an Alder Lane just round the corner and my post keeps going to the wrong house.
Alder Close, then, number 46. Thanks. Now, do you mind telling me what you do for a living? It's only because some employers have an agreement with us, so you might be entitled to a reduction.
I'm a physiotherapist. I've started at the Eastgate Clinic, which is the private one behind the cinema.
Physiotherapist. No, I'm afraid the clinic isn't on our partner list, although hospital staff are. Never mind, I'll note it down anyway. Which route will you use most?

Well, the 41 goes right past the clinic door, but it only comes every half an hour, as far as I can tell. My neighbour says I should take the 14, which runs along the river every ten minutes, and then walk the last bit from the stop.
Your neighbour's right. Most commuters on that side of town choose the 14. So, would you like a weekly, a monthly or an annual pass?
I was tempted by the annual one, because it works out cheaper per week, but I'm still on probation at work. So I think I'd better go for monthly.
Very sensible. If the job doesn't work out, you haven't paid for a whole year. When would you like it to start?
The first of February would be ideal. That's my first proper week.
Ah. Our system is being updated that weekend, so nothing can be activated on the first. The earliest I can start it is 2 February. Is that all right?
That's fine. I'll manage one day on foot.
Lovely. Now the price. A monthly adult pass is £64, but are you under twenty-six?
I'm twenty-five. Until June, anyway.
Then you qualify for the Young Traveller rate, which is £48 a month. That's quite a saving, so it's worth the paperwork. You'll need to show proof of age, and proof of address as well.
I can bring my driving licence for the age part. What counts as proof of address? I've got a bank statement somewhere.

A bank statement used to be fine, but we stopped taking those last year, because so many people have gone paperless and can't print them. It has to be a utility bill, dated within the last three months.
Oh, that's easy. I've got one from December, so I'll bring that along.
Perfect. Now, you can have the pass posted to you, which takes about five working days, or you can pick it up on the same day from one of our travel shops.
I'll pick it up at the station shop. That's the most convenient for me, because I pass it on the way home.
Ah, the station one is closed for refurbishment until April, I'm afraid. The Dockside shop is open, though, and it's only two stops away on the 14.
Oh, right. Dockside is fine, then. Do I need to make an appointment?

No, just walk in, but avoid the lunch hour if you can, because it gets busy with office workers. I'll put your details on the form. Your reference number is on my screen now, and you'll need it at the counter. It's T-B-5-5-2-8, so TB5528 all together.
T-B-5-5-2-8. Let me write that on my hand. And should I pay now or when I collect?

When you collect, by card or cash. You'll also be able to load the pass onto our app afterwards, so you won't need to carry the card around if you don't want to. We'll send you an email with the details by this evening.
That's brilliant. Thank you so much for your help, Gareth. You've made it much easier than I expected.
My pleasure. Enjoy the 14, and I hope the new job goes well.

Right, if everyone's got a lanyard on, we'll make a start. I'm Hilary Strand, and I run operations here at Fennick Interchange, which, as of last Monday, is officially open. Thank you for coming on a preview morning. You're the first members of the public to go round, so please tell me anything that doesn't work.

First, a little background, because I know the old bus station had its fans. A lot of people assume we knocked it down because it was falling apart, but the building was perfectly sound. It wasn't too small either; there was room for far more buses than we ever sent there. The real problem was the layout. Buses had to reverse out of their bays into a busy road, which was dangerous for pedestrians and caused long delays at peak times. That's why it had to go.

The new interchange has 16 bays. Our original design had 18, but we gave two of them up to make room for the cycle store that you'll see later. The old station had only 12, so it's still a big step up. Every bay is numbered and colour-coded to match the route maps in the shelters, so if you know your route colour, you know which way to walk.

Now, information. We have large departure screens in the hall, and they're very good, but our ticket office staff told us something interesting during testing. When a bus is delayed, the app updates before the screens do, because the screens only refresh once a minute. So if you see the word Delayed on a screen, the quickest thing to do is check the app for the revised time, rather than joining the queue at the desk. The staff will always help, of course, but you'll get your answer faster that way.

You'll also notice people in yellow jackets walking around. They're called Bus Buddies, and I want to be clear about what they do, because on the first day several visitors thought they were ticket inspectors. They don't check tickets, and they don't sell them either. They're here for anyone who feels unsure about using the bus, perhaps somebody who has never travelled by bus before, or somebody who finds the ticket machines confusing. They'll walk you to the right bay and explain how to pay.

A word about timing. Between half past seven and nine in the morning, and again from four until six, the hall is very crowded. If you're pushing a pram, using a wheelchair or travelling with a lot of luggage, you'll find it much easier between 9.30 and 11. Lunchtimes are busier than you might think, because of the shoppers, and after seven in the evening it's quiet, but fewer services run, so it isn't ideal either.

Right, let me take you round the facilities, and I'll point each one out on your plan as we go. If you look at the map in your hands, I've marked seven locations with letters. We'll start with the lost property office. You might expect it to be by the main doors, because that's where the old one was. But we found that people were using the doors as a shortcut, and the queue was blocking them, so it's now tucked away behind the lifts. It's a bit hidden, I admit, so the Bus Buddies will point you there.

Next, something we're proud of, the quiet room. Some passengers find a busy station overwhelming, particularly children and people with anxiety, so we've created a small room with soft lighting and no announcements. It's on the first floor, and the lifts take you straight there. Please don't use it for meetings, as some people did in the first week.

Moving down again, there's the cycle store. Now, we considered putting it near the main entrance, but cyclists told us they'd rather not wheel their bikes through a crowd of people, so it's beside the taxi rank, with its own entrance from the road. It holds sixty bikes, and there's a repair stand where you can borrow a pump and some basic tools.

While you wait for your coffee, you can charge your phone. We've installed lockers with charging cables, and they're opposite the café, so you can keep an eye on things while you drink. You choose a code, and you can leave your phone for up to an hour. We've found they're used mostly by commuters on the evening shift.

And finally, the accessible toilets. In the original plan they were going to go under the big clock, which is a lovely meeting point, but wheelchair users told us it was too far from the entrance, especially in winter. So we moved them to the very first thing you see as you walk in, right next to the main doors. They're open around the clock, and there's an alarm cord in every cubicle.

That's the end of the tour, but before we go for a cup of tea, I'd like to ask each of you to fill in a short card. It takes about two minutes, and I promise nobody will read your handwriting aloud. We'll be making changes over the next few months, and what you tell us this morning will decide the first of them. Thank you very much, and mind the step on the way out.
Come in, both of you. Jess, Anwar, sit wherever you like. Right, your project on bus travel. I've seen the draft, and I'd like to hear how the survey went before we talk about the presentation.
It went quite well, in the end. We'd hoped to hand out the questionnaires on the buses themselves, but the bus company wouldn't allow it.
Really? Was it the passengers who objected?

No, passengers were friendly enough. Some of them did say they didn't have time, because they were watching for their stop, but that wasn't the problem. The company said having students walking down the aisle was a safety risk, so we asked people at the stops instead.
Which turned out better, actually, because people waiting at a stop have time to talk.
Good. And you got how many responses?
A hundred and twenty. We spent three days at four stops in different parts of the city.
Fine. Now, what did you find? I read your summary, but I'd like it in your own words.
The thing that came up most often was people not knowing when the next bus would arrive. Even with the app, the times on the screen don't always match what happens in the street.

And the second most common was the route maps at the stops. People said they were confusing, with too many colours and lines, and nobody could tell where a bus actually goes after the third or fourth stop.
Interesting. So not overcrowding, which is what I would have guessed?
That came third, which surprised me too. A lot of people mentioned it, but it was far behind the other two.

What surprised me most, though, was the fares. I thought price would dominate, but hardly anyone complained about it. Only about one in ten even mentioned it, and most of those said the fares were fair.
That's useful, and it makes a good point for your discussion section. Now, about the sample. A hundred and twenty is fine for a student project, but did you look at who answered?
We did. It's mostly people between eighteen and thirty-five.

Which isn't surprising for a city with two universities. But you should say that clearly. I notice you've got only seven respondents over sixty-five, and older people are exactly the ones who tell you about the steps onto the bus and the time given to sit down.
We know. We did try to speak to more of them, but they tended to wait at the stop in the middle of the day and our timetable didn't allow it.
Then just be honest about it. A limitation stated clearly is worth more than a bigger sample that you can't explain.
Okay. We'll put it at the start of the discussion.
There's one other thing. In the questionnaire there was a question on fares, and it doesn't seem to tell us much. Should we delete it from the report?

I wouldn't delete it. You've got the data, and the fact that people aren't bothered about fares is a finding in itself. But it doesn't deserve a long discussion. Give it its own short section, a paragraph or two, and move on.
That makes sense. I'd wondered about redoing the question, but we haven't got time to go back out.
No, don't do that. One more thing on the method. Did you tell people what the survey was for, and did you take any names?
We explained it was for a university project, and we didn't take names, only the age group and the route they used most.
A few people asked what we'd do with the answers, so we gave them the email address from the information sheet, in case they wanted to see the final report.
Good. Put a sentence about that in the method, because markers like to see that you thought about it. It costs you ten words and earns you credit. And did you survey at the weekend as well?
Only on weekdays, between eight and six. We haven't got any evening data at all.

Then that goes in the limitations too. Now, the presentation. You've got fifteen minutes, so let's be practical. Jess, your introduction takes up three slides at the moment, which is far too many. What does the audience need?
Why we did it and what we asked.
Exactly. So make it much shorter, one slide at the most. Anwar, the method section is fine, but one thing is missing. Why did you choose those four stops?
We just picked places we knew were busy.
Then say so, and explain why that matters. Someone in the audience will ask, and you want an answer ready. It's also worth saying that two of the stops are on routes the council plans to change.
Right, I'll add that.
Now, the results. You have two tables with lots of percentages. In a talk, nobody will take those in. Could you turn them into a chart? Even a simple bar chart would work better.
We've got the numbers in a spreadsheet, so that's easy enough.
Good. And the recommendations. You've got six, which is a lot. Whatever you keep, make sure each one points back to something you found, so people can see where it comes from.
Should we compare our city with another one? We found some figures from a city in the south that did a similar survey.
It's tempting, but I wouldn't. You'd need to explain how their survey was different from yours, and you haven't got room. Leave it for the dissertation, if you carry on with this topic.
One last question. Are the numbers in the report all right? Anwar added them up last night, and I think some of the percentages come to a hundred and one.
Rounding, probably. It happens all the time, and a short note under the table will explain it. But do check them once more before you submit.
Will do. Thank you, Dr Hollis. That's really helpful.
You're welcome. Send me the slides on Thursday, and I'll have a look before the day.

Good morning. Buses carry more passengers than trains in most cities, yet they receive only a fraction of the design attention. Today I'd like to ask what happens when a city decides to take buses seriously. I'll use a case study from a city I'll call Northbury, because the council asked us not to name it.

Let's start with the network as it was. Northbury had 62 routes, and they had grown over decades. Each time residents complained about a service, a route was bent a little to pass their street or a new housing estate. The result was a map that looked like a plate of spaghetti. Routes were long and winding, doubling back to visit a hospital, then a supermarket, then a station. The journey from one side of town to the other might take an hour and a quarter by bus, and twenty minutes by car.

Now, when planners asked residents why they avoided the buses, you might expect the main answer to be price, or speed. It wasn't. The main barrier was uncertainty. People simply didn't know where a bus would take them, or when it would come. If you don't understand the system, you won't risk it, however cheap it is.

So the city started again. The new network has 24 routes, and the aim was clarity above everything else. They concentrated resources on the main roads, and on those roads a bus comes every 10 minutes, all day and into the evening. I should mention that the plan began with every 15 minutes, because the budget was tight, but a late decision found the extra money, and the 10-minute version is what launched. The idea is what the planners called turn up and go. If a bus comes every ten minutes, you no longer need a timetable. You just walk to the stop.

Of course, high frequency costs money, and the city found it by making buses faster. The first step was to look at the stops. The old network had a stop roughly every 200 metres, which is very convenient but very slow, because every stop costs a bus thirty seconds or more. The first proposal was to increase the spacing to 300 metres. But after modelling the effect, the planners decided that 400 metres would give much better journey times, and that's what they adopted. Naturally, some residents objected, and I'll come back to them.

The second step was payment. Before the redesign, passengers queued at the front door to pay the driver in cash. Now they can touch a contactless card on a reader at any door. The time spent at each stop is known as dwell time, and the effect was striking. The average time to board a passenger dropped from five seconds to just 2. On a busy route with hundreds of passengers, that adds up to many minutes saved over a day.

The third step was giving the buses space on the road. On the main corridors, the city created bus lanes, and, so that nobody could claim they hadn't noticed them, the surface was painted red. Painted lanes are only as good as their enforcement, though. Northbury installed cameras that record parked cars blocking the lane and automatically send a fine to the owner. In the first six months, there were many fines, but after that the number fell sharply, which suggests that drivers learned.

I should say a word about information, because it was the root of the problem. At the old stops there was a different route map at every pole, drawn by different people, and none of them agreed. The city replaced them all with a single simple diagram, in the same style at every stop, showing only the main routes and where they meet. It looked less impressive than the old maps, but people could read it in a few seconds, and that was the point.

Finally, signals. At many junctions, the traffic lights were programmed to detect an approaching bus and give it an early green light. It doesn't sound like much, but a bus that doesn't stop at red lights keeps to its schedule, and that makes the frequency promise believable.

So did it work? After the first year, passenger numbers had risen by 6 per cent, which was disappointing for the council, because they had hoped for 10. But the effect built up as people discovered the new system, and after two years the rise was 14 per cent. That's a remarkable figure for a city of that size, and it came without any increase in fares.

But there were losers, and I promised to come back to them. The people who lost out were mostly residents in the hilly districts on the north side, where a stop 400 metres away is a real climb, particularly for older people. The council didn't ignore them. Instead of restoring the old routes, it introduced a minibus service, which runs on demand to people's doors and connects them to the main corridors. It costs more per passenger than the big buses, but it keeps those residents inside the system.

So what can we learn from Northbury? Three things, I think. First, a network that people can understand will attract people who've never tried it. Second, speed and frequency support each other, because a faster bus needs fewer vehicles to run the same service. And third, the people who lose out from a redesign need a real answer, not a promise. Next week we'll turn to a different question, which is how to measure whether passengers actually feel safe at night. Please read the two articles on the course page before then.
You've reached Wick Lantern Walks, and this is Dominic. Sorry about the wait, we've got a school group in the office.
Oh, no problem at all. I'm hoping to book a tour for my book club. We've been reading a novel set in Ashby Wick, and somebody had the idea of walking round the places in it.
What a lovely idea. Which novel is it?
The Salt Road. Do you know it?
I certainly do. We get asked about it constantly. We can take you past three of the real locations. Let me open the booking sheet. Could I take your surname?
Teague. That's T-E-A-G-U-E.
Teague, lovely. And how many will you be?
There are twelve of us in the club, but a couple of the members want to bring their husbands along, so, er, 14 altogether.
Fourteen, that's fine. We can take up to twenty on a single walk. Did you have a date in mind?
We usually meet on Thursdays, so I was thinking of the 15th of May.

Ah, that one's no good, I'm afraid. Gethin, our best guide for literary walks, is away that week, and you really want him because he's read the book three times. Could you manage the Thursday after? That would be 22 May.
Yes, 22 May should be fine. I'll check with the others, but I can't imagine anyone minding.
And what time? Our evening walks usually start at seven.
Hmm. Several of us have a long drive home afterwards, so could we start a little earlier? Half past six would suit us better.
No problem at all. 6.30 it is. Now, where would you like to meet? Most groups gather at the castle gate.
Yes, I was going to suggest the castle gate, because it's easy to find.

I'd steer you away from that, actually. There are roadworks outside it until the summer, and the coaches drop off right there, so it's chaos. The Market Cross is much easier, and it has benches for anyone who arrives early.
The Market Cross, then. That's near the church, isn't it?

Just opposite. Now, there are three routes. The Castle Loop is the most dramatic, but it's steep and has a lot of steps. The Quay Steps has the best views, but it's hilly too. And the Ropewalk follows the old rope-makers' lane through the lower town, and it's almost completely flat.
One of our members walks with a stick, so the Ropewalk sounds the sensible choice. Does it pass the places in the book?
Two of the three. The third is the bookseller's yard, and we can reach that with a short detour at the end.
Wonderful. Does the guide read from the book at all?
Gethin does, a few short passages at each location. He'll ask for volunteers to read, so I'd warn your members in advance. Some people love it, and some hide behind the nearest wall.
I'll tell them. We've got at least three who'd read the whole book aloud if we let them. And how long does it take?

Most people expect two hours, because that's what it says on the website, but that includes a lot of stops. For a group with a member who needs to go slowly, we'd allow about 90 minutes, with plenty of pauses to sit down.
That would suit us very well. And what's the cost?
Our standard price is £12 a head, but groups of ten or more get a reduction, so it's £9 per person.
That's a good deal. Where does the walk finish?

Back down by the quay. A lot of groups go on to the Ferryman, which is the pub with the long back room. It actually appears in chapter six of your novel, so people like to see it. They do hot food until nine, but I'd book a table in advance.
Could you do that for us? I'd hate to arrive with fourteen people and find nowhere to sit.

I'll ring them this afternoon and let you know. Now, the last thing is a deposit. We ask for a quarter of the cost in advance. We used to take cheques, but we don't any more, and the card machine in the office has been giving us trouble, so the easiest way is bank transfer. I'll email you the details.
That's fine. I'm the treasurer of the club, so it'll be no trouble at all.
Perfect. You'll get a confirmation by email within the hour. And if anyone's unwell on the day, just ring us before six, and we'll sort something out.
Thank you, Dominic. You've been very helpful.
My pleasure. I hope the weather behaves.

Good, I think that's everyone. Gather in a bit closer, if you can, because the traffic is noisy on this corner. My name is Colin Maddox, I'm a volunteer with the Kelmoor Civic Society, and this morning we're launching the Kelmoor Heritage Trail. It's been two years in the making, so you'll forgive me if I get a little excited.

First, the basics. The trail begins here in Fish Street and winds through the old town to the harbour and back. Our first draft was five kilometres, but we tested it on some friends and they were exhausted by the end, so we trimmed it to three and a half. If three and a half still sounds too much, there's a shortcut that skips the harbour, which is two and a half kilometres, and it's marked with orange discs instead of blue ones.

You'll notice there are no signposts. We did ask permission to fix them to the old walls, but the conservation officer refused, because so many of the buildings are listed, and you can't drill into them. It was never about cost, as it happens, because the money came from a lottery grant. So, instead, there are small blue discs set into the pavement. Just follow them, and you can't go wrong. Some of them are a bit worn, I admit, so please tell me if you lose one.

A word about the ground. The oldest part of the trail runs along a cobbled lane called the Shambles, and it's lovely, but it's uneven. Trainers are fine in dry weather, but in the wet, smooth soles can be treacherous, so wear shoes with a good grip. There's a handrail on the steep section by the church steps, but it's only a few metres long, so don't rely on it. And please don't walk in the middle of the lane. Delivery vans do use it, early in the morning.

Now, the audio guide. You can download it free by scanning the code on the leaflet. It's not a lecture, I promise. It includes a lovely set of archive photographs, many from the 1900s, which you can compare with what you see in front of you. It also has recordings of residents, some in their eighties, talking about what the harbour was like when they were children. We did consider adding the local legends, the ghost of the customs man and so on, but they're in the leaflet, so we left them out. We also considered notes on the architecture, but they made each stop too long, so we dropped those as well.

Right, let me tell you about some of the buildings you'll pass, because a lot of them have changed what they do. First, the old customs house, the grand building with the pillars. A lot of visitors take it for a hotel, because of the entrance, but it's actually the town museum, and it's free on Sundays.

Next, the wool exchange, on the corner of Mill Lane. Until a couple of years ago, that was the library, and quite a few older residents still call it that. Now it's an art gallery, and it holds the work of local painters.

A little further on you'll see the Tanner's Hall, with its crooked beams. For years, it was empty, and then somebody had the idea of turning it into a bookshop. It's called the Hide and Seek, and it has a tiny café at the back where you can get tea. Half the town drops in on Saturdays.

Then there's the chapel, at the top of the hill. You might expect it to be a place of worship, but the congregation shrank, and the building was sold. After the wool exchange became a gallery, the library needed a new home, so it moved into the chapel, and the stained glass is still there.

Finally, the corn mill by the river, where the trail turns back. The wheel doesn't turn any more, but the building is in use again. It's a bakery, and the bread is made with flour from a farm up the valley. If you arrive before ten, you'll smell it from the bridge, so I'd suggest saving your coffee break until then.

A few practical points. There are public toilets by the museum, in the car park behind the bookshop and down at the harbour, and they all close at six. If it rains, you can shelter under the arcade at the customs house. Dogs are welcome, but they must be on a lead in the churchyard, because of the nesting birds.

One more thing. We'd love to know what you think of the trail, and there are feedback cards at the museum and in the bookshop. If you have any trouble finding a disc, or you think a stop is badly placed, please tell us. Any questions before we set off? No? Then follow me, and mind the kerb.
Come in, Freya, Luis. Sit down. I've read your outline for the walking project, and it looks interesting. Remind me, which town are you looking at?
Hartsmoor. It's a small market town, with a medieval centre, and the council wants to create a new walking route through it for visitors.
And why Hartsmoor, in particular? I know there are plenty of old towns.

Partly because it's typical, but mostly because the council has been counting pedestrians in the centre for three years, and they've agreed to give us the data. That would have taken us months to collect ourselves.
Freya grew up there, as well, but we decided that wasn't the main reason. It might look like bias.
It's not a bad thing to mention, though, as long as you're honest about it. Now, what have you done so far?
We've spoken to residents. We held two drop-in sessions at the library, and about forty people came.
Who came, mostly? Retired people tend to be over-represented at that sort of event.
They were, yes. About two thirds were retired, which is why we also put a short questionnaire through the doors on Cooper's Row, to hear from people who are out at work in the daytime.
We delivered sixty and got twenty-two back, which isn't bad.

That's a decent response for a leaflet drop. Make sure you say how many you delivered and how many came back, otherwise a reader can't judge it. And what about the shopkeepers? They'll have strong views too.
We've only managed to speak to five so far. Most were positive, but one said tourists look in the window and never come in.
That's worth a line in your report. Visitor numbers and visitor spending are not the same thing, and the council will want to know the difference. Now, what did they think about the proposed route?

Mixed, to be honest. Some people welcomed it, because it would bring customers to the shops. But the people who live along the route were worried, and their concerns were mainly about two things. The first was noise. Groups of visitors talking in a narrow street can be heard in every bedroom.

And the second was privacy. The houses on Cooper's Row open straight onto the pavement, so people walking past can look into the front rooms. One woman told us she'd already stopped using her living room in the summer.
What about litter, or parking?
A few people mentioned litter, but only in passing. And parking isn't affected, because the route is pedestrian only.
I see. And damage to the doorsteps? Some residents complain about that with heritage routes.
Nobody mentioned it, actually.
Good. What about the mapping? You said in your outline that you'd planned a map of the route.

Yes, and that's been a bit of a problem. The standard map we downloaded is at too small a scale. It doesn't show the passages between the buildings at all, and in Hartsmoor, those are the most interesting part. Some are less than a metre wide.
So how are you handling that?
We're walking the whole centre with a measuring wheel and drawing the passages in by hand. It's slow, but it's already shown us several that aren't on any map.
That sounds like a real contribution. Now, you've included a lot of photographs in the draft. I like them, but I'm not sure they do enough work.
We thought they made the report more interesting.

They do, but a photograph on its own just shows what a place looks like. If you add labels, showing what a walker would see and where the problem is, the same picture becomes evidence. I'd mark them up.
Okay, that's easy enough to do.
Now, the next phase. You'll need your own counts of pedestrians, not just the council's. How will you do that?
We considered cameras, but we'd have needed permission from the council and from the shops, and we don't think there's time. We also thought about using phone data, but that costs money.
So we're going to count by hand, standing at fixed points for twenty minutes in each hour, with those clickers you press.

That's practical, and it means you'll see what people do, as well as how many there are. Fine. Now let's go through the route. You've picked out four sections that need improvement. Tell me about the market square.

It's the busiest point, and visitors get lost there, because there are six exits and no signs. We thought of adding benches, but there are plenty already, so our suggestion is information boards, one at each corner.
Sensible. And Cooper's Row?

That's the narrowest lane, and two groups can't pass each other. We considered banning bicycles at busy times, but there aren't many cyclists in there anyway. So we'd make it one-way for walkers, with arrows painted on the ground.
Will that really work? People don't follow arrows.
They do, in a narrow place. We've looked at other towns.
Fair enough. And the harbour steps?
Those are the problem for wheelchairs and pushchairs. There are fifteen steps, and no alternative. Our suggestion is a ramp beside them, built from stone to match.
That'll cost a lot, and the conservation officer will have views. But it's right to suggest it. And the last section?
The churchyard path. It's very pleasant by day, but it's dark in winter, and people feel unsafe. We'd add low lighting along the edge, nothing bright, so it doesn't spoil the atmosphere.
Good. I'm happy with that. One last thing, your timetable. When are you planning the counts?
In the week after the exams, so the students are away and the town is back to normal.
Avoid market day for your first counts, because it will distort the figures. Do one market-day count separately, though, so you can show the difference.
That makes sense. We'll mark it clearly in the data.
Good. Send me the revised outline by Friday, and then we'll plan the fieldwork.

Good afternoon. Last week we looked at new towns designed around the car, and we saw how difficult they are to walk in. This week I want to go in the opposite direction, and ask why the old centres of our towns, which nobody planned in the modern sense, are often so pleasant on foot. I'll use a town in the south-west that I'll call Wexcombe, because it's a very typical case.

Let's start with the layout. Most old towns grew around a central market, which is where people gathered to trade, and every street led towards it. You can still see the pattern today. The streets radiate out like the spokes of a wheel, and the market square is the hub. The point is that nobody had to be told where the centre was. You simply followed the street downhill, or followed the crowd.

The streets themselves are narrow. In Wexcombe, many of them are less than 6 metres wide, and some are barely 3. They were built for people and horses, not for vehicles, and that's the reason they feel so comfortable to walk in. Planners today often talk about the human scale, and that's what they mean.

The blocks between the streets are also small. In a modern housing estate, you might walk for five hundred metres without a junction. In Wexcombe, you reach one every forty or fifty metres, so an old town has many more junctions than a new one. That means walkers always have a choice of ways, and when there's a choice, people explore. The shortcuts between the main streets have their own names. In northern England they're ginnels or snickets, and in Scotland they're called vennels.

Now let me turn to why people enjoy it. The first reason is distance. Because the buildings are close together and the streets bend, you never see very far ahead, and that has an odd effect. Distances seem shorter than they are, and people are willing to walk further. In a modern street, a straight road of five hundred metres looks like a long way. In an old town, the same distance feels like a stroll.

The second reason is what we might call visual interest. The ground floors are full of shops, with windows, signs and displays, and the upper floors have different roof lines, balconies and chimneys. There's something new to look at every few steps. Researchers who study walking say that this keeps people moving, because a boring wall makes them hurry, while a window makes them slow down.

There's also the question of edges. Old streets have a hard edge, a line of buildings right at the pavement, and that gives a sense of enclosure. People feel more secure in a space with a clear edge than in an open car park, where they feel exposed. And at night, lit windows above the shops mean the streets are overlooked by people at home, which is one reason that old centres often feel safer than modern ones after dark.

Does it make a difference to behaviour? A survey in Wexcombe found that visitors spent an average of 55 minutes on foot in the old centre. I'd compare that with the retail park on the edge of town, where the figure was only 40, even though the retail park has far more shops. People came, parked, shopped and left.

But I don't want to give you a romantic picture, because old towns have problems for walkers too. The most obvious one is the surface. Cobbles are beautiful, but they're very difficult for wheelchair users and also for people pushing prams. A few towns have cut smooth stone tracks into the cobbles, which look rather good, but they cost a great deal, and they have to be done carefully, so they don't spoil the appearance.

The second problem is traffic. Many of the old streets are still used by delivery vehicles, because the shops have to be supplied. Wexcombe used to allow them at any time, and the result was a series of near misses in the morning. The council first proposed to restrict them to before ten, but shopkeepers objected, because their customers arrive from ten onwards and they needed to unload earlier. In the end, they settled on 11, with a short window in the afternoon for urgent deliveries. Complaints dropped by half.

Finally, many towns have gone further and closed the centre to vehicles completely on one day a week. In Wexcombe, that's Saturdays, which is the busiest shopping day. At first, the shopkeepers feared they would lose trade. In fact, takings rose, and some of the shops now open later on Saturday evenings.

So what can we learn from places like Wexcombe? I think there are three points to take away. First, a good walking environment doesn't have to be designed all at once. Wexcombe developed over centuries, with many small decisions, and that variety is part of the attraction. Second, any change, even a good one, will affect someone, and the planners who succeeded were those who talked to the shopkeepers and residents before making changes. Third, the best old towns don't try to be museums. They stay in use, and the people who live and work there are the reason visitors enjoy walking through them. Next week, we'll look at what happens when that balance goes wrong, and a town is given over to tourists. Please read the two case studies on the course page.
Hello, is that the Lighthouse Rest? Oh, good. I was worried I'd have the wrong number, because the website lists two.
Easily done. The other one is an old listing from the previous owners, and I keep asking the directory to take it down. We're the one with the blue door, on Kittiwake Road.
That's the one. I saw your notice about winter breaks, and I wondered whether you've still got any rooms in January.
We have, more than you'd think. January is our quietest month, which is why we put the breaks together in the first place. Shall I take some details?
Please. The name's Quaife. That's Q-U-A-I-F-E.
Quaife, thank you. And which dates were you thinking of?
We'd hoped to arrive on the 10th, but my wife has a hospital appointment that morning, so it would have to be a few days later than that.
How about 14 January? That's midweek, and the room I have in mind is free.
14 January, yes, that should be fine. I'll just check with Alison that she hasn't made other plans, but I don't think she has.
Lovely. And how many nights?
Two, I think. We're really after a long weekend, nothing more than that.

Well, you might want to think about three. The package I'll tell you about works out better value over three nights, because everything is included from the first day. And in January, there isn't much of a rush to leave.
You've talked me into it. Three nights, then, 3 nights.

Which room would you like? We have the sea-view room at the front, which is lovely, but it's being redecorated in January, so I can offer you the garden room at the back instead. It's actually bigger, and it has its own door onto the terrace.
The garden room sounds fine. Do you get much of a view?

Of the garden, mainly, but you can hear the sea, which most people prefer when they've got a book. Now, the package. We have two offers. The Storm Watcher includes a guided walk along the cliffs, with waterproofs provided, but it only runs at weekends. Since you're arriving midweek, I'd suggest the Winter Warmer.
That sounds cosy. What does it cost?

Our usual winter rate is £85 a night, and in the summer it's £110. With the Winter Warmer, it comes down to £70 a night, because we'd rather have the rooms full. And that includes afternoon tea each day, which our guests tell us is the best part.
Afternoon tea. My wife will be delighted. She loves a scone.
Do you allow dogs? We might bring Biscuit, our spaniel.

Dogs are welcome in the garden rooms, in fact, which is another reason I'd suggest it. There's a charge of eight pounds a night, and he's not allowed on the beds, although I gather that's a rule most guests break.
Biscuit has his own blanket, so we'll manage. And what's the town like in January? Is anything open?

More than you'd expect. The shops mostly close at four, but the bookshop stays open late on Fridays, and the pub on the harbour does hot food every night. It's quiet, but quiet is what most of our winter guests are after.
Good. Do you have any dietary requirements? Breakfast is a full cooked one, but we can do alternatives.
Well, my wife is vegetarian. Actually, no, I should say vegan. She gave up cheese in the autumn, and I keep forgetting.
Vegan is no trouble at all, but it helps to know in advance, so that I can order the right things. I'll make a note.
And parking? Is there anywhere near you?

We haven't got a car park of our own, but there's a free one behind the church hall, which is about two minutes away. Please don't use the harbour car park. It charges, and in winter it closes at four, so you could find the barrier down.
The church hall, behind it. Thank you. I'm glad you mentioned that.
Check-in is from 3 pm. When are you likely to arrive?
We're driving, and I want to stop for lunch on the way, so probably about 5.
Right. Let me put that down.
Actually, the coast road is slow when it's wet, and I'd rather not be rushing in the dark, so make it 4.30.
4.30 it is. If you're running later than six, do ring us, because we lock the front door at seven.
I will. And thank you, you've been wonderfully patient.

Not at all. One more thing, just so you know. If you need to cancel, you can do so up to a week before and get everything back, so there's no risk in booking now. I'll send the confirmation by email tonight.
That's very reassuring. Thanks again.
January is a lovely month for it, as you'll see.

Evening, all. If you could find a chair, and those at the back, there are a few more down the side. I'm Kiri Waite, from Tarawai Bay Tourism, and I'm going to talk for about fifteen minutes about the winter programme, and then I'd like to hear from you. I know some of you came out on a Tuesday night in the rain, which I think proves my point that this town does not stop in winter.

Let me begin with the money, because I know it's what everyone wants to hear about. When we applied to the regional fund, we asked for 90,000 dollars. We didn't get that. Last year's grant was only 40,000, and a lot of you said that wasn't enough to do anything. This time the figure is 60,000, which is a decent start. Another 10,000 may come from the council, but that isn't confirmed, so I won't promise it.

Why spend it on winter at all? Well, we ran a survey last year of people who visited between May and September. The most interesting thing wasn't that they were few. Most were from within two hours' drive, which tells us that the visitors we have are local and not very far from home, and that we haven't been marketing to anyone else. Many of them said they'd come again, if there were more to do.

The second thing the survey told us is what put people off. We expected them to mention the weather, but hardly anybody did. Their main complaint was that many shops and cafés close at four, and by five the town is empty.
