One visitor wrote that they'd come all this way and found the street dark with a single fish and chip shop open.

So, here's what I'd like to ask of you. We aren't asking you to stay open all winter. We're asking you to open until seven on event nights only. There'll be about six of those, and we'll tell you the dates well in advance, so you can plan your staff. I'm not asking you to pay a levy, and I'm not setting up a loyalty card scheme either, although several people suggested both.

Let me go through the calendar, month by month. In May, we'd originally planned a kite festival. But the weather in May is too unpredictable for kites, so we've moved it to September, when the spring winds are steadier. In May instead, we'll have a storytelling night in the old woolshed, with locals telling tales about the bay, and a bit of music. It's a small thing, but the people who've seen it say it's moving.

June has the shortest days, so we thought, why not make a virtue of it? On the longest night, there'll be a lantern parade down the main street, ending at the beach. Children make the lanterns in school, which means that their parents will come as well.

In July, the nights are cold and clear, and the sky over the bay is wonderful. We've talked to the astronomy society, and they'll bring telescopes down to the headland for star-gazing evenings. We did consider a surf competition, because we've got some excellent winter waves, but it needs permission from the harbour authority, and that takes months.

August is the oyster season, and several of the restaurants have already said they'd like to join a seafood trail. People will walk from place to place, tasting something at each stop, and you'll be able to buy a passport that gets stamped. The restaurants share the cost of printing.

A word about publicity, because there's no point having events if nobody knows about them. We'll be advertising in the weekend papers and on regional radio, and every event will have a poster. We print them, you put them in your window, and we'd like them up on the first of each month, not the day before. We'll also have a page on the website with the whole calendar, and I'll send each of you a link as soon as it's ready.

And finally, September. As I said, that's the kite festival. And before somebody asks, no, we haven't forgotten the craft market. But we hold that every summer, and we thought it would be unfair to ask the stallholders to do it twice.

Now, how do we keep in touch? Some of you asked for a monthly meeting. But when we tried that in the spring, only seven people turned up, so I think a meeting isn't the best way. We've set up a group chat instead. Anyone can post an idea, or a problem, and I'll see it within the day. Please don't email the office, because the messages can sit for a week, and by then the moment has passed.

I'll stop there. I know there'll be questions about parking and about the toilets on the headland, and I'll take those in a moment. But first, can I ask for a show of hands? Who here can open until seven on a Friday?
Hamid, Poppy, come in. Sit down. I've been looking forward to this one. Your project on tourism outside the peak season. Where have you got to?

We've done the first stage, which was choosing the case studies. We're comparing two seaside towns, Marlow Sands and Port Teasdale, because they're similar in size, but Marlow Sands has a winter programme and Port Teasdale doesn't.
At first we thought of studying just one, but you said in the seminar that a single case can't tell you whether anything worked. So we're comparing two. We should have thought of it ourselves.
Good. A comparison doesn't prove anything, either, but it gives you something to hold on to. So what data have you collected?

Mostly accommodation figures. We asked the hotels and guesthouses for monthly occupancy. The difficulty is that only the large hotels keep records, and the small guesthouses say they don't, or they won't say. So we've got a lot for the big ones and very little for the others.
That's a bias you'll need to discuss. Large hotels might fill up differently from small guesthouses. Did you interview any of the owners?
Not yet. We were going to start next week.

One thing I'd say about that. Owners will tell you what they think you want to hear, particularly about how much trade they do. So ask about things they can't exaggerate, like how many staff they keep on in winter, and compare their answers with the figures.
That's a good idea. We did look at employment, in fact. In Marlow Sands, about a third of the people who work in hospitality are laid off in November. In Port Teasdale it's more than half.
Which is interesting, because it suggests the winter programme has kept some jobs.
It might. But be careful with that. It could also be that Marlow Sands has a larger local population, so people find other work. You can't claim a cause from those two numbers alone.
No, that's a fair point. We'll say it's consistent with the idea, but not proof.
Also, when did the winter programme start? Because if the layoffs were already falling before it began, that tells a different story.
It began four years ago. We've got the layoff figures for the last eight, so we can see the trend before and after.
Before the programme, the numbers were about the same in both towns, which is a point in our favour.

It is. Put a simple graph of both towns over the eight years in the report, with a line where the programme started. That single picture will do more for your argument than a page of words. And did you ask whether anything else changed at the same time? A new road, say, or a big hotel closing?
Port Teasdale lost its biggest hotel two years ago, which we hadn't thought about. It must have affected the figures.
It certainly would. Mention it, and be careful how much you claim.
Good. Now, the report. How long are your case studies at the moment?
About two thousand words each. We were worried that was too long.
The total word limit is five thousand, so two thousand each leaves you very little for anything else. I'd cut each one by half and put the detail in appendices.
Right. That makes the report much easier to read, I suppose.
It does. Now, let's talk about what Marlow Sands actually does. What's in the winter programme?

They have several things. There's a food festival in October, with stalls on the front. There's a storm-watching walk, which is just what it sounds like, people in waterproofs on the sea wall. There's a wellness weekend, with yoga and spa treatments, and they've started a discount scheme for parking.

Our view is that two of them are the most promising. The food festival, because it brings people who would not come otherwise, and the wellness weekends, because those visitors stay for two nights and spend more. The storm walk is fun, but it only attracts about forty people, and the parking discount seems to help local shoppers rather than visitors.
That's a reasonable analysis. Can you show it, though? How do you know about the spending?

That's the problem. We've got three possible sources of information, and they've all got weaknesses. The first is the hotel records. They tell us who stayed and when, but only for the large hotels, as I said.
The second is the visitor survey that the council does every summer. That's more detailed, but it's out of date, because the last one was done three years ago, and the programme started after that.
And the third is the mobile phone data, which would show where people go. But the council won't release it, because of privacy rules, and we'd need special permission.
Hmm. So hotel records only cover the big places, the survey is old, and the phone data you can't get. Which would you choose, if you had to?
Honestly, the survey. We could ask the council to run a short winter one, even for a week.
Then write that up as your recommendation. It's the kind of practical suggestion that examiners like. And a short survey is something the council might genuinely agree to.
I'll draft an email to them this afternoon.
And one more thing, about your references. Several of them are websites with no date and no author. Try to find at least five academic sources for the discussion.
There's a journal article that compares seasonal patterns in several European resorts. We'll start with that.
Good. Send me a copy before you send it. I know one of the officers there, and it might help if I put in a word.

In our last session, we looked at how tourists choose destinations. Today I'd like to turn to a problem that destinations face once they've been chosen, which is that tourists don't come evenly. Visits bunch together. Economists call this seasonality, and it's one of the most stubborn problems in the industry.

How bad can it be? One simple way to measure it is to compare the busiest month with the quietest. In some Mediterranean resorts, the busiest month has ten times as many visitors as the quietest, and a few hotels close completely for half the year.

Let me begin with the causes. They are often divided into two kinds. The first are natural causes. Weather is the obvious one, but I'd say that temperature on its own doesn't explain it, because many tourists happily visit cold places. What matters more is the number of hours of daylight. People want to be outside, and a coastal walk at four in the afternoon in December simply isn't possible.

The second kind are institutional causes, and these are often more powerful than the weather. The best example is school holidays. Families with children can only travel when schools are closed, and since most schools in a country have the same holidays, millions of people want to go to the same places at the same time. Public holidays do the same thing. A destination can have good weather in September and still be nearly empty, simply because everyone is at school or at work.

What does this mean for a resort town? Think about the jobs. Most people working in hospitality in a seasonal resort are on short-term contracts. They're hired in spring and let go in autumn. That makes it hard to train people, and it means experienced staff move elsewhere. Employers complain about it, but they can't afford to pay people all year.

Then think about the buildings. A hotel owner might tell you that occupancy in winter is about 30 per cent, but when researchers checked the actual records, it was nearer 25. That's one room in four, and the rest are empty, while the costs of heating, insurance and maintenance carry on. And in the peak month, which in most northern resorts is August, the opposite problem arises. The car parks are full, the roads are blocked, and local residents can't get into their own town.

So what can a destination do? The aim isn't to remove the peak, which is neither possible nor desirable. It's to lengthen the shoulder seasons, which are the months between the peak and the off-peak, so that the quiet period gets shorter. There are three main strategies, and I'll give you examples of each.

The first is events. A festival gives people a reason to travel in a month when they otherwise wouldn't. The most successful events are the ones that use the season rather than fight it. A winter festival of light, say, or a storm-watching weekend. They work because they offer something that is only available at that time of year.

The second is to target different people. Families are tied to school holidays, but retired people aren't. They can travel on weekdays, and they often prefer quiet places. Many resorts have discovered that a group of retired visitors arriving by coach on a Tuesday in February is worth more than a family on a Saturday in August, because they spend more per day and stay longer.

The third is price. Midweek discounts are the most common form, and they're simple to understand. They work best when the discount is generous enough to matter, but not so large that the destination looks cheap. Some hotels have also experimented with packages that include meals and activities, so the visitor knows in advance what the break will cost.

There's a fourth approach, which is to weatherproof the destination, by building indoor attractions such as a swimming complex or a covered market. It works, but it's expensive, and it can change the character of a place. A water park in a quiet fishing village may fill the hotels in February, but the people who liked the village may stop coming.

Does it work? Let me give you the example of a resort in the north-east of England which I'll call Harrowby Bay, because the name isn't important. Before it started its programme, around 70 per cent of its annual visitors came in the three peak months. Over a period of ten years, it introduced a festival, set up a retired visitors' scheme, and offered midweek discounts. By the end of that time, the proportion in the peak months had fallen to 52 per cent. It hadn't fallen to the 50 per cent the council had hoped for, but it was a considerable change, and the number of year-round jobs had risen.

I want to end with a caution. Not every destination should try to become a year-round resort. Some places are small, and their residents value the quiet winter, and some natural environments need a rest from visitors. The question is not how to get more tourists in January, but what kind of year the community wants. For next week, please read the two articles on carrying capacity, and bring one example of a destination that has decided not to grow.
Spoke and Chain, Ewan speaking. Hold on a second, let me turn the radio down. Right, sorry about that.
No worries. I'd like to book my bike in for a service, if you've got any space this week. I've been using it every day since I started commuting, and it's beginning to make some alarming noises.
Alarming noises are our speciality. Let me bring up the diary. Could I have your surname?
It's Haldane. H-A-L-D-A-N-E.
Haldane, thanks. And what sort of bike is it? A road bike, a hybrid?
It's a folding one. I take it on the train as far as Millbank, and then I cycle the last four miles. I did think about a hybrid, but there isn't room for one in the carriage.
How long have you had it?

About three years. I bought it second-hand from a colleague who was moving abroad, and I'll admit I haven't looked after it very well. It lives in the hall, and the dog sleeps next to it, so it's usually covered in hair.
Folding bikes are lovely, but they do get hard use, because the wheels are small and everything works harder. What seems to be the trouble?
Well, the brakes are a bit soft, and the tyres look worn. But the main thing is the chain. It slips when I go uphill, and sometimes it jumps right off, which is a bit frightening on the main road.
That's no good at all, especially in traffic. Probably the chain is stretched, and it's wearing the gears down with it. It would be worth replacing the chain and the rear cogs together.
Is that something you'd do in a basic service?

No, a basic service is just cleaning, oiling and checking the brakes and tyres. For what you're describing, I'd recommend a full service, which includes replacing worn parts and adjusting the gears. It takes longer, though.
I'd rather do it properly, then. A full service.
Good. Now, when would you like to bring it in? We can do a Tuesday, but we're very busy on Tuesdays because of the cycle club, so it might take two days.
Could I drop it on the Wednesday? I'm working from home on the Thursday, so I won't need it.
Wednesday works well. What time will you drop it off?
I'd like to do it on my way to work, so about 8.15. Is that too early?

We open at eight, so that's fine. I'll make sure someone's here. Now, the cost. A basic service is £45. The full service is £65, and that doesn't include parts. The chain and cogs will be about £30 on top of that, but I'll ring you before I fit anything.
That's fine. I'd rather know first.
Of course. Is there anything else you want us to look at while it's here?
Yes, actually. It's been so wet recently, and my back is covered in mud by the time I arrive. Do you sell mudguards that fit a folding bike? I saw something online, but I wasn't sure about the size.
We do. They're small, and they clip on without drilling. I'll fit them at the same time for you, and the cost is about fifteen pounds.
Perfect. Will that take long to fit?
Ten minutes at the most. It's the sort of job that I can do while the kettle boils.
Good. And what about lights? My front one has stopped working, but I've got a spare in a drawer.
Then use the spare. Make sure it's bright, though, because the back lanes are very dark in the evening. We can check it when we fit the mudguards.
Good idea. And when would the bike be ready?
We'd have it done by Thursday afternoon. We close at 5.30, so you'll need to collect it before then. If you can't, you can pick it up on Friday morning instead.
Thursday afternoon will be fine. Is there a loan bike I could borrow in the meantime? I wouldn't want to go without it for two days.
We do have a small fleet of loan bikes. They're free to use, but we ask for a £20 deposit, which you get back when you return the bike. We take cash or card.
That sounds fair. I'll bring the money with me, so there's no confusion.
One more question. Do you do those short courses on cycling in traffic? A friend of mine mentioned one.

We do, on the first Saturday of the month, and it's free for customers. It's a two-hour ride with an instructor, and you practise turning right across traffic, which most people find the scariest part. I'll leave a leaflet at the counter for you.
Thank you, I'd like that.
Great. I'll put all of that down. We'll see you on Wednesday morning, then. Don't forget to bring the key if it has a lock.
I won't. Thanks, Ewan. You've been very helpful.
No trouble. Take care on the roads, and I hope the noises go away.

Morning, everyone. Can everybody hear me at the back? Excellent. For those I haven't met, I'm Saskia Brandt, the workplace travel coordinator for Hallam Park Business Estate, and this is the briefing for Bike Week, which starts on Monday. I'll try to keep it short, because I know you'd rather be having your coffee.

First, the numbers. When I first put the sign-up sheet up, I hoped for forty. We've got 54 so far, which is far more than I expected, and it's a fair proportion of the whole estate, which has 65 staff on this site. The rest of you still have time to join, and I'll be going round with a clipboard at lunchtime.

There's also the question of where to leave your bikes. The shed is nearly full, so the council has lent us some temporary racks, and they'll go next to the loading bay. The shed is locked with your pass, and we've put a new camera on the door, so please don't leave expensive lights or bags on the bikes overnight. If anything goes missing, tell me the same day, because the recording is only kept for a week.

Now, the opening event. We'd originally planned a breakfast outside in the car park on Monday morning, with a gazebo and a barbecue. But the forecast is for heavy rain, and I'm not going to ask anyone to stand in a puddle for a bacon roll. So it's been moved inside, to the canteen, and it starts at half past seven. Please don't go to the car park looking for it.

Now, a practical point. The men's showers on the first floor are being repaired, and they won't be working until Wednesday. The plumber says it's a leak in the pipes, nothing dramatic, but it means that, for the first two days, everybody needs to use the ground-floor showers by the gym. There are only four, so I'd suggest arriving a little early, or be prepared to queue. The water's perfectly warm, so that isn't a problem.

Next, the incentives. In previous years, we've offered a prize draw to anyone who cycled every day of the week. That's still on, and the prize is a pair of good waterproof trousers, which I can personally recommend. But a few people pointed out that it's unfair on those who can't ride five days, so this year there's something for anyone who cycles on four days. They'll receive a voucher for a free service at the cycle shop on the high street. You can claim it from reception.
Let me explain how we'll check. Each morning you tap your pass on the reader at the bike shed, and it'll record that you've arrived by cycle. If you forget, ring me, and I'll add it by hand.

Now, safety, because that's what this week is really about. We've set up four stations on the estate, and they'll run all week. At the main entrance, there'll be a team from the local council offering route advice. If you're thinking of cycling to work but you're not sure which roads are the quietest, they'll look at your journey and suggest an alternative. Many people find that a route they haven't tried is much safer.

In the loading bay, we'll have the police cycle unit, who'll be marking bikes. They'll etch a code on the frame, and it goes on a national database, so that if your bike's stolen, it can be traced. It's free, and it only takes about five minutes.

In the canteen, between twelve and two, there'll be someone fitting helmets. A lot of people wear them badly, too far back on the head, or too loose, and an expert can fix that in a minute. If you've never worn a helmet, they can talk to you about the different types.

And in Car Park B, we've got a stand where you can collect free lights. Front and rear, a limited number, so it'll be first come, first served. If your own lights are working, please leave them for the others.

Finally, the group ride on Friday afternoon. It's about twelve kilometres, mostly on quiet roads, and it's at a gentle pace, with a stop in the middle. It's led by two experienced riders, and everyone's welcome, even if you haven't cycled for years. There are two things I'd ask you to remember. First, wear something bright, a jacket or a vest, because we'll be riding in a group and need to be seen. I'll have some spare ones if you haven't got one. And second, please arrive fifteen minutes before the start. The leaders will want to check your tyres and brakes. You don't need to bring ID, although it's sensible to carry your phone, and there's no need to bring lunch, as we'll have a snack at the halfway point.
Thank you very much, everyone. I think that's everything. If you've got any questions, come and find me, and please sign up before Monday.
Beth, Rahul, come in. You wanted to talk about the cycling project, if I remember. How's it going?
Quite well, Dr Whitlock. We've been analysing the collision data for the commuter routes in Brightmoor, and we think we've got something interesting.

The first thing is where the collisions happen. We assumed they'd be mostly on narrow streets, where cyclists and cars are squeezed together, but they aren't. Most of the serious ones are at junctions, where a vehicle is turning across the cycle lane.
That fits with what the research says in other cities. What about roundabouts? They tend to have a bad reputation.
They do, and they do account for some collisions, but fewer than we thought. The junctions with turning vehicles are the main problem.
Good. And what did you find about helmets?

That was the surprise for me. I expected a big difference between people who wore helmets and people who didn't, in terms of injuries. But the numbers are too small to say anything. In the records, most of the people who were injured were wearing one, simply because most commuters do.

That's a fair point. Remember, you can't draw conclusions about helmets from collision data alone, because you don't know how many people cycled without one and had no collision. I'd leave it as an observation.
Yes, I'll put it in a footnote.
Now, I looked at your numbers for the last five years. There were forty-three recorded collisions with injuries. Is that all?
That's what the police records show.

I suspect it's an underestimate. Many minor accidents, a fall in the wet, a scrape against a car, are never reported. Studies suggest that perhaps half of cycling injuries don't appear in police data. You should say that clearly, and not treat the figure as the whole picture.
We did wonder about that. We could look at hospital admissions, but we don't think we'll get access in time.
Then just discuss it. And the survey you mentioned. How many people answered?
A hundred and twelve. We put it online, and the cycling club shared it with its members.
Which means you've mostly heard from keen cyclists, who tend to be braver and more experienced than the average commuter. I'm not saying throw it away, but you need to be upfront about that.
We did get some answers from people who only cycle in summer, from a poster we put up at the station.
How many?
About twenty.
Then report them separately. They're closer to the people you actually want to reach. Now, tell me about the recommendations. You've looked at five places in particular.

Yes. The first is the Station Road junction, where a lot of commuters come off the main road. At the moment, cyclists have to wait in the same lane as cars, and the lorries turn left across them. Our suggestion is a separate signal for cyclists, so that they move off a few seconds before the traffic.
That's been shown to work. What about advance stop boxes, the painted areas at the front of the queue?
We thought about those, but they only work if the cars stay behind the line, and in Brightmoor they often don't. So it would have to be the signal.
Fair enough. And the second site?

The Mill Bridge. It's narrow, and the cycle lane is only about a metre wide, with cars passing very close. We looked at widening it, but there's no room, because of the stone parapet. So we're suggesting flexible posts along the edge, to keep the cars further away.
Posts won't stop a determined driver, but they send a message. All right.
Third is the Park Street roundabout, which is the one where we found the most near misses in our survey. We suggest a raised crossing at each entry, so that cars have to slow down.
That makes sense. And the underpass on the ring road?

That's different. The problem is the surface. It's full of potholes, and when it rains, the water collects at the bottom and people ride through the middle of the road to avoid it. So we're recommending resurfacing, with a proper drain.

And the last is Chapel Lane. It's a quiet street, but the cars drive very fast, because it's straight. We thought about speed cameras, but they're expensive, and the council says it doesn't have the budget. So we'd widen the cycle lane there, since there's space.
Good. It's a sensible list. Now, before you write it up, I want to talk about the limits of your study. What would you say are the weaknesses?
Well, the sample is small, but I don't think that's the main one, because forty-three collisions is a reasonable number for a city this size.

We think the biggest weakness is that we haven't got any data on near misses. Our survey asked people about them, but only a few answered, and they're not in the police figures. That would give a much better idea of where the danger is.
And the survey was only done in the daytime. We never asked anyone who rides in the dark, and that's when many commuters are going home in winter.

Those are the two I'd highlight, yes. The size of the sample is less of a worry, and you're not claiming to speak for other cities, so you can leave that out. One more thing on presentation. Your maps are very small. Put the five sites on one large map with numbers, and add a small photograph for each.
We can do that. We took photos on all the site visits.
Include one of a place that already works well, so readers have something to compare.
There's a path by the river that's completely separate from the road. People love it.
Perfect. Right. Write it up, and bring me a draft in two weeks.

Let's begin with a question. Suppose I asked a hundred people in your home town whether they'd consider cycling to work. How many would say yes? A planner in the United States once tried to answer that, and what she found has shaped cycling policy ever since. She divided people into four groups. A very small number are strong and fearless, and will ride anywhere. Another small group is enthusiastic and confident. At the other end, about a third will never cycle, whatever you do. But the big group, and it's the one that matters, is the people who are interested but concerned. In most surveys, that comes to about 60 per cent of the population.

So why don't they cycle? You might assume it's the hills, or the weather, or the cost of a bicycle. But when they're asked, the commonest answer is fear of traffic. And if you dig a little deeper, it's not all traffic. The thing that frightens people most is being close to heavy vehicles, and in particular lorries, whose drivers may not be able to see them. That fear is rational. A collision with a lorry is much more dangerous than one with a car.

Now, many cities have responded by painting a cycle lane on the road. It's cheap, and it looks like action. But I'd suggest that a painted line offers no real protection. A line of paint won't stop a lorry, and it doesn't make anyone feel safer. Researchers who've interviewed non-cyclists say that the painted lane doesn't change their minds at all.

There's another problem with painted lanes, particularly beside parked cars. If a driver opens a door without looking, the cyclist has no time to stop. It's known as dooring, and it can cause serious injuries. Engineers recommend that a lane beside parked cars should leave a gap of at least 1 metre, although I'd say that in practice, a lot of cities leave only half that.

So what's the alternative? A protected lane. This is a lane that is physically separated from traffic, by a kerb, or a row of bollards, or in the best cases, by planters, which also make the street look better. The principle is that a child of eight, and a person of eighty, should both feel safe on it. If it doesn't pass that test, the interested but concerned will stay at home.

Let me give you an example. I'll call the city Dunmere, although it's not the real name. In 2017, Dunmere set out to build a network of protected lanes. The original plan was for 15 kilometres, but there were arguments about parking and the budget, and in the end 12 kilometres were completed. That's a smaller network than planned, but they were well-chosen routes, linking the university, the hospital and the main shopping streets.

What happened? The council had forecast a rise in cycling of about 25 per cent over five years. In fact, it rose by 40 per cent. Cycling doubled on some streets, and there were fewer drivers on those streets, as well.

What about safety? In the first year, the council announced that injuries had been halved. That was a bit premature, because the numbers were small, and the figure was affected by one unusually quiet winter. When researchers looked again, over a full five years, they found that the number of injuries per kilometre cycled had fallen by a third. I'd say that's a more reliable figure, and it's still impressive, because the number of cyclists had risen so much. If more people ride, and the risk to each of them falls, then something is working.

And who were the new cyclists? The greatest increase was among older people, particularly women over fifty, who'd said in surveys that they felt unsafe sharing the road. That's the very group that painted lanes had never reached.

Of course, no system is perfect, and Dunmere still has problems. The most difficult places are junctions, where the protected lane has to cross the road. A turning vehicle is the biggest danger there, because the driver may be looking at the oncoming traffic and not at a cyclist coming up beside them. The solution is to design the junction so that vehicles turn at a slower speed and at a sharper angle, which gives the driver a better view. Dunmere is rebuilding its busiest junctions in this way, one at a time, and the early results are promising.

One more finding is worth mentioning. Shopkeepers had objected to the lanes, because some parking spaces were lost, and they feared that trade would suffer. But later surveys showed that people who arrive by bicycle visit more often, even if they spend less each time, and total takings on the main streets were no lower than before. The pattern has been seen in many cities, although the evidence is still developing. And weather matters less than you'd think. In cities with snow, the cycle lanes are often cleared before the roads, because they're narrower and quicker to do.

Let me finish with a point about policy. It's tempting to say that the money would be better spent on training cyclists, or on encouraging them to wear helmets, and that's what a lot of governments have done. But training doesn't change the way a lorry driver behaves, and a helmet doesn't change the layout of a junction. If you want the interested but concerned to cycle, you have to change the street. Next week, we'll look at what happens to bus journeys when a lane is taken away from traffic, and whether the argument still holds.
Morning. I was given your number by the library, who tell me you do group visits for older people. I hope I've come to the right department.
You have. Imogen here, in visitor services. We do quite a few of them, and they're some of my favourite bookings. Which group are you with?
I help run a day centre. We'd like to bring some of our members to the museum, but a few of them have difficulty getting around, so I'm trying to find out what's possible.
Of course. Let me open the booking form, and we'll go through it together. Could I have your surname, to start with?
It's Alderton. A-L-D-E-R-T-O-N.
Alderton, thank you. And what's the name of the day centre?
Meadow View. Sorry, no, I always say that, and it's wrong. It's Meadowside. We changed it two years ago, and the signs outside still say the old name.
Meadowside, got it. And how many people will be coming?

There are fifteen members who want to come. But we need three carers with them, so that makes 18 altogether. I did think it might be twenty, because two more members asked yesterday, but they've decided they'd rather not.
Eighteen is fine. We can take up to twenty-five in a single group. Have you thought about a date?
Our outings are usually on Wednesdays. I was wondering about the 5th of March.
Ah, I'm afraid the main gallery is closed that week, for the lighting to be changed. The Wednesday after would be better, which is 12 March. Would that suit you?
That should be fine. I'll confirm with the others, but I'm sure it's all right.
Lovely. And what time would you like to arrive? We open at ten, but I'd suggest coming a bit later than that.
Why's that?
Because the first half hour is when school groups come in, and the lifts get busy. If you arrive at 10.30, the lifts are free, and you'll have the galleries almost to yourselves.
That sounds sensible. Half past ten, then. Is it easy to get around inside? Some of our members use frames or wheelchairs, and most of the others get tired quickly.

We've made a lot of changes recently. The whole building is step-free now, and there are lifts to every floor. And for people who tire easily, we lend folding stools, which you can carry from room to room and sit on in front of an exhibit. We have thirty of them, so there'll be plenty.
Are there accessible toilets? That's the first thing my members ask about.
On every floor. The one on the ground floor is the largest, and it has a hoist and a changing bench, and a member of staff can show you where it is as soon as you arrive.
That's wonderful. Our members will love that, because they hate having to keep moving. What about wheelchairs? We bring our own, but I wondered whether you lend any.
We do have four, but I'd suggest bringing your own if the people are used to them. And the stools are the thing that people like most.
Good. And do you offer anything other than just walking round?

We have several options. There's a guided tour, which lasts an hour, and there's a handling session, where visitors can hold real objects, like old tools and pieces of pottery. For older groups, the handling session is far more popular. People talk about the objects, and the memories they bring back.
I think the handling session would be perfect. Some of them worked with tools like that when they were younger. What does it cost?
Normally it's £6 per person for the museum and the session, but for groups of ten or more, it comes down to £4. Carers come in free.
That's very reasonable. I'd assumed it would cost a lot more.
Many people do. And lunch? Do you want to eat here, or somewhere else?
We'd like to eat at the museum, if possible, so that nobody has to walk too far.

The café is small, and it can't take eighteen people at once. But we can reserve the Garden Room for you, which is on the ground floor, and has its own entrance onto the terrace. It's very quiet, and the caterers bring the food in.
The Garden Room would be ideal. One last question, about the coach. We're hiring a minibus. Where would it stop?

The main entrance is on a very busy road, and it's hard for the driver to stop. I'd ask the driver to use Mill Street, round the corner. There's a ramp from there, and a member of staff will meet you at the door.
Mill Street. I'll tell the driver. Thank you, Imogen. I feel much better about it now.
I'm glad. We'll send you a confirmation this afternoon, and a plan of the building, so you can show your members what to expect.

Right, if everybody could sit down, I'd like to start, because there's a lot to get through, and I know some of you have been on your feet all morning. For those who don't know me, I'm Tobias Reeve, head of visitor experience, and these are the briefing notes for the new Harbour Museum, which opens to the public a week on Saturday.

You're our greeters, which means you're the first person visitors see, and it's what they'll remember. Everything in the building has been redesigned around that idea, so let me take you through the main changes.

First, the entrance. Many of you know that it used to be on the harbour side, with six steps and a heavy door. A lot of people assume we moved it to be nearer the car park, but that's not the reason. It was to give level access, because a ramp at the old entrance would have been too steep, and would have spoiled the façade. The new entrance is on the south side, it's completely flat, and the doors open automatically.

Now, what do you say to people when they walk in? We tested several approaches. Asking whether they've been before wasn't helpful, because people felt they were being examined. Offering help immediately didn't work either, because most people said no, and then felt silly if they needed it afterwards. What worked best was asking how long they had. If someone says they've got an hour, you can suggest the highlights, and if they say all day, you can point them to the quiet corners. It sounds simple, but it makes people feel that they're in control of their visit.

The audio guides have changed as well. You may remember that they used to be available in three languages. They're now in eight, and the new ones were chosen after we looked at where our visitors come from. They aren't free, I'm afraid. They're included in the ticket price, which isn't quite the same thing, and I'd rather you didn't tell visitors they're free. And they're not only on the app. We still have handsets for people who don't have a smartphone, and there's a charging point by the desk.

Next, the quiet hour. This is something we're very proud of. Every Tuesday morning, between ten and eleven, the lights are dimmed, the announcements are turned off, and the volume on the videos goes down. It's designed for people who find museums overwhelming, for example visitors with autism, or those with young children who get easily distressed. We tried the Saturday afternoon, but that's when we're busiest, and Sunday mornings were no better. So it's Tuesday mornings, and we'd like you to mention it to anyone who looks uneasy.

You'll also notice that there are seats in all the galleries. People sometimes assume they're there for story sessions, and they are used for that occasionally, but that isn't why we put them in. The real reason is tiredness. Research on museum visitors has shown that they tire quickly, and when they're tired, they leave sooner, and enjoy it less. A bench every few metres means they can sit, look at the room, and carry on. It's cheaper than a café, and in some ways more effective.

A question I'm often asked is about photography. In the old museum, it was banned altogether, and we received a lot of complaints. The new rule is that visitors may take photographs in most galleries, as long as they don't use a flash. The exception is the textile room, where light damages the fabrics, and there, no photography at all. If somebody asks why, you can explain, and most people understand.

Now, let me tell you where things are, because visitors will ask you. I'll take the activities one at a time, and you'll find them marked on the plan you've been given. The family trail starts in the Tide Gallery, which is the big room on the left as you come in. There's a bag of activity sheets by the door, and children collect stickers.

The handling collection, where visitors can touch real objects, is in the Boatyard Room, at the back. It used to be in the basement, but we found that hardly anyone went down there, so it was moved. It's now one of the most popular spaces in the building.
School workshops take place in the Learning Studio, which is on the mezzanine, up the stairs or in the lift. Please don't send anyone there on the day, unless they've booked, because it's very small.

And the temporary exhibition, which is a display of seaside photographs from the nineteen-thirties, is in the Long Gallery. It was meant to go in the courtyard, but the roof isn't finished, so we've had to move it. If anyone asks about the courtyard, tell them it opens in the summer.

One last thing about language. Please avoid saying that something is for the disabled, or that a visitor has special needs. Say what is available, and let people choose. For example, we have stools you can borrow, and a quiet hour on Tuesdays. Most visitors would prefer to hear about an option than be labelled.

I think that's everything, but if I've forgotten anything, I'll find out the hard way next Saturday. Thank you all very much for coming, and for all the work you've put in. There are tea and biscuits in the staff room, and please take a copy of the plan on the way out.
Ah, good, you're all here. Ines, Jonah, Kofi. Sit wherever you like. I wanted to hear how the museum project is going, because you've been very quiet since the last seminar.

We've been busy doing fieldwork, to be honest. We visited three museums, the Harbour Museum, the Textile Museum and the Railway Museum, and we've been looking at how well each of them welcomes visitors.
Remind me why you chose small museums. There's far more material on the big national ones.

That's exactly the reason. There's a lot written about big museums, and hardly anything on small ones, even though most people in this country visit small ones. We thought it would be a better contribution.
Good. And the larger museums wouldn't have made it easy for you to do fieldwork, either, I suppose.
No, we didn't try. We assumed it would take too long to get permission, but that wasn't the main reason.
All right. So, what did you do at each one?

Three things. We walked round as visitors and noted everything that helped or hindered. We observed what people actually did for two hours at each one. And we interviewed about twenty visitors on the way out.
Start with the walk round. What did you notice?

Signs, mostly. At every museum, the signs were at a standard height, and the text was small. That's fine if you're standing up, but Ines took her cousin, who uses a wheelchair, and he couldn't read most of them. The labels are too high, and the lettering is tiny.
That's a useful observation, because it's the sort of thing that people on their feet never notice. Did the museums use different styles of sign?
Yes, in the Railway Museum especially, but that's a smaller point, so we left it out.
Now, the interviews. How did you find them?
Quite difficult, honestly. People are in a hurry, and they've often just been round, so they're tired. We started with closed questions, like, did you enjoy your visit, and the answer was always yes.
Of course. People are polite. What you want are open questions, where they have to describe something. Ask them what they remember best, or what they found confusing. You'll learn far more.
That's what we did in the end, and it worked much better.
Good. Make sure you say that you changed your approach, and why. Now, what did people say about what they valued?

We asked them to choose from a list. The two things that came up most were friendly staff and clear labels. Free entry and seating were mentioned, but not as often as we expected. And hardly anyone mentioned the café.

Several people said that a member of staff who said hello made them feel they were allowed to be there. One woman said that she'd never gone into a museum before, because she thought it wasn't for her.
That's a lovely quotation. Use it. And did you ask permission from the museums before you observed people, and from the visitors before the interviews?
The managers all agreed in writing. For the interviews, we explained it was for a university project and asked people if they minded, and we didn't record any names.
One manager asked to see the final report before we hand it in, which worried us a bit.

It's reasonable for them to read it, but they can't change your conclusions. Offer to send them a summary afterwards instead, and say clearly in the method that the findings are independent. Now, the observation part. Were there any problems?
There were two. The first was that people noticed us. We were standing in the corner with clipboards, and some visitors changed their behaviour when they saw us, or asked what we were doing.

And the second was the weather. We'd planned to observe on Saturdays, but it rained at two of the museums, and the numbers were much higher than usual, because people came to get out of the rain. So the results are probably not typical.
You can't control the weather, so just record it. The clipboards, though, you could solve by sitting down and pretending to read. Did any of the museums close on the day you'd planned?
One of them did, but it was only for the morning. That was a nuisance, but it didn't affect the data.
Then it's not worth a mention. Now, I'd like to hear your impressions of each museum. Starting with the Harbour Museum.

That's the best of the three. The whole building seems organised around the idea of making people feel welcome, and the effect starts the moment you walk in. There's a greeter, and a clear sign, and a place to sit.
And the Textile Museum?

That was the hardest one. The displays are lovely, but there's no obvious route, and the labels don't explain how the rooms connect. We saw several people turn round and walk back the way they'd come.
And the Railway Museum?
It's very good for families. There's a trail for children, and a play area, and a lot of things they can press and turn. The adults are less well served, but the children didn't want to leave.
That's a good summary, and it will make a clear table. Now, I've read your plan for the final report. I'd say it needs a floor plan for each museum, so readers can see what you're describing.
We've got those already. We drew them during the visits.
One more question, for the discussion. If a small museum had very little money, what's the first thing you'd tell them to change?
Honestly, the greeting. It costs nothing, and it makes the biggest difference.
I'd say the labels, but they cost money to reprint, so Jonah's right.

Then say so, and say why. That's the kind of practical conclusion that makes a project worth reading. Good. And I'd add some quotations from the interviews, because they make the report real. But keep them short. Let me have a draft in a fortnight.

Let me begin with a word that's been in use for more than a hundred years. In 1916, an American researcher wrote about what he called museum fatigue. He'd noticed that visitors, however interested they were at the start, seemed to become exhausted after a short time, and that it wasn't ordinary tiredness. It was something to do with the way museums were laid out, with long rooms, hard floors and rows of cases, and it made visitors stop looking. That observation started a whole field of research, and I want to take you through some of it today.

The next step came in the nineteen-twenties and thirties, when researchers began to follow visitors round museums, with stopwatches and floor plans. It sounds crude, but it produced some surprising results. The first was a habit that nobody had noticed. When visitors came through the entrance and faced a choice of directions, most of them turned right. It wasn't because of the layout, because the effect appeared in different buildings. It seemed to be a natural preference. The consequence was that the exhibits on the right-hand side received far more attention, and the ones on the left were often missed.

The second finding was about the length of the visit. The researchers measured attention by counting how many exhibits people looked at and for how long. In one study, which I'll call the Linden Museum study, attention fell sharply after about 30 minutes. Some people think the figure is nearer an hour, but in this case it was 30, and after that, visitors began walking past things they would have stopped for at the start. They weren't bored. They were tired.

So what can designers do about it? The first response is the simplest, which is somewhere to sit. In the Linden Museum, benches were put at the end of each gallery, rather than in the middle, so that visitors would take a rest before moving on, and not just in front of a display. It sounds minor, but it changed the pattern of the visit, because people who'd rested went on to look at the next room with fresh eyes.

The second response is to think about order. If attention falls over time, then the most important objects shouldn't be at the end. The curators at the Linden Museum rearranged the displays so that the key objects were close to the start, and the less important ones came later. They also stopped putting the shop at the exit of the last gallery, because visitors who reached it were exhausted and in no mood to look at anything.

There's one more early finding that I should mention, which is sometimes called the exit gradient. As visitors approach an exit, they increasingly head for it, and ignore the displays beside the door. So an exhibit placed right next to the way out is often overlooked, however good it is. Designers now treat the area near the exit as a place for thanks and feedback, and not for new content.

Third, text. Most visitors don't read long labels, and they certainly don't read them when they're tired. The old labels at the Linden Museum often ran to 200 words. The new ones are limited to 60, and the longer explanation is available on request, on a card or an app. The labels are also set at a height that works for wheelchair users, as well as for people who are standing, and the lettering is larger. A label that is easy to read is more likely to be read.

Fourth, navigation. One of the main causes of fatigue is confusion. If you aren't sure where to go, you spend energy deciding. The Linden Museum put coloured markings on the floor, running from room to room, so that visitors could follow a route without needing a map. People who preferred to wander could ignore them, but those who wanted guidance had it, and the number of visitors who asked staff for directions fell by half.

Now, did it work? Before the changes, the average visit at the Linden Museum lasted 55 minutes. Afterwards, it lasted 70 minutes at first, and then, once the new layout had settled in and the staff were used to it, it reached 75. That's a rise of more than a third. Visitors also reported that they felt less tired, and they said they'd noticed more of the collection.

But I think the most interesting result was about the visitors' attitude, and not about time. The museum surveyed people on the way out, and asked them whether they felt welcome. Those who said yes were far more likely to come back, but also far more likely to become members. In that sense, a comfortable seat in a quiet corner was a better investment than an advertisement.

There's a warning, though. It would be easy to take these findings and apply them everywhere. But a museum is not a shop, and a visitor isn't a customer to be moved through a route. Some people want to be lost, and some of the best experiences come from stumbling on an object nobody pointed out. The designer's job is to remove the obstacles, without taking away the wandering. Next week, we'll look at how digital displays are changing that balance, and whether an interactive screen helps or hinders. Please come with an example of a museum visit you remember, and be prepared to say why.
Sorry about that, I was just wrestling a rack of paddles back into the shed. Morning! Are you after a boat for today?
Not today, no. I'm thinking ahead. A few of us want to paddle the Tarawai River some time this month, and a friend told me to talk to you before the good weekends fill up.
Your friend's right, they go quickly once the weather warms. I can pencil you in now, if you like. Let me grab the booking form. Right, can I start with your surname?
It's Hargreave. H-A-R-G-R-E-A-V-E.
Hargreave, lovely. And have you got a type of boat in mind? We have single kayaks, and we have tandem canoes, which take two people.
Tandem, I think. Most of us haven't paddled for years, and I'd feel better if we shared. Although, is it true couples argue in those?

We call them divorce boats, but I've honestly never seen one end badly. The person at the back steers, and the person at the front just looks scenic. So, a tandem canoe. What date were you thinking of?
I was hoping for Saturday the 14th of March.

Ah, that's the one weekend I'd steer you away from. The irrigation board is releasing water from the dam that week, so the river will be high and fast, and I wouldn't send beginners out in it. The Saturday after, though, should be back to normal. That would be 21 March.
Then the twenty-first it is. That's actually better, because my sister doesn't finish her exams until the 18th.
Perfect. What time would you like to set off? We open at 8, so you could start at 9 if you wanted to be first on the water.
Oh, I'm not really a morning person, and we'll be driving in from the coast. Nine sounds a bit keen. Is there anything later?
The next slot is 9.30, and the minibus runs up to the weir every half hour from then. Most groups find that's a comfortable time.
Then 9.30, please.
Great. And how many people in your group?
Four of us. Me, my sister Gemma and two of her friends. Oh, hang on, Gemma's just texted me. Her boyfriend wants to come too, so make it 5.
Five, no problem. Then you'd want two tandems and a single kayak. The single is a bit more wobbly, but whoever takes it will cope, as long as they've paddled before.
That'll be the boyfriend. He's done a lot of sea kayaking, apparently, so he can show off.

Good. Now, where would you like to finish? Everyone starts at the weir. Most groups stop at Alder Bridge, which takes about an hour and a half. If you want a proper day out, you can carry on to Kettle Bridge, which is closer to four hours. And there's the Ferry Landing as well, but I'd only recommend that for experienced paddlers because of the rapids just before it.
Four hours is probably too much for people who haven't paddled in years. But an hour and a half does sound a bit short, to be honest.

Well, there's a lovely picnic spot just beyond Alder Bridge, and if you stop there for lunch, you can take it easy all the way down to Kettle Bridge in about three hours. A lot of people do exactly that.
That sounds ideal. Let's finish at Kettle Bridge, then, with a long lunch.
Wonderful. Will you need any extras? Lifejackets and paddles are included. Some people hire a waterproof barrel for their lunch, or dry bags for phones and cameras.
A barrel sounds heavy. I think dry bags, a few of them, for our phones and wallets.

Sensible. Right, let me work out the price. The tandems are $60 each, so that's... oh, no, sorry, that's the summer price. In March it's $50 each, so $100 for the two, then $35 for the single kayak, and a flat $10 for as many dry bags as you want. That makes $145 in total.
That's fine. Do I pay now?

No, we take payment on the day. Now, since you'll finish at Kettle Bridge, our minibus will bring you back. It picks up at Mill Lane, which is about two minutes' walk from the bridge. Please don't wait at the bridge itself, because the bus can't turn round there.
Mill Lane, got it.
Last thing. We post out a short river safety leaflet before the trip, so what's your postcode?
It's 4172. We live on Redfern Street, number 9.
Thanks, Oliver. That's everything. I'll put you down for the twenty-first, and we'll see you at the shed at twenty past nine.

Good morning, everyone, and thank you for coming along to the Hallowby Mill Heritage Weekend. My name's Helen Strachan, and I'm one of the volunteers who organise it. Before you all disappear into the village, let me go through a few practical things, and then I'll explain where everything is.

First, parking. Most of you will have come in on the lane from the main road, and you'll have noticed that the car park beside the church is already packed. I'm afraid it always is by ten o'clock. It's really kept for visitors with limited mobility, so if you've arrived without a badge, please don't be tempted. The best place for everyone else is the playing field behind the school. There's a marshal at the gate who'll wave you in, and it's only a five-minute walk back down to the mill. There's also a lay-by on Mill Lane, but that's for residents, so please leave it clear.

Now, tickets. Entry to the whole village for the weekend is five pounds for adults. Last year it was four, and a few of you who came before have mentioned it, so yes, it has gone up, but it still includes the guided walk, the exhibition and a hot drink. Children under sixteen are free, and so is anyone who can show a library card from the parish. Please keep your wristband on, because the stewards will ask to see it at each of the stalls.

The highlight for many people is the guided walk along the restored stream. It was a ditch full of supermarket trolleys ten years ago, and now there are kingfishers. The walk was meant to leave at eleven, but we've moved it back by half an hour because the vicar has asked us not to walk past the church during the service. So it will leave from the footbridge at eleven thirty, and it takes about forty minutes. A word about what to wear. The path beside the water is uneven, and after the rain we've had this week it's quite slippery in places. You won't need a waterproof, because the forecast is dry, and the path is shaded by trees, so hats aren't necessary either. But please do wear sturdy shoes. We had a lady last year who came in sandals and spent the walk holding on to a hedge.

One more rule. Dogs are very welcome, but please keep them on a lead, particularly near the stream, because we have nesting ducks and the herons don't appreciate being chased. The only place dogs can't go is the school hall, because of the exhibition.

A word about the mill itself, because you will want to go in. It was built in 1794 and ground flour until the nineteen-fifties, when it became a warehouse. The wheel has been restored by a group of retired engineers, and on the hour a volunteer will start it turning, so if you want a photograph, be there at five to. Inside, the machinery is roped off, and I must ask you not to climb on it, however tempting. The top floor is reached by a very steep staircase, so if you have a pushchair, or find stairs difficult, the ground floor displays tell the story just as well.

Right, now let me tell you where things are. Imagine you're standing at the entrance, with the old mill wheel on your left. If you walk straight ahead, you'll come to the High Street, and that's where most of the stalls are.

The pottery demonstration is the first thing you'll see. It's set up in a marquee at the top of the High Street, so you can't miss it. Our potter makes a bowl in about four minutes, which is irritating for those of us who've been trying for years.

Children are well looked after, too. The treasure hunt starts under the chestnut tree, which is in the middle of the green. The children get a map and a pencil, and they have to find ten wooden animals hidden around the village. Please don't give them any hints, because the winners get a prize.

For tea and cakes, you have two choices. The village hall is often full, but there's a much quieter spot just behind the old mill wheel, in what used to be the cart shed. The cakes there are baked by our local women's group, and I can personally recommend the lemon one.

If you'd like to look at old photographs of the village, they're on display in the school hall. It's the long building on the right as you come up the High Street. Some of them show the stream before it was restored, and you can see a gentleman fishing out a bicycle.

Finally, if anyone needs first aid, or if you've lost a child, a phone or a very small dog, you'll find the stewards' desk by the main car park, next to the toilets. And that's all from me. Have a wonderful day, and please do leave a donation in the buckets on your way out.

Ah, there you are. Maya, Jonah, do sit down. I've read your draft on Larkin Brook, and I'd like to go through it with you before you submit. First of all, remind me why you picked that particular stream.
Honestly, it's only ten minutes by bike from the campus, so that helped. But that wasn't the real reason.

No. The main reason was that the council restored one stretch three years ago and left the stretch just downstream as it was, in a concrete channel. So we had a restored section and an unrestored one in the same stream. It's like having a built-in comparison.
Yes, that's a good pairing, and it's one of the strengths of the design. Now, you sampled the invertebrates by kick sampling. How did that go?

Mostly fine, although it took us a while to get a consistent method. We nearly lost a net in the first week, but the real problem was that Maya and I kicked for different lengths of time. I'd count to twenty, and she'd stop when she got bored.

That's not fair. I just wasn't counting out loud. But it's true, the first two sampling days aren't comparable. After that we used a timer on my phone, three minutes per spot, and every sample was done in exactly the same way.
Good, but you must say that in the report. Don't hide it. Now, you've got three sites. Two in the restored section and one in the concrete channel. I'm a bit uneasy about that.
We did wonder whether it was enough.

It's workable, but I'd like to see a fourth site, further upstream, above the town, where the stream has had very little interference at all. That would give you a reference point, something to show what a healthy stream in this catchment actually looks like. You wouldn't need many samples. Even two visits would do.
I suppose we could get up there next week. The access is a bit muddy, though.
Wellington boots are cheap. Now, the results. They looked interesting. What do you make of them?

Well, we expected the restored section to have more animals overall. But actually, the concrete channel had more animals in total. It was full of worms and midge larvae. The restored section had fewer individuals, but far more of the sensitive species, like mayfly and stonefly larvae.
That's a very good finding, and it's the sort of thing that a simple count would miss. So you should lead with the sensitive species. The council will care about that more than total numbers.
Should we explain how we identified them? We used a laminated key from the library, but a few of the specimens were tiny, and I'm not sure we got every one right.

Say so. Identifying small larvae is hard even for experts, and nobody expects a second-year student to be perfect. If you're unsure, group them by family rather than guessing the species, and put a note in a footnote. Markers are much more forgiving of honesty than of confident mistakes.
That's reassuring. We did photograph the doubtful ones, so we could put a couple in an appendix.
An appendix is fine, but keep it to a single page. Nobody wants to read six pages of photographs of worms, however lovely the worms.

We did think there might be some things that distorted the results, though. There was a heavy storm about a week before our second sampling day, and it could have washed a lot of the animals downstream.

And one of the restored sites is under a lot of trees. It's shaded for most of the day, so the temperature and the amount of algae would be quite different from the open sites. We weren't sure whether to count that as a problem or a feature.

Both of those are worth discussing, so please do. You've mentioned a possible sewage leak in your notes, but you found no evidence for it, so I'd leave that out. And the water temperature didn't vary much between sampling days, so you can safely ignore that too.
Right. So, what about the structure of the report itself?

Let's go through it section by section. The introduction first. You spend three pages on the history of the culverting in the town, which is interesting, but it's too much for a report this size. I'd cut it by half, to a page and a half at most.
Okay, that's painful but fair.

The methods section is clear enough in the text, but I couldn't picture where your sampling points are. A simple diagram of the stream, with the sites marked, would make it much easier to follow. Just a sketch is fine.
I can do that with the map we used in the field.

Then the results. The graphs are well presented, but none of them has error bars. Without some indication of how much your samples varied, I can't tell whether the differences are real, so please add them, and say plainly where the uncertainty is.
We weren't sure how to calculate them.

It's one line in the spreadsheet. I'll show you afterwards. And finally your conclusions. They're sensible, but they float in the air. The council has published targets for stream health for the next ten years, so link what you found to those targets. It makes your work look useful, not just academic.
That's a great idea. We can do that this weekend.
Do you want us to present anything in the seminar, or is the report enough?

Just the report this time. But I'd encourage you both to offer a short talk to the group of volunteers who look after Larkin Brook. They meet monthly, and they'd be delighted to hear what you found, particularly about the shaded site.
I'd like that. They might even have older records that we could compare with.
They do, actually. Ask for Mrs Ibbotson. She has kept a notebook of the stream for fifteen years.
Good. Send me the revised draft on Friday, and I'll give you a quick read before the deadline.

Good morning, everyone. Over the past few weeks we've looked at how cities change the way water moves through the landscape. Today I'd like to focus on one of the most visible results of that, the urban stream, and on a rather surprising idea that has taken hold in many cities over the last thirty years, which is digging them up again.

Let me start with the problem. Ecologists use the phrase urban stream syndrome to describe what happens to a stream when its catchment is covered with roofs, roads and car parks. Rain can't soak into the ground, so it runs straight into drains and then into the stream. The result is that the water level rises very sharply during a storm and falls again just as quickly. We call this a flash flood, and for animals living on the stream bed it is devastating, because they are literally swept away. The second problem is the quality of the water. The rain that runs off roads carries oil, rubber from tyres and traces of metals, and all of that ends up in the stream. Farmland has fertiliser, but in the town the main source of pollution is the roads. Streams with this kind of treatment tend to lose their sensitive species and end up dominated by a few tough ones, such as worms.

Now, in many cities the situation is worse still, because the stream isn't there at all. It's been buried. During the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, thousands of small streams were put into underground pipes. These are known as culverts, and a culvert can be a brick tunnel or a concrete pipe, but in both cases the water is out of sight. Why did our ancestors do it? Two reasons. The first was health. Streams in towns had become open sewers, and people were afraid of disease, particularly cholera. Covering them seemed an obvious solution. The second was land. As cities grew, there was pressure to build, and a stream running through the middle of a site is an inconvenience. So the pipe went in, and the land above was used for housing. Many of you may be living on top of one. I certainly was, during my first degree.

From the 1980s, people began to ask whether this had been a mistake, and the answer was a practical idea called daylighting, which means taking a stream out of its pipe and letting it flow in the open again. Let me use a case study. The city of Dunmarrow has a small waterway called Corran Brook, which was piped in the 1930s. The council decided to open up a six hundred metre stretch beside a primary school.

What does a project like this involve? The first step is always to find out what is actually down there, and rather than guessing, engineers send a camera through the pipe. In Dunmarrow, this revealed that the pipe was in better condition than expected, but had one collapsed section, which had to be repaired. The second step is design. Most daylighting projects don't simply put the stream back in its old line, because the land above has changed. Instead, they create a wider, shallower channel with gently sloping banks, and, importantly, a floodplain beside it, a low area of grass that is allowed to flood. In Dunmarrow, this has meant that a storm which would once have overwhelmed the pipe now spreads out harmlessly across the park.

Now, what is the biggest obstacle to daylighting? You might expect me to say cost, and cost is certainly a factor, but in my experience the real problem is usually ownership. A buried stream often runs under dozens of private gardens or several commercial properties, and every owner has to agree. In Dunmarrow, negotiations took almost three years before the first digger arrived. The cost, I should add, was lower than many people feared, because the council reused soil from the site.

And what about the results? Once the stream was open, nature moved in quicker than the planners expected. I had assumed it would be a decade, but the first invertebrates arrived within a few months, and the monitoring team recorded sensitive species such as mayfly larvae after about 4 years. Fish took longer, because the pipe downstream was still a barrier, and the council had to build a small ramp to let trout through. There was also an unexpected economic result. The council had commissioned a study of house prices near the stream, and found that homes within a short walk of the open water had risen in value by 12 per cent more than similar homes elsewhere in the city. That figure is an average, of course, but it was enough to convince several other councils to consider similar schemes.

It is also worth saying that these projects often succeed or fail on public attitudes rather than engineering. In Dunmarrow, residents at first complained that an open stream would attract rats and mosquitoes, and some worried about children falling in. The council held evening meetings, put up fences only where the banks were steep, and invited the school next door to adopt a section of the bank. Within a year the children were monitoring the water quality themselves, and the complaints had almost disappeared. A project that the neighbours feel they own is a project that nobody vandalises.

I'd like to end with a word of caution. Daylighting is not a cure-all. In a heavily built-up area, the stream's catchment may still be so hard-surfaced that it floods. Real recovery usually means doing something about the surrounding streets as well, with rain gardens, permeable paving and green roofs, which is the topic of next week's lecture. So please read the chapter on sustainable drainage before you come.
Try a slice of the nectarine, love, they're going for next to nothing this morning. Oh, hello, you've been hovering by the sign for a while. Are you interested in the veg boxes?
I am, yes. A colleague of mine gets one every week, and she says she hasn't thrown away a carrot in months. I'd like to know how it works.

Simple enough. We pack a box on Wednesday night with whatever the farms around Wollerton have picked that week, and we bring it to your door. I'll just fill in a form as we go, if you don't mind. Can I take your surname first?
It's Brannigan. That's B-R-A-N-N-I-G-A-N.
Brannigan, got it. Now, we do three sizes. Small is good for one person, medium suits a couple, and large is for a family with hungry teenagers.
There's only me, so small sounds right. Although, I do like cooking at the weekends, and I always end up making too much. Perhaps medium, then. I can always freeze what's left.
Spoken like a true convert. Medium it is. Which day would suit you for delivery? We can do Wednesday or Thursday.
Wednesday would be perfect, I'm in on Wednesdays.
Ah, sorry, I should have said. Wednesday is when we pack the boxes, so we deliver on Thursday and Friday. I got that wrong.
Oh, right. Then Thursday, please. I work from home on Thursdays.
Thursday, lovely. And where do we leave it? Address?
It's 14 Wattle Street, that's W-A-T-T-L-E, in Hartfield. If I'm not there, you can put the box on the porch, under the bench.

Under the bench. I'll make a note. Now, here's a question that people think is odd, but it's very useful. Is there anything you don't like? I'd rather leave something out than have it end up in your bin.
Beetroot, I think. No, actually, I've started to like it, my sister roasts it with honey. Mushrooms, though. I can't stand the texture. Please leave those out.
No mushrooms. That's easy, since I hardly ever put them in anyway. Now, would you like any extras? We work with a few local producers, so you can add eggs, a loaf of sourdough, or a jar of honey.
Honey would be tempting, but I've got plenty. I won't say no to eggs. Half a dozen, please. I'm not sure about the bread, because it never lasts the week in my house, and it goes stale.
Eggs, then. Okay, the price. A medium box is usually $42 a week, but there's a discount at the moment for new customers who sign up at the market. So you'll pay $38.
That's quite a bit less than the supermarket would be, actually. When can I start?
The next delivery slot with room is 3 May, which is a Thursday. Is that too soon?
No, that's fine. It gives me a week to clear the fridge.
Good idea. Now, payment. Most people use direct debit, because it saves them having to think about it, but you can also pay each week by card when the box arrives.
Direct debit is fine. Will you send me the details?
I'll email you a link tonight. One last question, and it's just for our records. Where did you first come across us?
Well, my colleague first, but I'd also seen it in the school newsletter. My niece's school has a notice on it, because the veg boxes support a fund for their garden.

That's right, we donate a little from every box to the garden. Then I'll put down the newsletter, because that's where most people say they've seen us. Don't worry, your colleague will still get her credit, though. She gets a free jar of honey for every friend she brings in.
She'll be delighted. She mentioned that there's a recipe card in every box, is that true?

Every week. We try to tell people what to do with the odd things, like kohlrabi or a whole cabbage the size of a football. People are much less likely to throw things away if they know how to cook them. And if you get stuck, you can message me and I'll send you an idea.
What if I go away on holiday? I travel a bit in the summer.

Just text me by Monday night and we'll skip that week. No charge, no fuss. We'd much rather skip a box than see it wilting on your porch for a fortnight. You can skip up to four weeks a year without losing your discount.
That's generous. And do you take the empty crates back?
We do, we collect them the following week. Just leave them folded by the bench, and we'll swap them over.
That's very kind. Right, I'll let you get back to your customers. Thank you.
Thanks, Tessa. Take a nectarine on your way out. They won't last until tomorrow.

Hello, everyone, and thank you for squeezing in. I'm Greta Hallam, and I coordinate the volunteers here at the Marlow Street Community Fridge. For those of you who've never seen one, a community fridge is exactly what it sounds like. It's a fridge, and a couple of shelves, that anyone in the neighbourhood can fill with spare food and anyone can take from, without being asked a single question. Tonight I want to explain how ours works, and what we need from you if you're thinking of joining the team.

First, where we are. A lot of people walk past us, because we're a little hidden. You'll find the fridge at the back of the library, in what used to be the staff kitchen. If you go through the main doors and turn left, you'll see a red door with a handwritten sign. It's also reachable from the rear lane, which is useful for anyone arriving with a trolley full of food.

We open every morning at half past eight and we shut at six, apart from Sundays, when we close at two. Over the summer we tried opening until eight in the evening, but hardly anyone came after six, and it made the volunteers' rota very difficult, so we went back to the old hours.

Now, what can people leave? The rules are simple, and they're there for everyone's safety. All food has to be in a sealed container or the original packaging, and it must show a use-by date. If it doesn't, we can't accept it, however good it looks. And there are things we can't take at all. You might expect it to be mostly the obvious things, such as alcohol, but in fact our biggest problem is raw meat. Nobody can check how long it's been out of a fridge, so we turn it away. Raw fish and homemade items with raw eggs go the same way.

Every volunteer has to complete a short course in food hygiene before their first shift. It takes about two hours online, and the council pays for it. You'll also be given a badge, and a green apron, so that visitors know who to ask.

Let me tell you where our food comes from. About half of it is donated by neighbours, which is lovely, but it's not enough. The rest comes from two supermarkets, which pass on food that's close to its date, and from a bakery on the high street. The supermarket food is collected by our volunteer drivers, in a van that was lent to us by a plumbing firm. The bakery is different.
