The owner brings the bread over himself on his way home, but he only comes on weekdays, so at weekends we're usually without bread.

People often ask me what goes first. You'd think it would be the fruit, or maybe the yoghurts, but it's actually the salad. Bags of salad leaves that are one day from their date are the most common thing the supermarkets pass on, and people seem to love them. The bread goes quite quickly too, but by the end of the afternoon there's usually a pile of tinned beans, which people already have at home.

At six o'clock, we clear the fridge. Anything left that is still safe to eat goes to the women's refuge down the road, and anything that isn't goes into the compost bins in the library garden. Last month we sent forty kilos to the refuge, and only two kilos went to compost. I have to say that figure makes us very proud.

I'd like to say a little about what the fridge has done for the neighbourhood, because it isn't only about food. I thought the main thing would be fewer bags in the local bins, and that has happened, though the amount is small compared with the whole street. What has surprised me is the friendships. People who'd lived on the same street for twenty years and never spoken now meet at the fridge, swap recipes, and some have even started cooking together. I hadn't expected that at all. We haven't created any jobs, although a couple of regulars have used the fridge as a place to practise their English, which is wonderful. And the café next door hasn't noticed any difference in custom, at least not that I know of. Nor have our own volunteers saved money, I'm afraid. Most of them take food home, but they give far more than they take.

A typical shift lasts three hours. You'll start by checking the temperature of the fridge and writing it in the log, then wipe down the shelves, and after that you'll mostly be greeting people, sorting donations and keeping an eye on the dates. It's much quieter than people expect, and it's a good time for a chat. We always have two volunteers on at once, so you'll never be left on your own, and there's a kettle in the staff kitchen, which is the real attraction.
So that's us. If you'd like to join, please see me at the end, or write your name on the sheet by the door. We need people for the Tuesday and Saturday shifts in particular. Thank you very much.
Hana, Mark, hello. Take a seat, and tell me how the household waste project is going. I've seen your data tables, and I'd like to hear the story behind them.
It's been quite an adventure, hasn't it, Mark? We started with the idea of a questionnaire, because it's quick, but we dropped that.

Yes, the trouble with a questionnaire is that you're asking people to remember what they threw away last month, and nobody does. Most of us can't remember what we had for lunch on Tuesday. So we asked households to keep a diary for two weeks and note down everything that went in the bin.
That's a sensible choice. And how many households actually completed it?
Fifteen signed up, but three dropped out in the first week. So we ended up with twelve.
Twelve is small, but it's fine for a student project, as long as you don't claim too much from it. Did anything go wrong in the collection?

Not with the equipment. We gave everyone a set of kitchen scales, and they worked well. The real difficulty was that some people clearly felt embarrassed about what they were throwing away. One family told us afterwards that they'd quietly put a whole lasagne into the bin outside, so that it didn't show up in the diary.
Which means that our figures are probably lower than the truth. We called it under-reporting. We weren't sure whether it ruins the study.

It doesn't ruin it, no, but you can't hide it either. Every study of this kind suffers from it, and a good report says so honestly, in the limitations section, and then explains which way it would push your numbers. I wouldn't try to correct for it statistically, because you'd only be guessing. Markers prefer honesty to cleverness.
Before we go on, how did you recruit the households? If you chose friends, I need to know.
Mostly through a notice at the community centre. Only two of the twelve are people we knew, and we've said so in the report.
Good. And I assume everyone signed a consent form, and you've removed their names from the diaries?
Yes, each household has a number now, and the originals are locked in the departmental cabinet.
Then you're ahead of most of the second years. Good. Let's move on.
Good, that's a relief.
Now, what about the reasons? That's the part I'm most interested in. Why do different households waste food?

We were struck by how different the groups were. We interviewed one household of each type, and they gave us quite different explanations. The young professionals, for example, said they bought a lot of fresh food with good intentions, but then they were away for work so often that most of it was off by the time they returned.

The families with toddlers were the opposite. They were at home all the time, but the children refused to eat anything they hadn't eaten before. One mother said she'd cooked the same pasta so often that she'd stopped counting the portions she threw away.
That's very recognisable. And the older households?

The retired couples said they'd spent forty years cooking for a family, and they still make too much, even though it's only the two of them. One man said that he simply couldn't make a smaller pot of soup. They don't mind eating leftovers, but they often forget them in the fridge.

The students in the shared flat said that most of the waste came from not knowing whose food was whose. If something had been in the fridge for a week, nobody dared to eat it, in case it belonged to someone else, so it stayed until it was disgusting.
And finally the shift workers. They said they just didn't have time to plan their meals. They were sleeping when the shops were open, so they bought what they could, when they could.
That's a rich set of answers. Did anyone mention special offers, or confusion over the labels on food? Those are often the first things people say.

They did, in fact. Several people said they bought more because of special offers, and one or two were unsure about the labels. But when we asked them what the main reason was, they all gave something more personal.

That's the interesting finding. You should say it clearly. Now, about the presentation next week. You've got ten minutes, and you have far too many slides. I'd cut down the number of charts, because charts of small numbers don't convince anyone. What would be much more memorable is one household's story. Choose the one that tells the best story, perhaps the lasagne family, and tell it from start to finish.
We'd have to ask their permission.
Of course, and you'd have to anonymise it. But I think the audience would remember it for far longer than any bar chart.
Should we send the households a summary afterwards? Several of them asked what we found.

Yes, a one-page summary in plain English, with no jargon, is a lovely thing to do, and it's good practice too. People who give up two weeks of their time deserve to see the result. Just don't name anyone, even if they'd be happy to be named.
Right. One more thing. Should we mention what we think households can do about it?

A little, but keep it modest. Say what the households told you they'd try, and leave it at that. You're not experts yet. If you'd like to read more about it, the course library has a very good set of papers on household behaviour, and I'll email you the link. Right, I think that's everything. Come and see me on Thursday if you hit a problem.

Good afternoon, everyone. Last week we looked at food waste in farming and in the supply chain. This week I'd like to bring it closer to home, in fact right into your kitchens, because the surprising fact about food waste in a country like ours is that most of it doesn't happen on farms or in shops. It happens in houses.

Let me begin with the scale. If you add up all the food that is wasted after it leaves the farm, studies in this country suggest that about 70 per cent of it is thrown away by households. Supermarkets, restaurants and manufacturers together account for the rest. So when we talk about waste in the food system, the biggest single source is an ordinary family with an ordinary bin.

Why does that matter? Three reasons. The first is climate. When food rots in landfill, with no oxygen, it produces methane, which traps heat in the atmosphere far more strongly than carbon dioxide does over a short period. The second is more hidden. Every piece of food that ends up in the bin took water to grow, to process and to transport, and that water is lost along with the food. A single wasted hamburger, for example, represents thousands of litres. And the third reason is the simplest one: money. The average household in this country throws away several hundred pounds' worth of food every year.

So why do we do it? Let's start with the labels. Many people confuse the two main date labels on food. Best before refers to quality. After that date, the food may not be at its best, but it is perfectly safe. Use by, on the other hand, is about safety, and it is the only date that really matters. Surveys show that large numbers of people throw food away on the best before date, when it's perfectly good. Some supermarkets have started to remove best before dates altogether from fruit and vegetables, to see whether people use their eyes and noses instead.

The second cause is what happens in the shop. Supermarkets are very good at persuading us to buy more than we need, and the most effective tool is the multi-buy offer. Three for the price of two feels like a bargain, but if you can only eat one, it isn't. A study found that households buying fresh food on multi-buy offers wasted a good deal more of it than households that didn't.

There is also a cultural factor. In many households, throwing food away has become a sign of being well provided for. A full fridge feels reassuring, and an empty one feels like failure. Older people, who remember shortages, tend to waste less, and people who grew up with plenty tend to waste more. That's a generalisation, of course, but it fits what the surveys tell us, and it suggests that attitudes matter at least as much as information.

The third cause is the one that happens at home, in the kitchen. We simply cook too much. Most of us find it very hard to judge portions, particularly for rice and pasta, and we tend to prepare for the hungriest possible version of ourselves. The result is a plate or a pot of leftovers that nobody wants.

Now, does it help if you make people aware of this? Let me tell you about an experiment that was run in a city in the north of England. Researchers asked sixty households to keep a food diary for a fortnight, writing down everything that they threw away, together with the reason. Nobody was given advice, and there were no lectures about guilt. But when the researchers compared the households' waste afterwards with that of a control group, they found that the diary-keepers had reduced it by 25 per cent. Simply paying attention was enough. The households told them that once they had to write down 'lettuce, went slimy' for the third time, they started to buy less lettuce.

What practical steps can households take? Let me give you three. First, plan your shopping and take a list. Second, learn where food belongs. Many things we store in the fridge, such as bread, bananas and tomatoes, last longer outside it. And third, organise your fridge so that you can see what's in it. A lot of families now keep an eat me first shelf at eye level in the fridge, for things that are nearly at their date. It sounds trivial, but it is one of the most effective things you can do. And of course the freezer is your friend, for bread, for portions of soup, even for milk.

I should mention one thing that surprises people. Peelings, bones and coffee grounds are often counted as waste too, but researchers separate food that was edible from food that never was. The edible share is the part that could have been eaten, and it is the part everyone is trying to reduce. So when you read a statistic, always check which of the two it measures. Technology can help at the margins, too. Some shops now have apps that offer shoppers a bag of unsold food at a fraction of the price at closing time. But nobody has yet found a gadget that is as effective as a shopping list.

Finally, what can governments do? There is a lot of discussion about whether the rules should be tougher. Several countries have started with the supermarkets. The first to take a really strong step was France, which in 2016 passed a law that bans large supermarkets from destroying unsold food. They must either donate it to charities or send it for animal feed or compost. Other countries, including Italy and Czechia, have followed. Whether such laws reduce the waste that happens in homes is a different question, and it's one I'd like you to think about for your reading this week.
Hello, is that Mr Chalmers? It's Sunita from the Redcliffe Allotments office, returning your message from yesterday. You were asking about a plot, I think.

Oh, hello, yes, thanks very much for ringing back. I left the message rather late, so I wasn't sure it would reach anyone. I've been meaning to do this for years, and I finally got round to it on Sunday.
Well, I'm glad you did. Shall I take your details now and put you on the list? It only takes five minutes.
Please. Fire away.
Lovely. Surname first, please. How do you spell it?
Chalmers. C-H-A-L-M-E-R-S. Ewan Chalmers.
Thank you. Now, do you have any experience of growing things? It doesn't matter if you haven't, but it helps us decide which plots to offer.
A bit. I live in a flat, so it's all been in pots on the balcony. I've tried herbs, mainly basil and mint, and I managed a few tomatoes last summer. The mint did best. It took over the whole balcony.
That's mint for you. It's the same on the allotments, we keep it in buckets. So tomatoes, you said?
Tomatoes, yes, though the herbs were what I really enjoyed.

Fine. We'll put tomatoes on the form, since people always ask. Now, what size plot are you after? We have full plots, which are 250 square metres, half plots, and quarter plots, which are about 60. A lot of new tenants find a full plot rather overwhelming.
I'd have guessed a full one would be best, but I work full time, so I think I'd better start small. Half a plot, then. Is that the 125?
That's right, 125 square metres. A good size for a beginner. I should warn you that the waiting list is quite long. At the moment, for half plots, it's about eight months.
Eight months! Gosh. That's longer than I'd hoped.

I did say last year it was a year, so it's coming down. And if somebody gives up their plot, we might be able to call you sooner. Now, the rent. For a half plot it's £36 a year. A full plot is £48, and there's a reduction for pensioners and students, but I don't think that applies to you.
No, I'm afraid I'm neither. Thirty-six pounds is very reasonable. Does that include water?

It does. There's no mains water on the plots themselves, but there are taps spread around the site, shared between several plots, and you can fill your cans from those. Some people also collect rainwater in barrels, which is encouraged.
Excellent. And what about rules? I'd hate to break one without knowing.

The tenancy agreement is long, and I'll send you a copy, but there are a few main points. You can put up a small shed, and keep bees, if you have permission from the committee, but you're not allowed to light bonfires. Lots of people didn't know that, and we had a few complaints from the neighbouring houses last winter, so it's very strict now.
That's fine. I wasn't planning on one.

Another rule is that you must start cultivating your plot within six weeks of getting the keys. I know it sounds severe, but otherwise the weeds take over and the neighbours complain. It doesn't mean you have to plant everything, just clear the ground and get something going.
Six weeks should be fine. Is it a terribly strict site?

Not at all. We're a friendly lot. Actually, one more rule. We ask every tenant to come to a work party once a season. It's a chance to do the jobs that benefit everyone, such as clearing the paths, mending fences and tidying the shared compost area. Most people enjoy them, because there's tea and cake afterwards.
I'll be there for the cake, anyway. Is there any sort of induction for new people?
Not formally, but each new tenant is paired with someone who's been on the site for a while. They'll show you around and answer all your questions.
That sounds wonderful. What happens when my name comes up?

We'll ring you and offer you a plot, and you'll have a week to accept. Then you can collect the key from the pavilion, which is the little green building by the main gate. It's open on Saturday mornings from ten until twelve. Don't go to the gatehouse. That's for the groundsman, and it's not staffed at weekends.
The pavilion. Got it. Is there anything else I need to do?
Just a short form from me by email. I'll send it this afternoon. Thanks for your patience, Mr Chalmers. I think you're going to enjoy it.
Thank you, Sunita. I'm already planning the first bean row.

Hi, everyone, and thanks for coming on such a damp afternoon. I'm Ayesha, and I'm the head gardener here at the Rushmere Street Community Garden, which is a grand title for somebody who's mostly in charge of the wheelbarrows. I'll take you round in a moment, but first let me tell you a little about how the place came about, and how it works, so that the tour makes sense.

The garden stands on what used to be a bowling green. The club closed in 2012, when it ran out of members, and for two years the green was left to go to seed. It was a few of the neighbours who decided to do something about it. They didn't want to see it fenced off and sold for flats, so they went to the council and asked if they could look after it. You might think that the garden is owned by a housing association, because the blocks of flats on three sides are, but the land itself belongs to the council, who lease it to us for a pound a year. We don't think that is a bad deal.

People often ask how we pay for everything. We had two grants at the start, which paid for the fencing and the first polytunnel, but those are long gone. These days membership fees cover the insurance, and the rest comes from selling plants. We raise seedlings from March to May and sell them from a trestle table at the gate, and in a good year that brings in more than anything else we do. We also have a small shop, but it mostly sells jam, and I wouldn't say that it makes much money.

What are our problems? People expect me to say vandalism, because we're in the middle of a city, but I'm pleased to say that we have almost none. Nor is theft a real difficulty, though somebody does take the odd cabbage. The real challenge is volunteers on weekdays. We have plenty at weekends, but between Monday and Friday there are often only three or four of us, and the garden is far too big for that. If you can spare a Wednesday morning, you'll be very popular.

Now, what do we do apart from gardening? Every month we have a seed swap, in the village hall just across the road, where people bring the seeds they've saved and take home something new. We hold a pruning workshop in the winter, but that's only once a year. We tried a monthly film night in the polytunnel, but it was too cold and the screen kept blowing away, so we stopped. The beekeeping lessons are held only in summer, and the children's art class, which is run by the school, takes place every Friday, not once a month. So the thing that happens every single month, besides the seed swap, is our open volunteer morning, when anybody can come and try a bit of gardening without any commitment.

Right, let me explain the layout. We'll start at the main gate and walk straight down the central path. As you go in, you'll see a large shed on your left, which holds the tools. Don't go in. It's a mess. Behind the shed are the compost bays, three of them, each at a different stage. We call them the bank, because everything we put in comes back out as soil.

Carry on down the path and you'll reach the two polytunnels, one on each side. Between them, there's a little spiral of stones with herbs growing in it. It's called a herb spiral. The idea is that the herbs that like dry soil go at the top, and the ones that like it damp go at the bottom, so you can grow rosemary and mint a metre apart. Ours is rather scruffy, because the mint has escaped, but it still works.

On the right, there's the old orchard, just a dozen apple and pear trees that were here when the club closed. Under the trees we've put up an insect hotel, which is a stack of pallets stuffed with bamboo canes, pine cones and bits of bark. Solitary bees and lacewings move in during the spring. The children love it, though they keep adding sticks of their own, which doesn't help the bees.

Right at the end of the central path, where the old pavilion used to be, we have the wildflower meadow. We sowed it three summers ago with a seed mix of cornflowers and poppies, and last year it was so full of butterflies that a couple of people came just to photograph it. The pond, which you can see on your left as you walk down, is also part of the same wildlife area, but we don't let the little ones near it without an adult.
Right, that's quite enough from me. Put your hoods up and follow me, and please be careful of the wet steps by the polytunnel.

Layla, Ravi, come in, and mind the boxes on the floor. They're the remains of somebody's soil samples. I've read your proposal for the community garden survey, and I think it's got real promise, so let's go through it. How many gardens have you got in mind?
In the draft we said five. But one of them, the one on Calder Road, has just been closed for building work, so we're down to 4. We're a bit sad about it, because it had the best pond.
Four is fine, as long as they're properly different from each other. Remind me of how you chose them.

We wanted a range. Two are old gardens that have been going for twenty years or more, one is a school garden, and one is quite new, only two years old. We thought that would let us see whether the age of a garden makes a difference to the wildlife.
Good thinking. Now, the methods. You propose to count the plant species with quadrats. How many in each bed?
We wrote ten, but that was a guess.

Ten per bed is a great deal of work for a little bed. I'd say 6 is enough, as long as you choose the positions at random, with a throw of a marker, say, and not simply where it looks interesting. Otherwise you'll sample all the pretty bits.
Six, then. That's much more manageable. And we'd planned to go in June.

I'd think again about that. In June, the spring flowers have gone over and the summer ones haven't properly arrived, so you'd miss a lot. Most gardens peak in July. The weather's more settled too, which is important for the insect traps. I'd go in July, and keep all four visits within the same fortnight, so the conditions are comparable.
Right, July it is. We hadn't thought about that. For the insects, we plan to use pitfall traps, just plastic cups sunk into the soil. How long should we leave them?

Twenty-four hours is the usual minimum, but I'd leave them for 48. You'll catch more of the nocturnal beetles, and since you'll be returning anyway, it costs you nothing extra. One warning, though. Don't set them if rain is forecast. A flooded trap is a drowned trap, and your catches will be useless.
I hadn't thought of that either. We'll check the forecast.
And you do have permission from each garden's committee to put the traps in?

We've got permission from three. The school garden wants to speak to us first, and I'm a little nervous about that. The gardeners there are very protective. And another thing that worries me is that the gardeners might change something during the survey. If somebody decides to dig up a bed or put down weedkiller halfway through July, we'd lose a whole set of data.

That's a fair worry, and it's why you need to talk to them beforehand and ask them to leave the beds alone for those two weeks. I suspect most will agree if you explain. Gardeners tend to be very proud of what they've got, and they're usually delighted that anybody's interested.
We'd also have trouble identifying some of the insects. Is there anyone we can ask?

You could try the local naturalists' society, though I should warn you that they only meet once a month and it's a volunteer group. What I'd suggest instead is the museum. The curator of insects there, Dr Osei, has said she'd happily check specimens for any of my students, and she's much quicker than a society.
That's brilliant. We'll email her this week.
Should we use a diversity index for the analysis? I've seen the Shannon index in a few papers, but I only half understand it.

Use it, but explain it in a sentence or two, so that a reader who has never met it can follow. It rewards a garden with many species in similar numbers over one that has a lot of a single weed. Calculate it by hand for one garden first, so that you understand what it's doing, and then let the spreadsheet do the rest.
That sounds like a sensible way to learn it. Thanks.

Now, a couple of things to think about for the write-up. You're only surveying for one season, and that's a limitation you should state plainly. You can't say anything about how the gardens change through the year. And the gardens differ enormously in size. The old ones are several times larger than the school garden, so you can't just compare the number of species. You'll need to take the area into account, or the biggest garden will always win.
We'd thought about the area, but not about the season. Would it matter that we're not surveying private gardens as well?

I wouldn't worry about that. That's a different project. And I wouldn't worry about the weather either, as long as you record the temperature and cloud cover on each visit. Just remember to put it in your notebook.
What should we do with the results once we've got them? I'd like it to be of some use to the gardens.

I'd like that too. Rather than leaving it in a report that sits in a drawer, offer to give a short talk to each of the garden committees. Show them what lives in their garden, and suggest one or two changes that might help, such as leaving a patch of long grass, or building a log pile. People respond to a talk much better than they do to a document. And it will give you practice presenting.
Okay. That's something to look forward to, I suppose.
Good. Send me the revised plan by Friday, and then you can start ordering the cups.

Good morning, everyone. When we talk about biodiversity in gardens, most people think of wildlife, of birds, hedgehogs and bees. This morning, though, I'd like to talk about a different kind of biodiversity, one that's easier to overlook, and that is the diversity of the plants we actually grow and eat. And I'd like to argue that community gardens are playing a surprisingly important part in protecting it.

To begin with, the problem. Over the last hundred years, farming has become more and more efficient, and one of the reasons is that it has become more uniform. Commercial agriculture now relies on a very small number of varieties, bred to ripen at the same time, survive transport and look identical on the shelf. That's convenient, but it's also risky. If a disease arrives that attacks one variety, it can attack all of them, because they're genetically almost the same. The Irish potato famine is the classic example. More recently, the same thing has threatened bananas.

Let me give you a more familiar example, the humble apple. In the United Kingdom, there were once around 2,000 varieties of apple. Some had names that sound like poetry, such as Ashmead's Kernel, or Ribston Pippin, and some were like nothing you'd find today, russet-skinned and nutty, or with flesh that was pink all the way through. Now go into any supermarket and count the varieties on the shelf. In most shops, there are fewer than 10. The rest have simply vanished from the commercial world. They're not extinct, but they only survive in old gardens and orchards, and in the care of a few enthusiasts.

Why does that matter? Old varieties often have things to offer. Some have a flavour that modern types have lost. But, more importantly, many have resistance to particular diseases, or are adapted to local climates, such as a cold hillside or a wet valley. That kind of resilience may be extremely valuable if the climate changes, and if we lose the varieties, we lose it too.

So what can a community garden do? One of the most interesting ideas to emerge in the last few years is the seed library. It works exactly like a book library. You join, you borrow a few packets of seeds, you grow them, and then at the end of the season you give back seed from your own harvest, so the library never runs out. Gardeners get unusual varieties for free, and the varieties stay alive, because somebody is always growing them.

It sounds simple, but there are some technical issues. Seed saving is easiest with plants that pollinate themselves, such as beans, peas, lettuce and tomatoes, because the seeds you collect will be true to type. Things like squash and courgettes are much trickier, because the flowers are visited by bees, and they cross with each other very readily. You may plant what you think is a pumpkin and end up with something like a gourd. Experienced seed savers get around this by covering the flowers with fine netting before they open, and pollinating them by hand. It takes patience, but it works.

There is also a legal wrinkle that you should be aware of. In some countries, the rules about selling seed only allow registered varieties, and registration can be slow and expensive, which suits the big seed companies but not a shoebox of heirloom beans. Seed libraries get round this by lending, not selling, which puts them in a rather grey area. Some authorities have granted exemptions. It is worth noticing how a rule designed to protect farmers from poor-quality seed can also make it harder to keep old varieties alive.

Let me tell you about one project, in a town I'll call Ashburn, because they asked me not to use the real name. A group of volunteers in a community garden started a seed library about six years ago with a shoebox and just 40 packets, which had been donated by an elderly gardener. Today, they have members from across the town, and the garden itself grows around 60 different varieties of tomato alone, in colours you'd never see in a shop, from almost black to a creamy white. The project has even been visited by a plant scientist from the university, who took samples of some of the oldest varieties for her own research.

That doesn't mean that everything has gone smoothly. When I asked the organisers about their biggest difficulty, I expected them to say money, or keeping volunteers, or finding space. But they said that the main problem was damp. The seeds were stored in tins in the garden shed, and in a wet winter, moisture got in and many of the packets went mouldy. They've now moved the tins into the library, with silica gel in each one, and the problem has gone away.

What I'd like you to take from this is that biodiversity isn't only the wild things. It's also the plants and animals that we've bred over thousands of years, and which can easily vanish when nobody is looking after them. A community garden is a small place, but a small place with many people looking after many different things can do a surprising amount. In the seminar this week, I'd like you to think about the opposite risk, which is that these projects become too dependent on a handful of enthusiastic people. The two short articles on the reading list will help you to prepare.

Sorry to keep you on hold. Our phones have been playing up all morning, and I think the line you were on went through three people before it reached me. This is Kerry, the manager at the Hopewell Hospice Shop. You wanted to arrange a collection?
Yes, please. I'm clearing my late aunt's flat, and there's far too much to take in a car. A neighbour said you collect furniture for free.
We do, though we ask for a small donation. I'm sorry about your aunt. Let me get the collection form up. May I have your surname?
It's Marchetti. M-A-R-C-H-E-T-T-I.
Marchetti, thank you. And what have you got for us? I'll need the main item first, because it decides which van we send.
Well, the biggest thing is a sofa, a big three-seater, but I suspect I'm going to hear that you can't take it.
Does it have a label on it with the words about fire safety? It's usually under one of the seat cushions.
I've looked. There isn't one, I'm afraid. It must be older than the rules.
Then I'm sorry, we can't accept it. It's the law, not us. Is there anything else large?
A bookcase, a good solid oak one, and a dining table with four chairs.
Lovely, solid wood goes very quickly in the shop. Let's call the bookcase the main item, and I'll put down the table and chairs as extras. Anything electrical?
A food mixer, a kettle and a sewing machine. The sewing machine was my aunt's pride and joy, and I'd hate to see it go to a skip.

It won't. We have a volunteer who tests every electrical item before it goes on the shelf, and sewing machines are very popular with our younger customers, which surprises people. I'll note the sewing machine as the electrical item. The mixer and the kettle are fine too, but I'll just put the main one down.
Thank you. That makes me feel better.
Now, the practicalities. The flat, is it on the ground floor?
I wish. It's on the second floor, and there's no lift. Sorry.

Don't apologise, our drivers are used to stairs, and there are always two of them. They'll bring the table down in pieces, if they need to. Now, when would you like us to come? We're free on Tuesday the 3rd of March, or on the Friday of that week.
The Tuesday would be ideal, but the flat has to be handed back to the landlord by Wednesday, and I haven't finished clearing the kitchen. Would the Friday be too late for you?
Not at all. The Friday is 6 March. I'll write that down. And would you prefer the morning or the afternoon?
Morning, please, if you can. I have to be at work by two.
We run morning collections between 9 and 12. The drivers will ring you when they're about twenty minutes away, so you don't have to wait around.
That's very thoughtful. What about parking? It's a very narrow street.

That's a good question, and it's one people forget. The van is quite large, so ideally we'd stop in front of your door. If that's impossible, they could park on a side street and carry things. What's it like?

Terrible, to be honest. There are double yellow lines all along the front. But there's a little side street called Ash Lane, round the corner, where there's usually space, and it's only about thirty metres from the door.

Ash Lane. Perfect, I'll write that on the form so the drivers know. Now, our suggested donation for a collection of this size is £15. That's the same for any collection, whether it's one item or fifteen. It all goes to the hospice, and if you're a taxpayer, we can claim Gift Aid on it.
That's very fair. I'll pay it on the day, if that's all right.
Cash or card, whichever you prefer. One last thing, I need a number to reach you on the day. Is it a mobile?
Yes. It's, well, I don't want to give you the whole thing, but the last four digits are 4471, if that's enough for your records.

That'll do nicely. We'll check it against the one that shows on our system. Oh, and before I forget, we can't take mattresses either, for hygiene reasons, so please don't leave any out for the drivers.
No mattresses, no. Only the sofa, and a friend of mine has offered to take that to the tip.
Good. Then I think we're done. You'll get a text this afternoon to confirm, and another the night before.
Wonderful, thank you so much. You've been very patient with all my questions.
Not at all. It's what we're here for. Good luck with the rest of the clearing, Ms Marchetti.

Right, if everyone's got their high-visibility jackets on, and I can see most of you have, let's make a start. I'm Nigel Probert, the site manager here at the Brackenfield Recycling and Re-use Centre, and this morning I'm going to take you round the site before you start your volunteer training. Please stay with the group, and please don't wander off towards the lorries. They have a very large blind spot, and I'd rather not fill in an accident form on your first day.

Let me begin with some general points about how the site works, because they'll answer the questions you were about to ask. If a visitor arrives in a van, we ask to see a permit. They're free, but they're issued by the council, and without one we can't let the van in, however nice the driver. Most people with a van are doing house clearances or small building work. It's not unusual, but it is how the council keeps trade waste out of the domestic site. Cars, of course, don't need a permit.

On busy days, particularly at weekends, we ask visitors to book a slot. It used to be possible to ring the office, but we withdrew that line last year, because nobody had time to answer it. These days, it's online only. I'd say about one in five of our visitors still turns up without a booking, and we're strict about it, because queues back up on to the main road and the neighbours complain, with some justification.

A few details on opening times. We open at eight every day except Christmas Day, and we close at six in summer, but at four in winter, because the light goes. The last vehicle is let in fifteen minutes before closing, and we do mean fifteen. If you're ever on the gate and somebody arrives at ten to four with a trailer full of fence panels, I'm afraid the answer is no, however sad their story. Also, children must stay in the car, and dogs too, on safety grounds.

Now, let me show you where things go. As you come in from the road, the first thing on your right is the yellow cage. That's where household batteries go. Not car batteries, which have to be handed to a member of staff, but ordinary ones, from remote controls and torches. People are always surprised how many they find in kitchen drawers.

Next to the office, you'll see the row of red bins. They look rather like fire hydrants, and they're for cooking oil. Please don't let anyone pour oil down the drain. Last winter we had a blockage under the high street that took the water company a week to clear. It was a fatberg, the size of a bus, and I'm told it was mostly from takeaways.

Behind the office is the blue shed, which is for paint, solvents and anything with a skull on the label. It's kept locked, and it's only open when a member of staff is present. Please never put anything into it without asking.

If you follow the main road round to the far end, you'll find the big green skip, for garden waste. Branches, grass, hedge clippings, that sort of thing. We send it to a farm nearby, where it's composted, and in the spring we sell the compost back to residents at a very modest price.

And finally, on the left as you leave, is the re-use shop. That's where anything in good condition goes, such as furniture, bikes, crockery and toys. It's in a converted shipping container, and it's one of the things I'm proudest of on this site. Please encourage people to leave working items there, instead of dropping them in the skips. The shop is staffed by volunteers like yourselves, and you'll be shown how it works this afternoon.

A word about electrical items. Every one that goes on sale in the shop is tested by a qualified volunteer, and it's given a sticker with the date. Nothing is sold as seen. If it fails the test, it goes to the recycling bay, and you'll never see it on the shelf. People sometimes ask whether they can try it before they buy, and the answer is yes, there's a socket by the till.

This year, we have also added a swap shelf, just inside the shop door. It's for books, toys and jigsaws, and you simply leave one and take one. It's been such a success that I had to add a second shelf in June. We did consider a café, and even a bicycle workshop, but neither fitted within the budget, so for now we are sticking with the swap shelf.

Finally, a word about our targets. When I started here, only about 5 per cent of what came through the gates was re-used. This year we have reached 15, which I'm quite proud of, and next year's target is 20. It doesn't sound very much, but every percentage point is several tonnes of furniture that doesn't go to landfill. Thank you for helping us to get there. Now, shall we go and meet the rest of the team?

Nadia, Tom, good to see you. I've had a look at your project outline on repair cafés, and I think there's something in it. Before we get into the details, remind me why you chose to work from the café logs instead of designing an experiment of your own.

Mainly because the data already exists, and it's unusually detailed. The Millbank café has recorded every single item that has come through the door since it opened, with what the item was, what was wrong with it and what happened in the end. It's all in a spreadsheet. The organiser did suggest it, but I'd say we'd have gone for it anyway, because it's so rare to find records like that.
We've got 640 items for the last year. That's a good number for a student project, although we weren't sure whether it was enough to say anything about different types of product.
It's enough if you're careful about it. What's the quality of the data like? Logs kept by volunteers are rarely perfect.

That's been our biggest headache. It isn't that entries are missing, or that the handwriting is bad, because it's all typed. The problem is that different volunteers use different words for the same thing. One writes broken, another faulty, a third not working. We've had to reclassify about a third of the entries by hand, and I'm still not sure that we've been consistent.

Then you need to say how you did it, and ideally ask someone else to classify a sample, so you can show how often you agree. Now, what has the data actually shown? I'd like to hear the results by product type.

The first thing is that the picture isn't what we expected. We assumed small kitchen appliances, things like toasters and kettles, would be the easiest to fix, because they're so simple. In fact, many of them are written off. The repair is often possible, but the volunteers say it isn't worth it, because a new one costs less than the part.

Laptops were the real surprise. We expected them to be difficult, and they are, but not because of the electronics. The main reason that they fail to be repaired is that so many have parts that are glued in, like the battery, so that you can't remove them without breaking the case. A few volunteers said they won't even try.
That's a well-known problem, and it's a good point to bring out in your discussion. What about the clothing?

That's the success story. The textile table has the highest rate of repair of anything in the café, and nearly all the jobs, like replacing a zip or taking up a hem, are finished while the owner waits. The only disappointment is that people don't bring enough of them.

Bicycles are different again. They're usually repairable, but they rarely get finished on the day, because the part isn't in stock. The owner has to come back with it, or the volunteers order it, and about a quarter of people never return.
Interesting, I'd like you to quantify that. And anything else?

Headphones, which are surprisingly popular. They're mostly a matter of broken wires, and the repair is possible, but it requires a soldering iron and a steady hand, so only two of the volunteers can do it. If those two aren't there, the headphones queue builds up.
That's a nice example of how a café depends on the particular skills of its volunteers. Right. Now let's talk about the second part of the project, the visitor survey. How many questions do you have?
For the analysis, we were going to use simple percentages. Is that enough?

For 640 items, yes, with one caution. Some of your categories are tiny. If only eleven pairs of headphones came in, then a repair rate of eighty per cent means very little. So show the number of items next to every percentage, and be careful about drawing firm conclusions from the small groups. A table with counts beside the percentages is perfectly good.
We'll add the counts, then.
Fourteen at the moment.

That's too many. People come to a repair café to have something mended, not to fill in a form, and they'll lose patience. I'd cut it to ten at the most, and I'd put the most important ones first, in case they leave halfway through.
We could offer a small prize draw, as an incentive.

You could, but I'm not convinced it's necessary. People who have just had something repaired are in a good mood, and they're usually happy to answer a few questions. What I would add is a question about what the visitor would have done if the café hadn't existed. Would they have thrown the item away, taken it to a shop, or bought a new one? That's what tells you about the real environmental benefit.
That's a good idea. That hadn't occurred to us.

Of course, you can't rely entirely on what people say they would have done, and you should mention that in your limitations. But it's much better than counting the items that were mended and assuming every one would otherwise have been thrown out.
Should we translate the survey? The café has a lot of visitors who speak Polish and Arabic.

It's a fair point, but for a project of this size I wouldn't, I'd just mention that it's English only, as a limitation. And I wouldn't interview the volunteers as well. It's tempting, but you'd be doubling your workload, and you've already got more than enough.
Understood. Then we'll cut the questions and add the one about alternatives.

Good. Send me the revised version by the end of the week. And have a think about the title. At the moment it's rather bland. Something with a question in it, perhaps, since your findings are more surprising than you seem to realise.

Good afternoon. In the last few weeks we've been looking at how economies handle resources, and today I'd like to turn to an idea that has moved, in about a decade, from the margins of environmental debate to the centre of government policy, the circular economy. I'd like to explain what it means, and then spend most of the time on one small, practical piece of it, which is repair.

Let me start with what we have now. Our economy is, for the most part, a linear one. We take materials out of the ground, we make them into products, and when the products have done their job, we throw them away. Take, make, waste. It's a simple model and it has served us extraordinarily well, in the sense that we've become richer. But it has an obvious flaw, which is that it assumes that the supply of materials is endless and that the planet's capacity for absorbing rubbish is endless too.

Electronics make the point very clearly. The world now produces more than 60 million tonnes of electronic waste every year, and only about a fifth of it is documented as having been properly recycled. Part of the reason is a design habit that's often called planned obsolescence. The phrase suggests a conspiracy, and I don't think it's always that. But products are frequently designed with a limited lifespan, with batteries that can't be replaced, parts that are glued, and software that stops being supported after a few years. It makes economic sense for the maker, because a customer who has to buy again is a customer who comes back.

There is, however, a business model that points the other way. Some companies now lease their products instead of selling them. A customer pays for each wash, say, and not for the washing machine, and the maker keeps ownership. That changes the incentive completely, because the maker now profits from a machine that lasts, and has every reason to repair or refurbish it afterwards. It hasn't taken over the market, and critics point out that it can simply shift the problem to subscriptions, but it shows that design and business model are closely linked.

Against this, the circular economy proposes something different. The most widely used framework, developed by a foundation in the United Kingdom, has three principles. The first is to design out waste and pollution from the start. The second is to keep products and materials in use for as long as possible. And the third is to regenerate natural systems, which is to say, not only to do less harm, but to restore the soil, the water and the habitats that the old economy has used up.

The second principle is where repair comes in. It's helpful to think of a hierarchy of options. At the top, you simply reduce what you use. Then you re-use, then repair, then refurbish, then remanufacture, and recycling comes at the very bottom. People are often surprised that recycling is last, since it's what most of us do. But when you recycle a washing machine, you are crushing the machine to recover the metal, and you throw away all the labour, energy and design that went into building it. What is lost, in other words, is the value of the thing itself. Repair keeps it.

So what stops us repairing more? Part of it is design, as I mentioned, but a big part is access. If the manufacturer won't sell you the part, you can't fix the appliance. That's why campaigners have pushed for what are called right to repair laws. In several countries, the law now requires manufacturers to supply spare parts for a stated number of years after the product goes on sale, along with manuals and, in some cases, diagnostic software. It's a modest step, but it changes the economics, because the product can be fixed by the owner, or by a local shop, and it doesn't have to be sent back to the factory.

Governments can also change the price of repair. Sweden has done something very interesting here. Since 2017, it has cut the tax on repairs of items such as bicycles, clothes and shoes, from 25 per cent to just 12. The idea was that it would be a little more attractive to mend a pair of boots than to buy a new pair. Early evidence suggests that the effect has been modest, but it has certainly pushed the issue on to the political agenda.

That brings me to repair cafés. The first one was held in Amsterdam in 2009, and the idea spread incredibly fast. There are now many thousands around the world. The model is simple. Volunteers with practical skills sit alongside visitors, and together they try to mend whatever the visitor has brought. It's free, apart from a donation. In the data I've seen, around 70 per cent of the items brought to a typical café are repaired, which is remarkable, considering that many are items that the owners had already given up on.

But I don't think the main benefit of repair cafés is in the kilos of waste they avoid. Measured that way, they are very small. The most significant effect, in my view, is social. People who have never met each other work on a problem together, and a neighbour who is good with zips shows another neighbour how to use a needle. Researchers who have studied the cafés report that what they build is trust between neighbours, and trust is a resource that no recycling bin can provide. I'd like you to think about whether that can be measured, and if so how, for the reading discussion next week.
You look as though you've run here. Grab a seat by the fan, and have a cup of water. It's the only thing we've got that's colder than the pool. Now, what can I do for you?
Thanks, I think I will. I've just been told that the only way to survive this summer is to swim every morning before work, so I'd like to find out about a membership.
Sensible advice. Half of the town has had the same idea this week, so I'll take your details now, and then we can talk about times. Surname first, please.
Whitcombe. W-H-I-T-C-O-M-B-E.
Whitcombe, thanks. Now, we do several kinds of membership. Adult, family, student and senior. Which would suit you?
Family is out, there's only me. I was going to say adult, but I'm still a part-time student, and I've got a card to prove it.
Then you're eligible for the student rate. I'll put that down, and I'll need to see the card when you come in. When would you like to begin?
As soon as possible. Could I start tomorrow?

Tomorrow's the 30th, and the memberships start on the first of the month, I'm afraid. The system won't let me change it. So the earliest would be 1 December. You're welcome to pay for a single swim in the meantime.
That's fine. I can last a day.

Now, we run early sessions from six o'clock, then seven, and so on, but the first session of the day is the most popular, because it's the coolest. It's usually quite full, with lots of splashing and queues at the ends of the lanes. The next one is at 6.30, which is much calmer. Which would you prefer?
I do like an early start, but I don't think the very first one is for me, if it's as crowded as you say. Let's say 6.30.
Good choice. Which lane do you want? We've got slow, medium and fast. Be honest, because the fast lane is not forgiving.
I'd say fast, I swam a lot at school, but it was a long time ago. I've probably lost it. Medium, please.

Wise. People in the medium lane tend to talk to each other as they swim, so it's a good one for newcomers. Now, there are some extras. Most people want a locker, and the key needs a deposit. That's $20, refundable when you return it.
Fine. Are there showers, and do I need to bring my own towel?

Showers and hairdryers are free, but we don't supply towels, so you'll have to bring one. The changing rooms get crowded around seven, so if you want to be in and out quickly, the 6.30 session is perfect. And there's a bike rack by the side door, under the shade cloth. It's the only shady spot in the car park, so it fills up early.
Good to know. And what's the monthly fee? I should have asked that first.
The adult rate is $55, but the student rate is $49 a month. It's the same price whether you swim once a week or every day, so you might as well use it.
That's reasonable. Is there anything else I can add? I've seen a poster for classes.

We have aqua aerobics on Tuesday evenings, and lane swimming lessons on Saturdays, and a water polo club, though the water polo people are a bit competitive. Any of those, and it's an extra $8 a session.
Aqua aerobics sounds like fun. I'd like to do that, please. My mother does it, and says it's much harder than it looks.
She's right. Put you down for the next block. Now, for safety, I have to ask for an emergency contact. Whom should we ring?
My brother, Callum. He lives only ten minutes away, and he's usually on his phone.
Callum, brother. Thanks. And is there any medical condition we should know about? Our lifeguards like to be told, but we don't share it with anyone else.
Yes, I have asthma. It's mild and well controlled, but I always carry an inhaler, and I'll bring it poolside.
Perfect. Lifeguards will want to know that. Can you leave the inhaler somewhere visible on the side, such as on the end of the lane? Most people do, and it's no trouble at all.
Of course. Is there a discount if I pay for the whole summer in advance?
There is, actually. Three months in advance gets you one month free. It's popular with students, because they can budget for it. But it's entirely up to you.
I'll think about it and decide on my first morning, if that's all right.
Of course. I'll have your card ready at the desk on the first. Stay cool, and I hope the lane behaves.

Good evening, everyone, and thank you for coming out on what I'm told is the hottest evening we've had this year. I'm Fiona Bell, the council's resilience officer, and I'm here to explain the Heat Ready Summer plan that the council agreed last month. I'll talk for about fifteen minutes, then I'll take questions.

A word of background first. Last summer, the town recorded eleven days above 30 degrees, which was roughly twice the usual number, and the ambulance service told us that calls from elderly residents rose by almost a third. That is what prompted the plan, and it is why the council has tried to keep it as simple as possible.

Let me begin with the bit that most people want to know, which is how you'll hear about a heatwave. We already have a flood warning system, and the heat alert works on the same principle. When one is issued, everyone who has signed up will receive a text message. Not an email, which people don't check, and not a phone call, which people ignore if the number is unknown. A text message. If you haven't signed up yet, there are forms on the table by the door, and it takes only a minute.

So what's a heatwave, in our terms? The national weather service has its own definitions, which vary from one region to another, but for our town, we've decided that an alert goes out when the daytime temperature is forecast to go above 32 degrees. I should say that when we first drafted the plan, the figure was 30, but the health service advised that this was too low and would trigger so many alerts that people would stop paying attention. So we agreed on 32.

Now, what will the council actually do? First, water. We'll be giving out free bottles of drinking water, and refilling stations will be open at the town hall. I know some of you were hoping for the library, but the library's plumbing can't cope, so the town hall it is. We're also working with the pharmacy so that anyone who needs a refill of an important medicine will be able to get it, even if the weather makes it difficult to travel.

Second, people. The people at greatest risk in a heatwave are the elderly, those who live alone and those with chronic illnesses. We've recruited a team of 40 volunteer buddies, who will each phone or visit four or five residents every day during an alert. I know that sounds a lot, and it isn't enough, so we're still recruiting. You'll find the forms at the same table. We had hoped for 50, but 40 is what we have.

And a very practical point. Not everyone has a phone, and some people don't want to ask for help. So we've invented a simple system. If you're an older resident and you'd like someone to check on you during a heatwave, you can put a green card in your window. We'll give you one. The idea is that a neighbour or a buddy walking past will see it, and knock. If the card isn't there, nobody will bother you. We tried red at first, but it looked too much like a warning, and green is friendlier.

Finally, cool spaces. In a hot spell, you don't have to stay at home. The council has agreed with several buildings that they will open their doors to anyone who needs to cool down. Let me go through them. The library is open on weekdays, from nine until five, as normal, and nothing changes there. The leisure centre is the main one for the evenings. It'll stay open every day until eight, and the pool will be free for the first hour of an alert, from ten o'clock. The museum has agreed to open on weekends only, because on weekdays it's busy with school groups, and there simply isn't the space.

Next, the community hall on Fletcher Street. That's open on Monday to Thursday, because on Fridays it's used for the market, and on weekends there are hired events. And, perhaps the most surprising, the church hall behind the post office has volunteered to open at any hour, day or night, throughout a heat alert. They have a very large basement, and it's the coolest building in town. It's a lovely offer, and I hope that nobody needs it in the middle of the night, but if they do, it's there.

Before I stop, I'd like to say something about what you can do yourselves. Close curtains on the sunny side of the house during the day, and open the windows at night when the air is cooler. Drink water before you feel thirsty. Check on neighbours, particularly elderly ones. And if you have a pet, please remember that it feels the heat as much as you do. Those are small things, but a lot of the risk comes from forgetting them. Right, that's all from me. Who has the first question?

Ruth, Karim, hello. Do shut the door. The air conditioning in this corridor has been broken since June, so we'll all keep it out as best we can. I wanted to talk about your heat vulnerability map of Marlow Green. It's a good topic for this summer. How did you build it?

We combined several layers. The first one came from satellite images, which we used to work out how much tree cover each street has. The second was census data, which tells us how many residents are over seventy-five, and how many of them live alone.

We'd hoped to add a third layer, from hospital records. We wanted to see which areas had the most admissions for heat illness last summer. But the hospital said no, because of patient confidentiality, and we couldn't argue with that.
Quite right, they couldn't have released it. What about the council's tree register? That's a ready-made source.
We looked at it, but it hasn't been updated since 2015, and it only covers street trees, not those in gardens. We decided that the satellite images were more reliable.
Good. And what about measuring the actual temperatures? A map of risk is one thing, but you'd want some evidence that the hot areas are in fact hot.

That was the fun part. We didn't have the budget for fixed weather stations, so we each walked a set route through the town, one in the morning and one at three in the afternoon, carrying a handheld logger. It was about eleven kilometres altogether, and we sweated quite a lot.
We did think about strapping the loggers to bicycles, which would have covered more ground, but the readings were affected by the wind, so we gave up on that.
A wise decision. Walking speed is much better for this kind of work. Now, the satellite images. Did you have any difficulties?
When did you do the walks? Were the days comparable?
We did them on three consecutive days in the same week, when the forecast was for clear skies and about thirty-three degrees. We skipped the Wednesday, because it clouded over.
Good. A single day can mislead, and three days of similar weather is far more convincing, although you should say that it was one week in one summer.
Yes, we'll put that in the limitations.

Only one big one. We were hoping to count individual trees, but the images aren't sharp enough. Each pixel covers about ten metres, so a single tree can't be picked out. We had to treat canopy cover as a percentage of each block, which is much less precise.
That's a limitation, but a common one, and there's nothing wrong with a block-level estimate if you say so. Were there any surprises in what you found?

Yes, quite a big one. We assumed the hottest part of the town would be the industrial estate, because of the tarmac and the warehouses. It was hot, but not the hottest. That prize went to the new housing development on the eastern side. It has hardly any trees, because they were removed for building and the replacements are still saplings, and the houses are packed together with dark roofs.
And many of the residents are young families with small children, which makes it even more worrying.

That's a very useful finding, and I'd put it in the abstract. Now, I've had a look at the map itself, and I have one concern. Your colour scale runs from deep blue to bright red. That can be misleading. It makes a difference of one degree look like a dramatic change. I'd choose a scale that's more restrained, or at least show the actual temperatures beside the colours, so that the reader can judge for themselves.
Fair point. I suppose red does look very alarming.
Precisely. A map should inform people, not frighten them. Now, the last section, your recommendations. You've suggested actions for several places in the town. Let's go through them.
For the primary school, we recommended planting trees. The playground is a big expanse of tarmac with no shade at all, and the children have to sit inside at break time on hot days.
Good, and it's a visible project that parents will support. And the market square?

That was harder. The square is completely paved, and we found out that there are pipes and cables under it, so you can't just dig holes for trees. We considered fountains and misting sprays, but fountains get vandalised, and the sprays use a great deal of water, which isn't sensible in a drought. So we suggested shade sails, big pieces of fabric stretched above the stalls.
That's practical. Cheaper than trees, and fast. What about the retirement flats on Orchard Road?

They're a real concern. The flats were built in the nineteen-seventies, with large south-facing windows and no air conditioning. We thought about changing the roof, but it's the council's building, and it would cost too much. Instead, we recommended that the residents' lounge should be turned into a cool room, with a large fan and a supply of cold water, so that people have somewhere to go in the afternoon.
An excellent idea, and much quicker than any refurbishment. And finally the bus station?

The bus station has a huge metal shelter that gets painfully hot to the touch, so people choose to stand in the sun. We suggested coating the roof with a reflective paint. It's inexpensive and it can be done in a weekend.
Do you think the council would be interested in the map?

Quite possibly. The council's resilience officer has asked whether students might share their findings, so I'll put you in touch, but only once the map is finished. I don't want her to see the red version.
Well done, both of you. That's a very strong set of recommendations. Revise the colour scale, add the temperatures, and send me the final version on Monday.

Good morning, everyone. In the last lecture we looked at why towns get hotter than the countryside around them. Today I want to ask a more practical question. Given that summers are getting hotter, what can a town actually do about it? I'd like to begin with an event that changed the way that governments think about heat, and then work through the main responses, from warning systems to trees.

Let me begin in the summer of 2003. A heatwave hit much of Europe in August, and it lasted for about two weeks. At the time, it was reported mainly as a weather story, with pictures of dried-up rivers and sunbathers in fountains. It was only afterwards, when the statistics were compiled, that the scale became clear. Researchers estimate that it caused more than 70,000 deaths across the continent. That was far more than any previous natural disaster in Europe in living memory, and almost nobody noticed while it was happening. Many of the victims were elderly people who lived alone. They didn't have anyone to open a window or bring them a glass of water, and in some cases, nobody realised they were in trouble until days later.

After 2003, many countries introduced what are called heat-health warning systems. The idea is the same as with storms or floods. If the forecast says that temperatures will reach dangerous levels, the authorities issue a warning, and a set of actions follows automatically. The warning matters because it tells hospitals to prepare, and it tells carers, schools and care homes to change what they do.

How is the threshold decided? It's not a single fixed number, which surprises people. A temperature of 30 degrees means very different things in Stockholm and in Seville, because people in the south are used to it, and their buildings are designed for it. So each city sets its own level, and most of them require the forecast to stay above it for a number of days in a row. A typical rule is that it must be exceeded for 3 consecutive days, because it's the build-up of heat that makes people ill, rather than a single hot afternoon.

A warning is not much good if it doesn't reach the right people. That's why many cities now keep a register of vulnerable residents, such as the elderly, people with heart conditions and those who live alone. When a warning goes out, staff or volunteers phone the people on the list. There are privacy questions here, of course, because the register is made up of sensitive information, and different cities have given very different answers.

Let me turn now to the physical side. The cheapest of all measures is what's called a cool roof. It simply means a roof that reflects more sunlight than it absorbs, and the simplest way to do that is to paint it white. This isn't new. Many towns around the Mediterranean have whitewashed their houses for centuries, long before anyone talked about climate adaptation. Modern reflective coatings can lower the temperature inside a top-floor flat by several degrees, and they cost very little.

Trees are the other great tool, and they work in two ways. They give shade, and they release water vapour, which cools the air. Measurements on a hot day show that a shaded pavement can be up to 15 degrees cooler than one in direct sun. But there is a catch, which is that trees aren't an instant solution. A newly planted sapling casts very little shade, and it can take twenty years to reach full size. And in the first few summers, it needs regular watering, or it will die. A surprising number of planting schemes have failed, not because the trees were the wrong species, but because nobody was assigned to carry the water.

What about air conditioning? It's an obvious response, and in a hot spell it does save lives. But it has drawbacks. It uses a great deal of electricity, which, if it comes from fossil fuels, adds to the problem. It also pushes hot air out into the street, which makes the outdoor temperature higher, and the people who can't afford it end up in the hottest places. So cities that take adaptation seriously treat air conditioning as a last resort, and aim to cool buildings in other ways first, with shutters, ventilation and insulation.

For people who have no way of cooling their homes, many towns now designate a network of cooling centres. These are public buildings, such as libraries, community halls and swimming pools, which are kept open longer during a warning. They're not expensive to run, because the buildings already exist, and they work best when people know where they are and can walk to them.

Finally, there is the longer term. Town planners can change the rules for new buildings, so that the problem doesn't get worse. In some places, new housing is now required to include shading on windows that face the sun, such as external shutters or deep overhangs. It's easier and cheaper to put it in when a building is designed than to add it afterwards. Of course, it will take decades before most of the housing stock has been replaced, which is why all the other measures I've mentioned still matter. For next week, please read the case study on the city of Ahmedabad, and be ready to say what it did right.
Hi there. I hope I've come through to the right place. A friend of mine said you rent out those little satellite messengers for walkers?
We do, yes. This is Tarn and Trail Outdoor Hire, and I'm Tessa. Are you planning a long walk?
A long one, yes. I'm going to do the Cape Wrath Trail, from Fort William right up to the lighthouse at the top. I've wanted to for years, and now I finally have the time.

Oh, lovely. That's a proper adventure. It's about two hundred miles, and there's hardly any phone signal for most of it, so you've made a sensible decision. Right, let me bring up the booking screen. Shall we begin with your surname?
It's Hargreaves. That's H-A-R-G-R-E-A-V-E-S. Two As, and no E after the G, which people always seem to add.
Hargreaves, got it. And a mobile number, in case we need to reach you before you collect the device?
07700 900 358. Thank you. I'll put the route on the form as well, because we load the right maps onto the device before you pick it up. That's Cape Wrath, yes?
That's right.
And when do you set off?

I'm aiming for the twelfth of June. Actually, hang on. That's the day I start walking. I'm taking the sleeper train up, so I'd really want to collect the device the day before. Would that be all right?
That's no problem, but our hire period starts from the day you collect it, so the booking would run from 11 June.
Fine, then put 11 June. I don't mind paying for the extra day.
And how long do you think you'll be out?

I'd say two weeks, so fourteen days. But it's the sort of walk where the weather decides, and I'd rather not be charged extra because I'm a day late. So let's say sixteen, to be safe. Can you do 16 days?

Of course. Sixteen days it is. Now, there are two kinds of messenger. The standard one costs £4.50 a day, and it sends your messages and has the emergency button. The other has live tracking as well, so people at home can follow your route on a map. That one is £6.50 a day.
My sister wants to watch my progress, otherwise she'll worry herself sick. So I'd better have the tracking one.
Then it's £6.50 a day. The deposit is £100 for the standard model, but £150 for the tracking one. We take it as a hold on your card, and it's released when you bring the device back undamaged.
That's fine. Is the battery going to last? I'll be out for more than two weeks, and there won't be many plugs on the way.

With tracking on and a position sent every ten minutes, it lasts about two weeks, so it's worth turning that interval down to half an hour. Most people don't need a spare battery pack. What a lot of them do take is a waterproof case. The device is rated for rain, but not for being dropped in a river, and it only costs a pound a day.
Then I'll take the waterproof case, please. I'm terrible at keeping things dry.

Added to the form. Now, one important thing. When you press the emergency button, the message goes to a rescue centre, and they will try to contact somebody on your behalf. Who should we list as your emergency contact?
It's my sister, the one who'll be watching the map. Alison Reid. Her surname's different from mine, because she's my half-sister. That's A-L-I-S-O-N.
Alison Reid. And does she have a mobile number we could put down?
I'd have to look. Can I email it to you this afternoon?
Yes, that's fine. The address is on the confirmation message. Last of all, which branch would suit you best for the collection? We have shops in Fort William, Callander and Oban.

Fort William, I suppose, since that's where I'm starting. Oh, but no. The sleeper gets in early, and you won't be open until nine, and I want to be on the trail well before that. And I'll be collecting the day before anyway. I live near Stirling, so Callander would be much easier.
Callander it is, then. We're open until six on the eleventh, so there's no hurry. I'll send the confirmation to your email in a few minutes, and if you reply with Alison's number, you'll be all set.
Brilliant. And the device works out in the middle of nowhere?

It does. It talks to satellites rather than mobile masts. It uses the Iridium network, which has satellites right across the globe, so you'll get a signal on the wildest bit of the route. Just try to give it a clear view of the sky when you send a message. Trees and steep valley sides can block the signal.
Good to know. Thanks so much, Tessa. You've been really helpful.
My pleasure. Enjoy the walk, and don't forget to send us a postcard from the lighthouse.

Morning, all. Hats on, if you've brought them, because there isn't much shelter out in the fields. And mind the step down into the yard, it's slippery after last night's rain. My name's Moira, and I'll be showing you round Kestrel Fold Farm this morning. The tour takes about two hours, so we should be back at the tea tent by half past eleven. Actually, I've just been told that the soup is arriving late, so let's say twelve o'clock. Anyone who needs to leave earlier, just tell me.

This farm is three hundred hectares, and it's run by two people and a lot of technology. Many of you have asked what the technology actually is, so let's start with the obvious one. You can see the tractor by the barn. Look at the screen in the cab. That tractor drives itself in straight lines across a field. The driver only has to turn it round at the end of each row. It does that by using satellite positioning, the same system your phone uses to find the nearest café.

Now, you might think a tractor can manage perfectly well in straight lines without help, and you'd be right, up to a point. But a person steering by eye is out by perhaps twenty centimetres on each pass. Ours is out by about two centimetres. That sounds trivial, but over a whole season it means we don't overlap rows, we don't waste seed, and we don't leave gaps that grow weeds. To get that accuracy, we need a fixed base station that corrects the signal. It's the white mast just behind the grain store, and you'll see it in a few minutes.

The second use of satellites is less obvious, and it's the one I find more exciting. Every few days, a European satellite photographs this entire farm from space. We download the pictures for free, and a computer program turns them into a colour map showing how healthy the crop is in each part of the field. Where the colour is pale, the plants are struggling. We then walk out to look, and about nine times out of ten there's a simple reason, such as a drainage problem.

That brings me to what the farm has gained. People assume the main saving is fuel, and that's true, we do use less diesel. But the real change has been fertiliser. Because we can see which parts of a field need it, we spread it only there. Since we started, we buy roughly a tenth less every year. That's good for the bank balance, and it's good for the river downstream, because less of it washes off the land.

Some of you have been asking whether you'd need expensive equipment to do something similar on your own land. You wouldn't. The satellite pictures are free for anyone. You don't pay the cooperative, and you don't need to ask the council. You simply go to the Copernicus browser on the internet, type in the name of your village, and there is your field. It takes about ten minutes to learn, and there's a leaflet in the tea tent that explains how.

Now, I'll describe the layout of the farm, because we'll be splitting into two groups later, and I want you to know where everything is. As you can see on the plan in your leaflet, the main gate is at the bottom of the map, next to the car park. The farmhouse is to the right of the gate, and the barn is straight ahead. The first thing we'll visit is the weather station. It isn't near the buildings, as you might expect. It's on the hill above the farmhouse, because the wind there is a fair test of what the crops get. We measure rain, temperature and wind speed, and the readings go on the farm's computer every ten minutes.

As I said, the base station is behind the grain store. From there, we'll walk down the lane towards the demonstration plots. There are six small plots at the end of the lane, planted with different crops, so you can compare what the satellite pictures show with what's actually growing. It's the best way to understand them. We'll spend some time there.

Next to the orchard, between it and the barn, there's a flat area of mown grass. That's where we launch the drone.
