The drone gives us much sharper pictures than the satellites, but it only covers a small area, so we use it just on problem spots. Please keep well back when it's flying. If anything goes wrong, we'll ask you to stay behind the white line, which is painted on the grass.

Finally, the refreshments. The tea tent is beside the pond, at the far side of the orchard. In summer we get ducks, and this morning there are a few. Please don't feed them. If you are hungry earlier, there are biscuits on the table by the barn door.

Last of all, a word about safety. The farm is a working place, and there are vehicles moving about, so stay together, keep to the marked paths, and please keep your children close. There are no toilets on the tour route, so do use the ones in the car park before we leave. And if you have any questions, ask them as we go along. I'd much rather be interrupted than talk for two hours to people who have lost the thread. Shall we begin? Follow me, and mind that puddle by the gate.

Right, you two, shut the door behind you, would you? Nina, Callum, take a seat. I've had a look at your slides for the flood mapping project, and I'd like to hear how it's been going before I say anything.

Well, it's gone better than we expected, mainly because we changed the plan halfway through. We originally wanted to use ordinary satellite photographs of the Lincolnshire fens during the flood in January.
But the whole area was under thick cloud for nearly two weeks. The pictures just showed white. We couldn't see the water at all.
Yes, that's the classic problem with optical images. So what did you do?
We switched to radar. Callum found out that the European radar satellite can see through cloud, and it works at night too.

That's right. The only trouble was that radar pictures are harder to read. Flood water looks dark, almost black, because the smooth surface bounces the signal away from the satellite. But I had a problem with it at first. On one of the days, the wind was strong, and the water was rough, so some flooded fields looked bright, like dry land.
That's a well-known problem. How did you deal with it?

We compared that image with the one from three days earlier. If a field is dark in one picture and bright in another, it suggests flooding, even when the wind is a nuisance. It wasn't perfect, but it was convincing.
Good. But how do you know your flood map is right? You're relying on a computer's guess.
We haven't checked it properly yet. I thought we could ask a few farmers whether the fields flooded where we say they did.

That's a nice idea, but it's very slow, and people's memories are not reliable. What I'd do is compare your map with the river gauge records. The Environment Agency publishes the water levels for every station, every fifteen minutes. If your map shows flooding at the same time as the gauge peaks, you have strong evidence.
That makes sense. We'll download those tonight.
And label every gauge you use on the map, with its name and the date of the reading. Nothing annoys an examiner more than an unlabelled dot, except possibly a map with no scale.
We learned that the hard way in the last assignment. We lost marks because we forgot the scale bar and the north arrow.
Quite. Scale bar, north arrow and a legend, please, on every map, even the small ones.
Now, what about the limits of the method? Every method has them, and examiners like to see that you know yours.
The pixels are ten metres wide, so we can't see small ditches or a single flooded garden. And the satellite passes over only every six days or so, so we may have missed the worst moment.
We could also mention that the radar can't see flooding under tall trees or in towns, because buildings confuse the signal.

Include all three. Examiners like to see that you understand the weaknesses of your own method, and it makes the rest of your claims more believable. Now, before we talk about the structure, is there anything you want to add to the presentation? You have a little room.
Should we include a time-lapse animation of the flood spreading? We've got the images for it, and it looks rather dramatic.
I think so, yes. It takes thirty seconds and it's what people will remember. Anything you'd add, Callum?

A list of the data sources at the end, so that people can find the images themselves. We used the free software from the European Space Agency, and it took us a whole weekend to learn, so I'd like to save other people the trouble.

Yes, do that as well, and put the dates of every image in it, so that somebody else could repeat your work. That matters more than it sounds. I wouldn't bother with a table of costs. There's nothing to pay for, and it would only distract from the main point.
Right. That's easy enough.

Now, the structure. Your introduction is clear, but it's too long. There's a whole slide about the history of satellites, which is interesting, but it's not what the assessment is about, and it takes up a fifth of your time for no marks. Be ruthless.
I like that slide, though.
I know you do. Your method section, by contrast, is a bit thin. You jump from the satellite straight to the map. Explain how the radar works, but briefly, say, on one slide.
We'll add a simple diagram showing the signal bouncing off water and off land.

Good idea. And then the results. The flood map is excellent. I'd put the two images side by side, before and after, so the audience sees the change at once. Don't put the figures on the same slide, because it will look crowded. The conclusion is where I'm less convinced. At the moment you just say that radar is useful. I'd like to see you say who would use this, such as councils or insurance companies.
We could mention that insurers already use it to check claims.

Exactly. That's what makes it relevant to everyday life, which is the theme of the module. One more point about delivery. You have twelve minutes, and at the moment you'd need about seventeen. Practise with a timer, and decide now who says what. Last year two students argued about it on the day.
I'll do the introduction and the method, if Callum takes the results.
And we'll share the conclusion. Fine by me.
Sensible. Send me the revised slides on Friday, and I'll give you written comments over the weekend.

Here is a simple claim to start with. You have almost certainly used a satellite today, and you probably didn't notice. Perhaps you checked the weather, or you paid for a coffee with a card, or you asked your phone for directions. In each case, the information came from space, from machines that you will never see and that most of us never think about. Today I want to look at four everyday uses of satellite data, and I'll start with the one most of us take for granted, which is navigation.

The American GPS system has about thirty satellites in orbit, and they circle the Earth at a height of about 20,200 kilometres. Each one broadcasts a signal that says where it is and exactly what time it is. Your phone listens to several of them and works out how long each signal took to arrive. To fix your position, a receiver needs signals from at least four satellites. You might expect three would be enough, because we live in three dimensions, but the fourth is needed to correct the clock in your phone, which isn't nearly accurate enough.

That brings me to something that surprises many people. The most valuable thing GPS gives us isn't location. It's time. The atomic clocks on the satellites are so precise that mobile phone networks use them to keep their masts in step. Without that accurate timing, calls would be dropped as you moved from one mast to the next. Banks use the same signal to put a timestamp on every transaction, so that millions of payments can be put into the right order. If the signal disappeared, a good deal of everyday life would stop.

Now let's move to the weather. There are two main kinds of weather satellite. The first kind is geostationary. These sit about 36,000 kilometres up, directly above the equator, and because they orbit at the same speed as the Earth turns, they appear to hover over a single spot. So they can watch a storm continuously and send a new picture every ten minutes or so. The second kind is the polar-orbiting satellite. These are much lower, at around 800 kilometres, and they travel from pole to pole while the Earth turns beneath them. They see the whole planet, and each place is covered roughly twice a day. Forecasters need both. The first gives a quick view, and the second gives much more detail, including the temperature of the air at different heights.

The third use is the one that has changed most in my own lifetime, and that is watching the land. The Landsat programme began in 1972, which makes it the longest continuous record of the Earth's surface. For decades, the images were expensive, and few people used them. In 2008, the American government made them free, and the number of users went up enormously. Then, in 2015, the European Space Agency launched the first of its Sentinel-2 satellites. Its pictures are sharp enough to show features 10 metres across, and with two satellites working together, the same place is photographed every five days. You can see a field, a new road, or a forest being cleared.

Farmers were among the first to realise what this meant. By measuring how much red and infrared light plants reflect, a farmer can see whether a crop is healthy before the human eye can. A field that is short of nitrogen will look paler in the infrared picture weeks before the leaves turn yellow. That gives time to act, and it means fertiliser can be spread only where it's needed. Governments use the same pictures to check subsidy claims, so inspectors don't have to visit every farm.

There's also a quieter use that I find rather charming, and that is tracking ships. Most large vessels carry a transponder that broadcasts their identity, position and speed. Satellites pick up those signals even in the middle of an ocean, where no land station could hear them. A port can then tell exactly when a cargo ship will arrive and organise its cranes accordingly, and coastguards can notice a fishing boat that switches off its transponder in a protected area. Much of what you buy has crossed the sea under the eyes of such a system.

The fourth use is disaster response, and here I want to mention a different kind of satellite. Optical cameras, like the ones I've just described, are blinded by clouds. But floods tend to happen under cloud. Radar satellites solve the problem, because radar passes straight through cloud, rain and even smoke, and it works at night. Flood water is smooth, so it reflects the radar signal away and looks dark on the image. Within hours of a flood, emergency teams can have a map showing which roads are under water and which villages are cut off.

I should add a word of caution before I finish. Satellite data is powerful, but it isn't magic. Resolution is limited, clouds still hide the ground from optical cameras, and a picture has to be interpreted by someone who knows what to look for. But the main lesson is how much we now depend on these systems without thinking about them. In the next lecture, I'll look at who owns them, and what happens when they stop working.
Bluegum Code Club holiday programme. You've come through to Dana on the enrolments desk.

Oh, thank goodness, a real person. I've tried your website three times this morning, and it keeps asking me to prove that I'm not a robot. I clicked on every picture of a bicycle I could find, and it still wasn't satisfied.
I'm so sorry about that. We're having trouble with the new security check, and I've told them it's driving parents mad. Never mind, I can book her in over the phone. Is it a daughter or a son?
A daughter. Her name's Matilda, and I'd like to put her in for the July holidays, if there are any places left.
There are, but they're going quickly. Let me bring up the form. What's your surname, please?
It's Lindgren. That's L-I-N-D-G-R-E-N. People always want to put an A in the middle, so I've learned to say it slowly.
No, that's fine, I've got it. And Matilda is spelled the usual way, with a T and a D?
Yes. M-A-T-I-L-D-A. Not Matilda with a different spelling, just the ordinary one.
Lovely. How old is she? We have two groups, one for seven to nine and the other for ten and over.
She's 9. She turns 10 in October, so I suppose that means she's in the younger group, although she thinks she's much older.
She'll go in the younger group, then, and I promise she won't be bored. We have robot building, game design and a web design week. Which would she like?
She told me she wants to make a computer game, with a hero who is a dog. I think she'd also love the robots, but the game is the one she keeps talking about.
Then game design it is. It runs the week starting 14 July, from Monday to Friday. Would that suit you?
That's perfect. I have a conference that week, so I'm glad it's a full five days. What time do the sessions begin?
Classes start at nine, but you can drop her off from a quarter to nine, so that's 8.45, and there are staff in the hall from then. Pick-up is at three.
Quarter to nine is excellent. I'll be able to get to work before ten.

Now, the fee for the week is $340 normally. We give a discount if you book before the end of the month, and it takes $20 off, so you'd pay $320. Lunch isn't included, but there's a fridge, and you can store her lunchbox there.
That's a bargain. Does the price include the laptop?

Yes, we provide the laptops, and the children don't have to bring any equipment from home. They can't take anything online while they're here, either, apart from the programs we've set up. It's a closed network, so that all the children are safe.
I like that. I worry about what she sees online. At the moment she's only allowed on one app, and I check it every evening.
A lot of parents tell me that. On the form there's a section about health. Does Matilda have any allergies we should know about?

Yes, she's allergic to peanuts. It's quite serious, and she has an injector, which she carries in her bag. She used to be allergic to eggs too, but the doctor says she's grown out of that, so you needn't worry about eggs.
Good. I'll put peanuts only. Our staff are trained to use the injector, and I'll make a note on her file. Now, who will be collecting her at the end of the day?
It'll be her grandfather for most days. He lives round the corner from the hall. I might pick her up myself on Friday, but I'll let you know.
That's fine. I'll put her grandfather as the usual person, and we'll ask him for identification on the first day, just as a precaution. He needn't worry, it's just our rule.
He'll be thrilled to have a job to do. He'll probably dress up.
Last of all, I need your postcode, so that we can post the confirmation and the receipt.
It's 3056. We're in Brunswick.

Thank you. I'll send everything this afternoon, and you should get an email as well, with a link to a short video for Matilda. It shows the club's rules and some of last year's games. She might like to see what she's in for.
She'll love that. And you won't ask me to prove I'm not a robot?
Not unless you want the link to the video. Thank you for ringing, Mr Lindgren, and enjoy the rest of your day.

Thanks for waiting, everyone. I know you've come in out of the rain for the toddler session, and I'm going to borrow just five minutes of your time. I'm Yasmin, the community librarian here at Northfield, and I want to tell you about a programme that starts in February.

Every year, on the second Tuesday of February, schools and libraries all over the world mark Safer Internet Day. This year, we've decided to do more than put up a poster. We're running a whole week of events. And the reason isn't a new law or a visit from an inspector. It's that so many of you have stopped me at the desk and asked, quietly, what you're supposed to do when your child is online and you don't understand what they're doing. We heard you, and this is our answer.

The first event is a workshop for children. It's for eight to eleven-year-olds. We did think about opening it to seven-year-olds as well, but the activities involve reading some quite long instructions, so it didn't seem fair on the younger ones. We'll look at how to spot an unsafe message, what to do when something online upsets you, and how to talk to a grown-up about it. Families are asked to bring a device that the child already uses at home. It might be a tablet, it might be a phone, it might be a games console. You don't need to bring a library card or sign anything. Just make sure the battery is charged, because we've only got a few sockets.

Now, the second event is for parents and carers, and it takes place in the evening, on Wednesday. People always assume we'll spend the time teaching you how to read your children's private messages, and I should say straight away that we won't. We think trust matters more than spying. There are two things we will cover. The first is how to set up parental controls on the most common devices and apps, step by step, and you'll practise on your own phone. The second is how to report a problem, for instance, when someone has been unkind to your child, or when you find something that shouldn't be there. Every app has a way of doing that, and most of them hide it, so we'll show you where to look. We won't be covering passwords this time, as we did that last spring, and we won't be looking at privacy policies, because, to be honest, they're written by lawyers for lawyers.

Now I'd like to explain where everything is happening, because the building is a bit of a maze, and last year somebody got lost on the way to the first aid course and ended up in the staff kitchen. The parents' evening will be in the meeting room upstairs. The lift is by the front desk, and there are signs. There will be a member of staff at the bottom of the stairs, so you can't go wrong.

On Thursday afternoon, there's a drop-in session for teenagers. It's a relaxed hour where young people can ask us anything about privacy, social media or gaming. Because we want it to feel like a normal place to hang out, it will be in the computer suite, where the teenagers already come after school. We won't push them, and nobody will be made to talk.

For younger children, we're running a puzzle trail throughout the week. The children collect clues from the bookshelves and solve a puzzle about keeping safe online, and the answers are hidden in the books. It starts in the children's section, right at the back, near the beanbags, and they can take part at any time while the library is open. There's a small prize at the end.

As you come in or leave during the week, you'll see an advice stall in the foyer, next to the noticeboard. There will be leaflets in six languages, and people from the local school and from the police who can answer questions. You don't need to book. It's open all day Tuesday, and then for two hours each afternoon.

Finally, on Friday, we're having a little presentation at the end of the week, where children who finished the puzzle trail will receive a certificate. We were hoping to hold that in the reading garden, because it's lovely out there, but of course it's February, and it's freezing, so we've decided to hold it in the community room at the back of the café. Never mind, it's warmer and there will be hot chocolate.

If you'd like to sign up for the workshop or the parents' evening, there's a sheet on the desk by the door. You don't need to put down your child's name, just the number of people. Thank you for listening, and I hope to see you all in February. Now, back to the rhymes. I can hear that someone is getting impatient.

Zoe, Rishi, perfect timing. The kettle's just boiled, so help yourselves if you'd like tea. I've been looking forward to this, because your design for the children's reading app is one of the more interesting ideas I've seen this term. Zoe, remind me what the app does.

It's called Pip's Library. Children between six and ten read short stories, and they collect stars and little animal stickers when they finish. Our main question was how to make it fun without making it risky.
And that's where the argument started, because the original plan had a lot of features that, looking back, weren't very safe.
Let's go through them. I have your list here. What did you decide about the chat feature? I remember you wanted children to be able to message each other about the books.

We spent a long time on that. Rishi wanted to remove it altogether, but I thought children enjoy talking about what they've read. In the end, we kept a form of chat, but only with fixed phrases, like "I loved this one" or "What happens next?" Children choose from a list, so they can't type anything and nobody can send an unkind message.
That's a good compromise. And the streak counter? The one that tells you how many days in a row you've read.
We took that out. We read about how some apps use streaks to make children feel guilty if they miss a day, and I didn't want a six-year-old crying because she'd lost a streak.
Good. I'd have asked you to drop it anyway. What about the sign-up screen? I noticed you asked for the child's birthday.

Yes, we had a box for the full date of birth. Then we realised we only need to know roughly how old the child is, so we've changed it to an age band, such as six to seven or eight to ten. That way we hold much less information.
That's exactly the principle of data minimisation. Collect only what you need. And the location feature?
That was going to suggest local libraries. We kept it, but it's switched off by default. A parent has to turn it on.
Excellent. And last, the certificates that children can share with their friends.
We kept those too, but a parent has to approve each one before it's shared. I think it's a bit annoying for parents, but it feels right.
One thing I'd press you on. Isn't there a risk that parents will simply tap approve without reading anything, after the fifth or sixth request?

Probably, yes. We thought about sending a weekly summary instead, but Rishi felt that a parent would lose track of what was being shared. So we've decided to keep the approval for each item in the first version, and to review it after a pilot.
That's honest, and it's the right order of events. Mention the pilot in your report.
Right. I'd like to ask about the testing. How did you find out what children really think of the design?
We made a paper version of the screens and took it to a primary school for an afternoon. Twelve children tried it, aged between seven and nine.
And did you get consent from the parents before you went in?
Yes, the school handled that. Every child had a signed form, and we didn't record any names, just numbers on the notes.

And they surprised us. We'd assumed that the stars would be the main attraction, but most of them preferred the stickers. And, oh, one little boy tapped the help button on every screen, just to see what it did.
That tells you something. Was there anything the children found confusing?

The sign-up screen, actually. We had a long paragraph explaining the privacy rules, and none of them read it. One of them said it looked like homework. So we've replaced it with a short picture story, which they understood immediately.
That's very good. Children's design needs to be tested with children, not just with adults imagining what children do. Now, I want to talk about the report. What will you cover in it?
We'd like to discuss the sign-up problem, because it was our most useful finding. And we'll have a section about how the app makes money, because that's one of the big questions with children's apps.
How will it earn money?
A monthly subscription paid by a parent. No advertising and no in-app purchases. That's a real commercial risk, because most free apps rely on advertising.
Which is exactly why the report should explain it. I'd hope you'd also write about age checks, but that's a very large topic, and I don't think you'll have room.
We thought so too. We'll mention it in the last paragraph, but we won't go into detail.
Sensible. What about the costs of running the servers, the technical side?
We'd leave that out. It's interesting, but it isn't about child safety.
Agreed. One last thing. Is there any issue you two disagreed about and haven't resolved?
Whether parents should be able to see what their child has read. I think they should, but Rishi thinks it's a kind of surveillance.
I'd say it's a matter of trust. A child should be able to read a story in peace.
Then put the disagreement in your report. It shows that you've thought about it properly, and that's worth far more than a neat answer. Right, send me a draft by the end of the month.

I'd like to start with a small thought experiment. Imagine you've designed a game for adults, and a nine-year-old downloads it. What happens? In the early years of the app stores, the honest answer was that nobody knew, and, more worryingly, nobody had planned for it. Today's lecture is about how that has started to change, and what it means to design an app that is safe for children from the very start.

Let me begin with the law, because it shapes everything else. In the United States, the Children's Online Privacy Protection Act, known as COPPA, has applied since the year 2000. It protects children under 13, and it means that a company must get a parent's permission before collecting personal data from a young child. In the United Kingdom, the approach is a little different. The Children's Code came into force in 2021, and it contains fifteen standards that apply to any online service likely to be used by children. It doesn't say what an app must look like. It says that the best interests of the child must come first.

To understand what safe design means, it helps to know what we are protecting children from. Researchers often group the risks into four categories, which they call the four Cs. The first is content, meaning harmful or unsuitable material. The second is contact, which means harmful interactions with other people, including adults who pretend to be children. The third is conduct, which describes the behaviour of children themselves, such as bullying. And the fourth is contract, which concerns the terms on which a child uses a service. That includes hidden costs, unfair terms, and, most commonly, pressure to make in-app purchases that a child doesn't understand.

Now, what do designers actually do about these risks? Let me give you three principles. The first is about defaults. Most people never change the settings of an app. So if the default is weak, nearly every user will end up with weak protection. For children, the default setting should be high privacy. Profiles should be private, and no stranger should be able to contact a child unless a parent has chosen to allow it. The Children's Code goes further, and says that location sharing should be switched off unless there is a very good reason for turning it on.

The second principle concerns what we call nudges. You will all have used an app that tries to keep you scrolling, or that sends you a reminder when you haven't opened it for a day. Those techniques work on adults, and they work even better on children. One of the most common examples is the streak, a counter showing how many days you have played in a row. For an adult, it's a mild encouragement. For a young child, it can feel like a duty, and losing a streak can feel like failure. A safer design drops features like these, or at least doesn't use them to keep a child on the screen for longer than they want to be.

The third principle is to collect as little data as possible. Every piece of information that an app holds is a piece that could be lost, stolen or misused. A children's app rarely needs a full name, a home address or an exact birthday. An age band is usually enough. This idea is called data minimisation, and it is one of the simplest and most effective safeguards.

So far, I've talked about what designers should do. But there's an important question about how they should find out what's needed, and here I want to mention a method that has become popular. It's called co-design. Instead of designing for children and then testing the result, the team invites children to take part in the design from the start. They draw, they sketch, they tell you what they find confusing. This is hard work, and it takes time, but it avoids assumptions. Adults are often surprised by what children notice, and what they ignore. Long explanations, in particular, are almost never read.

Another practical point concerns reporting. Even in the best design, something will occasionally go wrong, and a child needs a way to say so. The most important rule is that the reporting button must be easy to find, and, ideally, no more than two taps away from any screen. If it's buried in a menu, children won't use it, and neither will their parents. When a report is made, the app should respond quickly and in simple language, so the child knows that someone has listened.

Finally, safety isn't something you achieve once and then forget. Every software update can change how a feature works, and sometimes a harmless change in one place opens a risk in another. Responsible teams therefore review their safety measures after every update, and they keep records of what they decided and why. That's useful, because if a regulator asks, they have an answer.

To summarise: the law now expects designers to think about children from the very beginning. The four Cs give us a way to classify risk, and a handful of principles, strong defaults, no manipulative nudges, minimal data, children as co-designers, and easy reporting, give us a way to respond. None of these is difficult or expensive. What they require is the habit of asking, at every stage, what this will mean for a child. Next week we'll look at the harder question of how an app can tell how old its users are.

Hello, am I speaking to the volunteer office? A neighbour of mine told me to phone about the patient escort scheme, and I've been holding on for what feels like ten minutes, so I wasn't sure whether anyone was there.
You've found us, and I'm sorry about the wait. It's Ruth Penfold here, I look after the volunteers at Kereru Bay Hospital. Are you thinking of joining us?
I am, yes. I retired in the spring, and I've discovered that I'm hopeless at doing nothing. My wife says I've reorganised the garage three times.
That's how most of our volunteers begin. Let me open the registration form and take a few details. May I have your surname?
It's Aldridge. A-L-D-R-I-D-G-E.
Aldridge, thank you. And a number we can reach you on?
My mobile is 021 555 0147.
021 555 0147. Got it. Now, you said you'd retired. What was your job, if you don't mind my asking? We like to know, because it helps us decide where to place people.

I drove trucks for the first twenty years, delivering food around the Waikato. Then I got tired of the early mornings, and I spent the last fifteen years as a bus driver. So I'd say bus driver, really, because that's what I did for longest.

A bus driver. Wonderful. You'll be good with people, then, and you know how to be patient. Now, which days would you be free? Most of our volunteers do a half day. We have shifts on Monday, Tuesday, Thursday and Friday.
I'm free on Tuesdays. And I could do Fridays, but actually, no, I look after my grandson on Fridays, so I'd better say Thursday instead.

Tuesday and Thursday, then. And what sort of work would suit you? There's the information desk in the main entrance, there's the ward visiting scheme, where you chat to patients who don't get many visitors, and there's the escort service, where you take patients to appointments in a wheelchair.
The desk sounds a bit too still for me. And I think visiting needs a particular talent that I'm not sure I've got. I'd rather be moving. So it's the wheelchair escort for me.

That's a good choice. We're short of escorts. All new volunteers have to attend a training session, and the next one is on 18 March. It takes the whole morning, and you'll learn how to handle a wheelchair safely, how to use the lifts, and what to do if a patient feels unwell.
The eighteenth of March is fine. I'll put it in the calendar.
Excellent. You'll be given a polo shirt, which you'll wear on duty, so that patients can recognise you. Which size do you take? Are you large?
I used to be large, but I've lost a bit of weight with all the walking since I retired, so you'd better put medium.

Medium, then. Now, one thing we have to do for every volunteer is a police check. That's a legal requirement, because you'll be near vulnerable people. The form asks for proof of your address, so please bring a recent bill or a bank statement to the training day. A driver's licence isn't enough on its own, I'm afraid, because the address on it may be out of date.
No trouble. I have plenty of bills, unfortunately.
And do you drive to the hospital, or would you take the bus?
I'd drive. Where would I park?

Volunteers can park free at the north entrance, in the car park beside the garden. The main car park is for patients and visitors, and it fills up quickly, so please don't use it. You'll be given a permit to put on the dashboard at the training session.
That's very generous. Thank you.
Last of all, we need the name of someone who can give you a reference. It doesn't have to be a friend, and in fact I'd prefer it wasn't. Is there someone from your working life?
My old manager at the bus depot, Gareth Dunn. He's known me for fifteen years, and he'll say something nice, I hope, if he's in a good mood.
I'm sure he will. I'll write to him today. Thank you so much, Mr Aldridge. You'll receive a letter in the post this week, with all the details, and I look forward to meeting you on the eighteenth.

Thank you, Ruth. I'm quite looking forward to it, actually. It's good to have a purpose again. My wife says she'll finally get her garage back, although I suspect she'll miss having someone to complain about.
I'm sure she'll cope. Goodbye for now, and thank you again for calling.

Gather round, everybody, if you can, and keep away from the doors. If you'd all stand near the bottom of the stairs, we'll make a start. I'm Wilf, and I'm one of the porters here at St Aldric's Hospital. It's my job this morning to take you round on the open day tour, and I should say at the start that I've done this job for twenty-two years, and I've never had to share it with a robot until last winter.

Now, a few practical points before we set off. The tours start every half hour from the main desk, and the first one leaves at 10.30. Mine is the third, so you've plenty of time to have a cup of tea. Each tour lasts forty minutes, which is long enough to see everything but short enough that nobody's feet give out. Please wear one of the blue lanyards from the table. They show security staff that you're a visitor, and without one you won't get through the doors on the second floor.

A word about children. We're delighted to see you've brought them, and there's a drawing table for them near the entrance. But anyone under twelve may not go into the laboratories, for safety reasons, and I know that's disappointing for some. Photographs are welcome, as long as you don't show the faces of patients or staff. The one place where we ask you to put your phones away altogether is the pharmacy, because the records on the screens there are confidential.

Now, you've come to see the robots, so let me tell you about them. We have six at present. They're about the size of a large filing cabinet, and they run on wheels. They carry meals, laundry, medicines and waste between departments, mostly at night, when the corridors are quiet. At first, many of my colleagues thought they'd lose their jobs, but in fact, we've been moved to work that needs a human being, like moving patients and helping in the emergency department.

As you can see on the plan in your programme, the hospital is arranged around a central atrium. The main lift is at the north end. Our first stop is the robot charging station, which is opposite the café. That's where the six robots rest when they aren't working. Each has its own bay, a bit like a parking space, and you'll see a light on the front that goes from red to green when it is fully charged. The children generally like that bit.

From there, we'll go along the east corridor, and at the end of it there's the loading bay, where deliveries arrive from outside. The robots take the boxes of supplies from there to the wards. If we're lucky, you'll see one setting off. They have a little tune that they play when they're about to move, so that people know they're coming.

Then we come to the pharmacy. It's behind the reception desk, just past the information stand. You can look through a glass window and watch the dispensing robot at work. It picks out the boxes of tablets from the shelves, and it never gets confused. Pharmacists check every item afterwards, so there's a person and a machine looking at every prescription. Please remember, no photographs in there.

Next to the pharmacy, there's a small room where the hospital's own engineers work. We call it the workshop, and it's where the robots are repaired. You can't go in, but you can see through the door. Beyond that, beneath the stairs in the atrium, is the first aid post, which is staffed all day by volunteers from the ambulance service. If one of the children falls over, that's where to go.

Finally, I want to mention a demonstration. At eleven o'clock, we'll show how a robot delivers a meal to a ward. It will be in the corridor beside the main lift. A nurse will place a tray in the robot's cupboard, and it'll set off on its own. When it arrives, the nurse on the ward will type in a code, and the door opens. People find that the best part of the day.

I'd also like to thank our sponsors, who've paid for the robots, and I should apologise in advance. The robots are slow. They travel at a walking pace, and they stop if anyone steps in front of them. If you try to race one down the corridor, you'll lose, because it will politely wait for you. Anyone who needs a seat or has difficulty with stairs, please tell me now, because every route on the tour can also be done by lift, and I'd rather arrange it than have you struggle. Right, if everyone has a lanyard, and I can see that most of you do, we'll start with the charging station. Follow me, and please keep to the left.
Aidan, Sophie, thanks for being so punctual. Take a seat. I've read your proposal for the case study of robot deliveries at Westmoor Hospital, and I'd like to hear where you've got to.
Well, we spent the first week visiting the hospital and speaking to the managers. We wanted to start by understanding why they bought the robots in the first place.

And there were two reasons, in the end. Everyone told us that deliveries to the wards had been late for years, especially meals and laundry, and the hospital was getting complaints. The other reason was that the porters were having back injuries, because they were lifting heavy loads all day.
We had expected it to be about saving money, or a shortage of staff, but the managers said neither was the reason. In fact, they've hired just as many porters as before.
Did the managers say who chose the supplier, and whether the staff were consulted at all?
The managers chose, but they held two meetings with the porters before signing anything. A union representative came to both.
Which, according to the porters, is why nobody made a fuss when the robots arrived.
Interesting. That's the sort of detail that makes a case study worth reading. How did you collect your data on the deliveries?

We had two sources. The robots keep a log of every journey, with the time of departure and arrival. We were going to time the porters with a stopwatch as well, to compare them, but the hospital wouldn't allow it, because it felt like surveillance.
So we used the porters' own records instead. They fill in a sheet at the end of each shift. It isn't as precise, but it's something.
That's an important limitation, and you should state it plainly in the report. What have you found so far?

The surprising thing is that the robots aren't any quicker than the porters. In fact, they're slightly slower, because they travel at a walking pace and wait for lifts. But they're much more reliable. They don't stop for tea, and they don't forget a delivery, so meals now arrive within five minutes of the planned time almost every day.
So it's reliability rather than speed. That's a good point, and you should make it the centre of your argument. Now, you also wrote that you'd survey the staff. How's that going?
We sent a questionnaire to about two hundred people, and sixty-three answered. That's less than a third, which is lower than we hoped.

It's a typical response rate for a hospital, where people are very busy. But it does mean you shouldn't claim that the results represent everybody. I'd suggest that you add a few short interviews, to give some depth to the numbers.
We'd already thought of that. We have an appointment with a porter on Thursday.
Do you have ethical approval for that? Your questionnaire was anonymous, but an interview is different.
Yes, the department signed it off last month. We'll ask for written consent and we won't use his name, only the word porter.
Good. Record him only if he agrees, and offer to let him read what you write about him afterwards.
Good. Now, tell me what the different groups said about the robots. Start with the porters.

Most of the porters were positive, more than we expected. They said that the robots have taken over the boring night work, and that they now spend more time with patients. Though a couple of them said they missed the chats they used to have in the corridors.

The nurses were the most enthusiastic. They said the biggest benefit was that they no longer had to leave the ward to fetch supplies. But, and this was interesting, some nurses said the robots were a nuisance in crowded corridors, because they block the way.

The pharmacists were the most cautious. They liked the dispensing robot, because it reduces mistakes, but they insisted on checking everything by hand afterwards. They said they simply wouldn't trust a machine alone with medicines.
And patients, well, we didn't have time to ask them properly, but the few we spoke to were delighted. They'd given the robots names, and a couple of children had drawn pictures of them.

That's delightful, but be careful. A drawing isn't data. I'd mention it as an observation, not as a finding. Now, the one thing I'm slightly concerned about is your timetable. You have three weeks. What have you left to do?
The interviews, the final analysis, and the writing, which is the biggest job.
Then I'd suggest that you write as you go along, rather than leaving it all till the end. Send me a draft of the first half by next Friday, and we'll meet to go through it. Is that realistic?
It is. I think we've both been putting off the writing, so having a deadline will help.

One more practical point. Keep a list of your references as you go, with the date you read each one. Last year a pair of students spent a whole weekend trying to find a website they had read in March.
That's us, I'm afraid. I'll start a shared document tonight.
Good. I'll look forward to it. And don't forget to ask the hospital whether they're happy for you to name them in the report, because that could be a problem later.
We'll ask them today.

When most of us think of a hospital, we think of doctors, nurses and operating theatres. We rarely think of the thousands of objects that must be in the right place at the right time to make those things possible. A large hospital moves food, linen, medicines, specimens, waste and equipment around its buildings every hour of the day. That's what we mean by logistics, and it's an area in which robots are now finding an unexpectedly useful role.

Let me begin with what hospitals did before robots. For much of the twentieth century, they relied on two systems. The first was the porter, a person who pushed a trolley from one department to another. The second was the pneumatic tube, in which small containers are carried by compressed air through pipes in the walls. Tubes are excellent for blood samples and small packages, but they can't carry a meal or a bag of laundry. So most of the heavy work was done by people, and some of that work was done by nurses who should have been at the bedside.

The first thing I want you to understand is why this matters. In a ward I visited a few years ago, a nurse told me that she spent part of every shift searching for supplies, such as dressings, syringes and bags of fluid. If a robot brings these to the ward, she can spend that time on patients. The benefit isn't dramatic in any one hour, but it adds up over a year.

So how do these robots find their way? Most of the modern machines use a laser scanner, called lidar, which measures the distance to every wall and obstacle around the robot many times a second. During the first week, the robot is driven round the building, and it builds a map. After that, it knows where it is by comparing what the scanner sees with its map. This is much more flexible than the older approach, which used magnetic strips or wires in the floor, because if a corridor is closed for repairs, the robot can simply find another route.

Hospitals are multi-storey buildings, so a robot must be able to use the lift. It doesn't push a button. The lift is connected to the robot's control system by a wireless link, so the robot can call it, and the lift tells the robot which floor it has reached. People in the lift are given priority, and the robot waits if the lift is full. Robots do not climb stairs, and they cannot open a heavy fire door, so the doors on the robots' routes have to be fitted with automatic openers. That's an expense that managers often forget.

Safety is the next consideration. A robot weighing a couple of hundred kilograms moving through a corridor full of patients could be dangerous, so its speed is limited to the pace at which people walk, and it stops if anyone steps in front of it. Some also play a little tune or flash a light, to warn people that they're moving. The sensors are so sensitive that the robot sometimes stops for a plant or a coat hanging on a door, which can be rather irritating.

There's one more advantage that is easy to overlook, and that is hygiene. Soiled linen and clinical waste travel in sealed containers, and the less they are handled by people, the smaller the chance of spreading infection. A robot's smooth surfaces can be wiped down between journeys, and it doesn't cough or forget to wash its hands. Some hospitals also use a separate kind of machine that disinfects rooms with ultraviolet light, but that's a different technology, and I'll leave it for another day.

Now, what goes wrong? The most common problem, in my experience, is the corridors. Hospital corridors are often crowded, with beds, wheelchairs and equipment parked along the walls. Robots that are designed for a clear route get stuck, and staff then have to move the obstacles. The second problem is human. When hospitals first introduced these machines, many staff were suspicious. They worried that the robots would replace them, and some deliberately blocked them. The hospitals that did best were those that involved staff early. One hospital let its staff give the robots names, and, to everyone's surprise, that made a great difference. People stopped seeing them as threats and began to treat them as colleagues, and the robots became rather popular.

And what about the benefits? Obviously, a robot can work all day, every day, including nights, when it can use quiet corridors and there are fewer people to avoid. The hospital I mentioned estimated that its robots paid for themselves in about three years, though they admitted that it was difficult to measure, because some of the benefits, such as nurses' time, can't be put into figures.

To sum up, hospital robots aren't intended to replace the people who care for patients. They're meant to do the dull, heavy and repetitive work, so that those people can do what only they can do. Their success depends less on clever engineering than on very ordinary things, such as the width of a corridor, the doors on the route, and how the staff feel about them. In the next lecture, we'll look at a different kind of hospital robot, the machines that actually assist in surgery.
Morning. I'm ringing on behalf of my book group. We'd like to book a block of tickets for the talks on the Saturday of your science festival, if they haven't all gone.
Marlowe Science Festival box office, Jamie speaking. You're in luck, we still have a fair few left for the Saturday. Are you a regular visitor?
This will be our first time. A member of our group heard a talk last year and came back so excited that the rest of us felt we had to go. We usually read novels, so it's quite a change for us.
Well, you'll enjoy it. Let me open a group booking form. Could I take the name of the person who's organising it?
That's me. The surname is Ogilvie. O-G-I-L-V-I-E. It's Scottish, but I've lived in Gloucestershire for forty years.
Ogilvie, lovely. And does your group have a name? We list the groups on the booking, and it helps us find you at the door.
We're called the Wren Lane Book Group, after the street where we first met. Wren as in the bird, and Lane as in a country lane.
Wren Lane, perfect. How many of you will be coming?
There are twelve of us at the moment. Oh, but two more said yesterday that they'd like to join us, so I'd better say fourteen. Could you make it 14 to be on the safe side?

Fourteen it is. There's a rule that groups of ten or more can book a block together, so you'll be sitting side by side. Now, which talk are you interested in? There are three on the Saturday afternoon.
The one about the weather and the air above our cities. My husband's a keen gardener, and he's always looking at the sky. It's at two o'clock, I believe.

It was due to start at two, but the speaker asked for a longer lunch, so it has moved to half past two. The programme on the website still says two, I'm afraid, because we haven't had a chance to update it.
That's very useful to know. Half past two is better for us, because several of us are coming from out of town.
I'll put 2.30 on the form. Now, prices. A standard ticket is £9, and a concession ticket for over sixty-fives and students is £6.50. How many of your party would qualify for the concession?
Let me think. I'm in my seventies, and so are most of the others. Of the fourteen, I think ten are over sixty-five, but one of them is only sixty-four. So that makes nine.

Nine concessions and five standard tickets, then. The concession price is £6.50, which is a good saving. We won't ask for proof on the day, I promise, but we might ask the odd person if they're really over sixty-five.
I'm sure they'll take that as a compliment.
Does anyone in the group need any help with access? The lecture hall has step-free entry and wheelchair spaces.
One of our members has a hearing problem, and she says that she can never make out what a speaker is saying in a big room. Is there anything that would help her?
Yes, the hall has a hearing loop. If she switches her hearing aid to the right setting, she'll be able to hear the speaker directly. We'll also keep a seat free near the front for her.
That's wonderful. She'll be delighted. Now, I wondered about lunch. Is there somewhere we could eat beforehand?
The festival café opens at noon, but it gets very busy. I could reserve a table for you if you like. Would it be for the whole group?
Not the whole group. A few of them are bringing sandwiches, and I think a couple of others are going to the pub. I'd say a table for eight.

Eight, then. I'll note that down. Now, when you've paid, we can either post the tickets, or you can collect them. Collection is from the information desk, in the main entrance of the town hall, and it opens at nine on the day.
I'd rather collect them. I never trust the post, and I don't want to find that Margaret's ticket has gone astray.
Information desk, then. And for the confirmation, I need your postcode, just to complete the form.
It's GL5 4RT.
GL5 4RT. Thank you. We'll send you an email with the payment link in the next hour, and you'll have a week to complete the payment. Is there anything else I can help with?
I don't think so. You've been very patient with me, because I know I'm rather disorganised.
Not at all. It's a pleasure to talk to a group who are coming for the first time. I hope you all enjoy the weekend.

Right, I think we're all here, so let's make a start before the rain does. Thank you for coming out on a grey Saturday morning. My name is Arjun, and I'm the coordinator of the Riverside Clean Air Walk. For anyone who hasn't done one before, the idea is simple. You walk a fixed route across the city, carrying a small sensor that measures the tiny particles in the air, and your readings are added to a map that anyone can see. Let me explain the route and what you'll be doing.

There are five stops, and the whole walk takes about two hours. At each stop, I'd like you to do one particular thing, so please listen carefully, because the jobs are different. We start here at the market square. At this stop, we stand still for two minutes and each of you simply records the sensor reading in the notebook. It's a quiet place, so this is our reference. We want to compare it with the busy places later.

From the market square, we walk north to the bridge. This is the stop where I'd like you to count. Stand by the railings and count the number of buses that cross in five minutes. Don't count cars, there are too many, and you'd lose track. Just the buses. Buses are the biggest source of fumes in the city centre, and I'd like to see whether the number of buses matches the sensor reading.

After the bridge, we go along the river path to the park gate. Here there's a different job. There's a lamp post just inside the gate, and I'd like one of you to fix a sensor to it, using the cable ties in the bag, and we'll leave it there until Monday morning. It will keep recording by itself, even when we've all gone home, and a volunteer will collect it. Ask me later if you'd like to be that person.

The fourth stop is the school crossing on Hollin Road. This one's the most interesting for me, because parents often tell me they worry about the air outside the school. While we're standing there, I'd like you to talk to any parents or teachers who are passing. There's a short list of questions on your clipboard, such as how they travel to school and whether they've noticed any smell. If nobody wants to talk, never mind. We'll try again on another day.

And the final stop is the bus station, where the walk ends. At the end, we'll have a cup of tea in the café, and I'd like you all to swap the batteries in your sensors for fresh ones, because they're then ready for the next group. There's a box of spare batteries on the counter. That's the whole route.

Now a few practical points. First, the sensor itself. You'll each be given a device about the size of a mobile phone, and you hold it at head height. That's because we want to measure what you breathe, not what a dog breathes. The most important figure on the screen is labelled PM2.5. That stands for particulate matter, smaller than two and a half micrometres, which is about thirty times thinner than a human hair. Those tiny particles can get deep into the lungs, which is why we measure them.

When should you start walking? We'll leave at ten o'clock exactly. I know that sounds strict, but the buses change their timetable at half past ten, and I'd like the first two stops to be completed before then. If you're late, you can catch us up at the bridge, which is the second stop, and the route is shown on the map in the bag.

What if the sensor beeps? That's quite normal, and it's nothing to worry about. It means that the reading is high, not that the device has broken. Just note it down, and add a comment to say what was happening around you, for instance, a lorry passing. That's actually the most useful information we get.

What about rain? Light rain is fine, and the sensors are protected against it. But if it pours, I'll stop the walk and we'll shelter in the café, and I'll tell you then whether we'll continue or not. We did abandon one walk last year because of a thunderstorm, and nobody complained.

Finally, what happens to the figures? When we've finished, I'll upload all the readings to the city's open data website. You'll be able to find them there by next Friday, and I'll send everyone an email with the link. A journalist from the local radio may also use them in a feature, but only if you agree, so please say so if you'd rather not be named. Right, if you've all collected a sensor, let's go. Mind the puddles on the way.

Priyanka, Ewan, thanks for coming in on a Friday afternoon. I'd like to hear how your project on the low-cost air sensors is going, because the last time we spoke, you hadn't yet decided where to put them.

We have now. We chose Fenwick Road, which runs past the library. The main reason was that it's only fifty metres from the council's monitoring station, so we can compare our readings directly with the official ones.
We'd looked at the park as well. But it's two kilometres from the nearest station, and the air there is so different that a comparison would have been meaningless.
And what about permission? You can't just attach equipment to a street lamp.
The library has agreed to let us fix three of the sensors to its wall, and the council has given us permission for the other three, on lamp posts. They even sent a letter.
The power was the harder part. The library lets us plug a cable into an outside socket, and the others run on batteries that we change twice a week.
Then keep a log of every battery change, because the readings can drop when a battery is low.
That's sensible. Have you started collecting data?

We've had the sensors for two weeks. I had a problem with the first batch, though. I'd assumed that they'd work straight out of the box, but one of them kept giving readings that were twice as high as the others, even when they were side by side.
It turned out the fan inside was blocked by a bit of dust. Ewan cleaned it, and it was fine.
How did you know it was the dust and not a fault in the sensor itself?
I put it next to two of the others, and it was still high. Then I opened it up and saw the fan was clogged, so I cleaned it and ran the test again.

Interesting. That's a typical problem with cheap sensors, and you should write about it in the report. But I'm more concerned about humidity. Have you noticed that the readings go up when the air is damp?
Yes, we have. On the foggy mornings, our figures were far higher than the council's. We think that tiny droplets of water are being counted as particles.

Exactly. That's well known, and it's why the sensors need to be calibrated against a reference instrument. You can do that by comparing your results with the official station and then adjusting them. Do you know how?
We thought we'd draw a graph of ours against theirs and fit a line.
That's the right idea. How long do you plan to collect data? You mentioned a month, I think.
We'd like to, but Ewan has an exam in three weeks, so we've agreed to stop after twenty days. That still covers a couple of weekends, when the traffic is lighter.
Which I think is useful, because it gives us a contrast.

It does, and twenty days is enough to see a pattern, though not enough to say anything about the seasons. Say so in the report. Now, let's talk about the method itself, because I want to be sure that it's solid. How many sensors have you got altogether?
Six. We'll put three on each side of the road, one at each end and one in the middle, so that we can see whether the pollution varies along the street.
Good. And at what height will you fix them?

Two metres above the pavement. We read that the official stations take their air from somewhere between one and a half and four metres, so two seemed a fair choice, and it's high enough that nobody can interfere with them.
Good thinking. How often will they record?
Every five minutes. We considered every minute, but there'd be too much data, and every ten minutes seemed too slow to catch a passing lorry.
Five is a good compromise. Which of the council's monitoring stations will you use for comparison?

The one by the library, which is classed as a roadside station. There's also an urban background station on the other side of town, which measures the air away from traffic. We may use that as well, if we have time.
I'd stick to the roadside one, as a start. And what form will the final results take?
We'd like to draw a scatter plot, with the official readings on one axis and ours on the other. It would show clearly how closely the two agree.
Excellent. A scatter plot is exactly what an examiner wants to see. One more thing: how will you handle gaps? If a sensor loses its connection, there'll be missing values.
We'd thought of leaving them out and saying so in the report.
That's right. Never invent data to fill the gaps. A short explanation is much better. And where will you store the data?
In a shared spreadsheet, backed up every night to the university drive.

Good. Keep the raw files untouched and do all your calculations on a copy. Now, I'd like you to keep a diary of anything unusual, such as roadworks, a fire, or a street market, because those events will explain odd readings.
That's a good idea. There's a farmers' market on Saturday mornings, and the traffic gets very heavy around it.
Then write it down. I'm very pleased with the progress. Let's meet again in two weeks, and bring me the first graph.

Take a deep breath. You have just inhaled thousands of tiny particles and several different gases, and you have no idea how many. That is the problem that air quality monitoring tries to solve. Today I want to look at how cities actually measure the air, starting with the most accurate and expensive methods and moving to the cheapest.

Let me begin by saying what we are measuring. The main concerns are nitrogen dioxide, which comes mostly from diesel engines, ozone, and what we call particulate matter. Particulate matter is a mixture of tiny solid and liquid particles. The most worrying are the finest ones, known as PM2.5, which are smaller than 2.5 micrometres across. They are small enough to pass deep into the lungs and even into the bloodstream. In 2021, the World Health Organization lowered its recommended yearly limit for PM2.5 to 5 micrograms per cubic metre, which is half of the previous figure. Very few cities in the world currently meet it.

So how do cities find out what they are breathing? The standard approach is the reference station. These are installed by the authorities and housed in a small cabin, about the size of a garden shed, on the pavement or in a park. Inside, pumps draw air through an inlet on the roof. By international agreement, that inlet is between 1.5 and 4 metres above the ground, which roughly matches the height at which people breathe, while keeping it out of reach of vandals. Inside the cabin, each pollutant is measured by a separate instrument. The nitrogen dioxide analyser, for example, uses a chemical reaction that gives off light, and the amount of light is proportional to the amount of gas. Reference stations are accurate and carefully checked, but they are costly to buy and to run, and a typical city can afford only a handful of them.

Different stations also serve different purposes. A roadside station sits close to the traffic, and shows the worst case. An urban background station is placed away from roads, and shows what people breathe in most of the city. Comparing the two tells you how much of the pollution comes from the traffic itself.

One thing worth remembering is that pollution is patchy. The air beside a busy junction can be far dirtier than the air a hundred metres away, down a side street, and a single station tells you about only one spot. Studies that have put sensors on bicycles and delivery vans have found big differences between one side of a street and the other. That is one reason why cities have looked for cheaper ways to fill in the gaps.

Because reference stations are so few, many cities add a cheaper method, called the diffusion tube. It's a small plastic tube, about the size of a pencil, which is open at one end. A chemical at the closed end absorbs nitrogen dioxide from the air that drifts in. The tubes are cheap enough that a city can hang hundreds of them, usually on lamp posts, to build a detailed map. But they have a serious limit. They are left out for four weeks, then sent to a laboratory, so they can only tell you the average for the month. They cannot tell you about a bad hour on a Tuesday morning.

The newest method is the low-cost sensor. These are small electronic units that cost a few tens of pounds, and they work by shining a laser through a stream of air. When particles pass through the beam, they scatter the light, and the sensor counts the flashes. They can send readings every few minutes, which is a great advantage. In many places, community groups install them in their own gardens. But they are not perfect. Their readings are affected by humidity, because droplets of water scatter light too, and a foggy morning can look like a polluted one. So their data must be checked against a reference station before it can be trusted.

What happens to all these numbers? In most countries, they are combined into a simple index, so that the public doesn't need to know what a microgram is. In the United Kingdom, the index runs from 1 to 10. One to three is low, four to six is moderate, seven to nine is high, and ten is very high. Other countries use different scales. The American scale, for instance, runs from 0 to 500. The idea is the same everywhere: to turn a complex set of measurements into a colour and a piece of advice, such as whether you should avoid exercising outdoors.

A word about how the index is used. In some cities, a high reading triggers action: schools are told to keep children indoors during break, or older vehicles are kept out of the centre. In others, the figure is simply published on a website, and nobody is obliged to do anything. So measuring the air is only the first step. What matters is who is listening.

Finally, I want to say something about the future. No single method gives a complete picture. The most promising approach is to combine them, using a few accurate reference stations to correct a large number of cheap sensors, and then using computer models to estimate the air quality in places where there is no instrument at all. Satellites add a view from above, particularly useful in regions with few monitoring stations. None of this is cheap, but it is much cheaper than the cost of illness caused by dirty air. In the next lecture, we'll turn to what cities can actually do once they know what is in the air.
Hello? Hi. Is that the research centre? I'm hoping somebody can help me with a box of my grandfather's old letters, and a friend said the archive might know what to do with them.

You've come to the right desk, I think. This is Te Awa Regional Archive, and I'm Imogen. We can certainly look at them with you, and we can also show you what we hold on the same subject. Are you thinking of visiting the reading room?
I'd like to, yes. I've never been to an archive before, so I'm afraid I'll need to be told everything.
That's perfectly fine. Let me open the booking sheet, and we'll go through it together. First, could I have your surname?
It's Fairweather. F-A-I-R-W-E-A-T-H-E-R. It's an old Scottish name, but my family have been in Otago for four generations.
Marchetti, thank you. And a contact number, in case we need to change anything?
Yes, my mobile is 027 555 0192.
027 555 0192. Now, what is the subject of your research? We ask, so that we can have the right material ready for you.

My grandfather farmed sheep on the Taieri Plain, and he wrote a lot of letters to my grandmother during the war. I'd like to see if there are records of the farm, but mostly I want to learn how to look after the letters.
So I'll put letters from a sheep farmer. That's a very good subject, because we hold the stock registers for most of the district. When would you like to come in?
I was thinking of Tuesday the second, but I think I have a dentist appointment, so perhaps the following week. Is Tuesday 9 April possible?
The ninth is fine. We're open from nine to five, and there are two sessions. The morning session starts at half past nine, and the afternoon one at half past one. Which would suit you better?
Morning would be my first choice. But on the ninth I have a meeting until eleven, so afternoon will have to do.
Afternoon, then. Now, you can request up to three boxes for each visit, because we have to keep the others safe. Have you any idea what you'd like to see?
I thought five, because there seem to be several kinds of record, the stock registers, the farm accounts and the local newspapers.
I'm afraid the limit is three. You can come back another time for the rest. I'd suggest the stock register for the 1940s, the farm accounts, and the newspapers, and we can order any others later.
Then three it is. Is there a number I should quote for the stock register?
Yes, the reference is MS 2231. That's the manuscript series. I'll write it down, and the staff will have the box on the table when you arrive.
Thank you. And is there anything I need to bring with me? Do I need any identification?

You'll need one photo ID, just so that we can register you as a reader. And a word about writing. You aren't allowed to use pens in the reading room, because ink can damage the documents. Please bring a pencil only, and we'll lend you one if you forget.
That's easy enough. Can I take photographs of the documents? It would help me to read them at home.
You can, but there's a permit to buy. It's $12 for the day, and it allows you to photograph as many items as you like, as long as you don't use a flash. Without the permit, you'll have to make notes.
Twelve dollars is very reasonable. I'll buy one.

One more thing. Large bags and coats aren't allowed in the reading room, in case something is spilled, or taken by mistake. There are lockers near the front door, and it's free, but you have to put a coin in to get the key, and the coin is returned when you open it again.
A locker, then, and I'll bring a coin. Lovely. Is there anything I can do to prepare my grandfather's letters before I bring them in?

Just leave them as they are. Don't try to flatten them, or take out any pins, and please don't use sticky tape on anything. We'll show you how to store them properly, in acid-free folders, when you come.
Thank you so much, Imogen. You've made it all sound much less frightening than I'd expected.
It really isn't frightening at all. We're a friendly place, and we'll see you on the ninth.

Evening, all. Sit wherever you can find a chair, and if you can't find one, there are a few more in the cupboard by the stage. I'm Bronwen, and I coordinate the volunteers for the Milford Memory Day. It takes place next Saturday, and I want to explain how the day will work, because many of you have signed up to help.

The idea of the day is simple. People from the town bring along their old photographs, letters and certificates, and we scan them, free of charge, so that families have a digital copy, and a second copy is added to the town's community archive. We expect about a hundred and fifty people, and for most of them it's the first time they've shown their family papers to anyone outside the family.

Let me describe how the hall will be arranged, because it matters. When you come in through the main doors, the first thing you see is the registration table, which will be directly on your right. That's where visitors sign in and where each is given a numbered envelope for their items. Please don't let anyone wander past the table without a number, because we'll need it later to give back the right items.

Behind the registration table, along the back wall, are the scanning stations. There are four, and each has a scanner and a laptop. This is the heart of the day, and it's where most of you will be working. Next to them, at the end of the wall, is the area for recording stories. We have a small microphone and a quiet corner, and people who want to explain who is in a photograph can do so. The recordings are as important as the pictures, because a photograph without names is almost useless.

On the left side of the hall, by the windows, is the tea and coffee table. We'll need two volunteers there at all times. The stage at the far end will be used for the children's corner, with paper and crayons. We'd like the children to draw their own family tree, which keeps them busy while their parents are scanning. And finally, by the kitchen door, we'll have the table where visitors collect their items once they've been scanned. It's very important that this is separate from the scanning stations, to reduce the risk of anyone going home with the wrong envelope.

Now, let me deal with a few practical questions that people have asked me. First, how long will each visitor spend with us? Each scanning appointment lasts twenty minutes. We tried half an hour at the trial last year, and the queue was out of the door by eleven o'clock. Twenty minutes is enough for about a dozen photographs, and visitors who have more can book a second slot.

Second, what should visitors bring? We'll ask them to bring only the items they want scanned, and to carry them in a flat folder, not in a plastic bag, because plastic can make old photographs stick together. They don't need to bring identification or a form. All they need is their name.

Third, and this is the question I'm asked most, what happens to the originals? The answer is that they go home with the visitor, every time. We never keep anyone's original. The archive keeps only a digital copy, and only with the owner's written permission. We stress that we're not here to take things away from people. It's the opposite. We're helping people to keep their treasures safe at home.

And what about the captions? When a photograph is scanned, someone needs to record the details. A good caption says who is in the picture, where it was taken, and roughly when. Many people don't know the date, but they can usually say, for instance, that it was before the bridge was built. I'd like each volunteer to ask the visitor, and to write down exactly what is said, even if it's uncertain. Please don't tidy it up or guess. If a visitor says, "I think it's Uncle Frank, but it might be his brother," we write that down just as it was said. Archivists call that respecting the source.

Finally, a word about clothing and conduct. Please wear the green volunteer badge, which you'll collect when you arrive, and comfortable shoes, because you'll be standing for hours. If you aren't sure about anything, ask me, or look for the person with the orange lanyard. Thanks again for your time, and I'm looking forward to seeing you on Saturday.
Right, the three of you, sit anywhere you like. Mai, Josh, Tamsin, I wanted to hear how the digitisation project is going, because I've only seen the proposal, and that was a month ago.

It's going well, I think. We've now chosen the collection. It's about four hundred press photographs from the local newspaper, from the nineteen sixties and seventies, and the newspaper has agreed to let us work on them.

We spent a long time deciding which ones to include. At first, we thought we'd go for the most dramatic, the floods and the fires. But Tamsin pointed out that this would give a very strange picture of the town, as if nothing but disasters had ever happened.
So in the end, we agreed to choose by theme. We've picked the fishing industry, because it changed so much in those years, and the photographs show how.
And is four hundred realistic? Scanning always takes longer than students expect.
We've done a hundred and sixty so far. Each one takes about four minutes, once you include cleaning the glass and checking the result.
So we've asked the newspaper whether we can reduce it to three hundred. But we'd rather finish a smaller set properly than rush.
Wise. Record those timings, because they're evidence for your report.
That's a sensible approach. A theme gives your selection a reason, which is what appraisal is about. Now, the technical decisions. At what resolution did you scan?
We tested a few, and settled on 600 pixels per inch. The photographs are small, and at lower settings, the faces went blurry when we enlarged them.
Good. And the file format?
We'll keep the master copy as a TIFF, which isn't compressed, so nothing is lost. For the website, we'll make smaller JPEG copies, because TIFFs are enormous.
Exactly right. Never edit the master. What about naming the files? That's something students often neglect, and it causes endless trouble later.
We agreed on a system that combines the year with a number. So the third photograph from 1968 would be 1968 and then 003. It's dull, but it's logical, and it sorts properly in the folder.
And no spaces or special characters, please.
We found that out the hard way. The website refused one file because the name had an apostrophe in it.
That's a very common mishap.
Dull is good in file names. Now, copyright. This is where many projects stumble. Who owns the photographs?

That was complicated. The newspaper owns most of them, but about thirty were taken by freelance photographers, and we couldn't be sure who they were. In the end, we decided to ask the newspaper to give us written permission for all of them, and to say in our report that the ownership of the thirty is uncertain.
That's the honest approach. And storage? Where do your files live?
On the university server. And Tamsin is going to keep a second copy on an external drive, which will be stored off the campus, at her parents' house.
Who is allowed to change the files?
Only the three of us. The newspaper staff can read them, but not alter them.
Then set the masters to read-only, so that nobody overwrites one by accident. It happens more often than you'd think.
Good. Keeping one copy in a different place is the most important rule. Now, tell me about problems. Did you find any with the originals?

Quite a lot, actually. The biggest was that many of the prints had been stuck into scrapbooks with sticky tape, and the tape had left yellow stains. Some photographs tore when we tried to lift them, so we scanned them where they were, and noted the damage in the record.
That's the right decision. If you can't move something safely, don't. What about identifying the people in the photographs?
Most of the prints had no names on the back. We took copies to the fishermen's club, and some of the older members recognised faces. One man cried when he saw a photograph of his father.
But they didn't always agree. One picture was labelled Davy Crockett by one man and Davy Crosbie by another.
And what did you do?
We recorded both, and added a note to say that the name was disputed.
