Now, a delicate question. Some of these people are still alive, and some of the photographs show accidents. Have you thought about whether any should be withheld?
We've set aside nine pictures that show injured people, and we'll ask the newspaper's editor to decide whether they should go online.
Good. Say in your report that you made that choice, and why. An archive that hides things without saying so isn't being honest.

Excellent, that's exactly the best practice. I'd add a warning about the descriptions you write, which we call metadata. It's very easy to be inconsistent. If one record says fishing boat, another says trawler, and a third says vessel, then a search will miss two thirds of them. Decide on a list of terms and stick to it.
We've started a list, but it's only half finished.
Then finish it first, before you describe any more photographs. What do you plan to do for the final report?
We thought we'd include a section about the costs, and how many hours each stage took.

Yes, do that, and make it prominent. It's the part that people who want to start a similar project will read first. Right, that sounds as though you're on track. Josh: Will we be marked on how many photographs we manage to finish?
No. You'll be marked on your reasoning, and on how clearly you explain what you did and why. Send me the list of terms by Friday.

When people hear the words digital archive, they usually picture a website with a search box and a lot of old photographs. They don't picture the labour behind it, which is largely invisible and, I would argue, far more important than the website. Today I want to talk about that hidden work, because without it, digital archives would last only a few years.

Let's start before anything is scanned. No archive can keep everything. Most material that is created is thrown away, and a small fraction is selected for permanent keeping. The process of deciding what to keep is called appraisal, and it is the first and perhaps the hardest task. Archivists ask whether something is unique, whether it shows how decisions were made, and whether anybody is likely to want it in a hundred years. The answers are often uncertain, and every choice is a judgment.

Then comes capture. When a document or photograph is digitised, it is scanned and saved in a file, and the choice of file format is crucial. The master copy is usually saved as a TIFF, a format that does not throw away any detail. TIFF files are very large, so they are used mainly for preservation. For viewing on the web, the archive makes a second version in the JPEG format, which is much smaller and loads quickly. The two serve different purposes. One is for keeping and the other is for showing.

It is worth pausing to notice how slow all this is. A skilled technician may scan only a few dozen fragile items in a day, because each one has to be handled gently, cleaned, positioned and checked. A bound volume cannot be opened flat without damaging its spine, so it needs a special cradle. People who fund digitisation projects are often surprised that the cost of scanning is only a small part of the total bill.

Now, a digital photograph isn't useful if nobody can find it, and that is where description comes in. Descriptions of this kind are called metadata, which means data about data. A standard that is widely used is called Dublin Core, which has fifteen elements, including title, creator, date and subject. Creating good metadata is slow, skilled work, and many archives spend far more time on it than on scanning. Where the document is text, such as a newspaper page, the scanned image is processed by software that reads the letters. This is known as optical character recognition, or OCR, and it makes the text searchable. But it makes mistakes, especially with old type, so a search for a name may miss it because the machine read an S as an F.

The next stage is the one the public never sees: keeping the files safe. You might think that a digital file lasts for ever, but that's an illusion. Storage devices fail, and sometimes a file changes slightly without anybody noticing, which is called bit rot. To detect this, archives use a checksum. A checksum is a short code calculated from the contents of a file. If even a single bit changes, the code changes, and the archive's software raises an alarm. The checksums are checked regularly, often every few months.

Archivists also follow a rule of thumb called the three-two-one rule. You keep three copies of every file, on two different types of storage, with one copy kept in a different place, so that a fire or a flood at one site doesn't destroy everything. It sounds simple, and it is, but it needs to be done consistently and for ever, which costs money.

There's a further problem that is less obvious: obsolescence. The software needed to open a file may stop being made. Anyone who has tried to open a document from a thirty-year-old word processor will know what I mean. To prevent this, archives regularly migrate their files to newer formats, copying the contents into a format that is still supported. Each time, they check that nothing has been lost. It's a job that is never finished.

Everything I have said so far concerns material that began on paper. Increasingly, however, archives receive records that were never printed at all, such as emails, spreadsheets and websites. These are called born-digital records. There is no original to protect in a box. The record is a file, and sometimes it only makes sense on a particular machine. Some archives therefore keep software as well as documents, and a few run old programs inside a modern computer, so that a visitor can see a file as its creator saw it.

Finally, I'd like to say something about the web, which is perhaps the most fragile archive of all. The Internet Archive was founded in 1996, and it has been saving copies of web pages ever since, through a service known as the Wayback Machine. Why does this matter? Because the web forgets. In 2024, a study by a research centre in the United States found that 38 per cent of the web pages that existed in 2013 could no longer be reached ten years later. Links break, sites close, and the information simply disappears.

So what should you take from this? A digital archive isn't a finished product but a continuing commitment. The scanning is the easy part. The real work is the choosing, the describing, the checking and the copying, which must go on every year for as long as the material is to survive. In the next session, I'll look at the ethical questions, such as who has the right to decide what is kept, and whose stories are left out.
Hi, I hope this is the right number. I picked up a leaflet about lunchtime classes, and all it says is call the front desk, with no name and no opening hours, which is a bit mysterious.
Ah, yes, we keep meaning to reprint those. You've reached Pennine Wharf Community Hall, and I'm Fergus. Which class were you thinking of?
The one with the picture of a woman reaching for her toes. I assumed it was yoga, but it doesn't actually say.

It isn't yoga, I'm afraid. Yoga is on Tuesday evenings, and that's been full since September. The lunchtime one is called gentle stretch. It's slower than yoga, and several people have told me it's the only time all week they sit still.
That sounds ideal, to be honest. I retired last month, and my shoulders have been permanently up around my ears after thirty years of typing.
Then you'll fit right in. Shall I put you down? I'll take a few details for the registration form as we go.
Please. My name's Joanna Prendergast.
And how is that spelt?
Of course. P-R-E-N-D-E-R-G-A-S-T. Most people leave out the D in the middle.
Prendergast, got it. Now, the class runs on two days, Tuesday and Thursday. Which would suit you better?
Tuesday, I think, because Thursday is my volunteering morning at the garden centre.
Hmm, Tuesday's already full, and the teacher won't go above fifteen people. I can only offer you Thursday. Would the garden centre let you finish a bit early?
Oh, they'd probably let me swap. It's only a few hours, and nobody else wants to do the compost. Yes, Thursday's fine. I'll sort it out.

Lovely. It starts at half past twelve, so you can come straight from your morning. Oh, hold on, sorry, I'm looking at last term's timetable. This term it's a quarter to one, so 12.45, because the pottery group now have the room until half past twelve and they need time to clear away.
Quarter to one, fine. That actually gives me time for a sandwich. How long does the course last?
Normally ten weeks, but this one is shorter because of the half-term break, so it's 8 weeks, and it finishes just before the school holidays.
Eight weeks, good. And what's the damage?

The full price is £80. But you're over sixty, so you qualify for the concession, and for you it's £64. We ask for a deposit now to hold your place, which is £15, and you pay the rest on your first day.
That's fair. Can I pay the deposit now?

I'll email you a payment link in a minute, if that's easier. I'm not supposed to take card numbers over the phone. Right, nearly there. The leaflet says the class is in the Studio, which I should correct. Will that cause you any difficulty?
It might be. Isn't the Studio upstairs? I had an operation two years ago, and I don't love stairs.

It is upstairs, and there's no lift, so that leaflet is out of date. We've moved the class down to the Garden Room, on the ground floor. It opens onto the courtyard, and honestly it's nicer, because the light is better.
Oh, that's a relief. The Garden Room, then. I'll write that on my calendar.
Just so I can tell our funders, how did you hear about the class?
From the leaflet, as I said. It was on the shelf in the library, right beside the large print novels.

Ah, our friends at the library. I'll let them know it worked. One last thing. Is there any health condition you'd like me to pass on to the teacher? She likes to know in advance, so she can adjust the exercises.
Well, I've mentioned my shoulders, and that's the main reason I'm coming. But the thing she should really know about is my left knee. That's what the operation was for, and kneeling is difficult.
Right, your knee. I'll put that in the notes. She'll have cushions and blocks, so you won't need to kneel at all.
Do I need to bring a mat?

No, we provide those, and the blankets too. Just wear something loose and bring a bottle of water. There's no parking on site, I'm afraid, but the bus stops right outside, and the number 14 comes every ten minutes.
I'll take the bus. I've got a pass now, and I should use it. Is there anything I should sort out beforehand?

Only check your email in the next few minutes for the payment link. If it doesn't arrive, look in your junk folder, because it often ends up there. And when you come on the first day, come to the front desk and say Fergus sent you, and I'll walk you down to the Garden Room, because the signs aren't brilliant.
Thank you, Fergus. You've been very patient with a woman who couldn't even read her own leaflet.
Not at all. The leaflet was the problem. We'll see you on Thursday.

Thanks for coming in before the commuters do. I'm Odette Teague, the station manager here at Kellerby Central, and this is the first of three induction sessions for our new Calm Concourse ambassadors. I'd like to tell you why the project exists, how your shifts will work, and then walk you round the concourse as it now is, because quite a lot has moved.

First, the aim. You may have read in the newspaper that Calm Concourse is about getting fewer people through the station at busy times, or that it's about persuading passengers to spend more in the shops. Neither is true. Our passenger survey last year showed that the morning peak was the part of the journey people dreaded most, because of the noise, the crowding and the constant announcements. So the whole project is about making the busiest hour less stressful for the people who have no choice but to be here.

Now, your shifts. We had originally planned four hours each, but the volunteers in our pilot group told us that the final hour was exhausting. Talking to strangers is more tiring than it sounds. So each shift is three hours. There's a morning shift, from half past seven until half past ten, and an afternoon one, from four until seven. You can do as many or as few as you like, but we do ask for at least one a week.

You'll be recognisable by your jacket. The first colour we ordered was bright orange, but passengers confused ambassadors with the maintenance crews, and navy turned out to look too much like our ticket staff. So the jackets are a soft green, with your name on a badge. Please wear the badge on the left, where people can see it when they look at you.

Next, and this is the part I'd like you to listen to most carefully, what to do if someone looks distressed. Some of you may think the best thing is to call security, and I'd ask you not to, unless there's a danger to anybody. Your first step is simply to ask, quietly and from a little distance, whether the person would like some help or some space. Don't touch them, and don't crowd them. Only if they say yes should you offer the quiet room, which is the second step, not the first. Some people just want a minute on a bench, and that's perfectly all right.

You won't be doing this alone. Every ambassador will do a half-day of training shadowing an experienced colleague, and there'll be a refresher after your first month. At the end of that first month, we'll also share the results of the passenger survey with you, so you can see whether the changes are making any difference. I'd much rather you heard those numbers from me than read them in the newspaper.

Right, let's look at the layout. Imagine you've just come through the main doors, because that's where almost every passenger starts. Immediately on your left, just inside the entrance, is the ambassador desk. The original plans put it beside the information screens, but the screens are noisy and the glare is awful, so we moved it. You'll collect your jacket and badge from there, and so will anyone who needs help.

Walk a few steps further and you'll see the information screens in front of you. That's where people arrange to meet friends and relatives, so we've marked it as the official meeting point. There's a bench beneath it, and a small sign, so no more standing around wondering which of the many pillars somebody meant.

Now turn right, towards the café. Directly opposite the café is a row of water refill taps and charging points. These are the most popular new feature by far, and you'll be asked about them all the time. Please don't send people to platform 1 for water. There's a tap beside the entrance to that platform, but it's the old one, and it's often out of order.

Going back across the concourse, behind the main staircase, you'll find the accessible toilets. They are easy to miss, because the staircase hides them, and the original sign was on the wrong wall. So when people ask, point them behind the stairs, not up them. The footbridge at the far end has a lift at the top, but there are no facilities there, so don't send anyone that way unless they're going to platform 4.

Finally, the quiet room. You'd expect it to be near the entrance, but it's at the far end of the west passage, as far from the trains as we could put it. The passage is lined with soft panels, and the lighting there is dimmer. The room is open from six in the morning until ten at night, and it has a sofa, a few cushions and a window with a view of the car park trees. It's not glamorous, but it's calm.

That's everything for today. If you'd like to see the quiet room for yourselves, please follow me, and I'll show you the door. And there are some bacon rolls waiting for you in the café, which I can see some of you have noticed already.

Right, you two, come in and shut the door against the noise from the corridor, which is appropriate, given your topic. I've read your plan for the Wexcombe Square project, and I want to know how the fieldwork actually went.

Mostly fine, Dr Ashdown, though not everything went to plan. We observed the square on four days, with three time slots each day, and counted how many people stopped, how long they stayed and where they sat.
And we measured the noise at six fixed points, using a sound meter from the department.
Good. So what went wrong?
Well, the weather was the first thing. It rained on two of our four days, and the square was almost empty. The numbers for those days are so low that we can hardly use them.
That's frustrating, but you can't control the weather. I'd just say so openly in the report. What else?

The second problem was my fault. Before we borrowed the meter, I tried the first day with a phone app instead, and it turned out to be reading about four decibels too high. So we had to throw out the first morning's readings and start those again.
Better to find out on day one than on day four. Did the meter itself behave?

Yes, perfectly. I nearly forgot the spare batteries, but luckily the first set lasted. And a security guard did come over on the Friday, though only because he was curious. He thought we were from the council.
We'd also planned our visits to avoid Saturdays, because of the farmers' market. The stalls change where people walk, so we thought it wouldn't be a fair comparison.
Sensible. Now, tell me something. Why observation? Wouldn't a questionnaire have been quicker?

Quicker, yes, but it would only tell us what people say they do. We read that people tend to overestimate how often they sit outside, and they say they want quiet places while actually choosing busy ones. Watching them seemed more honest.
Good answer. Include that in your methodology, with the reference. Now, about your time slots. You counted at eight in the morning, noon and four. Why not later?
I suppose it gets dark early at this time of year, and we weren't sure about being there on our own.

I understand, but the evening is when many young people use the square, and you're missing them. I'd suggest adding one evening session. Go in pairs, stay near the café where there's light, and keep it to an hour.
All right. We can do that. Another thing. We weren't sure how to record what people were doing. Should we film them?

I wouldn't. You'd need ethics approval, and people don't like being filmed in public, even when it's legal. Photographs are the same. Stick to tally sheets and sketch maps, where each person is a dot and a little note. Then nobody can be identified, which makes the ethics section much easier.
That's what we've been doing, then. Good.
Now, the big weakness. You've got figures for today, but what do they mean? Without a comparison, a busy square could simply be a busy square.
We wondered about comparing with Marlow Street, because it has a similar size and similar shops, but it hasn't been redesigned.
Though actually, I found something better. The council did pedestrian counts in the square in the same months, before the redesign. I only found them last week, in a report on its website.
Can I ask about the noise readings, too? We took six readings at each point, but the numbers jump about a lot when a bus goes past. Should we average them, or just report the highest?

Report both. An average hides the sudden peaks that people actually notice, and the peak alone makes everything sound worse than it is. A simple table with the average, the highest reading and the quietest reading at each point will tell the story far better than a paragraph.
That's easy enough. I've already got the figures in a spreadsheet, so I can turn it into a table tonight.
That's excellent, Joel, and much stronger than a different square. The same place, before and after. Use the council counts as your main comparison, and mention Marlow Street only briefly, if at all.
Great. Shall we say what we found, then?
Please do. Take me through the features of the square, one at a time.

Let's start with the fountain. We expected people to gather round it, but really it was the sound that mattered. At the noisiest points near the road, the fountain made the traffic hard to hear, and people said the square felt quieter than the meter said it was.

The trees are different. They're only two years old, so there's hardly any shade. People walk under them, but hardly anyone stops. It's the least used part of the square, even though it's right in the middle.
That may change as they grow, so say that in your discussion.
The benches along the east side were interesting. They're busiest at lunchtime, but almost always with one person. Someone eating a sandwich, someone reading, hardly ever two together.
And the café terrace is where people stayed longest, by a long way. Some people stayed over an hour. Even though it's the noisiest corner, because of the espresso machine and the chairs scraping.

That's a nice contradiction. Noise matters less if you've chosen to be there. Right, I think you've got enough to write. I'll expect a draft in a fortnight, with the council figures in the results section.

Good morning, everyone. Today I want to ask what it takes for a public space to feel calm, and I'd like to start with a number. When the World Health Organization published its environmental noise guidelines in 2018, it recommended that average road traffic noise should stay below 53 decibels. Many people are surprised, because they assume the safe level is much higher. It isn't. Above that figure, studies link traffic noise with sleep disturbance and with a higher risk of heart disease, and over the years the evidence has become more convincing, not less.

But noise is only half the story, because calm is a feeling as well as a measurement. Two psychologists, Rachel and Stephen Kaplan, argued in their book The Experience of Nature, published in 1989, that city life tires out a particular kind of attention, the effortful kind we use to ignore distractions. According to what they called attention restoration theory, natural settings give that attention a rest, because they hold our interest gently, without demanding anything. They called this soft fascination.

A famous piece of evidence came from the environmental psychologist Roger Ulrich. In 1984, he compared patients recovering from gallbladder surgery in the same Pennsylvania hospital. Some had a room with a view of trees. Others looked at a brick wall. The patients with the view of trees went home sooner, took fewer strong painkillers, and the nurses wrote fewer negative notes about them. It was a small study, and it has been criticised, but similar results keep appearing, and designers still cite it today.

So how do designers use this? Let's start with sound. One approach is masking. A fountain or a stream doesn't remove traffic noise, but it can cover it, as long as the sound of the water overlaps with the sound you want to hide. Designers talk about frequency here. A gentle trickle at a very different frequency from the traffic won't help at all, while a broader splash will. The researchers use the word soundscape for the overall acoustic environment as people experience it, and there's now an international standard, ISO 12913, that describes how to measure it, partly by asking people rather than only using meters.

The next issue is the surfaces. Glass, stone and concrete are hard, and sound bounces off them. In a square surrounded by tall buildings, you get repeated echoes, and a conversation can sound twice as loud as it really is. Soft materials, such as planting, timber and fabric canopies, absorb sound. But here I must warn you against a common myth. People think a hedge works like a wall. In fact, a hedge alone typically reduces measured noise by perhaps 2 decibels at most. That's barely audible, because most people can't detect a change smaller than about 3.

And yet, when you ask people, they say the hedge made the place quieter. Why? Because it hides the source. If you can't see the road, your brain pays less attention to it. This is a good example of why calm isn't only an acoustic matter. A small reduction that people can notice, together with a screen that blocks the view of the traffic, can feel like a big change.

Now let's turn to layout. The Danish architect Jan Gehl spent decades watching how people use city spaces, and one of his best-known observations is that people prefer to stay at the edges. If you go to a square, you rarely stand in the middle. You stay near a wall, a tree or a doorway, where you can see without being seen. Gehl called these soft edges, and the lesson for designers is to make the boundaries of a space rich and comfortable. Put benches and planters there, and the middle will look after itself.

Calm spaces are also easy to understand. If you can't work out where to go, you feel anxious, even if the place is beautiful. So designers aim for clear sightlines, so that you can see the exit from where you stand, and for consistent signs, using the same colour, the same size and the same wording across the whole site. A single odd sign, in a different style, can break the pattern and cause people to stop and hesitate.

One last element is light. Bright white light feels busy and even slightly clinical, especially in the evening. Designers of calm spaces usually choose warm light, and the temperature of light is measured in kelvin. A warm evening light is about 2700 kelvin, similar to an old-fashioned bulb, whereas daylight is more like 6500. Combine that with lower light levels in resting areas, and the space tells people to slow down.

I should add a word about cost, because students often assume that calm design is a luxury. It isn't always. Moving a bench from the middle of a path to the edge of a lawn costs nothing. Choosing a quieter surface when you repave a street costs a little more, but the surface has to be replaced anyway. The expensive mistakes are the ones made early and discovered late, such as a beautiful stone plaza that turns out to echo like a swimming pool, and has to be partly covered over a year later at the council's expense.

To sum up. A calm space is quiet enough, which means somewhere below 53 decibels, but it's also soft at the edges, easy to read and gently lit. None of these is expensive by itself. What costs money is getting the designers to think about all of them together, from the very first sketch, rather than adding a fountain at the end and hoping for the best. In next week's seminar, we'll apply this to a real site, so please bring a photo of a public space that you find calming and another that you find stressful.
Hello, I'm hoping you can settle an argument. My sister says you can do a special-order cake with only two days' notice, and I say it takes a week.

You're both partly right. A plain cake takes two days, but anything with decoration needs five at least. This is Elowen at Marigold Bakehouse, by the way, in case you were wondering who you'd been arguing about.
Ha, then I'm mostly right, which I'll enjoy telling her. It's for a birthday, and the party is on the 15th, so we've got plenty of time.
Then you're fine. Let me find the order sheet. Could I take your name?
It's Dev Garrity. G-A-R-R-I-T-Y.
Garrity, thank you. And who's the cake for, Dev? Your mother? A friend?
My grandmother. She's turning eighty, and the whole family is coming to a lunch at the village hall, which she knows nothing about yet.
How lovely. And what sort of cake? Most people choose a Victoria sponge for a big birthday, and it's hard to go wrong.
I was about to say Victoria sponge, but that's what we always have. What my gran really made, every Sunday, in a huge tin, was lemon drizzle. Could you do that? Is it sturdy enough to carry in a car?
If we bake it as a tray cake and ice the top, absolutely. Lemon drizzle it is. How many people will it need to feed?
About twenty. Actually, no, hang on. My aunt has just texted to say her neighbours are coming too, so make it 24. I'd rather have leftovers than a hungry guest.
Twenty-four is a big tray, but we can manage it. Now, would you like a message on the top?
Yes, please. Happy 80th, Gran. No, wait. She can't stand being called Gran. We call her Nana, and so does everybody in the street. So Happy 80th, Nana, with an exclamation mark.
Nana, with an exclamation mark. Writing it down in capitals, so the decorator can't get it wrong. Last month someone ordered a cake for Marge, and it came out as Margie.
Oh dear. Please check mine twice. When can I collect it?
The party is on the 15th, so I'd suggest you collect it the day before. We bake on the morning, and it's at its best then. Does the 14th suit you?
Perfect. I finish work at three, so I can come any time after that.
We close at half past five. Would you like to say a quarter to five, so you're not rushing?
I'd rather come a bit earlier, to be safe. Shall we say 4.30?

4.30 on the 14th. I'll put 14 June on the sheet, and write your name next to it. Now, the price. A lemon drizzle for 24 people comes to £38, and the message and decoration add £8, so the total would be £46.
That's less than I expected, to be honest.
Could you deliver it? The village hall is about six miles away, and I'm a little nervous about driving a huge cake along those lanes.

We do deliver, but only within three miles, I'm afraid, because the van is old and the lanes are bumpy. A tray cake that size would be safer in your boot, flat on a folded blanket, with someone holding the corners at the bends. That's what most of our customers do.
A blanket and a passenger. My sister will have to be useful for once. Do I need to pay anything now?
Not for an order this small. You pay on the day. Just one more thing for the sheet. Does anybody who's coming have an allergy? I have to ask.
Good question. One of my cousins can't eat nuts. Walnuts especially, because he once had a nasty reaction to a walnut cake at a wedding. There's no walnut in a lemon drizzle, is there?

No, but I'll write no walnuts on the order, and we'll bake it on a clean tray, away from the nut cakes. That's standard for us. Now, the last decision is the decoration. People often choose a ribbon, or just icing.
Here's another reason I'm glad I rang. My grandmother loves violets. She grows them by the back door. Do you do anything with flowers?
We do. I can put crystallised violets on the top. They're made by hand, so I'll need to start them tomorrow. Would you like those?
Yes, please. That would make her cry, in the best way.

Then violets it is. I'll read it back to you. A lemon drizzle for Garrity, serving 24, with Happy 80th, Nana, to be collected on 14 June at 4.30, for £46, and no walnuts, with crystallised violets. Is that right?
That's exactly right. And you'll check the spelling of Nana?
Twice. It's an easy name, but you never know. I'll see you on the 14th, Dev, and I hope your grandmother has a wonderful day.
Thank you so much. My sister is going to be unbearable about this, but at least the cake will be good.

Good morning, and thank you all for coming to Alderbrook Mill on a Saturday. I'm Gavin Murdoch, the museum's food historian, and I'll be your host for Recipe Memories Day. I'll explain what we're doing, what you should do next, and then show you where everything is, because we've spread ourselves across the whole site.

First, why are we doing this? A lot of people assume today is a cooking class, or a sale of our new cookbook, and I can see a few of you have brought aprons. Put them away, I'm afraid. The purpose of the day is to record recipes that families have passed down, and, just as importantly, the stories behind them. A recipe tells you what to put in the pot. The story tells you why anybody bothered.

Each recording takes about twenty minutes. We originally planned for ten, but our test sessions showed that people only start to relax after the first five minutes, and the best stories come right at the end, when they think the interview is over. So please don't plan to leave early. There's tea waiting for you afterwards.

Now, what should you have brought? Many people assume they need the recipe itself, written down. That's welcome, but it isn't necessary, and some of our most interesting recordings came from people who had nothing written at all. What helps most is something that connects you to the dish: a photograph, a battered old wooden spoon, a stained card. Our volunteers will ask you about it, and it often unlocks things you'd forgotten.

What happens to the recordings? Please don't worry, we won't broadcast them. Some visitors ask about local radio, and we have no plans for that. Nor do we hand the audio back on a memory stick, because we don't have the equipment to do it fairly for everybody. Everything is kept in the museum archive, but only with your signed permission, and you can choose whether it's open to researchers or closed for twenty years. You'll receive a printed copy of the transcript.

A word about photographs. You're welcome to take pictures of the site and of your own family, but please ask before you photograph anybody else, and please don't take pictures inside the recording booths, because it puts people off. If you'd like a photograph of yourself with the recording equipment, a volunteer will happily take one when you've finished.

And a word about accessibility. The site is old, and some of the paths are cobbled, so wear sensible shoes. We have a golf buggy that can take anyone between the lodge gate and the long barn, and you only have to ask a volunteer, who will be wearing a red cap so that you can spot them from a distance. Nobody should miss the day because of a few cobbles.

At the end of the day, we'll hold a tasting. Volunteers have cooked a selection of dishes from earlier recordings, and you can try them and tell us whether they taste the way you remember. This is always the most popular part, and I should warn you that the lemon pudding disappears in minutes.

Right, let's look at the site. I'll go in the order you'll meet things. You've all come in through the lodge gate, and just inside it is the registration table. Please collect your number from the volunteer there, because that's how we'll call you for your recording. If you haven't registered yet, don't panic, you can do that on the spot.

The recordings themselves take place in the granary, which is the tall stone building on your right. The recording booths are on the upper floor, where it's quiet, so you'll need to climb the stairs. If anyone cannot manage stairs, please tell me, because we've arranged a ground-floor alternative.

After you've recorded, you'll want to get your recipe cards copied. The scanning is done in the old dairy, the low building behind the granary. There's a long queue on busy days, so go early. The mill yard, by the way, is for parking and for the food trucks, and I'd ask you to leave it clear, because the water wheel beside it is being repaired and the area is fenced off.

For anyone who's brought children, there's baking for the little ones in the garden pavilion. It's the glass building with the pointed roof, down by the herb beds. The children make small bread rolls, and they get to take them home. It gives you an hour of peace to record your own story, which I know is attractive to some of you.

Finally, the tasting table. That's in the long barn, where the museum's big wooden tables are. It's open from three o'clock, and each dish has a card to say whose family it came from. You'll be able to write a comment on the card, and it goes into the archive too. I think that's everything. Have a wonderful day, and please do ask any of the volunteers if you get lost.
Ah, Lucia, Marcus, there you are. Your project on family recipes is one of the more appealing ones in the group, if only because I'm hungry. Tell me how the interviews went.
Really well, Dr Quinlan. We interviewed eight people, all aged over seventy, and we asked each of them to talk about one dish that mattered in their family.
Most of them came from my grandmother's lunch club, which is why it was so easy to arrange.
That's where I'd like to start, actually. Eight is a small number, but that's acceptable for this kind of qualitative work. My worry is the sample. Is everyone from the same club?
All eight, yes. And I suppose we know it's a mixed group, but looking at the notes, most of them grew up within a few miles of each other and ate much the same food.
That's the weakness to acknowledge. You'll find a very particular local food culture, and you can't claim it's typical of everyone. You don't need to fix it, just say it clearly in your limitations.
We will. We'd also hoped to film the interviews, because we thought the hands would tell a story. But two of the participants declined, so we recorded the audio on a phone instead.
That's often easier. People talk more freely when there's no camera. Did you notice any questions working better than others?

Definitely. We began by asking for the recipe, step by step, and people went rather stiff. They said what you'd expect: flour, eggs, butter. But when we asked who taught them to cook the dish, they came alive. We had twenty minutes of stories about aunts and neighbours.
It was the people, not the instructions, that people remembered.
That's an important finding, and you should say it prominently. What surprised you most?
That hardly anybody had a written recipe. We expected dog-eared cards in every kitchen, but seven of the eight had nothing at all. It was all in their hands and their heads.
And did that cause trouble when you tried to reproduce the dishes?
A lot, actually. They said a pinch, a handful, a knob of butter, until it's done. We spent an afternoon trying to turn that into grams, and the first loaf looked like a doorstop.

The transcription was a nightmare, though. Each interview was about twenty minutes, and it took us nearly three hours to type up each one, because people talk over each other and trail off halfway through a sentence.

That's normal. A good rule of thumb is that transcription takes six to ten times as long as the recording. It does mean you know your material extremely well, which will help when you write. Did everyone sign a consent form?

Yes, all eight. We explained that their names would be changed, so in the report they're Mrs H and Mr F, and so on. Mrs Hale wasn't quite sure she wanted anonymity, because she likes the idea of being quoted.

Respect that, but only if she says so in writing, and only if what she said doesn't identify anyone else. Mention the discussion in your ethics section, because examiners reward students who have clearly weighed the ethics.
Wonderful. Include that. Now, let's talk about the dishes themselves. What did people connect them with?

Each dish had a memory attached, and it was never what we expected. Take the dumplings. We thought they'd be about a festival or a holiday, but what people described was the kitchen itself, their mother at the table, everybody folding them together.
The fruit cake was linked to a wedding. Mrs Hale told us it was made by her sister, and that she'd carried a piece in her handbag for a week.
And the fish pie was about money. Mr Foster said it was the only thing they could afford in winter, because the fish was cheap, and he still can't eat it without remembering that.
Then there's rice pudding, which for Mrs Daly meant her school holidays on her grandmother's farm. She said the skin on top was the best part, and there was a fight over it every time.
These are all lovely. The report will be much stronger if you let people speak for themselves. A table of dishes and memories, with short quotations.
That's what we were hoping you'd say. Is there anything else we should add?
We were also wondering whether to compare our dishes with published recipes, to see how far the family versions have drifted.

It's tempting, but I'd resist it for this report. You have limited time, and the comparison would pull attention away from the people, which is where your strongest material is. Put it in your conclusion as an idea for further research, and leave it there.
Fair enough. We'll keep it short.

Examiners like a student who knows what not to do. As for what you should add, there are two things. First, more extracts from the interviews. You have good material, and at the moment the report is too much about you and not enough about them. Second, a short glossary of the measurement words. A pinch, a handful, a knob. Nobody outside your region will know what they mean, and it's rather charming.
A glossary is a good idea. We could even try to put a rough weight next to each one.
Yes, but make it clear they're approximations. What about the transcripts? Did you send them back to the participants?
Not yet. We thought we'd wait until the end.

I'd send them now. People can correct what they said, and it also protects you ethically. I don't think you need to do anything more elaborate than that. Right, I think you're in good shape. Let's meet again when you have a draft.

Let me begin with a cake. Not a real one, I'm afraid, but the most famous cake in literature. In 1913, the French writer Marcel Proust published the first volume of his enormous novel In Search of Lost Time. In one scene, the narrator, who is no longer young, dips a madeleine into a cup of tea. A madeleine is a small shell-shaped sponge. And as the taste reaches his mouth, a whole childhood comes rushing back: his aunt's house, the village, the garden. It's one of the best-known descriptions of memory in all of fiction.

Now, Proust was a novelist, not a scientist, but he was onto something. When we smell or taste something, the signals take an unusually direct route in the brain. They travel to the amygdala, which deals with emotion, and to the hippocampus, which is vital for memory, without first being relayed through the thalamus, as most other senses are. That may be one reason why a smell can bring back a scene so quickly and so powerfully.

The psychologist Rachel Herz, who has studied this for many years, found that memories triggered by smell tend to be more emotional than memories triggered by other cues, such as sight or sound. People don't merely remember a place, they feel it again. This is sometimes called the Proust effect, although Proust himself would have been surprised to have a laboratory finding named after him.

So food is tied to memory. But food is also tied to people. Think about the family meal. For decades, researchers have looked at what happens when families eat together, and the findings are quite striking. A group at Harvard recorded dinner conversations and found that young children heard a large number of uncommon words at the table, words they wouldn't hear in everyday talk. Sharing a meal appears to support vocabulary, which is something you might not expect from the fish fingers.

Now consider what happens when families move. Migrants often keep their traditional dishes long after they've dropped other customs, for a simple reason. Food is the easiest piece of culture to carry in a suitcase. You can recreate it in any kitchen, with a few substitutions. Psychologists call these dishes comfort food, and for many families they become a way of keeping a place and a person alive, particularly when someone has died.

This raises a problem for those who want to preserve culture. Recipes are usually passed on orally, and often without exact amounts. You don't write down a pinch. Increasingly, this kind of knowledge is recognised in official heritage lists. UNESCO keeps a list of what it calls intangible cultural heritage, the traditions, skills and practices that people hand down. In 2010, it added the gastronomic meal of the French, which includes the order of the courses and the way people sit at the table, not just the food.

Another example is from Korea. Kimjang, the making and sharing of kimchi, was added in 2013. It's a community event, held every year in late autumn, when neighbours gather to prepare enormous quantities of cabbage and pickle it for the winter. The point of the listing is not the kimchi itself, but the cooperation. And in 2017, UNESCO recognised the art of the Neapolitan pizza maker, the pizzaiolo, whose skills are learned in the family, from a parent or a grandparent.

There is one more reason that food memories matter, and it concerns older people. In care homes, workers often use what is called reminiscence work, in which residents are given familiar objects, music or smells and invited to talk. Food is especially effective. Someone who struggles to follow a conversation may suddenly describe, in perfect detail, how their mother made a Sunday roast. The memory of the dish can survive when other memories fade, and families often say that the conversation that follows is the first real one in weeks.

But I should also give you a warning. Memory isn't a recording. Psychologists have shown, since the 1930s, that we rebuild memories each time we recall them, and a dish remembered from childhood is partly a construction. Everyone's grandmother, it seems, made the best cake in the world. That doesn't make the memories worthless. It means that when you collect recipes you're collecting the way people remember, not a perfect record of how they cooked, and a good researcher keeps those two things apart.

Of course, official lists are not the only way to keep this knowledge. Many museums and archives now invite families to submit recipes, and what they've discovered is that a recipe on its own is nearly useless. A list of ingredients, without a story, tells you very little. So the more thoughtful archives ask families to add a short note, saying who the cook was and why the dish mattered. In a sense, they're asking for the Proust moment to be written down.

Let's think about what this means for researchers. If you want to study a food tradition, you can't rely on cookbooks. You have to talk to the people who cook, and you have to listen to what they say about the people who taught them. For your seminar task, try doing exactly that. Choose one dish from your own family, ask a relative to describe it, and make a note of everything they say that isn't in the recipe. You'll be surprised how much there is.
Good, a real person. I've been through three menus already, and I think I may have accidentally ordered a pizza.
Ha, no pizza here, I'm afraid. This is Tidewater Community Transport, and I'm Gareth. Are you ringing to book a seat on the minibus?
I am, if there's one going to Brimley next week. A friend told me you take people to the market, but she couldn't remember which day.
We go on Wednesdays and Saturdays. I'll need to take some details for the booking sheet. Could I start with your name?
Heather Nowakowski. It's a Polish name, my late husband's. N-O-W-A-K-O-W-S-K-I.
Nowakowski, thank you. That's one of the longer ones I've typed this week. Now, which day would suit you? Wednesday or Saturday?
Saturday, I think. No, wait. Saturdays are when my daughter rings from Perth, because of the time difference. Wednesday, please. I'd much rather miss the market than miss her.
Wednesday it is, then. And the destination is Brimley Market, I take it? We also stop at the retail park on the way back, if you need anything from there.
Just the market. I want to buy some fish, and some of that sourdough that everyone talks about. Do you need my address for the pick-up?
Please. We collect from the door, so I need the exact house.
It's number 41, Ash Grove. Oh, no, I always say that. We lived at 41 for thirty years, and I've been at 14 for only two. It's 14 Ash Grove, I promise.
Fourteen, Ash Grove. Good. We'll collect at quarter past nine. Is that all right?
A quarter past nine is rather early for me. What's the latest you could pick me up?
The bus has other stops to make, so quarter past is the earliest, but I can say a quarter to ten, which would be 9.45. That would still give you nearly two hours at the market.
9.45 is much better. I can finish my tea and my crossword. And how long do I get?
The return leaves the market at half past twelve, so that's 12.30, and you'd be home before one. The driver waits for everyone, so you won't be left behind, but please be at the stop by twenty past.
That's plenty of time. How much is it?
It's a flat fare of £3.50 for the return trip. It used to be £4, but the council gave us a grant in the spring, so we've been able to lower it. You pay the driver, in cash or by card.

That's less than I'd pay for the taxi in one direction. I'll be telling everyone. Now, there's something else. I have a walking frame, and I'll need it for the market, because the cobbles are dreadful. Does the bus take that?

Of course. The minibus has a ramp and a folding rail, and the driver will stow the frame beside you. I'll write it down, walking frame, so he knows what to expect. If you had a wheelchair we'd need a bit more notice, but a frame is no trouble.
Thank you. And is it all right if I bring someone? My neighbour, Mrs Ellery, would love to come, but she's shy about asking.
Certainly. The bus takes twelve, and there are only five booked for Wednesday. I'll book Mrs Ellery as well, if you'll give me her surname. Though if she'd prefer to ring up herself, that's fine too.

Oh, I'll tell her myself. She'll be much happier if it's a surprise that I'm taking her along. She lost her husband last winter, and she hardly goes out. So put me down as travelling with my neighbour.
Will do. A neighbour, travelling with you. And I'll note the first-time passenger discount, which means the neighbour pays half price. Don't forget to tell her.
How kind. And do I get anything to say the booking is made? I'm afraid I'd forget it by tonight.
I'll read you your booking reference, and you can write it down. It's TW4471. That's T-W-4-4-7-1. If you ring up to change anything, just quote that number and we'll find you straight away.
TW4471. Thank you, Gareth. I've written it on the back of my hand, so I'll have to be careful in the washing-up.
What happens if I'm not quite ready? I'm not as quick on the stairs as I was, and I'd hate to hold everybody up.

Don't worry about that. The driver will wait five minutes at each house, and he's used to it. Most of our passengers take a little longer than they expect, and nobody minds. If you really are delayed, ring the office, and we'll tell him.
That should do it. The driver will ring your doorbell when he arrives, so you don't need to wait outside. And if there's any change in the weather, we'll telephone you the evening before.
You've been very kind. Much better than the pizza people.
Our pleasure. We'll see you on Wednesday, Heather.

Good evening, everyone, and thanks for coming out on such a cold night. For those I haven't met, I'm Isobel Calloway, the coordinator of Doorstep Check-in. I'd like to explain how the scheme works, answer the questions I know you have, and then talk through some situations that tend to come up, because they're the part that new volunteers worry about most.

Let me start with how often you'll call. When we launched, the plan was for every volunteer to ring their person every day, and I suppose we thought it would be rather lovely. Within a month we had volunteers who were tired and clients who were feeling watched, so we changed it. Now, each volunteer rings twice a week, at a time you agree together, and keeps to that time. Predictability matters more than frequency. If someone knows you'll ring on Tuesday and Friday at eleven, they're much more likely to be ready to talk.

Now, what if nobody answers? Please don't panic, and please don't go straight to the emergency services. Most of the time, the person has gone to the shops or is in the bath. Leave it for half an hour, then try again. If there's still no reply, ring the contact person on their sheet, usually a relative or neighbour, and ask whether they know anything. Only if that doesn't help do we start to think about a welfare visit, and that decision isn't yours to take alone. You'll ring me, and I'll decide.

A word about money, because it comes up every winter. You must never take or hold anybody's bank card, and you must never ask to borrow money, however good your reason. But we do know that sometimes a volunteer picks up a pint of milk for somebody on the way past. You may carry up to £10 for that, provided you keep the receipt and hand over the change at once. Anything more than that, ring the office first.

Looking after you is just as important as looking after them. Some of the conversations will be upsetting, and I don't want any of you carrying them home alone. So there's a group meeting on the first Thursday of every month, at the library, where you can talk about how things are going, with biscuits. It's confidential, and I'll be there. There's no individual supervisor, I'm afraid, because we haven't the money, but there is the group, and my phone.

Finally, when can you begin? Some of you were hoping to start next week. I'm sorry, but all volunteers need a police check before they speak to anyone, and it takes about three weeks. I'll help you fill in the form tonight. As soon as the check comes back, you can start. You won't need a first aid course, though we run one every spring if you'd like to take it.

Right, let's look at some situations. I'll go through five that have actually happened. The first is when the person sounds confused. Perhaps they ask what day it is three times in a conversation, or they mention a visitor who couldn't possibly have come. You are not a doctor, and it isn't your place to diagnose anything. But please do tell me the same day. Don't wait until your next call. A sudden change can be a sign of an infection or something else treatable, and the sooner somebody knows, the better.

The second is when they ask about medication. They might say a tablet is making them dizzy and ask whether they should stop taking it. This is the one situation in which it's tempting to be helpful. Please don't be. Whatever you say may be wrong, and the consequences could be serious. The right answer is always to suggest they speak to their GP, or the pharmacist, and offer to remind them to do it on your next call.

Third, sometimes a person says they don't want the calls any more. It may feel like failure, but it isn't. They have every right to say no. Don't try to talk them round, and don't ring again to check. Thank them, accept the decision, and let the office know, so that we can close the file gently. Occasionally, they change their minds in a few months, and the door is always open.

Fourth, and this is much more urgent. If someone tells you they've just fallen, or that they're in pain, or that they can't get up, ring 999 straight away, and then ring me. Don't ask whether they would like you to. Don't wait to see if they're all right. If you're unsure, ring. Nobody has ever been criticised in this scheme for calling an ambulance that turned out not to be needed.

And finally, the situation you'll meet most often. The person is upset about something that isn't an emergency, perhaps a family argument, or a daughter who hasn't phoned, or a friend who has died. There's no trick to this. You don't need to fix it, and you shouldn't offer advice. Just stay on the line and listen, and let them talk for as long as they need. In fact, that's the single most valuable thing you'll do. Shall we take some questions?

Come in, all three of you, and find a chair, if you can. I've cleared most of that pile. Right, your survey of people who live alone. I've read the outline twice, and I'd like to start with the concept, because I think it's the foundation of everything. How are you defining your group?
We've defined it as people over sixty-five who live on their own, whether or not they feel lonely. We're deliberately separating the two.
Good. Say a bit more about why.

Because living alone isn't the same as being lonely. When we started reading, we'd assumed that anyone who lived alone must be lonely, but a lot of people said they love their independence. And some people who live with others are very lonely.

Precisely. Living alone is a fact about your household. Loneliness is a feeling. The two overlap, but they aren't the same, and you must not slip into treating them as if they were. Make that clear in the introduction. Now, Keiko, you chose the measure, I think?
Yes. I looked at several, and in the end I recommended the three-item loneliness scale. The longer one has twenty questions, and the older participants might find it tiring, especially on the phone.
So shorter, for the respondents' sake. And it's well established, I assume?
It's been validated in large national surveys. So we don't need to prove that it works, only to use it correctly.
Good. Don't be tempted to add your own questions to it, or you'll lose that validation. Now, recruitment. How did you plan to find people?
The original plan was to go through community centres and lunch clubs. We've got contacts at three of them.

I'd worry about that. People who go to a lunch club are by definition not at the most isolated end. The people you most want to reach are the ones who never leave the house. I'd suggest approaching the library's home delivery service. They already visit people who can't get out, and they may be willing to pass on your information sheet.
That's brilliant. We hadn't thought of that. The library is only two streets from the university, so it wouldn't be hard to arrange.
We've also been wondering about numbers. We'd like around sixty responses, but we don't know how many people to approach.

Assume that perhaps one in three will reply, which is typical for a mailed request to older adults, so you should approach about two hundred. It sounds like a lot, but it would be worse to end up with twelve. And do offer them a choice of replying by post, by phone or online, because some will have no internet.
That's a good point. We'd been planning on a web form, which would have shut out exactly the people we want.
Good. Now, you piloted the interviews. How did that go?

Very well, except that they took far longer than we expected. We'd planned for fifteen minutes and some ran to an hour. People wanted to talk. One man told us about his wife for nearly the whole time.
That's data in itself, though you may find it hard to use. It brings me to the ethics. What will you do if someone becomes upset during a call?

We've talked about that. We'd stop the interview, of course, and ask whether they'd like to continue. But we're not counsellors, so we've prepared a short leaflet with the numbers of two support services, which we'll post to everyone, whether or not they're upset.

Posting it to everyone is a good idea, because nobody is singled out. Make sure the information sheet says that at the beginning, so that people know what to expect. Next, the limitations. What will you say about the weaknesses of your study?
We were wondering about the scale. It's only three questions. Is that a weakness?

Not really. It's a recognised instrument, and I'd rather you didn't apologise for it. The real weakness is who won't take part. If somebody is very lonely, they may well be the very person who declines to answer. Say so plainly, and say what it might do to your results. That's the first thing.
And also that we're only sampling one town, so we can't claim our results would hold elsewhere.
Exactly, that's the second. What about the interviewing itself? Is it all done by one person?
Yes, Keiko is doing most of the calls. We thought that might be a limitation, because the results depend on one voice.
I'd say the opposite. One interviewer means the questions are asked in the same way each time, and that's actually a strength. Mention it as such.
Great. I'd rather present it as a strength.
Now, let's settle who's doing what, so that nobody is surprised in three weeks. Priya, you're keen on the ethical side, I know.
I'd like to write the ethics statement, yes. I've already read the university guidance. And I'll do the information sheet, if Tom can't.
I'd rather do the sheet, actually. I did a similar one for my work placement. What I'd really like to avoid is the literature review. Could Keiko do that? She knows the scale better than any of us.
I'm happy to. But then someone else has to contact the library, because I'm hopeless on the phone, which is awkward given the survey.
I'll do the library as well. I've got a contact there already.

Then it's settled. Priya, the ethics statement. Tom, the information sheet, and the contact with the library. And Keiko, the literature review. I'll look forward to the draft, and do remember the leaflet.

Good afternoon. Today I'd like to talk about a subject that sounds simple and turns out not to be: people who live alone. In many wealthy countries, close to three households in ten now contain a single person, and the proportion has been rising for decades. It would be easy to assume that these people are lonely, and that is exactly the assumption I'd like to challenge, because it leads to bad policy.

Let's start with definitions, which matter more than you might think. The psychologists Daniel Perlman and Letitia Peplau defined loneliness in 1981 as the distressing experience that arises when there is a gap between the contact people want and their actual contact. Notice that the definition is about a gap. Two people can have identical social lives, and one can feel lonely while the other feels perfectly content. Social isolation is different. It's an objective condition, measured by something like the number of contacts a person has in a week. You can be isolated without feeling lonely, and you can be lonely in a crowd.

Why does this matter? Because of the health evidence, which is now considerable. The most cited study is a meta-analysis by Julianne Holt-Lunstad and her colleagues, published in 2010. They combined the results of 148 separate studies, covering more than three hundred thousand people, who had been followed for an average of seven and a half years. Those with stronger social relationships had a 50 per cent greater likelihood of survival than those with weaker ones. That's a very large effect.

To put it in perspective, the authors compared it with other well-known risks. They concluded that the influence of poor social relationships on the risk of death was comparable to that of smoking up to 15 cigarettes a day, and larger than that of obesity or physical inactivity. You'll often see that comparison in headlines, and it's worth being careful. It's an observational finding, which means we can't be certain about cause and effect. People who are ill may become isolated, as well as the other way round. But the pattern has been found again and again.

One more complication. It is often said that loneliness is a problem of old age, but that is not what the surveys show. In a large BBC survey in 2018, people aged 16 to 24 reported feeling lonely more often than people over 75. There are good reasons. Young adults move to new cities, change jobs, and compare themselves with other people online, while many older people have built up friendships over a lifetime and, crucially, have chosen how much company they want. So when we talk about people who live alone, we should resist the picture of an elderly widow, because it is only one of many possible people.

Governments have noticed. In the United Kingdom, a commission set up in memory of the MP Jo Cox reported in 2017 that loneliness affected millions of people, and the government responded by appointing the world's first minister for loneliness, in 2018. Japan followed in 2021, having already grappled with the phenomenon called kodokushi, lonely deaths, in which people die at home and are not found for weeks. Whatever one thinks of the idea, it shows that the problem has moved from private sadness to public policy.

So what actually helps? One approach used in the National Health Service is social prescribing. A doctor who meets a patient with no medical problem, but a great deal of loneliness, doesn't write a prescription for tablets. Instead the doctor refers the patient to a link worker, who spends time finding out what the person likes and then helps them find a choir, a walking group or a gardening club. Early evaluations are encouraging, though the evidence is still thin, and a lot depends on whether the activities exist in the first place.

Another idea comes from Australia, where in the 1990s the Men's Shed movement began. Older men, in particular, often don't enjoy a coffee morning, and they're less likely to ask for help. But a workshop with tools, where you can repair a lawnmower or build a bird box, offers something to do with your hands, and conversation arrives as a by-product. The movement has since spread to many other countries, and the key lesson is that men talked more when they were standing side by side than when they were sitting face to face.

Which brings me to my final point. The most successful schemes seem to be those where participants are not treated only as recipients of help. Someone who lives alone may have decades of skills and stories, and what they often lack is a reason to share them. Schemes that turn clients into volunteers, so that they teach, repair, cook or simply keep watch over somebody else, tend to do better than those that offer a visitor and nothing else. Giving, it turns out, is a good cure for the feeling of being useless.

To conclude, living alone is a household fact, not a diagnosis. The aim of policy should not be to move people into shared homes, but to make sure that those who want contact can find it, and that those who value their solitude are left in peace. In the seminar this week, we'll look at how you might design a survey that tells the two groups apart. Please bring the reading on measurement scales, and bear in mind the point about gaps.
Lowther Window Furnishings. If it's about the sale, yes, it's still on until Sunday.

Not the sale, I'm afraid, though I wouldn't say no to a discount. I need blackout blinds for a bedroom. I work nights, and I sleep in the daytime, which means I've spent the last three months pinning a bath towel over the window.
That's more common than you'd think. We fit a lot of blinds for nurses and bus drivers. Are you looking for a measuring visit, or would you like to hear the options first?
The options first, please, then a visit. Do you want my details now, or at the end?
Let's do them now, and I'll fill in the enquiry sheet while we talk. What's your surname?
Ainsworth. A-I-N-S-W-O-R-T-H. People always want to put an E in the middle.
Ainsworth, no E. And which room are the blinds for? Your main bedroom?

Not the front one. That looks out on a street lamp, and there's a bus stop right underneath, so I moved into the back bedroom last winter. It faces the garden, but it gets the sun from about seven in the morning, which is exactly when I'm going to bed.
The back bedroom, then. Have you measured the window? We'll check it properly, of course, but a rough width helps me choose the right options.
I did it last night, with the kitchen tape. I think it's 110 centimetres. Hang on, let me look at my note. No, I wrote 112. I'd forgotten that the frame sticks out a little at one side.

112 is what I'll put down, and the fitter will measure it again anyway. Now, the type of blind. A lot of people think about Roman blinds, because they look soft, and with a blackout lining they work well. But the lining is thick, and the blind never quite lies flat.
I like the look of Roman blinds, but I'm not sure I want fabric that heavy in a bedroom. What's the alternative?

A roller blind with a blackout fabric. It's thinner, it's cheaper and it's easier to keep clean, and honestly it blocks light better, because the fabric is coated on the back. It's the one most of our night-shift customers pick.
Roller, then. That sounds more sensible. What colours do you do?
The popular ones are cream, grey and charcoal. Cream is lovely in a living room, but in a bedroom it lets a faint glow through, so I'd choose a darker shade.
I was going to say cream, because it's a small room and I wanted it to look bright. But if the dark one really does work better, then charcoal. I don't need to look at it when I'm asleep.

Charcoal it is. Now, here's the thing most people don't know. Even a perfect blind leaves a thin line of light down each side, and your brain notices it. We can add channels along both sides of the window, which are narrow tracks the blind runs in, and they close that gap completely. It's an extra, but I'd recommend them.
The line of light is exactly what I've been fighting with the towel. Yes, put the channels on. What does all this cost?
For a 112 centimetre window, in charcoal, with side channels, it's £89 fitted. The blind alone would have been £65, so the channels cost £24, and the fitting is free this week.
£89 is better than I feared. Does that include the old curtain rail coming down?
It does. The fitter will take it down and leave it in the garage, or take it away if you prefer. When would you like us to come and measure? We have a visit free on Monday afternoon, or on Tuesday.
I'm on shift on Monday night, so I'll be asleep in the afternoon, if I'm lucky. Tuesday would be better, because it's my first night off.
Tuesday is fine. We have a slot at 10, or at 2.30. Which do you prefer?
Ten is when I'm just getting to sleep, so definitely the afternoon. 2.30 would suit me very well.
2.30 on Tuesday, then. The fitter is called Mo, and he'll ring from outside, so you don't have to listen for the doorbell. And I'll need your postcode, so that he can find you.
It's HX3 8RW. That's H-X-3, then 8-R-W. The house is the one with the green door, next to the bus stop that kept me awake.
HX3 8RW, and a green door. Lovely. You'll get a text this evening to confirm, and the blinds will be ready about ten days after the visit. And do you want to put the towel away before then?
I'll keep it up until the day. It's the one thing that works. Cheers, that's been really useful.
You're welcome, Mr Ainsworth. Sleep well, whenever you do it.

Good evening, everybody, and welcome to St Aldric's, even if some of you have been working here for years and have simply never been shown this part of the building. I'm Rhys Pritchard, one of the occupational health nurses, and I'm here to tell you about the new Night Rest Room, which opens tonight. I'll explain why we built it, how to use it, and where everything is.

First, why. You might assume it came from a staff request for somewhere quiet to eat, and we did get plenty of those. But the real reason was a survey we ran in the spring. A worrying number of night staff said they'd felt too tired to drive home at least once in the past month, and two people reported a near miss on the ring road. The hospital decided it wasn't acceptable that people who look after patients all night should put themselves at risk on the journey home.

Now, the nap. You're allowed up to forty minutes in the Rest Room during your break, but the advice from our sleep specialist is to aim for about 20 minutes. Anything much longer, and you may fall into deep sleep, and wake up groggy and slow, which is the opposite of what we want. So set an alarm. There's one built into each chair, and a volunteer will knock on the door if you haven't stirred.

You might expect to find beds. We debated it for a long time, and decided against, for the same reason. If you lie flat, in the dark, you're more likely to sleep too deeply. So the room has reclining chairs, with blankets and eye masks. You can put your feet up, and close your eyes, but it isn't quite a bedroom, and that's deliberate.

Something else new, and I hope you'll use it. If you finish a shift and don't feel safe to drive, ask at the front desk for a taxi voucher. There's no form, no judgement and no need to explain. Each person may have up to four a month. If you need more than four, please come and talk to us, because that tells us something about your rota.

A few house rules, because a shared room only works if everyone keeps to them. There is no booking. It's first come, first served, and there are eight chairs, so if the room is full, please try again in ten minutes rather than waiting by the door. Please don't eat in there, and please don't make phone calls, even whispered ones, because sound carries further than you think in a room that quiet. Visitors aren't allowed, however sleepy they look.

Now, the practical details. The room is cleaned every morning, between five and six, so please don't leave belongings there. If you need to keep something, use a locker. And do put your phone on silent, because there's a sign on the door, but nobody has ever noticed it.

Right, let's look at the map. I'll take you on a walk through the hospital in the order that you'd meet things on a night shift. We'll start at the main entrance, and the first thing you'll find, beside the main lifts, is the staff canteen. It's open all night, with hot meals until three, and soup and sandwiches after that. A lot of people say they never eat properly on a night shift, so please use it.

If you carry on past the lifts, down the long ground-floor corridor, you'll reach radiology and imaging at the far end. That's not for you, unless you're scanning someone, but it's where the original plans placed the Rest Room. We moved it because the corridor is noisy, with trolleys going past at all hours, and the machines hum.

So where is the Rest Room? It's tucked next to the chapel, on the ground floor, which is the quietest part of the building. People ask if it's sacred. It isn't, but the chapel's stained glass keeps the lights low in that corner, and nobody holds meetings there.

Your lockers are in the basement, beside the laundry. I know that's an unattractive place, but the lockers are big enough for a coat and a bag, and it's warmer than it sounds. Each locker takes a padlock, which you can borrow from the desk.

On the second floor, above radiology, there's one more new feature, a light room. It has a bank of very bright lamps, which you can sit under for twenty minutes at the start of a night shift, and it helps some people to feel more awake. We'll explain how that works in the next session.

And finally, my office, the occupational health suite, is opposite the pharmacy. The pharmacy is where you'd collect prescriptions, so there's a sign, and you'll see my name on the door. Please come and see me if you're struggling with your sleep, and don't wait until it feels like an emergency.

Hello, Ben, hello, Sofia. Sit down. I've been waiting for this one, partly because I spent ten years on night shifts myself, before I came to the university. Your study of sleep in night-shift nurses is something I know a good deal about. How did it go?
We managed to complete it, Dr Mahlangu, although the methods were more difficult than we expected. We'd planned to use four different measures, and every one of them had a problem.
That's not unusual. Take them one at a time.

We started with the wrist monitors, the ones that detect movement. The idea was to wear them for two weeks, but several nurses said they were uncomfortable at night. They kept waking up because of the strap.

The sleep diary was my job. In theory, you write down when you went to bed, when you woke, and how well you slept. In practice, the nurses were so tired that they kept forgetting to fill it in, and some completed a whole week's entries in one go, on the last day.
Which isn't reliable, for obvious reasons. People's memory of how they slept three days ago is very poor. What about the sleepiness scale?

We used the Karolinska Sleepiness Scale, where you choose a number from one to nine. The trouble is that people use it differently. One nurse's six might be another nurse's four, so it was hard to compare them.
That's a known weakness of any self-rating scale, and you should say so. And the interviews?
Those were interesting, but they took too long. Each one ran to nearly an hour. We'd expected twenty minutes. And transcribing them took us a month.
Well, that's the price of rich data. Now, tell me about your participants. Why did you choose twelve nurses from the same ward?

We wanted everyone to be on the same rota, so that the pattern of nights was identical. If we mixed wards, we'd have people doing two nights, or five, or a mixture of day and night, and we wouldn't know what we were comparing.
That makes sense. It's a sound reason. And what about the number? Twelve is small.
We know. We were worried it might be too small to show anything at all.

It's not that small. For a study with this much detail, per person, it's quite respectable. You won't be able to claim that your results apply to all nurses, but you can describe what happened in this group very well, and that's what you're doing. Be modest in the conclusions.
One problem came up that we hadn't planned for. Several nurses took naps during their breaks, usually twenty or thirty minutes. We didn't know whether to count them as sleep.
What did you decide?
We asked the nurses to record the naps in their diaries, as separate entries. So we can look at the main sleep and the naps separately, or add them together.
Excellent. It's much better than leaving them out, because that would hide something real. Now, about your analysis. What have you done with the diaries?
At the moment, we've worked out the average hours of sleep across the whole fortnight, for each nurse.

I'd change that. An average hides the thing that matters most in shift work, which is the pattern. What you really want to compare is the sleep after the first night shift with the sleep after the last night shift in a run. Many studies find that people sleep fine after the first night, but get steadily shorter sleeps as the nights pile up. If you find that, it's a real result.
We could do that easily. We have the dates.
There was one thing we noticed that we couldn't explain. Two of the nurses seemed to cope far better than the others. They slept well in the daytime and reported hardly any sleepiness on the scale.

That's very common. People differ in what we call chronotype, which is whether they're naturally a morning person or a night owl. A night owl on a night rota may do rather well, and a lark may suffer badly. If you asked about chronotype, you can say that individual differences may explain some of the variation. If you didn't, say that too, and suggest that future studies should.
We didn't ask, so we'll mention it as a gap.

Honest and useful. Also, in the ethics section, make clear how you protected the nurses. The ward manager will be reading this, and nurses worry about being identified as the one who falls asleep at work.
We used numbers instead of names, and the ward manager has only seen the group results.
Good. Now, your conclusions. I'd like to hear what you're going to recommend.
We've got three ideas. A quiet place for naps at work, a limit on the number of nights in a row, and free blackout curtains for staff who've moved to nights.
We also thought about serving hot food in the middle of the night, because some of the nurses said they couldn't eat properly. And Ben wanted to suggest a later finish.
Let me be the voice of caution. You can only recommend what your data supports. Did you collect any information about curtains?
No, only what the nurses said in the interviews. So that's not evidence.
