Then leave it out, or mention it as an idea for further work. The same goes for the food and the finish time. But the other two have real support. The nurses with a place to nap said they felt less tired, and your diaries show that the sleep was shorter after four or more nights in a row. Those are the two I'd put in the conclusion.
That's a relief. Two clear recommendations are easier to write than five.

Good morning. Last week we looked at why sleep matters. This week I want to ask what happens when people are required to sleep at the wrong time, which is the situation for roughly one worker in five in many countries. To understand why night work is so hard, we need to begin with the body clock.

For a long time, scientists believed the human body clock ran on a cycle of about twenty-five hours. In 1999, a team led by Charles Czeisler at Harvard tested this more carefully, by keeping volunteers in dim light for weeks. They found that the average was much closer to 24.2 hours. That tiny difference matters a great deal. It means that left to itself, the body clock drifts later each day, which is why most of us find it easier to stay up late than to get up early.

Of course, we don't drift, because the clock is reset every day by cues from the environment. The strongest of these is light, and the technical term for such a cue is a zeitgeber, which comes from the German for time giver. Light reaching the eyes in the morning shifts the clock earlier, while light in the evening shifts it later. Other cues, like meal times and exercise, matter too, but they're weaker.

Two signals from the clock are worth knowing. Melatonin, the hormone that signals night to the body, starts to rise in the evening, a couple of hours before habitual bedtime, as long as the lights are dim. And core body temperature falls during the night, reaching its lowest point about 2 hours before you normally wake. That's the moment when alertness is at its worst, which is why a night-shift worker is most likely to make a mistake at around four or five in the morning.

Now, what does this do to health? The evidence is not simple, but it's worrying. In 2007, the International Agency for Research on Cancer, part of the World Health Organization, classified shift work that involves circadian disruption as probably carcinogenic to humans, in its Group 2A. The agency reviewed the evidence again in 2019 and kept the classification. I should stress that the absolute risk is small, and that it's based mostly on studies of nurses and flight attendants. Shift work has also been linked to a higher risk of type 2 diabetes, and to heart problems.

So what can people do? Let me start with the rota. The best evidence suggests that if shifts must rotate, they should rotate forward, from mornings to afternoons to nights, rather than backward. Why? Because a forward rotation asks the body to stay up later, which fits with its natural drift. A backward rotation asks it to sleep earlier than it wants to, which is much harder.

Before the second strategy, a word about individual differences. People have different chronotypes, which means different natural preferences for when to sleep. Roughly speaking, there are morning types, evening types and a large group in between. Evening types tend to adapt to night work more easily, while morning types often struggle. This is partly genetic, and it changes with age, so a person who coped well with nights at twenty-five may find them harder at fifty. Employers who understand this can offer a choice, which makes a real difference to people's health.

I should also tackle a popular belief, that the blue light from phone screens is the main cause of sleep problems. Blue-enriched light does suppress melatonin more than warm light, and that finding is solid. But the brightness and the timing of light matter at least as much as its colour, and most studies of phones show a modest effect. So the advice to put your phone down is sensible, but the larger gains come from controlling the bright light you meet on the way home and in the bedroom.

Second, the nap. In the 1990s, NASA researchers led by Mark Rosekind studied long-haul pilots. Pilots allowed a planned nap of up to 40 minutes, with an average of 26 minutes' sleep, improved their performance by 34 per cent, and their alertness by 54 per cent, compared with pilots who had no nap. That's a striking result, and it's the basis of much of the advice we give now. But notice the length. Short naps avoid the grogginess I mentioned.

Third, caffeine. Coffee works, but its effects last longer than people realise. The half-life of caffeine is about 5 hours, which means that half of the caffeine from a cup drunk at midnight is still in your blood at five in the morning. So the advice is to drink it early in the shift, and to stop several hours before you want to sleep.

Fourth, consistency. Researchers speak of anchor sleep, an idea developed by Minors and Waterhouse in the 1980s. The principle is that, even on days off, you should keep the same 4 hours of sleep every day, at the same time, for example from eight in the morning until noon. It means your body clock isn't whipped back and forth every weekend, and it's more realistic than expecting people to keep a full night schedule on days off.

Finally, light on the way home. When you finish a night shift at seven, the morning sun tells your clock it's time to wake up, which is exactly wrong. So many sleep specialists recommend wearing sunglasses on the drive or walk home, then going straight into a dark bedroom. It's a very cheap intervention, and quite effective. Next time we'll turn to what employers can do, since individual tricks can only go so far.
Hello, is this the right place to ask about Saturday mornings? Because the website says one thing, and the club's Facebook page says another, and I've given up guessing.
Ah, you've found our little problem. This is Ridgeway Cricket Club, and I'm Dougal, the junior secretary. I do apologise for the confusion. Is it junior cricket you're asking about?
It is. My son has just discovered that his friends all play, and now he wants to join. I'm Farah Haddad, by the way.
Pleased to meet you, Farah. Shall I take his details for the registration form? It's easier than explaining it all twice.
Please. I'll spell my surname, because it throws people. H-A-D-D-A-D.
Haddad, got it. And your son's first name?
Idris. I-D-R-I-S. He's eight. Would that put him in the Under 8s? Or is that for the really little ones?

Not quite. Our groups are named after the age limit, so the Under 8s are children aged seven and younger. An eight-year-old goes into the Under 9s. He'll be one of the younger ones in the group, which is no bad thing, because they learn fast from the bigger children.
And the website says sessions start at ten o'clock, but Facebook says nine. Which is right?

Neither, I'm afraid, and that's my fault. The website hasn't been changed since last season. The Facebook post was for the first week only, when the coaches wanted to start early. It's now half past nine, so 9.30, every Saturday, and it finishes at eleven.
9.30. And where do we go? The ground looks enormous.

There are two grounds, and everyone gets this wrong. The Upper Ground is for the seniors, and it has the proper pavilion. Juniors play on the Lower Ground, down the hill, past the tennis courts. It's the flat one, with the white fence. If you can see the sea, you've gone too far.
The Lower Ground, then. Thank you. How much does it cost?

The season fee is £45. But if you pay before the first of April, it comes down to £38, which is what most families do. And it includes a bat, a ball and a club shirt, which Idris will get on the first day.
I'll pay before April. That's very reasonable. What else does he need to bring?

We lend helmets and pads, and bats too, so the only thing he really must bring is a sun hat. The coaches are very strict about that, because the ground has no shade. A water bottle is useful, but there's a tap by the pavilion.
A sun hat, I can manage. One thing I should mention is that Idris has asthma. It's mild, but he sometimes needs his inhaler when he runs.

Thank you for telling me. I'll put it on the form, and I'll tell the coach, who'll keep his inhaler in the first-aid bag, if you'd like that. A lot of the children carry their own, and it's quite normal here.
I'd like him to carry it, if that's allowed. What do you need from me, as a parent?

Well, the club depends on parents. We usually ask each family to do something on a Saturday morning, once or twice a season. Some people help with the barbecue, some help put out the stumps, and some do the scoring.
I don't know much about cricket. I'm not sure I'd be any good at scoring. Is it complicated?
It looks it, but we teach you in ten minutes, and the scorebook has a guide in the front. Honestly, parents who've never watched a match are often the best, because they concentrate.
All right, then, put me down for scoring. I might regret it, but I'll learn.
Wonderful. Now, how would you like to pay the fee? We accept cash, or a bank transfer, or you can set up a direct debit, which splits it into three payments.
Splitting it is easier for us. A direct debit, please.
What happens if it rains? I've seen the sky over there, and I don't trust it.

If the ground is unfit, the coaches decide by eight o'clock on Saturday morning, and a message goes to the parents' group chat. You'll be added to it when you register. If you don't use that sort of thing, tell me, and I'll put you on the list for text messages instead. We try never to leave a family standing at the gate in the drizzle.
A group chat is fine, as long as nobody expects me to answer quickly.

Nobody ever does. Mostly it's photos of the children looking muddy, and the occasional lost sock. One more thing. We take photos for the club newsletter. If you'd rather Idris wasn't in them, just tell the coach, and we'll make sure he's not in the pictures.
I'll email you the form tonight, and the coach will contact you on Thursday. And please do correct us on the website, if you find it's still wrong. I'd be glad of someone who actually reads it.
I will. Thank you, Dougal, you've been very patient.

Right, let's get started, because the climbing wall opens in twenty minutes and I can see exactly where half of you are heading. I'm Mereana Pene, the manager of the Kauri Park Sports Hub, and welcome to our open day. I want to tell you what's different about this place, explain a few rules, and then show you around.

First, money. Everything today is free, and I've seen a few raised eyebrows. Normally, a taster session costs £2, which is cheap, but it's still more than some families want to risk on a sport they might not like. So we waive it today, and we waive it for the first visit all year. After that, the sessions are on a membership, or pay as you go.

How are sessions organised? Many clubs separate people by age, and others by ability, so you get a top team and a bottom team. We've deliberately done neither. At the hub, sessions are grouped by activity only. If you want to play basketball on a Tuesday evening, you play basketball with whoever turns up, whether they're fifteen or fifty, and whether they play like a professional or a beginner. It's chaotic sometimes, but people say it's the reason they keep coming.

A bit of news. Last year, we received a lottery grant. A few of you will remember that we spent some of it on a new hoist for the pool, but that was actually from an earlier grant. This year's money has bought a set of lightweight sports wheelchairs, which anyone can borrow. They're not just for people who use wheelchairs in daily life. Plenty of people try wheelchair basketball for the first time, and it's a fantastic workout, and humbling for the able-bodied.

Now, something that's become one of our most popular sessions. The quiet hour is on Sunday mornings, from eight until nine. The lights are lowered, the music is off, and there are no whistles. It was designed for people who find noise and crowds overwhelming, including autistic children and adults, but plenty of other people come because they like it. Don't come on Saturday morning looking for it, because that's our busiest time, and it's loud.

What about our coaches? Everyone who coaches here, volunteer or paid, has to complete a one-day inclusion workshop in the first month. They already have first aid certificates, and many have coaching qualifications. But the workshop teaches them to adapt a session so everyone can join in, which is a different skill. It was so successful that the council now sends its own staff.

A few practical points before we move. Parking is limited, so if you can, please walk or take the bus. The number 7 stops right outside the main entrance, and the driver will lower the ramp for anyone who needs it. If you do drive, the car park by the tennis courts has the most spaces, and there are six marked bays beside the entrance for blue badge holders. Please keep those clear, even if you're only stopping for a minute.

Let's go through the site. I'll start at the car park, because that's where most of you arrived. Right beside the car park entrance is the registration desk. Please collect a wristband there. It tells the coaches which session you've chosen, and, if you want, whether you need any support. There's no need to explain, but it helps.

Now walk into the building, and you'll reach the main hall. At the very back of it, past the badminton courts, is the area we've marked out for wheelchair sport. The floor there is smooth, with no lines to confuse the chairs, and there's plenty of space to turn. Our coach, Dev, runs a session there at eleven.

Upstairs, on the first floor above reception, is the quiet room. It isn't the same as the quiet hour. It's open all day, and anyone can go and sit for a few minutes if they feel overwhelmed. You'll find beanbags, soft lighting and a volunteer who won't ask any questions. Some people use it to take a break, and some use it to change into their kit in peace.

The climbing wall is through the double doors beside the gym. Please don't go through the squash courts, because they're being resurfaced, and the way is blocked. The wall has routes of every grade, from very easy to very hard, painted in different colours, and the instructor can adjust the harness for anyone. It's the most popular thing on the programme today, so go early.

Finally, our Changing Places toilet. Many people don't know what this is. It's a large room, with a hoist and an adjustable bench, for people who can't use an ordinary accessible toilet. Ours is beyond the pool, at the end of the east corridor, and it's open all the time. The café, by the way, is opposite the main entrance, and the coffee is free today. Enjoy your visit, and please ask a volunteer in a blue shirt if you have any questions.

Come in, Rory, come in, Jess. Sorry, I'm just finishing an email that has been sitting there since Tuesday. Right. Your study of girls dropping out of community sport. I've read the draft of your methods, and I'd like you to talk me through what you found.
We surveyed girls aged fourteen to sixteen, and held three focus groups. The survey went to 150, and 62 replied.

That's about forty per cent, which is quite respectable for a survey of teenagers. People often get under thirty. I'd just say it plainly in the report, so that the examiner sees you know it's not perfect. Now, the findings. What did the girls say?

We gave them a list of reasons for giving up, and they ticked the ones that applied. The one picked most often was that their friends had left. Many of them said they only joined because their friends did, and once they went, there was no reason to stay.

The second, and this surprised us, was feeling judged. Not on how good they were, but on how they looked. Their kit, their bodies, what they looked like when they were red-faced and sweaty. Several girls said they'd stopped going because of boys watching from the other side of the park.
That fits what the national surveys show. And the others? Did cost matter?

It did for a few, but it was only fourth on the list. Coaching was third, mostly because a coach had only picked the best players. Exams were last, which surprised me, because everyone says that girls give up sport for schoolwork.
A nice finding. People assume it, but your data don't support it. Make a point of it. Tell me about the focus groups. Where did you hold them?

In a café, near the school, rather than at school. We thought the girls would be more honest if there were no teachers around. They really were. In the school, they said what they thought we wanted to hear, and in the café they said things like the changing rooms were embarrassing.
Excellent reasoning. Did you have any problems?
One group was dominated by a girl who'd had a bad experience. Everyone else seemed to agree with her, and we couldn't tell whether they really did or were just going along.

That's classic. A trick I like is to ask everyone to write their answer on a card first, before anyone speaks. Then you read them out, and the loudest voice can't set the tone. You could use that in the second round, if there's time.
We'll try that. Another thing. Rory wants to use one of the quotes in the introduction. It's a very striking one, from a girl who said she felt rubbish every time she walked on to the court.
It's a powerful line. But think about the ethics. Did she give permission for it to be used?
She agreed at the time, but she didn't see the actual wording.
Then check with her again, and take out anything that could identify her, such as the name of the club. I'd rather you used a gentler quote with full permission than a better one you can't defend.
Fair enough. We'll go back to her.

One thing worries me. We sent the survey through the school, so the girls who replied were all the ones who were still there. We haven't heard from the girls who left the school, or who didn't answer.

A good point, and you should raise it yourselves, as a limitation. Any survey like this has some voices missing, and you can't fix that now. What you can do is be honest about who they are. Say that your findings describe girls who stayed in contact with the school, and that those who had dropped out of everything may feel differently. And remember to keep the survey anonymous, as you promised. No names, no initials, and no tiny details that point to a single person.
We did that. The survey only asked for age and the sport they'd stopped.
Now, recommendations. What will you suggest to clubs?
We had a long list. Fifteen items, actually.

Too long. No club will read fifteen recommendations. Choose three or four, make them specific, and make them affordable, because most community clubs have almost no money. Avoid something like 'change the culture', which means nothing, and aim for something a volunteer could do on Saturday.
Right. We'll cut it down. We did find a few good examples, though, from the clubs we visited.
Tell me about those.

The netball club runs a social session once a week, with no ladder and no scores. They call it no-pressure netball, and the girls who'd dropped out of the competitive team said it was the only reason they were still playing.

The swimming club lets people join sessions whenever they can, rather than committing to a fixed night. A lot of the girls said that made it possible to keep going, because they had exams, or part-time jobs, or a sick relative to look after.

And the athletics club has what they call a bring-a-friend week, where members can invite someone for free. It helped with the friends problem, because the girls arrived together, and stayed together.

Those are lovely, and they link directly to your findings. Use them. A recommendation that comes with a real example is always more persuasive. Send me a new draft in two weeks, and keep the quotes short.

Good morning. I'd like to begin today with a hospital in Buckinghamshire. In the 1940s, Stoke Mandeville Hospital took in soldiers and civilians with spinal injuries, at a time when many doctors expected such patients to live only a few years. The neurologist in charge, Ludwig Guttmann, took a different view. He believed that sport, properly organised, belonged in the treatment itself, because it restored strength, but also confidence and a sense of purpose.

In 1948, Guttmann organised a small archery competition for wheelchair users at the hospital. It took place on 29 July, the very same day that the Olympic Games opened in London, and that was no coincidence. He was making a point, that for him sport was a central part of rehabilitation, not a reward for finishing it. Sixteen competitors took part, and from those beginnings the Stoke Mandeville Games grew. The first official Paralympic Games, with athletes from many countries, followed in Rome in 1960. So the idea that disabled people belong in sport is not new, but putting it into practice, at community level, is a different matter.

Let's look at the present. Sport England runs a large annual survey called Active Lives, and its results are consistent from year to year. Disabled people are roughly twice as likely to be inactive as non-disabled people. Similar gaps appear for women compared with men, for people from lower-income households, and for some ethnic minorities. Notice that these gaps haven't closed, even though facilities have improved in most places.

One explanation is that exclusion isn't usually deliberate. It's built into the way sport is organised. Think of a club that holds its sessions at seven in the evening, in a building up a flight of steps, with a fee that must be paid in a lump sum. No one meant to keep anyone out, but a worker on shifts, a wheelchair user and a parent with no spare cash are all excluded, without anyone saying a word.

A well-known example of changing the message came in 2015, when Sport England launched a campaign called This Girl Can. The research behind it had found that many women were put off by a fear of being judged, as we heard from the girls' study last week, and the campaign showed ordinary women, sweating and wobbling and enjoying themselves. It was often described as one of the most successful public campaigns of its kind, though measuring its true effect on activity is difficult, because many things were changing at once.

Now, what can a coach or a volunteer actually do? A practical tool is a framework called STEP, which is used in many coaching courses. The letters stand for space, task, equipment and people. If a game isn't working for someone, change one of the four. You can change the space, by making the court smaller. You can change the task, by removing the competition. You can change the equipment, by using a lighter ball. Or you can change the people, by putting players in different groups. It's simple, and the idea is that you adapt the activity, rather than expecting the person to adapt.

Another example is parkrun. The first event was held in Bushy Park, in south-west London, in October 2004, with just 13 runners and a handful of volunteers. It was free, it was timed, and nobody was left behind, because there's always a volunteer at the back, called a tail walker. Today there are events in many countries, and what it shows is that removing cost and removing pressure took away two of the barriers I mentioned earlier. It also let walkers and runners share the same course, which is rare.

I'd like to say a word about sensory needs, which are often forgotten. A leisure centre can be a very hard place for a person who finds noise and bright light overwhelming. More and more venues now offer sensory-friendly sessions. They reduce noise by turning off the music, they stop the whistles, and they dim the lighting, and they cost almost nothing. For many families, it's the difference between a child coming to the pool and not coming at all.

A word on cost, because it's the barrier clubs find hardest to talk about. Fees, kit and travel can easily add up to several hundred pounds a year for a single child, and families rarely say that this is why they've stopped coming. They say that the child lost interest, or was too busy. Some clubs now offer a kit swap, where outgrown boots and shin pads are passed on for free. Others keep a quiet fund, so that nobody has to ask for help in front of the rest of the team. Neither idea is complicated, but both only work if they are offered discreetly.

Another thing worth knowing is that disabled sport has moved beyond the Paralympics. The Special Olympics, which began in the United States in 1968, was built around the idea that people with intellectual disabilities should be able to compete at their own level, in a spirit of friendly rivalry. Its founder, Eunice Kennedy Shriver, started with a summer day camp in her own back garden. Many local clubs now run unified sessions, where athletes with and without disabilities play side by side, in the same team, and I find that the most persuasive example of what inclusion could look like.

But I should end with a caution. Inclusion isn't the same as integration. It's possible to put a disabled child on a team and ignore her. Real inclusion means asking the participants what they want. That sounds obvious, but the evidence suggests that clubs rarely do. For next week's seminar, choose a local sport club, and write down three changes that you'd make, then consider who you would ask before making them.
Morning! Come in out of that wind, you'll be blown halfway to Ireland. Let me guess. It's the beach huts you're after. Everybody who comes to this window in May wants the huts.
Is it that obvious? Yes, it is. I've got a leaflet here, but it's a bit crumpled and I can't work out how the whole thing is meant to run. Do I just turn up and pick one?
Not quite, but it's easier than it looks. I'll fill in an enquiry form while we chat, and then I can see what's free. Can I take your name first?
It's Hector Pargeter.
And how do you write that?
P-A-R-G-E-T-E-R. Like the decorative plasterwork on old houses.
Pargeter, lovely. Right. When were you thinking of starting? The leaflet says the season runs from the middle of May.
That's what I'd hoped. I'd like a week at the end of May, if there is one.

Ah, I'm sorry, that leaflet is a year old. We had to move the opening because the council repainted the whole row this spring and it won't be dry until early June. The first hire day this year is Saturday 6 June. All the hires run from Saturday to Saturday.
Well, that's fine, then. Let's make it 6 June. Is it possible to have more than one week?
Yes, you can hire for as long as you like if the hut is free. How long were you planning to stay?
I was going to say two weeks, but my daughter and her children are coming over in the school holidays, so it might be better to have it for three. I think I'll go for three.
Three weeks from 6 June. That's a long time to have a sea view. Now, the huts come in four colours. Which would you like?
Blue, please. My granddaughter picked it out from the leaflet. She's seven, and she's quite particular.

Oh dear. The blue ones have all gone, I'm afraid, and they went in January. There are still white ones, a few yellow ones, and some in a sort of sage green that's actually very popular with people who don't want to stand out.
Hmm. I don't think she'll accept white, and yellow's too bright for me. Let me ask her. No, I'll decide, because I'm the one paying. I'll take the sage green.
Good choice. Now the price. For the weeks in June, it's £155 a week.
Oh. That's more than I expected. The leaflet says £140.

I know. I'm sorry. That's last year's price. There was a rise in April, and the leaflet really should have been thrown away. If you take three weeks, though, we take a little off the third week, and I'll put it on the invoice.
That's kind of you. And is there anything to pay on top?
Yes, a deposit for the key. It's £25, and you get it back when you return the key at the end of your hire. Don't lose it, because the replacement lock costs far more than that.
I'll tie it to something heavy. What's inside the hut?

A table, a shelf, a kettle, and two folding chairs. If you need more seats for the family, you can add deckchairs for £6 a week each. A few people hire a windbreak as well, which is useful on a day like this, but that's from the kiosk, not me.
I think we'll have the deckchairs. We're a family of five on the day they all come. Is there a gas stove, by any chance?
No, I'm afraid gas isn't allowed in the huts, because of the fire regulations. The kettle is electric, and there's a socket in every hut.
That's no problem. And what about the car?

There's a car park behind the sea wall, and you can't park on the front in summer. There's a permit that you can buy for a day or for a week. Most hirers choose the weekly one, which is £12 and works out much cheaper.
Then I'll take the weekly permit. I'll need one for each week, I suppose?
Yes, one for each. Now, which hut? Number 14 is free, and it's right next to the café, so you can get a hot drink without walking.
Hmm, that sounds convenient, but I've heard the café plays music all day, and the arcade is just beyond it. I'd really like somewhere a bit quieter, if there is one.

Then you want the far end, where the huts are away from all that. Number 31 is free for those weeks. At night you only hear the tide coming in, which some people find very soothing, and some people say keeps them awake.
I'll risk it. Number 31, then.
Lovely. Last thing. I need an address for the invoice. Where should it go?
It's 22 Kittiwake Lane, in Ludwell. Kittiwake is spelled K-I-T-T-I-W-A-K-E, like the bird.
Kittiwake Lane, Ludwell. Got it. You'll have a letter from us within a week, and then you can pay the first instalment by post or in person.
Wonderful. Thank you for sorting all that out so quickly.
My pleasure. Enjoy the sea air, Mr Pargeter. And mind that wind on the way out.

Hello, and a very warm welcome to Porthgwenna Lifeboat Station. I'm Verity. I've been a volunteer here for eleven years, and for the next forty minutes I'm your guide. Before we go in, I'll tell you a little about the building and the people who use it, and then we'll walk round together.

The first lifeboat here was launched in 1881, from a wooden shed across the harbour. You can still see the stone footings if you look across at low tide. The station moved to this side of the bay in 1962. A lot of people assume that the boathouse you're standing in dates from then, and for a long time it did. But in the winter of 1996, a storm took half the roof off, and the crew decided to rebuild the whole thing rather than patch it. The new boathouse opened in 1998, so it is younger than some of our crew.

Now, money. Visitors often ask whether we're paid by the government, and the answer is no. A government grant did help with the new roof, and the harbour authority lets us have the land for a very small rent. But the day-to-day costs, such as the training, the fuel, and the repairs, are met mostly by donations. The shop and the café are helpful, but together they bring in less than a fifth of what we spend. The rest comes from people's gifts, and from the legacies that some of them leave us in their wills.

A word about safety, because it matters. The crew are alerted by pagers, so there's no siren on the street. But there is a loud alarm in the boat hall as well, and if it goes off while you're here, please stay calm, and don't head for the exit. The crew will be coming in through the car park door and straight past you at a run. The safest thing is to go up the stairs to the viewing gallery, where you can watch the launch through the glass. We would far rather you watched than got in the way, and someone will tell you when it's safe to come back down.

The boat itself is launched by tractor. People sometimes ask why we don't simply slide it down the slipway, and I'll admit the boat is heavy, nearly seven tonnes, but that isn't the reason. The real reason is the tide. Here the sea goes out nearly three hundred metres across flat sand, and at low tide the slipway ends a long way short of the water. So the tractor pushes the boat out until it floats.

And what's new this year? We opened a children's room last spring, with a model boat that you can climb into, and that's been very popular. But the exhibit that people keep talking about is the new sound booth. You put on a pair of headphones and listen to recordings of real radio calls, made during rescues over the last thirty years. Some of them are quite moving. We played with a few ideas, including a wall of old crew photographs, but the voices were what everyone wanted.

Let me orient you, so that you don't lose each other. We're standing in the entrance hall. The ticket desk is on your left, and I know a lot of people think the shop is next to it. It isn't. The shop is just beside the main doors, on your right as you came in, so you can't miss it on the way out.

The café used to be opposite the boat hall, but we moved it two years ago, because the smell of toast was drifting into the hall where the boat is kept. It's now at the far end of the corridor that runs behind me. If you walk to the end, you'll see the door. The cakes are made by volunteers, and the scones are well worth trying.

The sound booth I mentioned is upstairs. When you get to the landing, you'll see it straight in front of you. It's small, and it only takes two people at a time, so don't be surprised if there's a queue on a busy day.

The first-aid point is directly below the viewing gallery, in the room with the green cross on the door. We have two trained first aiders on duty every day, and they are also members of the crew, so if the alarm goes off, there may be a short delay while they come out to help you.

And finally the toilets. There are some in the main building, but they're small, and they've had a few problems with the plumbing this week, so please use the accessible toilets in the separate block. You reach those from the car park. They're tucked away behind the tractor shed, so you have to walk round the side of the shed to find them. There's a signpost, but the wind has turned it round, so follow my directions rather than the sign.
If nobody has any questions, let me take you through to the boat hall, where you'll meet the boat, and then I'll introduce you to Bryn, who drives the tractor.
Come in, both of you, and shut the door against that draught. I read your outline over the weekend, but I'd rather you told me where you've got to. This is the sound-mapping project, yes?
That's right. The recording stage is finished and we're about to start writing up, so we wanted to check our approach with you first.
Especially the analysis. Shall I remind you why we picked Skelwick?
Please do. I remember something about the coastline.

We looked at three or four resorts. But we'd have needed a car to get from one site to another, and neither of us has one. Skelwick has a pier, a working harbour, a shingle beach and a promenade with an amusement arcade, all within about a kilometre. So we could record at all four on the same day, in the same weather, on foot.
The tourist office did say they'd like to see the results, but that wasn't the reason. It was about convenience, really.
Good. That's a sensible reason, and it makes your comparison fairer, because the weather is the same. Now, the equipment. How did you measure sound levels?
We used a decibel meter app on our phones, and a pair of small recorders for the audio.

Phone apps. Hm. I'm a little uneasy about that. They're fine for comparing one place with another, so long as you use the same phone every time, but the absolute numbers can be wrong by several decibels. If you present them as exact, someone will challenge you.
We did wonder. The engineering department has a properly calibrated meter that it lends out. I think we could borrow it for an afternoon and check our phones against it.

That's the answer. Check once, and report the difference in your methods. You don't need to repeat all the recordings, only apply a correction. Now, what went wrong while you were out there? Something always does.
Wind, mostly. On the pier it was blowing so hard that the first recording is mainly a roar, even with the furry covers on the microphones. We had to go back and repeat that one the next morning.

And people. You wouldn't believe how many stopped to ask what we were doing, and some of them started talking into the microphone. There's a lovely recording of a man telling us about his dog, but it's no use for the study.
Any problems with batteries, or rain?
No, we were lucky. It stayed dry, and we took spare batteries anyway. The tide didn't matter either, because the pier and promenade don't depend on it.
Good. Tell me about the survey.
We asked sixty visitors to rate each site on a scale from calm to unpleasant. We expected the ratings to follow the meter readings, so that the loudest place would be the least liked.
But they didn't. The harbour was the loudest by a long way, mostly because of the engines, yet people rated the arcade as the least pleasant, even though it was quieter.

That's interesting, and it's exactly the kind of result you should make something of. Loudness and annoyance aren't the same thing. People tolerate the sounds that fit the place, and a working harbour is supposed to be noisy. Now, what will you say about each site?

Let me start with the pier, since that's where we began. We expected the waves to dominate, but what we mostly recorded was the wind whistling in the railings. The gulls were there too, but they were quiet by comparison.
The harbour was easy. It's the boat engines, all day, from first light. There's a little traffic on the road beside it, but you can barely hear it over the engines.
On the shingle beach, the waves are what you hear. It's a lovely sound, a sort of rattle as the stones are pulled back. And there's almost nothing else, which is why people rated it calmest.
And the promenade is the arcade. We thought that the traffic would be the biggest sound there, because it's a busy road. But the machines drowned it out completely, even at ten in the morning.

Excellent. One more thing before we move on. In your outline you call the arcade unpleasant. Be careful with that word. It's the visitors' judgement, not yours, so quote the survey and keep your own opinion out of the results section.
Fair point. I think I was influenced by the headache I had on the Saturday afternoon.
He wore earplugs for most of the second day, which rather defeats the purpose of a sound study.
Then you can mention that in your reflection, with a smile, but not in the data. Now, about the report itself. You'll want to include your audio, I assume.
Yes, we've got some good clips. We were thinking of putting in a link to a recording from each site, perhaps a couple of minutes long.

Careful. The markers won't have time to sit through hours of audio, so keep each clip short, thirty seconds at most, and choose the stretch that shows your point best. Transcripts would be pointless, since you can't write down a sound. A link next to each table is plenty.
That makes it a lot easier. We were worried about the length of the whole thing.
Aim for the middle of the word limit, and put the calibration note in the methods, not an appendix. When can I see a draft?
The end of next week?
That suits me. Bring the draft, and bring a clip from the pier, because I would very much like to hear what that wind sounds like.
We'll bring the one we recorded on the second morning, not the first one.
Please do. Thank you both.

Hello again, everyone. For the next hour I want to turn our attention to a place that most of us associate with relaxation, the seaside, and ask a slightly odd question: what does it sound like, and why does that matter? Over the next hour I'll introduce the idea of the soundscape, look at where the sounds of the shore come from, and then consider how we might manage them.

First, the term itself. The word soundscape had been used occasionally by urban planners before, but it was in the 1970s that it became widely known, largely through the Canadian composer R. Murray Schafer and his colleagues. Schafer wanted people to listen to their surroundings as carefully as they look at them, and he proposed a simple vocabulary. He divided the sounds around us into three groups. Keynote sounds are the background ones that you stop noticing, like the hum of traffic in a city. Signals are the sounds that demand attention, such as bells or sirens. And the third group is what he called soundmarks, which are sounds so characteristic of a community that people would miss them if they disappeared.

Now let's apply that to the coast. At the seaside, the keynote sound is the surf. It is almost always there, and it's so constant that regular visitors often tell you they can't hear it any more. Signals might be a ship's horn or the cry of a lifeguard. Soundmarks are more local. For one town it could be the clock on the pier, for another it could be the bell that calls the fishing boats in, and I'll come back to one example in a moment.

Let me spend a few minutes on the sea itself, because it's less obvious than it seems. When a wave breaks, you might think that the roar comes from the water hitting the shore. In fact, most of the sound comes from air bubbles. As the wave breaks it traps air, and each bubble rings like a tiny bell as it forms and collapses. Add up millions of them each minute, and you get that hiss. That is why a calm swell that doesn't break is almost silent, even when the water is moving a great deal.

The type of beach changes the sound as well. On sand, the backwash makes a soft sigh, because the water sinks into the beach. On shingle, it's quite different. Here the characteristic sound is a crackle, which comes from pebbles being dragged back down the slope and rattling against each other. Some listeners compare it to frying, and a few say it's like applause.

Now to the human part of the picture. I want to describe a small example, and I should stress that it's imaginary, an illustration I made up to show how such a study might look. Suppose a researcher interviews 400 visitors at a resort I'll call Marram Bay. She asks them what they value most. Imagine that 52 per cent, no, I'm sorry, 62 per cent say it's the sound of the sea. That's the number I'm using in this illustration. Then she asks what they find most unpleasant, and the most common answer isn't traffic or crowds. It's jet skis, mentioned by more people than anything else, even though they are only used for a few hours a day.

Notice how this echoes something we saw in the fieldwork reports last week. How loud a sound is doesn't tell you how much people mind it. A sound that people feel is out of place, or that they can't escape, will bother them far more than a louder sound that belongs.

So what can a town do about it? A few councils have begun to treat sound as part of coastal planning, in the same way that they plan for views and for safety. One approach is to set aside quiet zones on a stretch of beach, usually away from the main car parks and cafés, where music and engines aren't allowed. These are popular, and they don't need much enforcement, because people who choose to sit there tend to look after the calm themselves.

Another approach is to find out what you've got, and the surest method is systematic listening. Some projects ask volunteers to make a short recording at the same place every month for a year. The place matters. If the recording point changes, you can't compare the results. Over time, the seasons show up very clearly in the recordings.

And the seasons matter, because a resort in winter is a completely different place. When the visitors go home, the soundscape loses its crowds, the music, and the engines, and what remains is the surf, the wind and the gulls. Some residents say that is the real sound of the town and that the summer one is only a performance for guests.

Finally, I want to mention that many of these sounds are fragile. A foghorn that has been in use for a century can be switched off for the sake of a few complaints, and the community only realises what it has lost afterwards. That has led some towns to treat their sounds as heritage. In a few places, recordings of harbour bells, fishing boats and the tide are kept in a sound archive, alongside the old photographs and the maps, so that future generations know what the place was like when it was alive.

So to summarise. The seaside has a soundscape that can be described, measured and, to some extent, protected. In the next session we'll follow the soundscape indoors, to shopping centres and railway stations. Please read the Schafer extract before then.
Hello? Is that the storage place on Quarry Road? Sorry, the line is dreadful. I'm standing in my late aunt's hallway, and the signal comes and goes.
Larkhall Self Store, yes, and I can hear you well enough. Go ahead, I'm all ears.
I need somewhere to put a houseful of things for a few weeks while the family sorts through them. Could you take some details?
Of course. I've got the enquiry sheet in front of me. Name?
Ingrid Ottoway. That's O, then double T, then O-W-A-Y.
Ottoway. Right. And which day would you like to begin? Tomorrow's possible, if you're in a hurry.
I was hoping to move everything on Saturday the 12th, because my brother is free then and he has a van.
Ah, the office doesn't do new rentals at weekends, because nobody's here to give out the codes. The first day I can offer is Monday. That would be 14 July.
Oh, I see. Then Monday it is. My brother will have to take a day off, but that's his problem. 14 July.
Lovely. What size of unit do you think you'll need? We've got three, two square metres, five, and ten.
Ten, I should think. It's a whole house, after all. Well, a small house.
Can you give me an idea of what's in it? People usually overestimate.

Let me think. A wardrobe, a chest of drawers, two armchairs, and maybe forty boxes of books and clothes. The thing I'm really worried about is the photographs. My aunt kept a hundred and fifty albums, as well as shoeboxes of loose prints, and nobody has ever looked at most of them.
Then I'd say five square metres, not ten. You'd be paying for space you don't use. Forty boxes will stack quite high, and we have shelves you can borrow for nothing.
Five is fine, then. I'll trust you.
And how long will you need it? Most people say a month.
A month, I'd have said, but my brother is worried it'll take longer, and the lawyers are slow. Let's say six weeks, to be safe.

Six weeks, then. You can always extend, but it's awkward to cut it short, because we charge by the week. Now, the price. For a five square metre unit it's £15 a week. Sorry, I've just looked at the website, and that was the old price. It's gone up, and it's now £18 a week.
That's all right. Does that include insurance?
It doesn't, I'm afraid. The insurance is extra. It's £2 a week for the contents, up to a limit of five thousand pounds. If you have anything worth more than that, you'd need your own cover.
The furniture isn't worth that, and I can't put a value on the photographs anyway, so I'll take the standard insurance.

Fine. Now, where do you want the unit? We have ground-floor units, which are handy because you can drive right up to the door. But I should tell you that two of them got a small leak in March, when the drain blocked in that heavy rain. The first floor is warmer and drier, and there's a lift and a trolley.
Then it has to be upstairs, with the photographs. I'd hate for the albums to get damp. I don't mind carrying boxes.
Good thinking. Damp ruins old prints very quickly. It's the first floor, then. I can offer you unit D23. It's at the quiet end, near the stairs, so you don't have to walk far.
D23. Perfect. Is there somewhere to leave the van while we unload? I don't want to block anybody.

There's a loading bay at the front gate. Thirty minutes is free, and after that you should move the van into the car park, which is also free for customers. Just don't block the gate first thing on a Monday, because the delivery lorries come then and the driver isn't a patient man.
Understood. And what about the opening times? My brother works until six.

The gate is open from 7 in the morning. In winter it shuts at 8 in the evening. But in the summer months, it's 10 at night, so you can come after work without a rush. The website still says 8, but that's wrong, and I'll fix it when I get the time.
Excellent. Is a lock included?

No, bring your own padlock. We sell them at the office, for £6, if you'd rather buy one. A cheap one is no good, though. Get one with a thick shackle, because we've had thefts at other sites, though not here.
I'll buy a good one. Thank you for being so helpful.
My pleasure. I'll send an email with the agreement, and you can sign it on Monday morning when you come in. Take care, Ms Ottoway.

Evening, all, and welcome to the Kererū Camera Club's new members' night. I'm Philippa. I've been chair for four years, which means I'm the one who gets the blame when the heater doesn't work. Let me tell you how the club runs, and then there's tea and some very good lemon cake.

First, meetings. For years we met on the first Tuesday of the month, and you'll see that on the old leaflets. But the church hall changed its booking system, and Tuesdays vanished. We tried Thursdays, but the choir has the hall then, so from this year we meet on Wednesdays, at half past seven. So if your leaflet says Tuesday, please don't turn up on a Tuesday. The caretaker will think you are burglars.

Now money. The subscription was $60 a year for a long time. I'm afraid it's gone up, and for an adult it is now $75. That covers the hall, the insurance, and the fees for our visiting speakers. Students pay half. Someone told me it was $90, and that is the household rate, when two people from the same address join together. Most of you will pay $75.

Competitions. Every term we hold one, with a theme chosen by the committee. Until last year, you had to print your photograph and mount it on card, which was expensive and a little stressful. This year there's a change. Entries are now sent in as digital files, one per member, by email, and the judge sees them on a big screen. We still hold a print night in the spring, for anyone who misses the card and the glue, but the regular competitions are digital.

Next, the darkroom. We've had one in the basement since 1987, and some new members assume it's for printing exhibition pictures. It could be, but those are sent to a laboratory these days. What the darkroom is really used for now is teaching. One Saturday a month, one of our older members shows beginners how to develop black and white film by hand, and people tell me that it's the best thing the club does. We also store the spare tripods in there, but please don't mention that to the fire officer.

When you join, you'll be given a mentor. Mentors aren't picked by you, I'm afraid, because we find that people choose their friends and then learn nothing, so the committee matches you. Before the first meeting with your mentor, we ask you to bring three of your own photographs. They aren't there to be judged, and they don't have to be good. They're simply a starting point, so your mentor can see what you like to photograph.
On to the outings, because that's what many of you are here for, and what to bring. I'll go through the first five in the programme.

The first is the estuary at dawn, in October. Some people bring a tripod, but there's enough light by the time the sun is up, and it's more of a nuisance in the mud. What you will need is a pair of waterproof boots, because the path floods at high tide and the mudflats are soft. Last year somebody lost a shoe, and we're still looking for it.

Second, the Saturday market, in November. It's a lovely place for people photography, but stallholders don't like a lens poked in their faces. So we suggest you bring a long lens and stand back a little. You'll get more natural pictures, and people will thank you.

Third is the evening at the observatory in December. The astronomers are very welcoming, but they need the dome dark, so bring a torch, preferably one with red cellophane over the front. A white torch will make you very unpopular, so please remember.

The fourth is the old railway tunnel, in February. It's very dim inside, and a lot of the pictures only work with long exposures, so a tripod is essential. Some of you will have a tripod that's very heavy. Think about that before you carry it a kilometre.

And the last one in this list is the walk up the glacier valley in July, in the middle of winter. It's lovely, but it's very cold, and cold drains batteries remarkably fast. Bring spare batteries, and keep them in an inside pocket, close to your body. We've had several members arrive at the best view and find their cameras dead.

One more practical point. We take turns to make the tea, and the rota is on the noticeboard by the door, so don't be fooled by anyone who tells you they have a bad back. The old club website is still online, but nobody has updated it for years, so ignore it and use the address on your welcome bag.

I won't mention the others tonight, as they're on the sheet at the back. There is a lens cloth for everyone in the welcome bags, so no one needs to bring one, and no one needs a plastic sheet to kneel on unless the weather turns bad. Right, any questions before tea? Yes, at the back.
Noor, Cormac, good to see you. I've been keen to hear about this one, partly because my own grandmother's albums are in a terrible state. Tell me about the restoration project.
Thank you, Dr Ibarra. We've collected twenty-six photographs from people in the town, and we're now at the stage of deciding how to treat them and how to write it up.
Perhaps we should say why we asked residents, and not the town archive. You asked us about that last time.
I did. I wondered if the archive had refused you.

No, they were quite happy to help. But their pictures were already catalogued, and most had been cared for. We wanted to hear what the owners had to say about them, and what each one meant to the family. Those stories were more interesting than the images themselves.
Good. That makes it a human study as well as a technical one. What condition were the photographs in?

Worse than we expected. We'd assumed that most damage would be fading, because many of them are forty or fifty years old. But the commonest problem is the albums. Lots of them have those sticky pages with a plastic film over the top, and the photographs have bonded to the page. When you try to lift them, the surface comes away.
Yes, those albums were very popular, and a disaster for photographs. The adhesive becomes yellow and the plastic traps moisture. What did you do?
We tried to ease one out with a plastic spatula, and it tore. We stopped at that point. We're worried about damaging the others.

Quite right. Don't try to separate them yourselves. Photograph the whole page as it stands, and take advice from a conservator before you attempt to lift anything. There are techniques, but they take training. For a student project, a good scan of the page is a perfectly respectable record.
That's a relief. I was afraid we'd have to leave them out.
Not at all. Now, the digital repair. Which software did you use?
A free editor to begin with, and then a program with a healing brush. It works well on scratches and spots, and the results are very convincing.
Convincing is the word that worries me. There's an ethical question. What do you do when part of a face has gone, say an eye, or half a mouth? It's tempting to paint it in.
We did that with one picture, and it looked quite good, but I felt uneasy. We were guessing.

You were. My advice is, only do it with the owner's agreement, and record what you've done in a note beside the picture. Then nobody is misled in fifty years' time, and the family feels part of the decision.
That's a good rule. We could add a caption to every restored image saying what was changed.
Do. Now, what is the final display going to include? I had the impression you were being very ambitious.

We were, but we've cut things back. We'd planned a timeline of photographic processes, and a short film about the restoration. We've dropped both, because there isn't time and we don't want it to look rushed.
What we'll keep is a display with each original next to its restored copy, so visitors can compare. And we'd like to produce a leaflet that explains how to store family photographs at home.
Excellent. I think those two are the most useful. What about the recordings of the owners?
We made several, but we haven't had permission from everyone, so we'll use them for the report only.
Wise. What did the owners make of the process? Did anyone object to the changes?

One woman was quite upset. Her photograph of her father had a scratch across his cheek, and we'd removed it, but she told us that the scratch reminded her of the day her brother dropped the frame. So we put it back.
It made us realise that damage can be part of the story. In the end we offered every owner two versions, the cleaned one and the plain scan of the original.

That's a lovely finding, and it ties in with what I said about notes. Make it a section of its own in the report, not a footnote. Plenty of students would have hidden it, but it's the most original thing you've found.
We weren't sure it was scientific enough.
Reports about people don't have to be all measurements. Quote them accurately, say how many people you spoke to, and you're fine.
Twenty-six owners, although a few were from the same family.
Say that too. Now, tell me about the individual photographs. Which problems did you meet?
There was a group of holiday snaps from the 1970s, and they've faded badly. The colours have gone orange, as if somebody had spilled tea over them.
The school group was a framed one. It had been hanging on a wall for decades, and it's stuck to the glass. We can't separate it without destroying it, so we've scanned it through the glass.

A christening photograph had water stains, probably from a flood. The owner told us that the whole family's pictures were in the cellar when the river rose. Another one, a portrait of a soldier, is covered in creases, from being carried in a pocket.
Did you find any mould?
Only on one, and it belongs to someone who asked us not to include it. We gave it back to her with some advice.

That was sensible. Mould can spread. One last thing, the title. As it stands, it reads Photographic Restoration Techniques, which sounds like a manual. Something that mentions the families would suit the project far better.
We'll think of something.
How about Whose Picture Is It Anyway?
Better than the first one, certainly. Right. I think you're in better shape than you feared. Send me an outline of the display by Friday.
We will. Thank you.

Hello, everybody. Last session we covered how photographs are made. This morning I want to move on to what happens to them afterwards, and to how we can look after them, whether in a museum or in a shoebox under a bed. I'll start with a very quick tour of the early processes, then explain why photographs deteriorate, and end with some advice you can use at home, including on digital repair.

So, the processes. The first practical method, the daguerreotype, was announced in 1839. It produced a single image on a polished metal plate, with no negative, so it couldn't be copied. For that reason daguerreotypes are rare and precious. Later, in the middle of the nineteenth century, the albumen print took over. Its name comes from the way it was made, because the paper was coated with egg white to hold the silver on its surface. Millions were produced, and many of them survive in family albums. Then, from the 1880s, came the gelatin silver print, which dominated photography for the whole of the twentieth century, and which most black and white prints in your family still are.

Now, why do photographs deteriorate? Each process has its own weaknesses, but there are some common ones. Let me take silver prints first. Over time you may see what's called silver mirroring. A kind of metallic sheen appears on the darkest parts of the print, rather like the surface of a cheap spoon. It's caused by tiny particles of silver moving to the surface, and it's often a sign that the print has been stored badly.

Colour prints behave differently. The image is made of dyes, rather than silver, and the three dyes don't all fade at the same speed. So a colour print doesn't just get paler, it changes colour. That's why so many photographs from the seventies look orange or reddish. The picture isn't wrong, it's just that one of the colours has faded much faster than the others, and the balance has gone.

What causes this? There are three main enemies. Light is one, and heat is another, but the one I'd like you to remember is humidity. Damp encourages mould and makes photographs stick to whatever is touching them. Incidentally, last year I said that heat was the biggest danger, and I've changed my mind. In the collections I've examined, damp does more harm than heat.

So how should we store prints at home? First, avoid the sticky albums I mentioned, the ones with sticky pages and a plastic film. They were advertised as modern and convenient, and they cause an enormous amount of harm, because the adhesive and the plastic react with the print. If you have photographs in one, don't pull them out. Ask an expert.

Second, don't hold stacks of prints together with rubber bands, because the rubber sticks and leaves a mark. And don't use paper clips either, because they rust and leave a brown stain. Use acid-free paper envelopes or archival boxes, and keep them somewhere cool and dry, not in the attic or the cellar. If you need to write on the back of a print, use a soft pencil, never a ballpoint pen, because the pressure leaves an impression on the front and the ink may transfer.

A word about colour, since I suspect plenty of you have shoeboxes of snapshots. The cooler you keep colour prints, the more slowly the dyes change, which is why serious archives keep their colour film in cold stores. You don't need a freezer at home, but a cupboard on an inside wall is far better than a loft, where the temperature swings from freezing to roasting. Steady conditions matter as much as low ones, because the expansion and contraction as a print warms and cools makes the surface crack. If you want to display a favourite, hang a copy and keep the original in its box.

Now to digital repair, which is where many people start. The first step isn't restoration at all, it's scanning. For prints you should scan at no less than 600 dots per inch. Last year I told you 300, and that's still fine for casual use, but if you want to enlarge or repair the picture, you need more detail than that. Save the file in an uncompressed format, and keep it as your master copy. Never work on it directly. Always make a copy, and edit the copy.

And what about ethics? This is the question that conservators care about most. The rule is that a repair should be reversible, or at least documented. Digital work is good in this respect, because the original isn't touched. But if you rebuild part of a face, you're inventing something that wasn't there, and a later viewer could mistake it for fact. So the best practice is to keep a log of every change, and to store it with the file.

Let me finish with a thought about why this matters. A photograph is a physical object as well as an image, and its condition tells a story. Fingerprints, creases and corners worn soft from handling, all show how people used it. A perfect restoration can hide that. So the question to ask before you begin isn't how to make it look new, but what you want to keep.
Before we meet again, read the chapter on the conservation of colour film, and bring a photograph of your own, with a note on how it has been stored.
Right, sorry about the noise, I was cutting vinyl in the back. You must be the lady with the street festival.
That's me. I'm Esme. I rang on Monday, and your colleague said to pop in once I'd made up my mind about the banner.
And have you?
Mostly. I've got a drawing here, and a long list of questions. Shall we start at the beginning?
Always a good idea. I'll fill in the order form as we go. Your surname?
Abernethy. That's A-B-E-R-N-E-T-H-Y. There's a lot of us in Scotland, but only one of me on this side of the border.
Abernethy. Got it. And is this a business order, or private?

Neither, really. It's for the Larch Street Residents' Association. We hold a festival every May, and this year we want a banner across the road, so that people know it's happening before they turn the corner.
Larch Street. I know it. Lovely trees. How wide were you thinking?
Three metres. That's what we agreed at the meeting, but nobody really measured anything.

Let me think. Across the road is the problem. The lamp posts opposite each other are about four metres apart, I believe. A three metre banner would be too short to tie between them, and you'd end up with ropes at both ends sagging into the road. I'd go for four.
Four it is, then. That's a good point, and I'm glad I came in.

Now the material. Vinyl is cheaper, and the colours look very bright. But Larch Street is open at both ends, and I've seen what the wind does down there. A solid sheet acts like a sail and either rips or pulls the lamp post over. I'd recommend mesh, which has small holes that let the wind through.
Will the colours still show?
Very well, as long as you keep the design simple. Big letters, no fine detail.
Then mesh. I had thought of dark blue for the background, with white writing.
That's a classic combination, but is it clear from a distance?
Hmm. The festival poster is teal, actually, and it would look odd if the banner were another colour. Let's go for teal, then, and keep the writing white.
Teal, with white lettering. Good. Anything else you want printed besides the banner?
Yes, flags. Little ones, to hang from the windows. We thought one for each house, so that makes thirty.
Thirty. The flags come in packs of ten. Is everyone on the street joining in?
I think so. Oh, wait. There are the new flats at the end of the road, with another eight households. We'd want those too, so that's thirty-eight, and I suppose you'd say forty.
Forty is easiest, and it gives you a couple of spares for the shop on the corner. They cost a pound fifty each.
That's very reasonable. And the banner itself?
The price on the phone on Monday was £85, but that was for vinyl, and your banner's mesh at four metres, so it's £96.
Ninety-six pounds. Fine. The committee gave me a budget of two hundred, so there's room.
Good. The next thing is timing. The festival is on Saturday 24 May, isn't it? Printing takes five working days, so I need your artwork a week before. Can your designer manage Friday the 16th?
She told me she'd have it ready by the Wednesday. That would be the 14th.
That's even better, but I'll put down Friday 16 May as the final deadline, so that you've some leeway. If it comes in later than that, I can't promise it'll be ready.
Sensible. And when would we collect it?
It should be ready by Thursday, the day before the weekend. We're shut on Friday afternoons, so that's easier for everyone.
I was going to suggest Friday morning, but I'm at work, and Thursday after six would suit me better. Can you stay open?
I'll be here until seven on Thursdays. Come at half past six, and I'll hold it for you.
Wonderful. And how do I pay? Is it on collection?
We ask for half as a deposit when you place the order. The banner's £96, and the forty flags are £60, which makes £156 altogether, and half of that is £78.
Seventy-eight pounds. I've got my card.
Brilliant. If you tap it here, we're done. I'll email you a proof, and please check the spelling, because I once printed three metres of banner with a mistake and the whole street never forgot it.
Thank you, I'll check it twice.

Morning, volunteers, and thank you for being here so early. I'm Delphine, and I'm coordinating the Fenner Street Mural Weekend. Over the next two days we'll be covering five walls with paint, so let me run through the practical details before we begin.

Let's start with registration. The leaflet says the town hall steps, but the builders put scaffolding up there on Thursday, and I've moved the desk. You'll find it now at the library entrance, just inside the glass doors. Please sign in each morning, and collect a badge, because the police like to be able to tell us from people who aren't supposed to be there.

Next, what to bring. The paint, the brushes, the rollers, the aprons and the gloves are all supplied, so there's nothing you need to bring. The one thing I can't provide is the right footwear. You'll be on a platform, or stepping over buckets, so please wear closed shoes. Last year someone came in sandals, and the less said about that, the better.

Now timing. On Saturday, painting runs from nine until five, with an hour for lunch. On Sunday, the leaflet says we finish at five too, but that's changed. The council needs to reopen the road, so we have to stop at four. That gives us a little less time on the second day, so I'd ask you to be punctual in the morning.

And the weather. I know you're all wondering about the forecast. We aren't going to cancel if it rains. The two walls under the arcade are covered anyway, and for the others we have large tarpaulins that we can put up. We'll carry on, but we'll take longer, so bring a waterproof jacket just in case.

A quick word about lunch. The café on the corner is providing soup and sandwiches on both days, free for volunteers, and the librarians have kindly agreed to let us use their staff kettle. Please don't carry food or drink onto the scaffolding. Spilt tea and wet paint are a bad combination, and a surprising number of walls have a cup-shaped patch somewhere on them.

One more thing about the finish. When all the walls are done, a contractor will come on the Monday and apply a clear coat to each one, which stops people from spraying graffiti over the top, and protects the colours from the sun. So please don't be tempted to touch up your work after the weekend, as it'll be sealed.
Let's turn to the walls. We have five, and each has its own theme, which came from a consultation with local people. I'll go round the street in order.

First is the west gable wall at the end of the bakery. This is the biggest. It'll show portraits of local people, nine of them, painted from photographs that residents sent in. We had a suggestion for a sunrise, since the wall faces east in the morning, but the portraits won the vote. We'll have a very experienced artist from the college leading that team.

Second, the chemist's shutters. They're long and narrow, which suits repeating patterns. The designs come from the old tiles that you can still see in the doorways of some of the older shops on the street. A group from the history society found them and copied them, so these are real local designs, not something invented.

Third, the bus shelter. It's a small wall, but a lot of people see it. It will have birds of the estuary, curlews and oystercatchers and so on, drawn by members of the local bird club. I think they're lovely, and they're the kind of thing that you notice while waiting for a late bus.

Fourth, the underpass beside the river. It's a dark space, so we need something bright. The mural will be a map of the river, from the hills where it starts to the sea, with the names of the villages along it. The underpass follows the river's path, so it makes sense. We did discuss painting the old tram that used to run on the street, but we couldn't find enough photographs to make an accurate picture.

And finally, the library fence. This one isn't a wall, but it's ideal for the youngest painters. The primary school is coming on Sunday morning, and each child will add a handprint in their favourite colour. When the day finishes, I expect the fence to look like a rainbow, and I hope the weather is kind.

And on Sunday, once the road is cleared, there'll be a small celebration in front of the bakery. The mayor is coming, but I've asked her to keep the speech short, so you'll all be on your way home by half past.
Now, if everyone has their badge, we'll go to the first wall, and I'll introduce you to your team leaders. Thank you again for coming, and I hope you enjoy the weekend.
Come in, Wilf, Cleo. Last time we spoke, you were still choosing a case study. I gather you've settled on the sculpture in Penwarren?
Yes. The Silver Run, the big steel salmon in the market square. It was put up last spring.
Remind me why you chose that one.

Mainly because it's so recent. People still remember the arguments, and the council's files are all there to read. With an older sculpture we'd have relied on people's memories, and those change over the years.
We did consider a statue in the next town, but nobody can say how the decision was made, so we dropped it.
Good, that's sensible. Now, what sources are you using?
Three. Letters in the local paper, interviews with people in the square, and a short online questionnaire.
Let's take them one by one. Start with the letters.

We found forty-three. In the weeks before the unveiling, almost all of them were negative, mostly about the cost. People wrote that the money should have gone on the roads. But after the summer festival, when the salmon was lit up for the first time, the tone changed completely. People wrote about taking their grandchildren to see it.

That's an interesting pattern. A word of caution, though. People who write to a newspaper are rarely typical. They tend to be the ones who feel strongly, and there may be many more who feel nothing at all. So I wouldn't treat the letters as a measure of opinion in the town. They're a record of the debate, not the whole picture.
Good point. We'll mention that in the methods.
Now the interviews. How many did you do?
Twenty, over two Saturdays. We stood by the fountain and asked people if they'd talk for five minutes.
Some of them talked for fifteen. Once people start telling you what the town used to be like, it's hard to stop them.
That's good material. What about the questionnaire?
We put it online, and we got ninety replies, but when we looked at the ages, nearly all of them were under forty. The older people just weren't there.

Then you have a gap in your evidence. I'd suggest handing out paper copies in the square, ideally on a market day when the older residents come in. There's no need to start again. Just add the paper responses to what you have, and mark which came from which.
We could manage that on Saturday. Honestly, I never thought of paper.
It's old-fashioned, but it works. One more point about the interviews. Did people know they were being recorded?
We asked each person, and we've got a signed slip from everyone. Two people said yes but didn't want their names in the report, so we'll use initials.
Exactly right. Keep those slips safe until after the marking.
We'd also like to include some quotations, but we aren't sure how many is too many.

Choose the ones that say something your own words can't, and no more than one or two for each group. Otherwise the report becomes a collection of quotes with no argument of your own. Now, what did people like about the sculpture?

The reason most people gave was that it reminded them of the fishing past. Penwarren was a fishing port until the sixties, and the salmon, even though it's abstract, made people talk about their fathers and grandfathers on the boats.

The second most common reason was that it brightens up the square. It used to be a car park with a few benches, and apparently it was rather grim. People said it made the whole centre feel looked after.
And you'd expect the council to be pleased about attracting visitors.
They hoped so, but almost nobody mentioned it. Only two or three people said anything about tourists.
Interesting. Tell me how different groups reacted.

The older residents were the most critical, and mostly for one reason. They didn't object to the salmon itself. What annoyed them was that nobody asked them. The decision was made by a committee, and they said they read about it in the paper after it was too late.

The shopkeepers surprised us. We assumed they'd say it brought them customers, and a couple did, but the main complaint was the lighting. After dark the square is rather dim, so people avoid it and the shops lose evening trade. They'd like better lights.
The teenagers loved it. They use it as a place to meet, and that's pretty much all they said. It's the one spot in the square where nobody tells them to move on.

And the families who've moved to Penwarren recently said it taught them something about the town. A few of them went to the museum afterwards to find out about the fishing industry. It gave them a way into the local history.

That's a lovely finding. I suspect it's the most important thing in your data, so don't bury it. Think carefully about how you present the results. A table of groups and comments might be the clearest way.
We were thinking exactly that.

Good. Finally, be upfront about what you can't say. You can't claim that the salmon caused the change in attitudes, only that attitudes seemed to change after the festival. Other things happened that summer, including a very hot July, which tends to make everyone feel kinder.
That's true. We might be tempted to say more than we should.
We'll put in a paragraph about the limits of the study.
Do. Let me have a first version of the findings before the month is out, and I'll look at it before you write the discussion.

Good afternoon, everyone. Today's topic is public art, and in particular, what it does for the way people feel about the places they live in. I'll begin with a definition, then talk about two famous examples, and finish with some of the arguments and risks.

So, what do I mean by public art? In the simplest sense it's art that stands in a place anyone can reach, rather than inside a gallery. But it's also usually paid for, at least partly, with public money, and that matters, because it means the public feels entitled to an opinion. Some cities have a rule that a small part of every large building budget must be spent on art. The figure is typically around one per cent. That sounds small, but across a whole city it adds up to a great deal.

Let me give you two examples that most of you will know. The first is the Angel of the North, the huge steel figure beside a motorway in the north of England, designed by Antony Gormley. It was unveiled in 1998. Its wings are not spread out sideways but angled slightly forward, and the wingspan is 54 metres, which is more than twice its height. When it was proposed, many local people objected. Some thought it was ugly, and some thought the funds should go on jobs. Now, though, it's widely regarded as a symbol of the region, and it appears on postcards, on football scarves and on tea towels.

The second example is a different kind of work. Another Place, also by Gormley, is on a beach near Liverpool. It consists of 100 cast-iron figures, spread out along nearly three kilometres of the shore. Each one is a copy of the artist's own body.
