They all face out to the sea, as if waiting for something, and the tide covers some of them twice a day. Visitors walk among them, and many say they find it moving. Again, it was controversial at first. There was some concern about safety, and for a while it was unclear whether it would be allowed to stay. Eventually it was, and now people would object if it were removed.

Notice what these two have in common. Both started as outsiders' ideas, and both were opposed. And both became part of the local identity. I'd like to be careful here, because that doesn't always happen. For every success, there are works that stay disliked, and we usually forget them because nobody takes their photograph.

Let me describe an imaginary case, which I've invented to make a point, so please don't go looking for it on a map. Picture a small town called Carrowby, where the council spends a large sum on a bronze statue of a local poet, chosen by a panel in the capital. The statue is well made, but it stands in a car park, and nobody in the town has read the poet. Within a year it has a traffic cone on its head. Now picture a second town, where the same money pays for a hundred benches, each one decorated by a different family. The benches are less impressive one by one. Yet people point out their own bench to visitors, and they'd be furious if it went missing. That contrast proves nothing on its own, but it shows how the process may matter more than the object.

So what makes the difference? One answer is participation. Research on community projects suggests that people who help make something feel a sense of ownership towards it. They defend it, look after it, and tell visitors about it. That is true even if the work isn't, strictly speaking, very good. If a work is simply delivered to a community, even a brilliant work, people may feel it's been done to them rather than with them.

Next, permanence. Not all public art is intended to last. Temporary works can be installed for a few days, and they're often linked to festivals, such as light displays or parades. Because they don't stay, they cost less, and people are more willing to try something strange. A few towns use them to test ideas. If the response is positive, a permanent version may follow.

Then there's the way art is made. Murals are a good example, because they are cheaper and quicker than sculpture. Many are painted together with local schools, with children helping at every stage. The children then bring their parents to see it, and that spreads the sense of pride through the community very quickly.

Let me raise a note of caution. Public art can be used cynically. There's a term, artwashing, which describes the use of art to make a controversial change look acceptable. Typically it appears in the argument about gentrification. A developer might commission a colourful mural on the side of a building, while rents rise and long-standing residents are quietly pushed out. In that case, the art isn't expressing local identity at all. It's covering up a change that threatens that identity. Critics ask whose identity is being represented, and who is paying.

For your assignment, I'd like you to choose a work of public art in a place you know. Describe it, find out who made the decision to install it, and ask at least five people what it means to them. Don't just ask whether they like it. Ask what they would miss, if it were gone. In my experience, that question gets a much more honest answer.
Lost property, Kingsmead station. And before you say anything, no, we haven't found anybody's umbrella today.
Ha. It isn't an umbrella, I'm afraid. I think I left a bag on a train last night, and I'm hoping somebody handed it in.
Let's hope so. I'll get a few particulars and then check the shelves. Can I have your name?
It's Petra Thistlewood. T-H-I-S-T-L-E-W-O-O-D.
Thistlewood. That's a new one on my list. Now, which day did you travel?
It was the 13th. No, hang on. The 13th was my sister's birthday, and I was at her house all evening. So it must have been the 14th. Yes, it was 14 October.
14 October. Which train was it?
The late one from the city, the one that stops at every little station. I got on at about ten to eight, and I was in coach D.
Do you remember where you sat? Seat numbers help us, because the cleaners write them on the bags they find.
I was in seat 74. No, that's wrong, because seat 74 was by the toilet and I moved. I was in 47, beside the window.
47. Good. And when did you realise it was missing?
Not until I got home. I put my keys on the table and thought, where's my bag? I rang the train company, but the line had closed for the night, so I came to you first thing this morning.
Sensible. Did you try the station at the end of the line?
I phoned them, and a man said he'd have a look, but he sounded as if he was eating his supper.
That'll be Gordon. He's very reliable, honestly, just hungry. Now, what sort of bag was it? A rucksack? A suitcase?
It's a shoulder bag. It looks a bit like leather, but it's actually canvas. The leather one is my sister's, and that's the one that I'm always being told to look after.
Canvas shoulder bag. What colour?
Khaki, I'd have said, but my friend says that's too brown, and that it's really olive green. Let's go with olive green.
Olive green. And what was in it? That's the part that helps us most.

A camera, mainly. I had two lenses with me, but I put those in my coat pocket, so they're safe. In the bag there's the camera body and some notebooks, a few pages of which I really need, because they have the notes for a project I'm working on.
So camera and notebooks. Anything else? Phone, wallet, keys?
No, thank goodness. Just those.
Does the bag have anything that makes it easy to recognise? A badge or a tag?
Yes, there's a keyring clipped to the zip. It's a little wooden fox. My niece made it at school, and it has a rather wonky tail.
A fox. That's very helpful, because I wouldn't have thought of that. Right, now I need to ask what it's worth. It's for the insurance side of things. What would you say the camera is worth?
Oh, it was about £800 new. But I bought it second-hand four years ago, so I'd say £600 now. And that doesn't include the sentimental value, naturally.

£600. That's fine. Let me explain what happens if we do find it. We don't keep items here at Kingsmead for long, because there's no room. Everything goes to the main depot in Harrowfield, and you can collect it from there.
Oh, that's a bit of a trek. Is there any way of having it sent to me?

There is, but it's expensive. Posting it costs £15, and it's cheaper to collect it in person. If you collect it yourself, there's a reclaim fee. For bigger items it's £10, but for a bag, it's £5. Sorry, I said ten at first, but that's for suitcases.
Five pounds is fine. When is the depot open?
Monday to Friday, until 6 in the evening, and on Saturday mornings. You'll need some photo ID, and if you can describe the camera, you won't have any problem. Do you know the serial number?
I do, because I registered it when I bought it. I'll find the email and write it down.

Excellent, that makes it easy. What I'll do is put a note on your file, and if the bag turns up on any train in the next two days, it'll be tagged for the depot. I'll also send you a text when it arrives, so there's no need to ring.
That's very kind. Thank you for being so patient with me.
It's what I'm here for. Try not to worry. Most things are handed in, and cameras especially, because people know how much they matter. I'll be in touch.

Welcome aboard, everyone, and mind the gap between the pier and the deck, because the tide is lower than it looks. My name's Torquil, and I'm your skipper this afternoon. This is the Marguerite, and she's been taking passengers round Port Alder harbour since 1974, which makes her older than most of the crew.

First, the practical bits. The cruise takes ninety minutes. Your leaflet says one hour, and I'm sorry, but that's the old route. This year we've added a loop round the island, because passengers kept asking, so everything now takes half an hour longer. If you have a train to catch, please tell me now, and I'll see what we can do.

Hot drinks. There's a small kiosk on the upper deck, but it's closed today because the person who runs it has gone to a wedding. So if you'd like tea, coffee or hot chocolate, you'll find the galley below deck, down the steps on the left. The tea is strong, and the biscuits are free, so don't be shy.

Next, a word about the sea. It's a calm day, but the harbour mouth can be lumpy, and some of you may start to feel queasy. If that happens, don't go below, because it makes it worse. Come up to the rail, stand on the open deck, and fix your eyes on the horizon, which helps most people. And tell a member of the crew, so that we know you're all right.

Lifejackets are under the benches, and I'm required to tell you where they are, so here goes. Lift the seat and you'll find them in orange bags. Children's sizes are in the blue box beside the steps. You won't need them, but I'd feel better if you knew. There's no smoking anywhere on the boat, and that includes the little electric ones, and please keep dogs on a lead.

Now, the route. We'll head out past the fish market, along the sea wall, round the island and back, and I'll give you commentary as we go. Some people ask whether we go under the old iron bridge, and unfortunately we can't. It isn't closed or being repaired. The problem is the height of our mast. At high tide there simply isn't room to get under it. But you'll get a good view from the water, and I'll tell you its story as we pass.

At the end of the cruise, we come back to the same pier, and you can stay on board while we tie up. Please wait until the crew say it's safe. There's an optional stop at the fish market, where you can get off if you want to buy something, and the boat will wait for twenty minutes. Last time, someone came back with an enormous crab, and I'm told it was delicious.
Now for the sights, so that you know what to look out for.

The first one, on the right as we leave the pier, is the lighthouse. It's the oldest on this coast, and people sometimes assume it's still working, but it's been replaced by an automatic light further out. It's now open to visitors on Sundays, and you can climb to the top for a very small fee, if you don't mind a lot of stairs.

Next, on the hill behind the town, is the castle ruin. I should say that it wasn't always a castle. It was used as a prison for about a hundred years, and then fell into disuse. The walls are still standing, and a lot of the stones were taken for building the town, so many of the houses you can see are built from a prison.

The big crane you can see at the end of the old shipyard is the next thing. It's not working any more, but the council has decided to keep it, because it's become a symbol of the place. At the moment it's covered in scaffolding, because they're repairing the rust. The work should be finished by the spring, and I'm told it will be lit at night.

Then there's the fort on the sea wall. It was built to defend the harbour in the eighteenth century, and it's the best-preserved of its kind in the country. It was moved to its present site, brick by brick, after the old harbour wall collapsed in a storm, which makes me wonder how well it's been preserved. It's a lovely building, anyway, and it's now used for weddings.

And finally the island. It's small, and nobody lives there, but it's covered with grey seals, especially in the autumn. They like to lie on the rocks and look as if they don't care about us. Please keep your voices down as we go round, because they're nervous animals, and the loop will take longer if we have to drift.
If anyone has a question, find me at the helm. Otherwise, sit back, and enjoy the harbour.

Come in, Bryony, Evander. I've been looking at the contact sheets you sent, which was a pleasure. Most students send me the best twelve pictures and hide the failures, and then I can't tell what they've learned. Tell me about the project.
It's a photo essay about the dawn fish market in Allerby. We went every morning for two weeks, from five o'clock, and we've got about nine hundred pictures.
Do you want us to explain why we chose it?
I do, because it affects how I read the work.

Partly it's about timing. The market's moving to an industrial estate next year, and the old building will be sold. So this is the last winter that anyone can photograph it in the place where it has stood for a hundred and forty years. We wanted a record.

My uncle works there, which helped with getting in, but that wasn't the reason we chose it. And it wasn't your suggestion either, Dr Palmer, though you did say we should find something with an end date.
I'm glad I said something right. What was the hardest part?
The first few days. We turned up with cameras, and everybody went silent. Some of them started posing, with fish held up to the lens, grinning. Nobody looked natural, and the pictures were hopeless.
One man told us to go and photograph the pier. We realised we weren't going to get anything unless they trusted us.
How did you get round that?
We went for the next three mornings without cameras. We just helped carry crates and drank their tea. After that, people ignored us, and the camera became part of the furniture.
That's what I'd tell any documentary photographer. Time is the real equipment. Now, there's a picture on your sheet that worries me, the woman lifting the cod. It looks as though she's done it twice.
She did. I asked her to do it again, because the first time I'd missed it.

That's an important question. Some people would say never ask a subject to repeat anything, because then it isn't documentary. I think it can be acceptable, so long as you say so in the caption. Readers can then judge for themselves. What's unforgivable is pretending a thing happened spontaneously when it didn't.
Then I'll put a note on that one.
Good. Now, how are you choosing the final set? Nine hundred is a lot.
We thought of picking the sharpest. But the sharp ones were mostly boring, and the blurry ones had some life in them.

In the end we stopped judging single pictures. We've been laying them out on the floor, and asking, does this one lead to that one? We want twelve that tell a story, from the dark hour before the lorries arrive to the empty hall at nine.
That's the right instinct. A good essay isn't the twelve best pictures, but the twelve that work together. Next, the captions. What do you plan to put?
We hadn't thought about it much. Perhaps the date and the place?

Those are the basics, but you can do better. A caption in documentary work tells the viewer who the person is. So give the name and the job of everyone you've photographed, with their permission. And if you have a short quotation, add it, because a few words from the person themselves can change how the picture feels. Don't bother with camera settings or the weather, because nobody wants to read that. And I wouldn't give the exact time unless it matters.
We've got a lot of quotations, so that's easy.
What about permission? Did everyone you photographed agree to be in the essay?
The stallholders did, and the managers. But on busy mornings we had lorry drivers and customers walking through the frame, and we can't ask everybody.

In a public working place, that's usually accepted for background figures. For anyone who is clearly the subject, though, you need agreement, and I'd get it in writing, even if it's only a note on a scrap of paper. And if someone changes their mind afterwards, take the picture out. It isn't worth losing a friend for one frame.
One of the older fishermen asked us not to use a portrait of him with his cap off, because he thinks he looks bald.
Then it's out. That's your answer. Remember too that the essay will be on show, so people in Allerby may well see it. Think of them as your first audience, not just the markers.
We're hoping to put it up in the café beside the market.

Even better. Then the workers will have the final say. Now, let me go through the pictures that you've shortlisted. The woman with the scales, who's weighing the boxes. She's a lovely subject, but there's a crate in the left of the frame that cuts her off. It needs cropping, so that the eye goes to her face.
I thought so, but I didn't want to lose the scales.
You won't. Next, the empty crates at dawn. That's the one I'd open the essay with. It has atmosphere, and it promises that something is about to happen, which is what an opening picture should do.
That's what I hoped.
The two men sharing a flask. The light is superb. The lamp makes a kind of halo over their hands. Don't change a thing.
That's my favourite as well.

And the auctioneer. He's got a good expression, but there's a poster behind him, with a bright red logo, and the eye keeps going to that. See if there's another frame where he's standing a little to the left.
There might be. I'll check the sheet.
Good. One last thing, the title. Allerby Fish Market is accurate, but it's flat. Think about it before Friday. Bring me the final twelve then, printed small, and we'll lay them on the table.

Hello, all. This hour is about the craft of documentary photography. I'll look first at where it came from, then at two key moments in its history, and then at the questions that every documentary photographer has to answer, about time, trust and truth.

Let's begin with the pioneers. In the 1880s, a Danish immigrant to New York, Jacob Riis, was a newspaper reporter, who wanted to show the middle classes how the poor lived in the tenements. The problem was that these rooms were dark. So he took to using flash powder, a mixture that exploded in a bright flare. It was dangerous, because a flare like that could easily start a fire. But it allowed him to make pictures that nobody could ignore, and his book of 1890 caused real alarm.

A little later, Lewis Hine took a different approach. He worked for a committee that campaigned against child labour, and he photographed boys and girls working in mills and mines. Sometimes he pretended to be a salesman, or a fire inspector, to get into the factories. His pictures helped to change the law on child labour. That shows something important, which is that early documentary photography was a tool for reform, not just for observation.

The second moment is the 1930s. In the United States, the government set up a project to document rural poverty during the Depression. It was part of an agency called the Farm Security Administration, which began its photographic work in 1935. The man who ran it was Roy Stryker, and I always tell students that he's one of the most important people in the history of photography who never took a famous picture. He gave his photographers lists of the things he wanted, such as a cotton field, a barn, a family at a kitchen table, but he allowed them time to work.

The best-known picture from the project was made by Dorothea Lange, who photographed a mother with her children at a pea-pickers' camp in California. She did it in 1936. I've seen the contact sheet, and she took only six exposures. People imagine that famous pictures come from a thousand frames. Sometimes they come from six.

Lange also wrote notes at the time about what the woman had said, and years later there was some disagreement about the details, with the woman herself remembering things differently. That's a useful warning. Even the caption of a famous picture can be disputed, and we should treat every account, including the photographer's, as one version of events.

Let me turn to a different tradition. After the Second World War, a group of photographers founded an agency, Magnum, in 1947. One of them was Henri Cartier-Bresson, who wrote about what he called the decisive moment. His idea was that there's a fraction of a second when the event in front of you and the composition of the frame come together, and the photographer's job is to be ready for it. Many students find that idea inspiring, but I want to offer a note of caution. Not every good documentary picture depends on a single instant. Some depend on patience.

Technology has changed the craft, though perhaps less than people think. Light, fast cameras let photographers work in places where Riis's flash would have caused a riot, and the phone in your pocket can record a photograph, a video and some sound in the same minute. But the questions haven't changed. A phone makes it easier to take a picture, and harder to decide whether you should. And because everyone now carries a camera, viewers are more suspicious. They ask whether an image has been altered, which people didn't do a generation ago, so a photographer's reputation for honesty has become the main thing that they have to sell.

So, to the questions that practitioners face today. The first is time. I want to give you a little arithmetic, and I should say that this is an imaginary example. Suppose a photographer spends a year on a project about a market, takes 9,000 pictures, and the published set contains just 24 of them. That's a ratio of about one in four hundred. It shows how much of the work is selection, which many people don't realise.

The second is trust, which anyone who has done fieldwork will recognise. In long-term projects, the photographer often spends weeks without taking a picture at all. People need to get used to a stranger, and only then will they behave naturally. That brings us to consent. Today almost every professional code says that you should seek informed consent, especially if you're photographing someone vulnerable. That means the person understands where the picture will appear. It isn't always easy, and in some situations it isn't possible, but the principle is that people shouldn't be surprised by how they're shown.

And the third question is truth. Documentary photographs can mislead without any lies. A photographer who tells you only half of a story, or crops out an inconvenient detail, is shaping what you see. The best defence is honesty about the process. That is why captions matter so much. A good caption gives names, dates and places, so that the viewer can check the claim, and it says if anything was staged or rearranged. If you remember one thing from today, remember that a photograph does not explain itself.
For the coming week, please bring along a documentary photograph that you admire, and be prepared to explain what the caption tells you, and what it leaves out.
Tui Cove Holiday Park, you've come through to reception. If it's about the hot water in the shower block, the answer is still soon.
Ha, no, nothing like that. I'd like to book a site for the new year, if you've got anything left. I imagine you're nearly full.
We're getting there, but let's have a look. I'll take your details as we go, if you don't mind.
Of course. The surname is Dalrymple. D-A-L-R-Y-M-P-L-E.
Dalrymple, with a Y. Lovely. When were you hoping to arrive?
We'd like to arrive on the 3rd of January. We're driving up from Dunedin, and we want to miss the traffic on New Year's Day.
Hmm. The 3rd is a problem, I'm afraid. All our sites with electricity are taken until the 4th. A few people leave that morning. I could give you a site from 4 January, if you can wait a day.
We can stay with my sister for one more night, so that's no problem at all. 4 January, then.
And how many nights?
Five. No, six. My wife has just reminded me that the school holidays don't end until the Tuesday, so we might as well use the extra day. Six nights.
Six nights. Now, what are you bringing? A tent, a caravan, a campervan?
A campervan, and it needs power, because we've got a fridge and a little heater that run off the mains. We can't manage without the fridge, because of the baby's milk.
Then you want a powered site, which is what I've put. Do you know the length of the van?
It's six metres on the paperwork. Sorry, that's without the bike rack at the back. If you include the rack, it's nearer seven, so let's say seven metres.
Thank you for checking. Some people don't, and then we have to move them at midnight. How many of you will there be?
Two adults and three children. Ellie is nine, and the twins are six. Oh, and the baby, but she's only eight months old.
So that's three children, and the baby is free, as long as she doesn't count as a camper. Children under five don't pay, so the twins and Ellie will each cost you something. Is that right?
That seems fair. What's the nightly price?
For a powered site it's $38 a night for two adults. On our website it still says $34, but that's the off-peak price, and January is peak. Each child is an extra $8.
Right. That's quite a lot with three children, but it's a lovely spot. We camped there when I was a boy, and I still remember it.
Most of our customers say the same. Do you have any pets with you?
One dog. A terrier called Biscuit. He's very well behaved, mostly.
Dogs can stay, provided they are leashed at all times, and there's a charge of $5 a night. We find that most dog owners are happier with that rule than the ones without dogs.
That's fair. Do you have any activities?

There's a playground, a games room, and a boat ramp. If you want to go out on the water, we hire kayaks and paddle boards, and the kayaks are very popular with families. You pay at the office, and they're $20 for the morning.
Oh, the kids would love that. I'll put us down for a kayak. We've got our own bikes, so we won't need those, and we've got a boat ourselves, so no paddle board either.
A kayak, then. A double one, I'd suggest, so that you can take one of the children along. Shall I write that down?
Please do. What are the rules about noise?

Quiet hours begin at ten in the evening, and the gate locks at eleven. If you're coming back late from the pub in the village, ring the bell and Colin will let you in, though he isn't always cheerful about it.
We have a baby, so we'll be asleep by nine.
Then you'll be perfect neighbours.
Is there anywhere to buy things on site?
There's a small shop at reception. It sells bread, milk, ice cream, and firewood, but not much else. The nearest supermarket is fifteen minutes away.
That's fine. Now, how do I pay the deposit?
The deposit is 20 per cent. I'm afraid our card machine has been broken since Monday, so I can't take it over the phone. If you can manage a bank transfer, I'll send the details by email.
A bank transfer is easy enough. I'll do it tonight.

Wonderful. Once the deposit has arrived, I'll send a confirmation, along with a map of the site. Check-in is from two in the afternoon. If you arrive earlier than that, you can wait in the car park and have a swim.
Thank you, Una. You've been very helpful.
Not at all. I'll look forward to meeting Biscuit.

Right, I think that's everyone, so I'll make a start. Welcome to Radio Wattlebird, and a big thank you for volunteering. My name's Maeve, and I'm the station manager, which means I'm the one who stops the teapot from running dry. Before we go through to the studios, let me tell you how the station works.

We've been broadcasting for twenty-two years, and we're entirely independent. People often ask where the money comes from. A few listeners give us donations, and the council gave us a small grant when we started, but the biggest share comes from local businesses, which pay to sponsor shows. The baker pays for the breakfast programme, the garage pays for the traffic report, and so on. They get a mention, and we get to keep the lights on.

Now, what happens to you as new volunteers. Everyone begins with a studio induction, which takes half a day, and it comes before anything else. You can't touch a microphone until you've done it. Some people are keen to make a demo show straight away, and some would rather follow a presenter around for a few weeks. Both are possible, but not until you've done the induction. It covers the desk, the fire exits, and what to do when the computer crashes, which it does, usually during the news.

Training sessions run on Wednesday evenings, from seven. Some of you may have been told Tuesday, but the church hall next door has a choir on Tuesdays, and the sound comes through the wall, so we moved it. Wednesday evenings, seven o'clock, in the training room upstairs. It's a friendly group, and the biscuits are better than the ones on Tuesday.

A few house rules while I have you. No food or drink in the main studio, and that includes my tea, which I'm told sets a bad example. Please switch your phone off before you go on air, not to silent, but off, because it buzzes on the desk and the microphone picks it up. And if you ever say something you shouldn't, don't panic. We run a short delay, so the engineer can drop it, but please tell the engineer afterwards, so there are no shocks at breakfast.

A word about music. We play a lot of local bands, and we're proud of that, but we also play well-known songs, and for those we pay licence fees. To work out the fees, we have to know exactly what's been played. So every presenter keeps a log of every track, with the title and the artist, and hands it in at the end of each show. It sounds dull, but if you forget, the treasurer comes looking for you, and she's more frightening than the fire officer.

What's new this year? We've been given a grant for a second studio, but it won't be ready until next year, so please don't ask. The big addition is the outside broadcast van. We picked it up cheaply from a bakery, and it still smells slightly of bread. It's fitted with an aerial, so we can broadcast live from the market, the football ground, wherever there's something going on. There's also a podcast team, but that's only three people, and they have all the volunteers they need.

Now, a quick tour of the schedule, so that you know which shows you're likely to hear about. The local news is read every weekday morning, and it's the heart of the station. If you want to know what the council decided last night, that's where you'll hear it. The garden show is on at lunchtime, Monday to Friday, with a retired nurseryman who answers questions from callers. He's been wrong about slugs twice, but he is otherwise reliable.

Folk music is on Thursday evenings. It started as a one-off, and it's been on air for fifteen years. Some of the performers come into the studio and play live, and we've had audiences of up to thirty people squeezed into the corridor.

The children's stories are read on Saturday mornings, usually by one of our older volunteers, who does all the voices. We get letters from parents saying that it's the only time the family sits still. And finally, the sports round-up, on Sunday afternoons. It covers everything from rugby to bowls, and the presenter has an unfortunate habit of shouting.

Overnight, the station plays music automatically, with no presenter, but somebody still has to check on it once a week, and there's a rota for that on the noticeboard. And one more practical point. The car park behind the building belongs to the church, so please use the street, or you may be towed.

You may be wondering about the late-night slot on Fridays. That's a music request show, but it needs a presenter with a very strong stomach, so let me know if you're interested. Right, that's all from me. Follow me, mind the cable on the stairs, and we'll start with the main studio.
Sit down, you two. I want to hear how the theatre project is going before you start writing. Remind me of the research question.
We're asking what small theatres contribute to their communities, apart from the performances themselves. By small, we mean fewer than a hundred and fifty seats.
We chose six in the Tamsdale area, ranging from a market town with a single theatre to a city suburb with three of them within a mile.
Why six? It's an odd number.

We wanted to compare different kinds of buildings. We've got a converted chapel, a room above a pub, a village hall, a purpose-built studio, and two others. We could have visited more, but I think the variety matters more than the numbers.
And six was what we could manage, to be honest. Two directors didn't reply to our emails, so we ended up with the ones who did.
That's a fair reason. What was your method for gathering data?

We interviewed the director of each theatre. They took about an hour each. And at every theatre we handed out short cards to the audience on the way in, asking where they lived and how often they came.

I'd like you to be careful with the interviews. Directors want their theatre to survive, and they tend to describe it in the best possible light. You'll hear how much it means to the town, how loyal the audience are, and not much about empty seats. So treat what they say as one view, and look for other evidence to check it against.
We thought of that, and that's partly why the cards matter.
Quite. What did the cards show?

Something we didn't expect. We'd assumed that people would travel from a long way to see something unusual. But in fact, most of the audience lived within three kilometres of the theatre. They walked or cycled.
Even at the studio, which is the most ambitious of the six. People like having it near their homes, and they said it felt like part of the street.
That's an important finding, and it supports the idea that a small theatre is a local resource. Now, you also mentioned the economic side. Are you going to say how much money the theatres bring in?
We'd like to, but we don't know how to calculate it.

Don't try to produce a precise figure. You'd have to guess too many things, and nobody would believe the result. What you can do is ask the audience where they go before and after a show. If forty per cent say they eat in the cafés nearby, that tells a more honest story than a calculation.
That's easier. We could add a question to the cards.
Do. Now, what did the directors say about staying small? It's quite unusual for an organisation to say no to growth.

Two reasons came up more than any others. The first was the audience. Several of them said that if the theatre got bigger, people would be sitting further back, and the actors would lose that sense of being close. They said that's what makes it special.

And the second was volunteers. Most of these places depend on people who give up their evenings for nothing, selling tickets and making tea. A bigger theatre would need more than they could find, and the directors don't think they'd cope.
Neither of them mentioned money?
A few did, in passing, but it wasn't the reason for staying small. Heating a large building is expensive, certainly, but nobody said it was why they stay put.
Good. Turning to the difficulties each theatre faces. I think that could be a useful table.
Yes. The chapel has a leaking roof, and the director said she spends most of her time raising money for repairs. It's the first thing she mentioned.

The room above the pub has a different problem. The pub downstairs plays music on Friday and Saturday evenings, and it comes through the floor. They've tried different curtains and carpets, but nothing really works.

The studio is the one that had the most funding. But the rules changed last year, and now it has to show that it reaches new audiences, which is hard for a theatre that people already like. So it's worried about losing the grant.
And the village hall theatre is simple. It runs entirely on volunteers, and the three people who do most of the work are all over seventy. If they stop, nobody will take over.
That's very telling. Parking, ticket prices, none of those came up?
Parking was mentioned once, but people mostly walk, so it isn't a real problem.
Excellent. Now, how will you structure the report? I'd like to see the six theatres treated as cases with some comparison, not just six separate descriptions.
We thought of a chapter for each theatre, then a comparison at the end.

That risks being repetitive. By the time a reader reaches the sixth chapter, they won't remember the first. Try organising it by theme instead: place, people, money and buildings. Then use the theatres as examples within each theme.
That would be shorter too. We were worried about the word count.

It also shows the patterns, which is what examiners look for. Cut the history of each theatre to a paragraph. And please use the real names of the theatres only if the directors have agreed. Otherwise, call them Theatre A, Theatre B and so on.
We have written permission from four of them.

Then anonymise all six, for consistency. Nobody will mind, and it protects you if a director changes their mind. Right. I think you have a good project. Start writing, and send me the introduction in a fortnight.

Afternoon, everyone. I'd like to start with a question that sounds simple. Why do small theatres matter? We all know that big theatres matter, because they employ hundreds of people and put on spectacular shows. But the little places, the ones with eighty seats and a creaky floor, have an influence out of all proportion to their size. I'll begin with where they came from, then say what they offer, and finish with the threats they face.

Let's start with the history. Many people trace the modern small theatre to what was called the Little Theatre movement, which began in the early twentieth century. In Europe and America, groups of enthusiasts set up small stages, often in converted shops or halls, to put on plays that commercial theatres wouldn't touch. They were reacting against the big, expensive productions of the time, and they wanted something more daring.

A later landmark was the Edinburgh Fringe. It began in 1947, when eight companies turned up at the first Edinburgh International Festival without having been invited. They simply found rooms, put on shows, and the audiences came. Today it's one of the biggest arts festivals in the world, and it began as a gatecrash.

A small point about vocabulary. In New York, theatres are classified by size. Broadway houses have 500 seats or more. Off-Broadway theatres seat between 100 and 499, and anything below 100 is called Off-Off-Broadway. I mention it because the labels show that people have long regarded size as a kind of ladder, even if the rungs aren't equal in quality.

So what do small theatres offer? The first thing is closeness. In a large theatre, the actors are tiny figures in the distance, and they need to project. In a small one, the audience can sit within a few metres of the performers. You can see their faces, hear them breathe, and sometimes feel them brush past. People who've experienced that often say that it changed what they thought theatre was.

The second is risk, and I mean financial risk. A large theatre has to fill a thousand seats a night to survive. That means it must choose safe plays, with famous names, because failure costs a fortune. A small theatre can try something odd, because the cost of an empty night is low. That's how new writers get their start. Many first plays have been staged in a small room above a pub, in front of thirty people, and some of those plays later reached the main stages.

The third is the effect on a place. Here is an example. I want to stress that these figures are illustrative, not real, but they're typical of what researchers find. Imagine a town of twenty thousand people, with a small theatre of ninety seats. It gives about a hundred and sixty performances a year, and on average 70 per cent of the seats are filled. That works out at roughly 10,000 tickets a year. Now suppose that each person spends, on average, £15 in nearby cafés, bars and restaurants on the night. That's a hundred and fifty thousand pounds a year, flowing through the high street, and the theatre itself may need only a modest grant.

And I should add that the benefits aren't only financial. Many small theatres run classes for children, host community groups, and provide a place where strangers can sit together in the dark and laugh at the same joke. It's difficult to measure, but people notice when it's gone.

There's also the training function, which is easy to overlook. Many actors, directors and technicians learn their craft in small venues, where one person might build the set, run the lights and then take a bow. A famous actor may spend years in a fifty-seat theatre before anyone has heard of them, and the skills they pick up there, such as how to hold an audience with nothing but a chair and a voice, last their whole career. If small theatres vanish, the route into the profession gets narrower, and only those who can afford to work for nothing will be able to follow it.

Now, the threats. The first is staffing. A great many small theatres rely on volunteers to run front-of-house, selling tickets, serving drinks, and taking coats. That's wonderful, but it's fragile. When the volunteers get old, or move away, the theatre may struggle to survive. A few places have tried paying a very small team, but that raises costs.

The second threat is money, and in particular the cost of the building. I used to think that the biggest problem was the funding for productions, but I've changed my mind. When I talk to theatre managers now, the thing they mention first is rent. Many of them occupy buildings that are in desirable areas, and when the lease runs out, the landlord can quadruple the price. Energy bills come second, but the rent is what closes them.

Finally, a word about what we can do. If you live near a small theatre, go, and take a friend. Buy a ticket even if the play doesn't sound like your thing. You may find that the evening you didn't expect to enjoy is the one you remember.

Before the next session, read the chapter on audience development, and visit a theatre that has fewer than one hundred and fifty seats, if you can find one. Bring a ticket stub to prove that you went.
Thanks for holding. I've got the visit calendar open now, so let's see if we can get you booked in. This is for the free home fire safety check, is that right?
That's the one. My daughter picked up a leaflet at the doctor's surgery and left it on my kitchen table with a sticky note that said "Phone them, Dad". So here I am.
Well, she sounds sensible. I'll fill in the booking form as we go along. Can I start with your name?
Gideon Abernethy.
Abernethy. That's A-B-E-R-N-E-T-H-Y?
That's it. People usually leave out the second E, and then the letters never arrive.
Not from us, I hope. Now, which building do you live in? Our crews do the blocks near the harbour every autumn, but I want to be sure you're in the right area.
It's Tolland House, on Quarry Lane. The one with the green balconies, opposite the bakery.
Tolland House, yes, I know it. And your flat number?
It's 14. Oh, no, hang on, that's my old flat in Leeds. I do that every time, I'm sorry. It's 41.
Flat 41. Don't worry, you wouldn't believe how often that happens. And which floor is that on? Some buildings number the flats in a way that doesn't match the floors.

Well, I always think of it as the fifth floor, because there are four flights of stairs below us. But the ground floor is G on the lift panel, and the button for my floor says 6. So it's the sixth, if you go by the lift.
Then I'll put sixth, because that's what the crew will see when they press the button. How many people live in the flat with you?
At the moment there are three of us. Me, my wife, and my grandson, who's staying until he finishes his course in the summer. Usually it's just the two of us.
Three, then. Now, do you have working smoke alarms, and do you remember when they were last tested?

We've got one in the hall and one in the lounge. The council fitted them, and an engineer came to check them last year. I think it was May. No, wait, it was March, because it was just before my wife's birthday, and she was cross that he turned up while she was icing the cake.

March it is. That's useful, because the batteries in some of those models only last about a year, so I'd suggest we check them again when we visit. Now, there's a question I ask everyone, and please don't take it the wrong way. Does anyone in the household need help moving around, or getting out of the building quickly?
Well, my wife can walk, but not far. She had a hip operation two years ago and she uses a walking frame outside the flat. Inside, she holds on to the furniture.

Thank you for telling me. That's really important, because the crew will want to talk with you about what to do if the lift is out of action. I'll note walking frame on the form. Is there any difficulty hearing the alarm, as far as you know?
No, her hearing is fine. Mine's the one that's going.

Then the crew can show you a vibrating pad that goes under the pillow, which isn't expensive. Right, now the visit itself. The crews work Monday to Friday, and I have places on Tuesday, Wednesday and Thursday next week.

Tuesday's no good because my wife has her physiotherapy. Wednesday's possible, but my grandson has his driving lesson, and I'd like him to be there too, since he's often the one at home during the day. So Thursday would suit us best.
Thursday it is. I can offer you either a morning slot at ten, or a later one at half past four.
Half past four, please. My wife is always more tired in the morning, so the afternoon is better for her.
I'll book 4.30, then. Each visit takes about forty minutes, and there are always two officers, both with identity cards, so please do ask to see them.
That's reassuring. Will they need to look around the whole flat?

They'll look at the hall, the bedrooms and the kitchen, and they'll also check your front door and the landing outside, since that's the way you'd leave. One last thing for the form. Is there anybody nearby who holds a spare key, in case there's ever an emergency while you're out?
Yes, our neighbour at number 42, Mrs Hepplewhite. She's lived there for thirty years and she waters our plants when we go away.

Hepplewhite. Lovely. We'd never use the key without your permission, but it helps the crew to know who is around on your floor. You'll get a text message the day before, and a reminder on the morning.
Wonderful. Should I tidy up before they come?

Only a little. The most useful thing is to make sure the hallway is clear, so they can see how easy it is to get to the front door. And if you could write down any medication your wife takes, that's helpful too, though it's not compulsory.
I'll do that tonight. Thank you very much, you've been very patient with my muddles.
Not at all, Mr Abernethy. We'll see you on Thursday.
Thank you. Goodbye.
Bye for now.

Right, if everyone could shuffle in from the lift area, I'll make a start, because I know some of you have dinner waiting. Thank you for coming. For those who haven't met me, I'm Ingrid Solvang, the building manager here at Larkspur Quay, and tonight is all about what happens when something goes wrong: a fire, a flood, a long power cut, anything that means we need to act together.

Let me begin with the good news. After last winter's false alarm, when half of you stood on the pavement in dressing gowns for forty minutes, the owners have agreed to pay for proper practice. Until now we've held one drill a year, which, frankly, isn't enough, because people forget. From this autumn there will be two, one in spring and one in autumn, and we'll announce the dates three weeks in advance. We won't tell you the exact time, though, because a drill that everybody expects isn't much of a test.

Second, the alarm system itself. It's checked every week, and the test used to be on Monday mornings at seven, which upset the people who work nights. After the survey you filled in, we've moved it to Wednesday at eleven in the morning. It lasts about ten seconds. If it lasts longer than that, it isn't a test, so please treat it as real.

Now, the assembly point. For years the sign in the foyer has said the car park, and that was a mistake, because the delivery vans use the side entrance, and a crowd of residents standing in the car park is both dangerous and in the fire crew's way. So we've changed it. The new assembly point is the bandstand in the small park across the road, about eighty metres from the front door. The new sign is up, but the old one is still by the post boxes until Friday, so please ignore it.

Lifts. This is something many people don't know. When the alarm sounds, the lifts do not simply stop where they are. They travel to the ground floor, the doors open, and then they're switched off, so nobody can use them. That means everyone has to use the stairs. I know that's hard for those on the top floors, and that's exactly why I want to talk about help. If you, or someone in your household, would find the stairs difficult, please register with the management office. We'll sit down with you and write a personal evacuation plan. It's a short document, it's confidential, and only the fire service and I will ever see it. You can come to the office any weekday between nine and twelve, or you can drop a note through the door and I'll come to you.
Now for the practical part, which is the equipment. A lot of you have asked where things will be, so let me go through them. You'll see a sheet on your chairs, but I'll tell you the main points.

First, torches. We're buying rechargeable emergency torches, and they'll be fixed to the wall in a small box on every landing, so wherever you are in the stairwell, you won't be in the dark. The box lights up if the power fails, so you can find it easily.

Second, the floor plans. At the moment there's a plan in the foyer, which is no use to anyone who is already on the fourteenth floor. The new plans show the exits and the stairwells, and they'll be fixed at the foot of the stairs, where the fire crew come in. I did think about putting them in the lift lobbies, but the lifts are going to be switched off, so nobody will be standing there.

Third, the first aid kit. I'd originally planned to put it in the concierge office, but the office is shut at night, and accidents don't only happen between nine and five. So it's going into the laundry room, which is open round the clock and has a sink. Please don't borrow plasters for your own use, because the kit is checked on the first of every month.

Fourth, the defibrillator. Several of you asked about this after the incident at the leisure centre. It'll be in a heated cabinet right beside the main entrance, outside the front doors, so that anyone can reach it, including people passing in the street. There'll be a recorded voice that tells you what to do, so you really don't need training, though I'm planning a short session in November.

And fifth, the emergency radio. It's a wind-up radio, with a spare set of batteries, and it's going to be kept in the concierge office, in a locked cupboard. If there's a long power cut, I'll bring it out and we'll get the news from the local station. A radio in the car park would be no use to anyone, so I'm afraid there's no plan to put anything out there.

One more thing before the questions. Some of you have asked about the bike store, and whether it counts as an exit. It does not. It's a locked room with a single door, and in a fire it's the last place to be. So please don't leave bikes in the stairwell, either. The crew need those stairs clear.

Please spare a thought for your own neighbours too. If you know that the flat next to you has an elderly person, or a family with small children, please just have a word with them about tonight. It makes a surprising difference when someone knocks on the door. Now, who'd like to ask a question first? Yes, the gentleman at the back.
Come in, both of you. I read your pilot report on the train this morning, so let's get straight to it. Tell me why you chose apartment buildings in the first place.

It was partly personal, actually. Last January the lift in my building broke down for three days, and I realised that nobody on our floor knew who to call, or whether there was any plan at all for people who couldn't manage the stairs. I started asking around, and it turned out nobody had a clue.

I was more interested in the fire side, because my cousin works for the fire service and says the same thing about every tall building. But the lift story makes a better introduction, so we kept Ottilie's version.
Good. A personal story is fine, as long as the question that follows from it is a proper one. Now, the pilot. You gave the questionnaire to twelve residents at Wren Court. What happened?

Eight replied, which was better than we'd hoped. But question four caused trouble. We asked, "Do you have an emergency plan?" Five of the eight said yes, but when we read the comments, it turned out they meant they'd put a torch in a kitchen drawer, or that they thought the fire notice on the landing counted.
And two of them thought we meant a medical emergency, so they wrote about their GP's phone number. One person even wrote that the question was too frightening to answer.

So the problem isn't that the residents are unprepared. The problem is that the phrase means something different to each of them, and you can't compare answers that don't measure the same thing. You'll have to define it on the form, perhaps with a couple of examples.
That's what we thought, and we've rewritten it. Now it says, "A plan is something you could explain to a visitor in a minute."

That's much better. Now, eight out of twelve is two thirds, which is excellent. But please don't expect it to hold. When you send a questionnaire to hundreds of people, you'll be lucky to get one in five back, so you should plan for that from the start.
That's why we were thinking of knocking on doors. Then people can't ignore us.

I'd advise against it, for two reasons. One is your own safety, because I don't want students alone in corridors in the evening. The other is ethics. Turning up at someone's door to ask whether they're prepared for a disaster could easily worry them, and the committee would ask a lot of questions. A printed form through the letterbox, with a return box in the lobby, is much safer. You could also add a code for people who prefer to answer on their phones.
That's fine. The managing agents have already said we can put a box beside the post boxes.
Good. Anything else you're worried about?

One thing. I keep thinking that the people who reply will be the ones who are already interested in safety. If they're the only ones, the results will look much better than the real situation, and we'll end up saying that residents are well prepared when they aren't.

That's a real weakness, and you should say so in the limitations section. You can't solve it, but you can reduce it. For example, you could compare the people who replied with the building's records to see who's missing, and you can follow up with a short reminder.
We could ask the managing agents for the number of flats on each floor, so we can see if one floor is missing.

Exactly. Now, let's look at the questionnaire. It's one page, which is sensible. I'd like you to add two things. First, how long the person has lived in the building. I suspect newcomers know less, and it would be a very clear result if they did.
Kwabena wanted to ask about pets as well, because people sometimes refuse to leave without them.
And Ottilie suggested a question about languages spoken at home, so we could see whether the notices are understood.

Both are good ideas, but you can't ask everything on one page, and the pets question is better for interviews. The language question is important, but save it for the interviews too. What I'd add, as my second addition, is a question about who they would call first in an emergency. Their answer tells you whether they'd phone the emergency services, the manager, or a neighbour, and that's more useful than asking if they have a plan.
That's clever. We'll put it in as an open question.
Right. Which buildings will you survey? You told me you want three.
Yes. Wren Court is the one from the pilot, and the residents there are mostly older, a lot of them retired. We'd keep it for comparison, since the replies were already good.

The second is the Mill Lofts, a converted warehouse. The managing agent told us that about half of the flats are let by the week to visitors, so it's a very different group of people. We thought it would be a good contrast.
And the third is Parkside Tower, which is the newest. It had sprinklers fitted last year, so we wondered whether people feel safer because of that, and whether it makes them less careful.
Interesting. Did you consider the Granary?
We did, but it has no lift, and it's too small, with only fourteen flats. We also looked at Dene View, which is managed by a housing association, but they haven't replied to our emails.
Fine. Three buildings is plenty for the time you have. Send me the revised form by Friday, and I'll look at it over the weekend.
Thank you. We'll do that.

Welcome back, everyone. I'd like to start with something that few of us ever think about until the alarm sounds, which is how people actually behave when they have to leave a building. Many of us assume that the moment an alarm rings, everybody stands up and walks briskly to the exit. In practice, that isn't what happens, and understanding why is the starting point for any serious emergency plan, especially in apartment buildings, where the people involved are not colleagues who have trained together but neighbours who may hardly know one another.

Let me start with a term you'll meet in every textbook on the subject. When engineers model an evacuation, they divide the total time into stages. First there is detection, when the building recognises that something is wrong. Then comes the alarm. Then comes the stage that surprises most students, which is the delay before people begin to move. That delay is known as pre-movement time, and it's very often longer than the time people spend walking to the exit. In some buildings it accounts for most of the total.

Why should people wait? Researchers have found several reasons. The first is that a bell on its own tells you very little. Most of us don't know whether it's a drill, a fault or a real fire, so the natural reaction is to look for more information. We open the door and look along the corridor, we phone a friend, or we go to the window to see whether other people are outside. A second reason is that people finish what they're doing. They turn off the cooker, they save a document, they look for their shoes. And a third reason, which is particularly relevant at home, is that people stop to collect valuables. Passports, laptops, the cat, a box of photographs. None of these are irrational choices, but every minute adds risk.

To show you the pattern, I'll use figures from an imaginary study, because the shape of the results matters more than the exact numbers. Imagine researchers observing drills in a block of apartments with about two hundred residents. The median delay before people began to leave was 75 seconds. That's the middle value, so half of the residents waited longer. A small group waited more than five minutes, and when the researchers interviewed them afterwards, a number of them said something very interesting. They said they'd assumed it was a false alarm, because the alarm in their building had been triggered by burnt toast so many times before. This is sometimes called the cry-wolf effect, and it's a serious design problem, because the more often a system sounds when there is no danger, the less seriously people take it.

What made the difference in the imaginary study? The biggest factor was social. People left much sooner when somebody physically came to their door. In the building I'm describing, volunteers called fire wardens went along the corridors during the drill and knocked on each door. The residents who were visited left, on average, almost a minute earlier than those who were not. That agrees with a lot of real research, which shows that an alarm tells people that something is happening, but a neighbour at the door tells them it matters to them.

Next, think about the route. When people do leave, they don't always choose the nearest exit. Many head for the entrance they know best, which in most apartment buildings is the front entrance that they use every day. They know where it is, and it feels safe, even if the fire exit at the end of the corridor is much closer. If the front hall happens to be where the fire is, this can be dangerous. So a good plan makes the alternative routes familiar, and one way to do that is to use them in drills.

The design of the building matters as well. Take signs. In our imaginary study, the researchers moved a set of exit signs from just below the ceiling to eye level, and the number of people who found the stairwell without help rose noticeably. It sounds obvious, but in many older buildings the signs are still where somebody thought they would look good. And the lifts, as the building manager at your last lecture may have told you, are normally switched off, so residents on the upper floors need to know that they have to use the stairs from the very beginning. Some will want to wait for the lift, because that's what they do every day, so the plan has to say, in plain words, not to.

So what can be done? Most of the evidence points to three measures. The first is drills. In the imaginary study, the researchers compared a year with no practice and a year with two drills, and the median delay fell by 40 per cent. People simply knew what to expect. The second measure is information that is clear and local, which means saying exactly where to go, rather than telling people to leave by the nearest exit. And the third is to give people who need help a plan of their own. In the building we've been discussing, those residents who had agreed a personal evacuation plan in advance left fastest of all, and also reported feeling least anxious. That last point is easy to overlook, because it shows that planning doesn't only make people safer, it reduces fear as well.

Let me finish with a caution. Everything I have said is about averages, and every building is different. A plan that works in a block with one stairwell may fail in a block with three. Your own work will need to look carefully at the people and the place involved, and that's what we'll turn to next week, when we look at how to design a questionnaire that asks the right things. Thank you very much.

Sorry, I'm still wrestling with the card reader, so bear with me. You're my first visitor of the day, which means you get the full speech. Have a look at the leaflet while I try to make this thing switch on.
No rush at all. A friend told me you lend out tools the way a library lends books. I thought she was pulling my leg.

She wasn't. We keep about four hundred items in a shed at the far end of the allotments, everything from spirit levels to wallpaper steamers, and members borrow them for a few days at a time. It saves everybody buying things they'll use twice. Right, I think it's working. Shall I take some details?
Please. Where do I start?
Your name, if that's all right.
Cormac Quigley. The surname is Irish, from my grandfather's side, and it always gets misspelt, so it's Q-U-I-G-L-E-Y.
Q-U-I-G-L-E-Y. Lovely. And where do you live?
Number 12, Marram Street. It's the little turning behind the library.

Oh, I know it. My sister had a flat there. Now, there are three kinds of membership. Single is for one adult, household covers everyone living at your address, and the group one is for clubs and schools.

I live on my own, so single, I suppose. Actually, hold on. My nephew is staying with me this term while he finishes his apprenticeship, and he's the one who really knows how to use this stuff. So perhaps household is better.

Household would be the sensible choice if he'll be borrowing too, because a single card can only be used by the person named on it. It does cost a bit more, though. Normally it's £30 a year for a household, and £20 for a single. But we're signing up founder members at the moment, and until the end of the month a household membership is only £18.
That's very cheap. Put me down for that.
Done. Now, how many items can you borrow at once? When the shed first opened it was three, but since the new shelving went in last month, members can take four at a time.
Four will be plenty. I don't think I've ever needed more than two tools for any job.
What are you hoping to borrow first?
I'm re-tiling the bathroom floor. I wondered about a tile cutter, but I'll need a trowel and a spirit level too. My neighbour keeps telling me a wet saw is the only proper way to do it.

We don't have a wet saw, I'm afraid. We only have the manual cutters, but they're perfectly good for ordinary ceramic tiles. I'll put down tile cutter, and you can add the other things when you collect it.
That sounds fine.
And when do you need it? We're open for collections on Thursday and Friday evenings, and on Saturday mornings.

I was going to say Saturday 2 May, but the plaster in the bathroom needs more time to dry, so I think I'd better start a week later. Saturday 9 May, then. My sister is coming to stay on the sixteenth, so I really would like it finished by then.

Then you'll want to collect the cutter on the Friday evening. Now, before anybody borrows anything with a motor, we ask them to come to a short safety induction. The tile cutter doesn't count as a power tool, but I expect you'll want the drill sooner or later.
Probably, yes. When are the inductions?
They're on Wednesday evenings, and they take about half an hour. There used to be one at half past seven as well, but it was always empty, so now it's just one, at 6.45.
That's fine. I'll come along next Wednesday, if there's a space.

There always is. Just turn up. And you'll find the shed behind the scout hut on Fordham Lane. It has a green door, and a very large sign saying "Tool Share" that someone painted last year and which now seems to be fading.
Behind the scout hut, got it. I think I walked past it on Sunday and thought it was a garden store.

Plenty of people do. The last thing is proof of address. We just need to see something with your name and the Marram Street address on it, something from the last three months. A bank statement is fine, or a utility bill. The only thing we can't accept is a mobile phone bill.
I have a gas bill from last month. Would that do?

That's perfect. Bring it on Wednesday and I'll scan it. You'll get your membership card then, and a little booklet with the rules. They're not scary, I promise. Mostly it's about bringing things back clean.
I'll try to remember that. Thanks for all your help.
Not at all, Cormac. See you on Wednesday.

Right, hands up if you've never held a pole saw. Good, I like honesty, and that's exactly why we run this talk for every new member. I'm Marit, and I look after the shed on Fordham Lane. Over the next ten minutes I'll tell you how borrowing works, what you can't borrow, and where everything lives, so that you're not wandering about on Saturday morning looking lost.

First, how long you can keep things. When we opened, the loan period was a week, and it turned out to be far too long. Popular tools like the carpet cleaner and the steam stripper were out for days when nobody was using them, and other people were waiting. So most tools now go out for four days. Big machines, like the floor sander, are different, and those are weekend loans only, from Friday evening to Monday.

Second, what happens if something comes back late. We don't charge fines, because we don't want people to feel they can't afford to borrow. What we do is stop your borrowing for a week, and that's usually enough. If something is damaged, you tell us at the hatch, and we'll tell you whether it's something we can mend ourselves. Accidents happen, and nobody will shout.

Third, training. Anyone borrowing a power tool for the first time needs to have attended the induction on a Wednesday evening, but that's only half of it. At the hatch, before you take the tool away, one of our volunteers will watch you use it for a minute or two, to check that you know how to switch it on and where the guard goes. It sounds fussy, but it has already prevented one or two near misses.

Now, what we don't lend. People always ask this, so I'll be clear. You'll see a list pinned up by the hatch. Pressure washers are fine, and so are hedge trimmers and extension ladders, though the long ladders need two people to carry them, so please bring someone. But we don't lend petrol chainsaws. Our insurer won't cover them, and honestly, I wouldn't feel comfortable either. And we don't lend nail guns, because the safety training takes a whole day, and we simply can't offer it. If you need one of those, there's a hire company in the industrial estate, and they'll be glad to help.

Right, let me take you through the layout of the shed, because it's a bit odd. It used to be a bicycle store, and it still has some strange corners. Walk in through the main door and the hatch is straight ahead of you. That's where you hand things in and collect them, and where I'll be most Saturdays.

Power drills and drivers are kept in the locked cage on your left. I know that seems over-cautious, but the batteries are expensive, and they're the thing most likely to disappear. The volunteer on the hatch will fetch whatever you ask for.

Garden tools, spades, forks, rakes and so on, used to be on the back wall inside, but it was too crowded in the spring, so since March they've been on a rack outside, under the little roof beside the door. You help yourself, but you still have to sign them out at the hatch.

Ladders are the awkward ones. They used to lean against the wall by the workbench, which wasn't safe, so we now keep them in the metal container behind the shed. You go out of the back door, and there's a blue container with a padlock. Ask a volunteer for the key.
The tile cutters, saws and similar tools, anything that cuts, are in the back room. It's quite narrow, so please don't go in unless you've asked, because there's very little space to move about.

And finally, paint equipment. Rollers, brushes, trays and the paint sprayer, if you've seen it, are in the loft, up the ladder at the end of the workbench. You can't go up there without a volunteer, partly because of the stairs and partly because we've had paint on the floor before. I don't think I need to explain that one. The workbench itself is at the side, and you're welcome to use it if you need to fix something before you take it away, though I'm afraid there's no tea.

One last thing, which is about reminders. A text goes out the evening before anything is due back, and you can ask to have it as an email instead. If you lose a tool, don't panic, and don't buy a new one without telling us, because we might already have a spare. We've had several members turn up with expensive replacements that were different from the original, and that creates much more paperwork than the loss itself.
That's me finished. Come through to the hatch, and I'll show you the booking screen. Mind the step on the way.
Right, let me see where you've got to. The title on your draft is "Borrowing and lending tools in neighbourhoods". Remind me what's actually new about it.

Most of the research we found looks either at formal tool libraries or at the sharing apps. Nobody seems to compare a library with the informal lending that goes on in a street, where somebody simply knocks on a door to ask for a ladder. So we want to interview people from both kinds.

I wasn't convinced at first. I thought the library would win on everything, because it has rules and insurance. Maren thought the informal way would be more popular because it's free. In the end we agreed to find out rather than guess.
Good. Comparing two arrangements is a legitimate gap, as long as you can say why the difference matters. How did you find the people for your first interviews?
We tried a poster at the library, and nobody replied. Then Maren put a message on her street's group chat and got six volunteers within an hour.
Which is a problem in itself, because they're all my neighbours, and they know me.

Exactly. I was going to raise that. People who like you will be polite, and they'll tend to say whatever they assume you are hoping for. That's fine for a pilot, because all you're testing is whether the questions work. But for the main study, ask the library to send a message to its members, and use a street you don't live on.
That makes sense. I hadn't thought about the politeness side of it.
What did the pilot tell you about why people borrow? I'd like to hear one or two actual results.

I was sure that cost would be the main reason. But the first person we interviewed said that what mattered most was not having to find space to store something she'd use once. Cost came second, though she did say that the price of a tile cutter made her wince.
The others agreed. Four of the six said that storage was the biggest reason, which I didn't expect at all, because I live in a house with a garage.
That's an interesting result, and it suggests the title should perhaps mention space and not only money. Now, what about the people who didn't join the library? Did you ask them why?

We did. A few of them said the opening hours didn't suit them, because the shed is only open on Thursday and Friday evenings and Saturday mornings, and some people work shifts. And two of them said it was simply too far away, because the shed is at the far end of the allotments and there's no bus.
One person said she hadn't heard of it, but she only said that once, so I wouldn't count it. And nobody complained about the fee. They all said eighteen pounds was cheap.
Good. Opening hours and distance are the kind of practical findings the council might actually act on. Now, let me ask about the recording. You've been recording the interviews on your phones.
Yes, with permission. Everyone signed the form first.

Good. Be careful with the files. I'd like you to delete the recordings once they've been typed up, and take the names out of the transcripts. If someone says that her neighbour never returns the lawnmower, you don't want that attached to a name in an appendix.
That's a good point. I'd been planning to keep the recordings until the end of the project, in case we needed to check anything.
You can check against the typed transcripts. Keep the recordings as short a time as you can.
Fine. We'll do that.
Now, the main study. You'll have the same questions for both groups, I hope?
Yes. Open questions, the same for each, so we can compare the answers directly.
Good, keep them the same. Otherwise you can't compare. How many interviews do you plan?
Five from each group. That would be ten altogether, which feels like a lot already.

I'd say ten per group, or twenty in all. Five is too few to see any pattern, and with only ten people one unusual person could change your whole picture. If twenty is too many to transcribe, you could do shorter interviews, but I'd rather have more voices than long ones.
Twenty. All right.
What about how long each interview should be? The first ones ran to nearly an hour, and by the end people were just repeating themselves.

Aim for about twenty-five minutes. Anything longer and you'll drown in transcripts, and the people you're interviewing will start to wish they hadn't volunteered. Have a small number of questions you really need answered, and then leave a little room at the end for anything they want to add. That's often where the best material turns up.
We could offer to meet them at the shed or at their own front door, whichever they'd prefer.
Their own front door is better for the street group, and a neutral place for the library members. It also means you can see the tools in the garage, which tells you something too.

And when you analyse the transcripts, don't just read them and pick out quotations you like. Code them properly, going through each transcript and labelling the themes, such as storage, trust, cost and convenience, and then count how often each one comes up in each group. That's what turns a collection of stories into a result.
We did start doing that by hand, with highlighters.
Highlighters are fine for a pilot. For twenty, use a spreadsheet. Send me the new plan by Friday and I'll comment over the weekend.
Thank you, Dr Imrie.

Good morning, everyone. Think for a moment about the tools in your own home. A drill, a ladder, a set of spanners, perhaps a pressure washer in the shed. How many hours a year do you actually use them? For most of us, the honest answer is almost none. Household tools spend nearly all of their lives unused, and yet each household buys its own. Today I want to look at what happens when neighbourhoods decide to do something about that, and what research tells us about how sharing arrangements succeed or fail.

Let me begin with a theoretical point, because it's one that students often miss. People used to believe that anything shared would be spoilt. If a resource belongs to everyone, the argument goes, nobody looks after it. The political economist Elinor Ostrom challenged that view, and in 2009 she won the Nobel Prize in Economic Sciences for her work. She studied how real communities manage shared resources, such as fisheries, forests and water systems, and she found that many of them did so successfully for generations. What mattered was not whether a resource was owned privately or publicly, but whether there were clear rules, whether people could see who was following them, and whether those who broke the rules were dealt with sensibly.

Now, how does that apply to a box of spanners? Here are some made-up figures, so you can see how the argument works, and please don't quote them. Imagine that researchers asked 800 households in a medium-sized town about their tools. Of these, 86 per cent owned an electric drill. That's not surprising. But when they asked how often the drill was used, the typical answer was about five times a year. Five times, for an object that costs more than a good pair of shoes. And when they asked whether they would be willing to lend it, most people said yes, in principle. In other words, there is a gap between ownership and willingness.

Why does that gap exist? The researchers asked those who owned tools but did not lend them, and the most common answer was fear of damage. People worried that the tool would come back broken, or that it wouldn't come back at all. A smaller number worried about being asked to lend something they didn't trust the borrower to use properly. And then there was a social reason, which I find fascinating: some people said that they would rather buy a new drill than ask a neighbour, because asking felt like admitting that they couldn't manage. In other words, the barrier to sharing is often as much about pride as about money.

So how do successful schemes overcome this? The first answer, perhaps surprisingly, is that trust is built through very small actions. Where informal lending works well, neighbours tell you that the tool must always be returned on time. That is the single behaviour that people mention most. Nobody expects a gift, though a bottle of something is always appreciated. But if a borrower brings back a ladder a week late, the lender doesn't say anything, and simply doesn't lend again. That's why a formal scheme, like a tool library, can be more reliable, because it takes the awkwardness out of the situation. The reminder doesn't come from a neighbour. It comes from the system.
