The second answer is clear lending rules. A good library tells people how long they may keep a tool, what happens if it is returned late, and what it will not lend at all. Notice that these are exactly the kinds of rules that Ostrom identified in her studies, applied to a very small community. The most successful libraries in the imaginary survey, and in the real research that it was modelled on, also had a short induction for anyone who wanted to borrow power tools, and a volunteer at the counter who could check that the borrower knew how to use the equipment.

The third answer is location. This seems trivial, but it turned out to be one of the strongest predictors of use. A library that people could walk to in under ten minutes, or that they passed on a regular journey, did much better than one in a quiet corner. The researchers in our imaginary study found that the best sites were beside a primary school, because parents pass the door twice a day, and a library that you pass twice a day is a library you remember when the shelf comes off the wall.

I want to finish with a caution. Sharing schemes tend to be started by people who are already comfortable with the idea, and they tend to attract people who resemble them. If we want a neighbourhood scheme to serve everyone, including people on low incomes, older residents and those who aren't online, we have to think about hours, about distance, and about who feels welcome. That's the subject of the lecture after next, on the practical side of running a community project. Please look at the two readings on the course page beforehand. Thank you.

Westerbrook Welcome Line, this is Hemi. Before we go any further, are you ringing about the leaflet with the sunflower on the front? I only ask because we had a printing mix-up and some of them went out with the wrong number.
Yes, that's the one, sunflower and everything. It was in a pile of post that came with the house, and I nearly threw it out with the pizza menus.
I'm glad you didn't. So you've recently moved to the area?
Yes, a few weeks ago. I'd better give you my name first, hadn't I? It's Paloma Sandoval. That's S-A-N-D-O-V-A-L.
Thank you, Paloma. I'll start a record for you. And which suburb have you moved to?
Havenside. We're in one of the new houses beside the old ferry wharf.
Lovely part of town. And when did you move in? I need the month, because the welcome package is different for people who arrived in the last three months.
Let me think. We collected the keys at the end of July, but the painters were late, so we didn't really move in until the first week of August. So I'd say August.
August, then. Now, who's in your household?

My husband and me, and the children. We've got three children. Oh, wait, no, I always say three because my niece is here so often, but she lives with her mother down the road. There are two of our own.
Two children, then, which will matter for the school information. Is English your first language, or would you like some of the materials in another language?
My English is fine for talking, though I find forms very difficult. My first language is Spanish. My husband would prefer everything in Spanish if he can.
We have the full pack in Spanish, so that's easy. Can I ask what sort of help you're looking for? Some people just want the welcome pack, and others want us to point them toward particular services.

A few things. We found a doctor quite quickly, because the surgery is next to the supermarket. But every dentist we phone has a waiting list of months, and my husband has a tooth that really needs looking at. So that's the first thing, a dentist.
I'll put dentist at the top, and I'll ask the team which practices are taking new patients. Now, your children. Which school have you chosen?
Sedge Lane Primary. My daughter is nine. At her old school she was in Year 3, but here they've put her in Year 4 because of her birthday. She's rather nervous about it.

That's very common, and the school is good with new arrivals. I'll put Year 4 on the form, and I'll make sure the pack includes the leaflet for parents. Now, we also run a buddy scheme. We match you with a volunteer who lives nearby and shares one of your interests. It's completely optional.
I like that idea. I'm a bit lonely, if I'm honest. All my friends are far away.
So, what would you say your main interest is? We have walkers, gardeners, a knitting group, and a lot of keen swimmers.
I'd say walking, but really, it's swimming. I used to swim every morning before work, and I haven't been in the water since we arrived.

Then I'll put swimming, and there's a volunteer called Joanne who swims at the harbour pool on Saturdays. She'd be delighted. When's the best time to phone you? The buddies like to call before they visit.
Mornings are difficult because of the school run, and in the afternoons I'm working from home with the door shut. Evenings are best, after seven.

Evenings, perfect. Last thing, the welcome pack itself. We can post it, but we'd rather deliver it in person, so we can say hello. The volunteer who delivers usually has a bag of local things, a map of the bus routes and so on. We could come on Thursday.
Thursday I'm at the school all day, because there's a parents' meeting. Could it be Friday?
Friday, no problem. Someone will bring it between ten and twelve. And you'll receive a text to say who's coming and what they look like, so you aren't surprised at the door.
That's very thoughtful. One more question, if you don't mind. My husband works nights at the bakery, so he sleeps in the day. Will the volunteer need to knock very loudly?

Not at all. I'll add a note to the record asking them to ring the bell once and wait. And if nobody answers, they'll leave the pack with a note, and we'll try again another day. Nobody will be offended.
Thank you so much, Hemi. I think I'll sleep better tonight.
That's what we're here for. Welcome to Westerbrook, Paloma.

Hello, everyone, and welcome to our open morning. It's lovely to see so many of you. Do come in a little closer, because the acoustics in this atrium are dreadful, and I'll tell you about the Westerbrook Welcome Hub, and then we'll walk round together. I'm Catriona, I'm the Hub's coordinator, and I've been here since the day we opened.

First, the basics. The Hub is open from nine until five, Monday to Friday. On Saturdays we used to open all day, but we found that very few people came in the afternoon, so since March we've been open on Saturday mornings only. That was a difficult decision, but it has freed the volunteers to run more sessions during the week, when the demand is greater.

Second, who pays for all this. A lot of people assume that the council funds us entirely. In fact the council provides the building, and not much else. The money for staff and activities comes from donations, a lottery grant, and a small amount from local businesses. Nobody is ever charged for anything here, and we want to keep it that way, which is why we spend a lot of time filling in funding applications.

Third, something new. Language has always been a barrier, and we have volunteers who speak a dozen languages between them, but not everyone has a volunteer who speaks theirs. So this year we've started a telephone interpreting service. If you come in and nobody can understand you, the receptionist rings a number, and within a minute you're speaking to a trained interpreter, who stays on the line for the whole conversation. It has made more difference than anything else we've done.
Now let me describe where things happen, because it's quite a rambling building. It used to be a primary school, and we've kept as many of the old classrooms as we could.

Our most popular session, by a long way, is the free English conversation group. It meets on Tuesday and Thursday mornings in the Garden Room, which is the one with the French windows opening onto the lawn. In summer we move the chairs outside and, honestly, the conversation is better.

Legal advice is on Wednesday afternoons, and it needs a quiet space, so it takes place in the Quiet Room, at the end of the corridor on your left. The solicitors are volunteers from a local firm, and they deal with everything from tenancy agreements to immigration questions. I should say that it's only for advice, not representation.

The job club meets on Thursday afternoons in the Studio. It's a bigger room, with computers along one wall, and the volunteers there help people write their CVs and practise interviews. Several people have found work through it, and we're very proud of that.

For families, there's story time for under-fives, which takes place in the Library Corner on Friday mornings. It's the cosiest spot in the building, with the beanbags and the picture books, and it fills up fast, so do get there in good time. The parents tend to stay and talk afterwards, and a lot of friendships have started that way.

The sewing group, which has become something of an institution, meets on Monday evenings in the Kitchen. I know that sounds strange, but the kitchen has the biggest tables, and there's an electric kettle, so the group is never short of tea. Members bring their own projects, and some of them are very ambitious indeed.

And finally, the weekly lunch, which we call Open Table, is held in the Meeting Room on the first floor, since that's where the long table is. It started with six people and now we regularly have forty. It isn't a service in any formal sense, just a chance to sit and eat with people you haven't met, but I'd say it's one of the most important things we do.

The Atrium, where we're standing, is the one place where there's no activity at all, because it's our front door, and we want people to be able to come in without being asked what they want. We have sofas, a noticeboard and a tea urn. Nobody asks anything of you.

One thing visitors often ask is whether they need to register before they come to any of these. The answer is no. You can turn up, give your first name if you like, and join in. We only ask for more details if you want to see the legal adviser, because the solicitors have to check for conflicts of interest, and that takes a few minutes. Everything else is just walk-in, and we've found that the less paperwork there is at the door, the more people actually come through it.

Before we start the walk, a quick word about the volunteers. You'll see people wearing yellow lanyards. They're all trained, and they all know the building, so if you can't find something, ask any of them. They'll be glad to help, and to hear what you thought of the morning. Shall we go?
Come in, both of you. Esme, Luka, thanks for sending the draft in advance. I've read it once, and I have questions, but first tell me where you've got to.

We're looking at whether welcome leaflets actually help newcomers. We collected twenty-five leaflets from towns around the region, and we also interviewed eight people who'd moved to the area in the last year.

People often ask why we started with paper rather than websites. The answer is that nearly every newcomer we spoke to said the first thing they received was a leaflet, usually from a landlord or a neighbour, and they didn't find the websites until much later. So the paper leaflet is the first point of contact, even though it's old-fashioned.
That's a good justification, and it's worth stating clearly in the introduction. What did you find when you looked at the language of the leaflets?

I used a free online tool to check the reading level, and most were fine on that score. The real problem was the abbreviations. One leaflet used CAB, GP, NHS and ASB within the first paragraph, with no explanation of any of them. It would be difficult even for someone who'd grown up here.
I'd say that's worse than the length. A few were very long, but a long leaflet at least has room to explain. The short ones were full of acronyms.
So the headline finding is that confusing abbreviations are a bigger obstacle than the reading level. That's useful. What did the newcomers say about the leaflets themselves?

Most of them kept the leaflet, but they put it aside to read later and never did. One woman had hers on the fridge for three months before she read it properly. By then she'd already worked out most of the things the leaflet was trying to tell her.
That's telling. It suggests that the timing matters as much as the content. Right, what about the number of interviews? You've done eight, and I know that's less than you hoped.
We were going to do fifteen, but several people didn't reply to our messages. I'm worried it's too few.

For an exploratory study, eight is acceptable. You're not trying to prove anything about every newcomer in the country, you're trying to find out what questions are worth asking. Provided you're open about it, I think you're fine. Just don't claim more than you've got.
We'll make that clear in the method section.

One more thing about that. When I wrote up the interviews, I noticed that people were very reluctant to criticise the leaflets. They kept saying that someone had clearly worked hard on them. It made the answers rather polite.

That's a familiar problem. People don't like to criticise something that was given to them in kindness. One way round it is to ask what a friend of theirs would find confusing, instead of asking what they found confusing themselves. It's a small trick, but it works surprisingly well, so you might use it if you go back for a second round.
We did try that with the last two people, and they were much more open.
Good, then say so in the method section. Now, which information did the newcomers say they wanted most? You mentioned that in the notes.

Everyone mentioned the doctor. Several people didn't know they had to register in order to see one, and one man spent a fortnight in pain because he assumed he could simply turn up. The second thing was transport. Specifically, which bus goes to the hospital, because that's a real worry for people who don't drive.

I'd have guessed that bin collection days would come up, since they're always at the top of the leaflets, but nobody said it. They worked it out from the neighbours. And schools came up, but only from parents, so it wasn't a main finding.

So there's a gap between what leaflets emphasise and what newcomers need. That's your finding. It's interesting. Now, let me say something about the structure of the report. I think the introduction is too long. You've got three pages about the history of welcome schemes, which is interesting, but nobody needs that much. Cut it to a page.
That's fair. I got carried away.

In the method section, tell me how you chose the leaflets. At the moment it says you collected twenty-five, but not where from or why those ones. A reader will wonder if you picked the bad ones deliberately.
We took whatever was available in the library and the council office, so it wasn't a very scientific selection.

Then say that. It's not a weakness, as long as you tell people. In the findings, include more quotations. Right now it reads like a list of numbers, and the quotations from the newcomers are the part people will remember. The woman with the leaflet on the fridge is wonderful.
We have plenty of those. I'll pick the best ones.

And in the recommendations, don't just say the leaflets should be clearer. Give examples of unclear phrases, with a rewritten version next to each. That's something a council could use straight away, which is the point of the whole thing.
We could do that as a table, the original wording on the left and our version on the right.
Perfect. I'd also considered suggesting a map of the towns, but I don't think it adds anything. Leave it out. Send me the revised draft in a fortnight.
Thank you, Dr Abara. That's really helpful.

Last week we looked at what newcomers need when they arrive in a new place. This week I want to ask a different question. Not what they need, but how they actually build a life, which is largely a matter of how they build relationships. Anyone who has moved to a new town knows the feeling of walking down a street where nobody knows you. The question for researchers, and for the organisations that try to help, is how that feeling changes, and what speeds it up.

I'd like to begin with a classic piece of sociology. In 1973 the American sociologist Mark Granovetter published a paper called The Strength of Weak Ties. His central idea was simple, but it overturned a lot of assumptions. We usually think that our close friends are our most valuable connections. Granovetter pointed out that weak ties, meaning acquaintances rather than close friends, matter in a different way. Your close friends tend to know the same people you do and the same information. Acquaintances belong to other circles, so they are the ones who bring you news from outside. In his study, the example was jobs. People often heard about a job from someone they saw only occasionally, not from a best friend. For a newcomer, that is very good news, because acquaintances are exactly what a newcomer can make quickly, long before they make close friends.

The second idea comes from another sociologist, Ray Oldenburg, who in 1989 wrote about what he called third places. His point was that people need somewhere that is neither home nor work, a place where you can turn up without an invitation and where status doesn't matter. Today we might think of cafés, libraries, barber shops, or the benches in a park, though I should say these are my examples, not his. For newcomers such places matter because they are where the weak ties form. You can't have a conversation with someone you never meet.

The figures I'm about to give you come from a survey I have invented, so please don't cite them. What I want you to notice is the shape. Imagine researchers who interviewed 300 newcomers during their first six months in a medium-sized town. They asked everyone where they had first had a friendly conversation with a neighbour or local person. The most common answer was the school gate. That was true even for people without children, who said it was the place where they first saw others talking, and who stopped there on their walk. Other answers included the doctor's waiting room, the supermarket queue, and a local café.

Now, the more worrying part. After six months, only 35 per cent of the newcomers said they had a neighbour they could ask for help with something practical, such as borrowing a ladder or collecting a parcel. Everyone else had met people, but not in a way that led to anything. That suggests that being friendly in a queue, though pleasant, isn't the same as having a relationship that you can rely on. The researchers called this the gap between contact and connection.

What narrowed it? The study compared newcomers who had attended a welcome event, such as a coffee morning or a street party, in their first month, with those who hadn't. Those who attended were twice as likely to have joined a local group within the six months, and a local group, as you'd expect, is a source of exactly those weak ties we've been discussing. Importantly, the event didn't have to be sophisticated. A cup of tea and a name badge were enough. Many of the best events were organised by volunteers with almost no budget.

One more finding is worth mentioning, because it complicates the picture. The newcomers who were most outgoing did not always make the strongest connections. Some of them met a great many people in their first month, but because they were always moving on to the next group or the next event, none of those acquaintances turned into someone who would lend a hand. Meanwhile some quieter people who simply went to the same café on the same morning every week ended up with more reliable contacts after six months. Repetition, in other words, mattered more than variety.

Notice what this means for the people who run welcome schemes. It is tempting to measure success by how many leaflets were handed out, or how many people attended an event. But the survey suggests that the better measure is whether, six months later, the newcomer has someone to ask. That is a harder thing to count, but it is the thing that matters. A welcome that ends at the door of the town hall has done only half its job. The other half happens months afterwards, in a kitchen or on a doorstep, and it is invisible to most statistics.

Finally, what did the newcomers themselves say would have helped? The answer came back almost word for word from several people. They wanted a buddy. Not a leaflet, not a website, not a list of services, but a named person to whom they could send a message. That one person acted as a bridge, introducing them to others, and explaining the unwritten rules of the neighbourhood, such as which day the market is busy and who to ask about the bus. Of course, a buddy scheme depends on volunteers, which brings us back to the question of who does the work, and that is where we'll begin next time. Please bring your notes from the reading.
Harvest Row, you're through to the donations line. I'll warn you now that it's a bit crackly because of the roadworks outside the warehouse, so do shout if you can't hear me.

I can hear you fine. I'm calling from a bakery, and we've got a problem that I think you might be able to solve. We're throwing away far too much bread at the end of the day, and my wife said I should ring you before I throw away any more.
Your wife is a wise woman. We'd love to collect it, as long as it's safe to eat. Let me open the donation booking form. Which business are you with?
Tansy Bakery. That's T-A-N-S-Y, nothing to do with the flower shop, though people always ask.
Tansy Bakery. And where are you based?
Number 8, Thornleigh Road, just past the tram stop. You'll see a blue awning with a wheat sheaf painted on it.
Thornleigh Road, got it. Now, what sort of items would you be giving us? We can take bread and rolls, but there are some rules about cream and fillings.
Mostly bread, and the small buns that we don't sell by closing time. We also have cakes, but most of those have cream on top, and I imagine you can't take those.

That's right, anything with fresh cream or custard has to be thrown away, I'm afraid, because we can't keep it cold on the van. But plain pastries, such as croissants, are absolutely fine, and people love them.
Then I'll put pastries on the form. They're all baked the same morning.
Lovely. Roughly how many loaves do you think you'd have each day?
On a Saturday we can have up to sixty left over. During the week it's more like forty.

I'll put forty as the usual number, and we'll adjust for Saturdays if we start collecting then. We'd start with weekdays, if that's all right. Which days would suit you best? We have a van going round your side of town on Mondays, Tuesdays and Fridays.
Monday's no use, because we're closed on Monday, and the oven's switched off. Tuesday and Friday, then.
Tuesday and Friday it is. What time would you be ready? The driver can't wait around, so I need a time that's reliable.
We close at six, but we need a good while to clear up and wash the trays. So any time after 6.15 would be fine. I'd rather say a quarter past than push it.
After 6.15, then. And where would the driver go? Some shops have a loading bay, and some have a back lane.
Not the front door, because it's locked as soon as we shut. There's a side door in the alley beside the shop. If you knock on it, someone will hear. I'll put a sign on it.

Side door, perfect. Now, packaging. We ask that everything is packed in crates, because paper bags tear and plastic bags make bread sweat. We can lend you a stack of crates to begin with, and the driver will swap them each time.
That's very kind. Crates are no problem, we've got a lot of old ones in the yard.

There's one more rule, which is a legal one. Each crate needs a label showing the baking date. It's something about food safety, and our volunteers check it before anything goes onto the shelves. If there's no date, we have to bin it.
I can do that. I'll write it on a sticker. The baking date, rather than the date it goes off, yes?

Exactly, the baking date. Finally, I should give you the name of the driver, so you know who to expect. Your route is covered by a volunteer called Wanda. She drives a small white van with our logo on the side, a bunch of carrots, which she says looks more like a rocket.
Wanda. I'll tell the staff to look out for her. Should we ask for any identification?

She carries a badge, so please do ask if you'd like to see it. She'll ring the bell on the first visit, and after that she'll just come round to the side door. We'll send you a text message with the confirmation, and a copy of the donor guide, which has the details about food safety.
That sounds ideal. I'd feel a lot better knowing that loaf is going to a family and not into a bin.
So would we. Thank you so much, Mr Tremaine, and we'll see you on Tuesday.

Hello, everyone, and welcome. Grab a biscuit if there are any left, and if there aren't, I apologise on behalf of last week's group. I'm Rowena, and I look after the volunteers at the Harvest Row Food Bank. This evening is the induction for new volunteers, so I'll go through how the food bank works, what we ask of you, and what a normal week looks like.

Let's begin with how people get food from us. Years ago, anyone could walk in off the street. That's no longer how it works. People come to us because another organisation has referred them, such as a doctor's surgery, a school or an advice charity, and they arrive with a voucher. The voucher means that someone has already spoken with them and understood their situation, which saves them from having to explain it again to us.

Next, how often a household can use us. This surprises some volunteers. People are not allowed to come every week. A household can use the food bank three times in six months. That's not because we want to be strict, it's because the food bank is meant to be a bridge. After the third visit, the referring agency usually offers some longer-term support. If someone is still in difficulty after that, we talk to the agency and we can arrange more visits, but the visit limit is how we make sure that the conversation takes place.

Now, something that changed this year. In the past we handed everyone a pre-packed parcel, and people complained, quite rightly, that there were things in it they couldn't use, like tins of sweetcorn when their family didn't eat it. Now it works like a small shop. Each client has a number of points, depending on the size of the household, and they walk along the shelves and choose for themselves. It's slower, but the difference in how people feel is huge. They're customers, and not recipients.

Which brings me to dignity, which is really the most important thing I'll say tonight. Our clients are in a hard moment, and some of them are ashamed to be here. Please be warm, but not sugary. If a client seems upset, don't make a fuss and don't hurry them. Offer them a seat and a hot drink, and then fetch the support worker, who is in the room next door on Thursday afternoons and knows what to do. You don't have to fix anything yourself.

Two things I'd ask you never to do. First, never ask a client why they need help. It's not your business, and they have probably been asked that a dozen times this month. If they want to tell you, they will. Second, no photographs. I know somebody will say they'd like a picture of the shelves for social media, and there's a place for that, but never when there are clients in the building, and never with a client in the background, even by accident. If you need a photograph for any reason, ask me first.

You might wonder about the other rules. Can you eat the food? Well, there's a staff cupboard for tea and biscuits, and you're welcome to that, but not the stock on the shelves. That's for clients, and even a tin that's passed its date goes in the recycling, not in a volunteer's bag.

Let me tell you what a typical week looks like. On Monday the building's closed to the public, and a small team does the cleaning, including the freezers, which we defrost every two weeks. On Tuesday the supermarket deliveries arrive. Three shops send us surplus food, and the van pulls up at the back door, so you'll need strong arms and sensible shoes. Wednesday is for sorting. We check the dates on everything, decide what goes on which shelf, and throw away anything unsafe. It's the quietest day, and I always say it's the best one for chatting, because you can talk and work at the same time.

Thursday is the day when the doors open to clients, from one until four. This is the busiest session, and most new volunteers are put on the reception desk to begin with, where they check vouchers and sign people in. It's a good way to learn the layout, because you'll be asked where everything is.

We don't open on Friday, but on Saturday we have the mobile pantry. A small team packs a van with fresh food and drives to the estate on the hill, where there isn't a shop within two miles. It leaves at nine, so you'll need to be here by eight.

I should mention training. New volunteers aren't left alone on day one. You'll be paired with someone who has done the job for at least three months, and after a month, we sit down and ask how it's going. We also run a one-hour food hygiene session in the first fortnight, which I'd recommend even if you've done something similar before.
I think that's enough talking. Shall we go through to the warehouse and meet the people you'll be working with? Do mind the pallets.
Come in and sit down, both of you. Philippa, Tomasz, I've read your proposal twice, and it's an interesting topic. Remind me how you got there.

It started with a poster. In the window of our local food bank there was a sign saying "Volunteers wanted" and it was still there more than a year later. I walked past it every week, and I started to wonder why they couldn't keep anyone.
I was less sure. I thought maybe there were just too many food banks competing for volunteers. But Philippa persuaded me that the interesting question isn't why people don't start, but why they stop.
That's a much better question. There's quite a lot of evidence that getting people through the door is the easy part. Tell me how you contacted former volunteers.
We couldn't ask the food bank for names, because of data protection. So the volunteer coordinator sent our questionnaire on our behalf, as an email from her, with a link to our survey.
Excellent. That respects people's privacy, and it's the correct way to do it. Did you get many replies?

Thirty-eight, from ninety people the coordinator wrote to. It's a decent number, but I'm a bit worried about who replied. Looking through them, nearly all of them said they'd left on good terms. Nobody who left angry seems to have answered.

That's an important observation. It means your picture may be rosier than reality. You can't fix it, but you should mention it in your limitations. Now, the questionnaire itself. Show me what you asked.
We asked sixteen questions, mostly tick boxes. One of them was a list of reasons for leaving, and people ticked as many as they liked.

I'd change two things. First, the list. If you give people a list, they tick from the list, and you'll never find out if there was something you didn't think of. So ask an open question first, in which they write in their own words, and only show the list afterwards. Second, sixteen questions is too many. People get tired. Try to bring it down to ten.
We can do that. We could drop the questions about their previous jobs, which weren't really connected to anything.
Good idea. Now, what about age? You collected it, I think.
Yes, in bands. The trouble is that only two of the thirty-eight replies were from people under twenty-five. We can't say anything meaningful about so few.
Then don't try to. Combine the youngest two bands into one group, under thirty-five, and compare that with the older volunteers. It's not perfect, but it's honest.
That makes sense.
So, what did people actually say about why they left? Give me the headlines.

The most common reason, mentioned by about half, was that the shift times changed. The food bank moved its client session from the evening to the afternoon, and a lot of people who work during the day simply couldn't come any more. A few said that they'd have stayed if they'd been told in advance.

The second reason, which surprised me, was that people felt nobody noticed what they did. They'd worked for months, and no one had ever said thank you. A few of them said that it wasn't the money, they just wanted a word of recognition. Very few mentioned physical tiredness, and only a couple said that the clients were difficult, which is what we'd expected to see.
That's a good result, because both of those are things the food bank can change.
We were thinking of recommending that the food bank gives every volunteer a thank-you card at the end of each month, and perhaps a small certificate after a year.

Be careful there. Your data shows that people felt unnoticed, but it doesn't show that a card would have kept them. You can suggest it as something worth trying, but say that you haven't tested it. Examiners are much more impressed by a modest claim that is supported than a big one that isn't.
That's fair. We'll phrase it as a suggestion for further work.
Now, tell me what else you're planning in the way of data.
We'd like to do some interviews as well, perhaps ten, and use the food bank's attendance records.

Let me take them in turn. The interviews first. Ten interviews, with transcription, in three weeks, is more than you can manage. They take a very long time, so I'd cut them to four or five, and choose people who gave different reasons. And the attendance records are useful, but you must remember that they only cover people who signed in at the desk. Anyone who came to the Saturday pantry isn't recorded, so they're helpful but incomplete.
We hadn't thought about the Saturday volunteers. I'll ask the coordinator about that.

Do. One more point about the write-up, since you have so little time. Don't spend three pages reviewing everything ever written about volunteering. Pick the four or five studies that really bear on your question, explain each in a paragraph, and move on. The marks are in the analysis, not in the reading list.
We found one on retention in hospitals, and another about older volunteers in charity shops. Would those count?

Yes, as long as you say how they relate. And send me the shortened questionnaire before you send it out. I'd like to see it, and if you could pilot it on a couple of friends first, that would be even better.
Will do. Thanks, Dr Tennant.

Think about the last time you gave your time to something for nothing. This lecture is about why people do that, and, perhaps more usefully, why they stop. You might think the answer is obvious. People volunteer because they are kind, and they stop because they get busy. But research suggests that the picture is much more complicated, and that organisations that understand the complications can keep their volunteers far longer.

Let me start with the most influential framework. In 1998 a group of American psychologists, led by Gil Clary and Mark Snyder, published a paper that introduced what they called the Volunteer Functions Inventory. Their idea was that volunteering isn't one thing. It serves different purposes for different people, and they identified six of these purposes, or functions. One is values, which is acting on beliefs about helping others. Another is understanding, which means learning new skills or seeing the world differently. A third is the social function, which is simply meeting people and being part of a group. Then there's career, which is gaining experience that will help in a job. The fifth is protective, which is using volunteering to escape one's own troubles, and the sixth is enhancement, which is about feeling needed and feeling good about oneself.

The practical consequence is that two volunteers working side by side at a food bank may be there for entirely different reasons. One wants to feel useful, and another wants company, and a third has been unemployed for a year and wants something to put on a CV. If the organisation treats them all in the same way, some will feel that their needs are not being met, and they leave.

I'll illustrate with an invented study. The figures are made up, but the pattern is the one that real researchers keep finding. Suppose researchers followed 240 volunteers at twelve food banks over two years. They found that the median volunteer lasted only seven months before stopping. Half stayed longer, half left sooner, but the figure itself came as a shock to the managers, who had assumed that volunteers stayed for years. Then the researchers looked at when people stopped. The most dangerous moment was not at the end of the first month, as you might expect, but after the third shift. By then the novelty had worn off, but the volunteer hadn't yet found a place in the team.

The managers were also surprised by who left. They had expected the youngest volunteers, the students, to drift away, and many did, usually at the end of term. But some of the most reliable people were also among the first to leave, and when the researchers asked why, they discovered a pattern. These were retired people who had been given the heaviest work, lifting crates and standing for hours, because they were so willing, and who quietly decided that it was too much. Nobody had asked them. This is the kind of loss that a short conversation could have prevented.

What predicted who stayed? The strongest factor in the imaginary study was whether the volunteer had been given a clear role. Those who were told, in effect, this is your job, this is what good looks like, and this is who to ask, stayed far longer than those who were told to help wherever they were needed. It sounds like freedom, but in practice it makes people feel invisible. Related to that was feedback. Volunteers who received a word of thanks from a named person, preferably the person who ran the session, said they were much more likely to stay. Anonymous thank-yous on a noticeboard barely registered.

The second theme I want to mention is the change in how people volunteer. Researchers sometimes distinguish between regular volunteers and what they call episodic volunteers. An episodic volunteer helps at single events, such as a collection weekend or a charity run, and may never come back to a regular rota. For years, organisations treated these people as less committed. But the evidence suggests that many of them are simply people whose lives don't allow them to commit to a weekly shift, and that many of them return when something suits them. A food bank that offers only fixed weekly shifts, and nothing else, may be losing a lot of potential help.

A word of caution about all of this, though. Most of what we know about motivation comes from questionnaires, in which people describe their own reasons, and people are not always reliable witnesses to their own minds. Someone who says she volunteers to help others may also be enjoying the company and the feeling of being needed, and she may not say so, even to herself. So the six functions are best seen as a useful way of asking questions, and not as a final account of what is going on inside a volunteer's head.

So what are the recommendations? There are three. Offer flexible shifts, including short ones, and tell people well in advance if the times are going to change. Give every volunteer a clear role and a named person who will notice what they do. And, perhaps the simplest, ask volunteers for feedback after the first month. In our imaginary study, food banks that did this lost far fewer volunteers in the following quarter, not because the feedback always led to a change, but because people felt that someone was listening. That is a lesson for any organisation, and it is one that's cheap to learn. Next week we'll turn to paid staff, who have different motivations and a different set of risks. Thank you.
You're through to the permits team at Calderside Council. Bear with me for a second while I close another application. Right, I'm with you. Is this about a resident parking permit?

It is, yes. My neighbour told me I could apply online, but the council's website has about six different pages about permits, and I couldn't tell which one was meant for me. So I thought I'd better ring.
You're not the first to say that, I'm afraid, and it's a known problem. I'll take your details over the phone and put them in myself. Could I have your name, please?
Dorothea Vanterpool. It's my husband's family name, and it's usually spelt wrongly. V-A-N-T-E-R-P-O-O-L.
Thank you, Mrs Vanterpool. And what's your address?
Flat 3, Linnet Mews. It's a tiny turning off the high street, behind the chemist.
Linnet Mews. And the postcode?
C-S-4, and then 7-H-N. So that's CS4 7HN.
Thank you. Now, which permit zone are you in? Some people know it from the last letter they received.
I think it was the Market zone. That's what my old permit said, anyway, the one that ran out in March.

Ah, that's changed. The boundaries were redrawn in the spring, and Linnet Mews moved into the Harbour zone. It's the same streets, more or less, but a different name on the permit. That might be why the website confused you.
That explains a lot. I did wonder why the map didn't look right.
It's a very common problem this year. Now, the vehicle. What colour is it?
It's grey. Well, to me it's grey, but my husband says it's silver, and I suppose the paperwork would say so. Silver, then.
The log book will be the final judge. I'll put silver, and if it doesn't match we'll correct it. What fuel does it use?
Petrol. No, wait, that's the old one. I traded it in last June. This one is a hybrid, so it's partly electric.

Hybrid, thank you. Does that make any difference to the permit? In some councils it does, but not in ours, so you pay the standard rate. Now, how long would you like the permit to last? We have a six-month permit and a full-year one.
Which one is cheaper in the long run?
The full-year permit works out cheaper per month, but if you might move or change cars, six months is safer.
I'm not planning to move, so I'll take 12 months.
Twelve months, then. The fee for a first vehicle is £45 for the year. A second vehicle in the same household costs £60. And for a six-month permit it would have been £30, if you'd wanted it.
Just the one car. Forty-five pounds is fine. Does the permit guarantee me a space?

Not exactly, I'm afraid, and I do get asked that a lot. It gives you the right to park in the Harbour zone, but doesn't reserve any particular bay, and at five o'clock on a summer Friday you may have to drive round for a while.
At least that's honest. One more thing before the paperwork. My son visits at weekends. Does he need a permit of his own?

No, he'd use visitor vouchers. They come in a book, and each one covers a single day. You scratch off the date, like a lottery card, and leave it on the dashboard. They're on the same page of the website as the permits, which is part of the confusion, so I'll make a note on your record that you'd like to be told when they're on sale.
That sounds easy enough. What do I need to send you?

Two documents. One is proof of address, such as a council tax bill or a bank statement from the last three months. And the other is the log book for the car, the V5C. We need to see the section with your name and address on it.
I have the log book in the drawer. I haven't had it long, since it only came in the post last month. Can I send you a photograph?
Yes, a clear photograph is fine. Email it to the permits address, and put your postcode in the subject line. I'll send you the address in a text message straight after this call.
Lovely. And how long will it take to arrive?

The permit will arrive by post, within ten working days of us receiving the documents. If you haven't got it by then, ring us, and quote your postcode. Please don't park in the zone before it arrives, because the wardens won't be sympathetic about a pending application.
I wouldn't dream of it. Thank you, Yusuf, you've been much clearer than the website.
That's the nicest thing I've heard all week. Goodbye, Mrs Vanterpool.

Thanks for braving the weather, everyone. I'm Gordon Haldane, I'm the waste services officer for Calderside Council, and I'm here to explain the new collection arrangements. I can see from your faces that some of you have already had a letter, and I suspect that some of you read it twice and are still confused. If so, you're in good company. So was I.

That's actually why the new system exists. Last year we received over four hundred complaints about the old letters. They were long, they were full of legal references, and nobody could tell which bin went out on which day. The council decided to rewrite everything from scratch, with a simple calendar on one page, and that's what's in your hand now. So the reason for tonight's change is not a new law, and it isn't to save money, though it may do that too. It's because people told us, quite plainly, that they couldn't understand us.

The next question everyone asks is when it all begins. The plan was for the first of September, and that's the date on some of the early leaflets. But the new bins arrived late, and we decided not to start without them. So the new system begins on the first Monday in October. If you see a leaflet with the earlier date, please ignore it, and I apologise.

Now, what if your bin is missed? Under the old arrangement you had to wait until the next scheduled collection, which could be a fortnight, and I know that wasn't good enough. Now, if you report a missed collection by phone, online, or through the app, the crew will come back within two working days. Please report it by nine on the day after, and not a week later, because the crew's schedule can't stretch back that far.

Let me move on to what goes where, because that's the heart of it. The blue bin is for dry recycling, and it's collected every two weeks. A couple of things have changed. Paper, cardboard, tins and drinks cartons are all still welcome. But black plastic trays are no longer accepted, because the sorting machines can't see them, so they pass straight through to the rubbish. I know a lot of ready meals come in them, and I'm sorry, but there's nothing I can do about it. And glass jars and bottles can no longer go in the blue bin. They now have their own small box, because broken glass spoils the paper.

Right, let me go through some items that people often ask about, and tell you where they go. Garden clippings, grass and hedge trimmings go in the brown bin, which is collected every second week from March to November. In winter it's monthly. For the leftover food from your plate, from peelings and tea bags, to the bones from the Sunday roast, you'll have a small kitchen caddy, which goes in the food bin at the front of the house. It's collected every week, and it's the one that will probably save you the most money.

Old batteries must never go in any bin at home, because they can start fires in the lorries. You can take them to any of the big supermarkets, which have a collection point near the entrance. Please don't leave them with the household waste. Broken electrical items, like a kettle that has stopped working or a toaster that has given up, go to the household waste centre on Ferrier Road. And if you have furniture that is still in good condition, please don't throw it out. Take it to the reuse shop beside the centre, where it's sold cheaply and the money goes to local charities. A good sofa can find a new home within a week.

The grey bin is for everything else, and we collect it once every three weeks. I know that's less often than before. The aim is that you throw away less in that one, because everything else now has a place. I'd suggest you keep the calendar on the fridge, and I'd also suggest you sign up for the text reminder. We'll send you a message the evening before collection, with a picture of the bin to put out. That was a suggestion from a resident, and it's already the most popular part of the scheme.

Before I take questions, one last thing. If there's a word in the leaflet you don't understand, please tell me tonight. If it confused you, it will have confused hundreds of others, and I'd rather fix it now than in next year's edition. Yes, the lady in the green coat. You have a question about the calendar?
Come in, you two. Odalys, Hamza, I've read your draft, and I think it's very promising. Let me start with the obvious question. Why did you choose a council tax letter?

It came from something that happened to my grandmother. She got a letter about a reduction she was entitled to, and she couldn't work out what she had to do or by when. By the time she asked me, she'd missed the deadline by a week. It wasn't that she couldn't read, she's a retired teacher. The letter was just hard to follow.

I was surprised, to be honest. I assumed that if a retired teacher couldn't follow it, then nobody could. But when I read it, I could see what she meant. There was a paragraph of seventy words with no full stop, and the deadline was hidden in the fourth paragraph.
Good. A real case like that makes a better introduction than a statistic. Now, tell me about your rewrite. What did you do first?
We moved the deadline to the opening line, and we cut the sentences down. The original averaged about thirty words, and ours are about half that.
And we added headings, so that the reader can find what to do, what to send, and who to call.
Sensible. Now, the test. You asked people to read both versions, I believe.
Yes, twelve people. They each read the original first, and then our rewritten letter, and answered ten questions about each.

That's the weakness in your design. By the time they read the second version, they'd already read the first, so they knew what the letter was about, and of course they scored higher. You can't tell whether the improvement is due to your rewrite or simply to the fact that they'd seen the content before. I'd strongly advise that each person reads only one version. Half read the original and half read yours, and then you compare the two groups.
That makes sense. We'd need more people, though.

Twelve is fine for this sort of study, provided you tell people. A larger sample would be better, but I'd rather see a small, honest design than a big, flawed one. Just explain in the method section why the number is small. How did you recruit them?
At the community centre where I volunteer. The manager let us put up a notice, and we paid for tea and biscuits.
That's helpful, but do be careful. People who go to a community centre may not be typical of the whole borough, and you shouldn't generalise. Say that it's a convenience sample.
We did have an ethics form, but it only covered the first round. If we're changing the design, do we need to submit a new one?
Yes. Any change to the design has to be approved before you test anyone, and it needs to be done before the second round. Please don't start recruiting before you hear from the committee.
We'll send it tomorrow.
And who marked the answers? Because the question about what the reader should do has more than one acceptable answer.
We both marked them, but not separately. We talked about every one as we went.

Then in the next round mark them separately, and compare afterwards, and report how often you agreed. If you only agree on half, that tells you the questions are ambiguous. If you agree on nearly all of them, the reader can trust your scores.
Now, the results. What made the most difference? Your notes said that people did better with the new letter overall, but I'd like to know which changes mattered.

The headings, mostly. When we asked people what they'd do if they were in a hurry, nearly everybody pointed at the headings. The second was putting the deadline in the first paragraph. Almost nobody missed it in the new version, while in the old one only a third found it.

We also removed the legal references, the numbers of the Acts of Parliament, but it made very little difference. People just skipped over them in both versions. And we tried a bigger font at the end, but that was only with two people, so we can't say anything about it.

That's a nice set of findings. When you write them up, don't scatter the numbers through the paragraphs. Put them in a table, with the two letters side by side, and a column for each question. A reader can take that in at a glance.
Right. A table. We'd thought about a bar chart, but there are only ten questions.

The table is better. Now, the limitations section, and I'd like you to be frank in it. Say that the participants all came from one community centre, and that the larger font was tried with only two people. Admitting that a sample was small doesn't weaken a report. It makes readers trust the rest of it.
We were worried it would look as though we were apologising.

It won't, as long as you say it plainly and move on. One last thing. I've been wondering whether you need a recommendation section at all, since you're only testing one letter. Do you think the council would do anything with it?
We'd like to send it to the communications team. They've said they're keen to improve their letters.
Then write it so that they can use it. Plain words, no jargon. Which, now that I say it, is rather the point of the whole project.

Good afternoon, everyone. Today we turn to a subject that sounds simple and isn't, which is writing clearly for the public. Every day, councils, hospitals and banks send out letters that someone has to understand in order to do something, claim a benefit, attend an appointment, pay a bill. When the letter is unclear, the cost doesn't fall on the writer. It falls on the reader, and often on the organisation too, in the form of phone calls, mistakes and missed deadlines.

Let me begin with a little history. People have been trying to measure how hard a text is for a long time. The best-known tool was created by an Austrian-born writer, Rudolf Flesch, who published his readability formula in 1948. It's still in word processors today. The formula is based on two things: the average length of the sentences and the average number of syllables per word. Short sentences and short words give a high score and an easy text. Long sentences and long words give a low score. It's a clever idea, and for a quick check it's useful.

But I want you to be sceptical. A formula counts what can be counted, and a good deal of what makes a letter clear can't be. It can't judge layout, for example. A letter in which every sentence is short, but the important date is hidden at the bottom of the second page, will score beautifully and still defeat the reader. It can't tell whether the order of the information makes sense. And it can't tell whether a word is familiar to the person reading, because a short word like lien may still be unknown.

Governments have taken this seriously. In the United States, the Plain Writing Act became law in 2010, and it requires federal agencies to write documents the public can understand. Other countries have similar guidelines. They mostly give the same advice: put the most important thing first, use everyday words, address the reader directly, and keep sentences short. None of that is complicated. The difficulty is that organisations find it surprisingly hard to do, partly because officials are afraid that plain language will sound less precise or less authoritative.

You'll sometimes hear people talk about a reading age, as in, this leaflet is written for a twelve-year-old. I'd urge caution with that phrase. It's a way of describing the difficulty of the vocabulary and the sentences, not the intelligence or the experience of the reader. A forty-year-old who has just moved to a country, or who is coping with a diagnosis, may be a skilled reader who is simply tired, frightened and short of time. Clear writing is a courtesy to everybody in those situations, and that includes the experts, who often say they prefer it, because it saves them effort too.

Does it work? Here is a made-up example, with figures I've chosen for clarity and not taken from any real report. Imagine researchers took a typical council letter, about a change to a payment, and rewrote it. They gave the original to 120 residents, and a revised version to a different 120, and asked each person a set of questions about what they would have to do. The original letter had an average sentence length of 34 words. It was a single block of text, the deadline was in the fifth paragraph, and it contained several references to legislation. The revised one had sentences averaging 18 words, short headings, and the deadline in the opening line.

What happened? On the original letter, only 41 per cent of the answers were correct. On the revised version, the figure rose to 78 per cent. But the figure that interested the council most was time. Residents were asked to find the date by which they had to reply, and with the original letter it took them an average of over a minute. With the revised letter it took 12 seconds. That's a tiny saving per person, but multiplied by thousands of letters, and by the phone calls that no longer needed to be made, it is a considerable amount.

There's one more result I want to mention. When the researchers asked residents which version they preferred, nearly everyone chose the revised letter, but a small number of older people said that it felt less polite. That reminds us that plain doesn't mean childish or curt, and that tone matters as well as clarity. You can say it simply and still say please.

So, what should an organisation do? The most important lesson of the imaginary study, and of the real research behind it, is that you can't know whether a letter is clear by reading it yourself. You wrote it, so you already know what it means. The only reliable way is to test drafts with real readers, preferably people who haven't seen the topic before, and to watch where they hesitate. If three people stumble in the same place, you've found your problem. Next week we'll look at how to run those tests. Thank you.
